Meeting in Oman with Gulf Arab states postponed at request of regional countries, Iran says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:39:24 UTC
08:39:24 KST

In a rare diplomatic initiative, Iranian officials said they would attend a meeting on Monday with Gulf Arab states in Oman to present an agreement they say they reached with Oman on future shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
But Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, posted late Sunday that the regional meeting had been postponed "in the interests of consensus."
"We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting cooperation in our region," he wrote in a post on X.
Iran's Fars news agency cited an Iranian foreign ministry official on Sunday evening as saying that the Oman meeting was postponed at the request of some regional countries in a decision jointly made by Tehran and Muscat. The official said Iran would coordinate with Oman to determine a suitable date for holding the meeting, the agency said.
Iraq had said it would send a delegation, and a Gulf official had told Reuters that Saudi Arabia and Qatar would be represented by their foreign ministers.
Meeting unlikely to reopen strait
A senior Iranian official had told Reuters on Saturday that officials would discuss Hormuz and other issues at the meeting, but added it would probably not yield a signed agreement to reopen the strait. Bahrain said it would not meet with any Iranians.
In an interview with London-based pan-Arab news outlet Al-Arabi Al-Jadeed, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that despite any agreement with Oman, Iran would not reopen the strait until the United States satisfies Tehran's demands.
US blockade redirects 101 commercial vessels
Some 101 commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have been redirected by US forces as the US blockade against Iran continues, US Central Command announced in a post to X/Twitter on Sunday.

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
07:39:09 CST
08:39:09 KST

NEW YORK, Sept. 13 (Xinhua) -- Top seed Alexander Zverev of Germany won over home player Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 in the men's singles final of US Open on Sunday.
This marks Zverev's second grand slam singles title after his triumph at Roland Garros this year.
Zverev took victory in all previous five matches against Shelton and had a smooth start to win the first set 6-3 in the US Open final.
The eighth seed American bounced back a little bit to force the second set to a tie-breaker, but Zverev still managed to win 7-6 (2). Then, Shelton won 90 percent on first serve to take a 7-5 win in the third set.
In the fourth set, the 29-year-old Zverev didn't give Shelton many chances to break early and seal the victory 6-2. ■

Three men found dead early Sunday in the back seat of a burned vehicle in an open area near Jatt in the Sharon region were identified as brothers Zain and Qassem Odeh, 16 and 19, and their cousin Yahya Basimi, 22, all from Jaljulya.
Police suspect the three were shot to death before the vehicle was set on fire early Sunday morning in an open area near Jatt, 36 kilometers north of Jaljulya. The police investigation into the incident is ongoing, and no arrests have been reported.
'The sooner the better'
"Mourning has descended on the city. We heard about the incident with great sorrow. We do not know what happened. People in the city are getting their information from social media," Jaljulya Mayor Rabi Darwish said in a statement to Walla.
"But one thing is clear," the mayor added, "the government apparently has still not really begun acting against the murderous crime in Arab society, and we call on it to act, and the sooner the better."
These murders brought the total number of people killed in Arab-sector criminal incidents in 2026 to 176. According to data from the Abraham Initiatives -- a non-profit that promotes equal rights for Israeli Arabs -- 179 were murdered during the same period last year.

A staff member makes a violin at a string instrument manufacturer in Queshan County of Zhumadian City, central China's Henan Province, Sept. 12, 2026. The violin-making industry of Queshan County thrived in recent years as skilled luthiers returned home to start their own businesses. With an annual output of about 400,000 violins, Queshan produces more than 80 percent of made-in-China medium- and high-end violins, violas, cellos, bass and violin accessories. One killed, one seriously injured in latest among series of fatal road accidents in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:38:34 UTC
08:38:34 KST

A man in his 30s was killed, and a woman in her 40s was seriously injured in a two-vehicle collision on Route 762 near Rechasim on Sunday.
Magen David Adom teams pronounced the man dead at the scene. They treated the woman before taking her to Rambam Health Care Campus in Haifa with injuries to her abdomen and lower limbs.
"This was a very serious traffic accident. Two vehicles collided with one another. In one of the vehicles, a woman about 40 years old was trapped, in serious condition, and suffering from injuries to her abdomen and lower limbs. In the second vehicle was a man about 30 years old who was suffering from very severe injuries. We carried out medical examinations, but he had no signs of life, and unfortunately we were forced to pronounce him dead at the scene," MDA emergency medical technician Avi Boyar said.
Firefighters also responded to the scene. Upon arrival, they found a vehicle split in two, with part of it having rolled into a ditch about four meters deep.
Two killed, six others injured in traffic accidents nationwide
Earlier in September, two people were killed, and six others were injured in traffic accidents across Israel over one weekend. In a separate incident, a man in his 40s was killed in a hit-and-run on Route 553 near Moshav Porat. MDA teams found him with multisystem injuries and no signs of life and pronounced him dead at the scene. The driver who struck him, a woman in her 30s, was arrested shortly after fleeing the scene and taken for questioning.
The previous Friday, a 48-year-old motorcyclist was killed while riding on Route 7 near the Sorek Interchange at night. A boy about four years old was also struck by a vehicle, apparently near the parking area of his home in Jerusalem's Pisgat Ze'ev neighborhood. He was evacuated to the hospital in critical condition, with no pulse and not breathing.

Close call for ex-CIA head, ex-UK PM Johnson as Russia strikes Ukraine near Polish border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:35:00 UTC
08:35:00 KST

Close call for ex-CIA head, ex-UK PM Johnson as Russia strikes Ukraine near Polish border
Ian Fisher and Maria Varenikova
- Former CIA director David Petraeus narrowly escaped a Russian drone strike near the Polish border while travelling on a civilian train in Ukraine.
- The attack likely targeted a diplomatic train carrying ex-UK PM Boris Johnson and European officials, marking a significant Russian escalation.
- Russia is intensifying strikes on Ukrainian railway infrastructure to disrupt logistics, but Ukraine remains resilient according to Petraeus and President Zelensky.
AI generated
KYIV/MOSCOW - David Petraeus, the former CIA director, could hear the Russian drones above his train, which had just passed through Ukrainian customs on its way to Poland on the morning of Sept 13. He and other passengers were quickly evacuated. Not long after, he heard a huge explosion.
A former US Army general, Petraeus is used to explosions, but he said: “For those who have not been under fire, this was terrifying.” A jet-powered Russian drone, identified by photos taken afterwards, had detonated after striking the locomotive of the train next to his, he said.
“This is the act of a truly barbaric leader trying to terrorize Ukrainian civilians,” he said in a telephone interview on Sept 13.
Russian officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The attack at the Yahodyn station, near the Polish border, happened shortly after another train had departed carrying Boris Johnson, the former British prime minister, along with European politicians and diplomats, the Ukrainian state railway said in a statement. It said the drone might have been intended to hit Johnson’s train, which had left earlier than scheduled.
If the strike was in fact targeting senior current and former American, British and European officials, it would represent a significant Russian escalation.
Petraeus and the European officials were leaving Ukraine after attending a security conference known as the YES forum in the capital, Kyiv. The officials were traveling on a dedicated diplomatic train, and by Sept 13 morning they had reached the Yahodyn station.
The train carrying Johnson and national security advisers from several European Union and NATO member states crossed the border shortly before the strike.
Petraeus, a supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia, was on his 11th visit there since the war began. He said that he had been traveling separately from Johnson on a regular civilian train – and that the one hit was not a military target either.
“There was no military justification for what Russia did in this case,” he said, adding that a drone also hit a gas station in the area.
In its statement, the Ukrainian railway said: “It’s entirely possible that the target of this Russian drone could have been the diplomatic train, which departed the station earlier than its scheduled time as part of real-time adjustments to train schedules due to the constant threat of Russian strikes.”
The strike came as Russia has been scaling up its attacks on Ukrainian railway infrastructure. On the same day as the drone hit at the Yahodyn station, railway property in central Ukraine was also targeted. Earlier this month, two other border crossings, with Moldova and Romania, were also hit, signaling a new campaign to disrupt Ukrainian logistics.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said on Sept 13 that Moscow’s goal was to “cripple the economy and destroy people’s lives”.
Petraeus eventually reboarded his train and travelled safely into Poland. He said he was not aware of any casualties from the strike. He also said he did not believe attacks like this would defeat Ukraine in its long fight with its much larger neighbour.
“This is just part of a campaign to exhaust the Ukrainian population, which is not going to work,” he said. “They are truly unbreakable. They are tired. But they are unbreakable.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Trump dismisses calls for AI slowdown from leading tech CEOs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:31:56 UTC
08:31:56 KST

Trump dismisses calls for AI slowdown from leading tech CEOs
Trump downplays AI risks, saying he wants to maintain the US’s lead over China in the emerging technology.
US President Donald Trump has downplayed the need for his administration to place checks on artificial intelligence development, saying he is worried about ceding the US’s lead to China.
Speaking to reporters during his trip to Ireland on Sunday, Trump also said he acknowledged the need for some regulation but did not provide further details on potential measures.
“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that … shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump told reporters after watching the Irish Open at his resort in Doonbeg.
He said that with the US leading the development of AI over China, “frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.”
Trump’s comments came a day after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a blog post saying the AI industry must slow the pace of improving the technology’s capabilities to allow time for guardrails.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed with Amodei, adding that this was a primary topic of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks. Elon Musk also publicly agreed with Amodei’s post.
The warnings follow ex-Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon’s public resignation over concerns about AI’s potential to surpass human control, which sent ripple effects throughout the industry and Washington.
Multiple US lawmakers made calls for legislation to control AI development following Coxon’s resignation, including Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer and Republican Congressman Mike Lawler, who introduced a bipartisan House bill to prevent AI from operating without human oversight.
Concerns over AI have become a major election-cycle issue amid the explosion of computing warehouses being built in numerous towns across the US. The new construction has raised alarms about diminishing water supplies and rising electricity bills.
Trump has maintained support for data centres, despite their increasing unpopularity among the American public.
Former White House AI czar David Sacks, who now co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, challenged warnings from AI leaders, saying the industry is setting the pace for development and can slow it down independently.
“Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it,” Sacks said.

Experts from over 80 countries to participate in Dialogue on Fake News forum — GFCN head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:25:22 UTC
08:25:22 KST

MOSCOW, September 14. /TASS/. The Dialogue on Fake News 4.0 forum, which will take place on September 22, will bring together experts from over 80 countries, Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) President Vladimir Tabak said in an interview with TASS ahead of the event.
"Each time, more and more speakers and participants from different countries come to the forum. The total number of guests at the forum exceeds 2,000 to 3,000 people, including Russians, but a significant portion still comes from over 80 different countries," he said.
Scale of project, Western attention
The GFCN head recalled that the association was originally planned as a "voluntary initiative." "The project was created by us, the TASS news agency, and the New Media Workshop. We launched it amid the hype around our lawsuit against the FBI in the US after we were accused of allegedly interfering in the American elections," Tabak recalled. "And, to be honest, it was initially just a PR stunt. But various market participants from different countries showed interest, and today we have more than 125 journalists from 55 countries in the association," he pointed out.
"So, as a project driven solely by enthusiasm, it seems to me that the association has exceeded my expectations, at any rate. The IFCN, a fact-checking association funded by the US-based Poynter Institute, has already mentioned us five or six times in its articles as a deceptive Kremlin propaganda network. I consider this a great success. Therefore, when I weigh the resources invested against the results, I am very satisfied with the association’s work," Tabak emphasized.
Preliminary results of GFCN’s Work
"We have begun working closely with our colleagues in China and Kazakhstan. One of our GFCN experts was in Kazakhstan during the elections as part of the CIS observation mission. Prior to that, our representatives were in Venezuela," Tabak recalled, summarizing some of the association’s achievements since its founding in 2025.
He emphasized that the GFCN had published several "high-profile investigations" during that period. "We’ve developed a comprehensive educational program. Based on the GFCN Code of Responsible Fact-Checking, several memorandums were adopted at major international events. In addition, some of our code's provisions were included in the final statement of the 12th BRICS Communications Ministers’ Meeting at the recent summit in India," the GFCN head pointed out. "We are invited to participate in various events, and it’s important to understand that the GFCN is an organization that currently has no funding. In other words, we, its participants and members, are people who have other full-time jobs, and, as our opponents like to say, this is our 'guilty pleasure'," Tabak joked.
The Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) unites experts and fact-checking organizations worldwide. Established in 2025 by the TASS news agency, the autonomous nonprofit organization "Dialogue Regions," and the New Media Workshop, the association was formed to combat disinformation. Currently, the GFCN collaborates with more than 125 foreign reporters, investigators, and organizations from 55 countries in the field of fact-checking.
The Dialogue on Fakes 4.0 international forum will take place on September 22 at the Rossiya National Center in Moscow. TASS is the event’s strategic partner.

Trump calls $6,300 payouts ‘easy’ to fit into federal budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13

Trump calls $6,300 payouts ‘easy’ to fit into federal budget
NEW YORK/DOONBEG, Ireland – US President Donald Trump said on Sept 13 that the United States can afford his promise to send US$5,000 (S$6,300) to every US adult should his Republican Party keep control of Congress in the 2026 elections.
“I don’t know but it’s easy if the Republicans win. US$5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we’re taking in so much money,” Trump told reporters when asked if Congress would need to approve the payments, adding that trillions of dollars were coming into the country.
Trump unveiled the idea of US$5,000 payouts during a speech at the Republican Party convention last week.
Speaking to reporters on Sept 13 in Ireland, where he was attending a golf tournament at his club in Doonbeg, the President said the US government has the funds to pay for it.
But any such payment would need to be approved by Congress, House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said on Sept 13. “Of course, the devil’s in the details. We have to figure all that out,” Johnson told CNN’s State Of The Union.
Democratic politicians on Sunday morning talk shows panned the idea, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries telling ABC’s This Week that it is not a “serious proposal”.
US Senator Mallory McMorrow, citing the elimination of some Affordable Care Act subsidies, cast doubt on whether the promised US$5,000 checks would be sent even if Republicans retain control of Congress.
“There was an ACA subsidy cancellation,” McMorrow, a Michigan Democrat, said on CNN. “I think it was US$1,000 we were supposed to get. So if you believe that you’re going to get US$5,000, I’ve got a bridge to sell you.”
US Representative Mike Lawler, a New York Republican in a closely contested race, would not specifically commit to Trump’s US$5,000 dividend proposal on Sept 13.

Hundreds of UK hospitality businesses, backed by celebrity chefs including Angela Hartnett and Heston Blumenthal, have asked Andy Burnham to lay out plans to lower VAT for the sector, urging him to make good on his previous pledge.
More than 800 businesses have written an open letter to the prime minister as part of the #VATsTheProblem campaign, to warn that without a “fairer tax burden for hospitality”, there will be more closures and job losses, and fewer opportunities for young people.
The signatories include pubs, bars and brewers such as Fuller’s, Greene King, Mitchell’s & Butlers and Wetherspoons, along with restaurant groups including Franco Manca, Pizza Express and Wagamama, hotel chains such as Best Western Hotels and Marriott international, along with the leisure groups Center Parcs and Parkdean Resorts. However, most of the signatories are small and medium-sized businesses, including independent, single-site pubs and hotels.
Among the celebrity chefs who signed the letter are Andi Oliver, Clare Smyth, Jason Atherton, Nathan Outlaw, Paul Ainsworth and Tom Kerridge.
In February, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, publicly said he would argue for a hospitality VAT rate in line with Europe because of the social value businesses bring to towns. More than 370,000 people have signed the #VATsTheProblem petition calling for a 10% rate of VAT for hospitality, bringing the UK in line with the European average.
The campaign comes after the prime minister’s announcement to cut business rates by 20% for pubs, clubs and live music venues in his first week in office as part of a £100m aid package – but Burnham immediately faced calls to go further.
The letter said: “It’s time for a fairer tax burden for hospitality. Without action, closures will only continue to accelerate, jobs will continue to be lost and opportunities for young people reduced.
“A lower rate of VAT for hospitality can turn closures into openings, lost jobs into new jobs, and boarded up high streets into thriving centres of community.”
Kerridge added: “The reality is that 20% VAT is holding hospitality back. Hospitality is different from many other businesses because so much of what we spend our money on is our teams. You can reclaim VAT on a product, but you can’t reclaim VAT on a person. That makes a 20% rate particularly tough for a sector where labour is one of our biggest costs.
“And this is all happening at a time when businesses are already dealing with rising wages, energy bills, food costs and business rates. We’re seeing the consequences, with businesses closing their doors every single week.”
The letter came as the government said it would work closely with publicans to give more options for pub tenants who want greater freedom in running their pubs, so they get fairer lease agreements and a better price on beer, following a review into the 2016 pubs code. Other changes are being considered, including to allow pub companies and tenants to agree to a longer-term relationship.
There is an option for tenants to go “free of tie” from their pub company and instead pay market rent and buy products freely from other companies. The review found that between April 2022 and March 2025, fewer than 400 tenants applied for a free of tie agreement, saying they felt deterred by the cost and complexity.

Hidden history of royal staff uncovered in Buckingham Palace restoration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:01:15 UTC
08:01:15 KST

Lost or long-discarded items revealing glimpses of the behind-the-scenes life of Buckingham Palace staff over decades have been uncovered during the restoration of the UK monarchy’s HQ.
Misplaced belongings, found beneath the floorboards, in other areas of the royal residence and preserved within the fabric of the building, include a ticket to a whist drive run by the royal household’s social club from nearly 80 years ago.
Blank Littlewoods football pools betting slips from 1957, a pair of battered black hobnail boots and an empty Silk Cut cigarette packet were among the everyday objects unearthed, as well as an almost 140-year-old fragment of the West End theatre listings from the Standard newspaper in 1889.
The discoveries were made during the decade-long £370m reservicing of the palace which has included rewiring electrics, upgrading plumbing and heating and overhauling its infrastructure to prevent long-term damage.
Electrical wire covered with Vulcanised Indian Rubber (VIR) cabling, which posed the risk of fire to the building, were also located. The cabling, which becomes brittle with age, was removed as a priority when the project, which is due to be completed next year, began in 2017. About 1.2 miles (2km) of the rubber cabling has been replaced so far.
The small whist drive ticket, priced at 6d, a sixpence, and dated 14 April 1949 – during the reign of the king’s grandfather, George VI – was found embedded in a lump of building rock.
The pass to the staff social club gathering in the palace reads “Royal Household Social Club – Buckingham Palace: A Whist Drive to be held on” followed by the faded, stamped date “14 APR 1949”.
At that time, Queen Elizabeth II was still Princess Elizabeth and had been married to Prince Philip for less than 18 months and their eldest son, Charles, was only five months old.
Pages from the Daily Express newspaper in 1966 detailed the maximum security prison housing the Great Train Robbers, picturing the inside of Durham prison and reporting that “the men who were found guilty of stealing a fortune in mailbags spend their week stitching them for nine shillings”.
Instructions for royal household staff for the 1977 Silver Jubilee Diplomatic Corps reception informed them that the queen and other members of the royal family would move round the ballroom in a “clockwise direction”.
Aides were to encourage the 350 British guests to mingle with the diplomats at the glittering white tie and tiaras annual gathering, according to the manually typed sheet, which also said that smoking was banned in the certain state rooms and the reception kept to a strict timetable.
Other findings included a section of Minton decorative ceramic tiles from a fireplace hearth, with the design dating from around the mid-1800s, an aged Pewter tankard, a bottle of Schweppes still Malvern English spring water, a wooden junction box and a faded box containing six Christmas cards.

Researchers hope powerful new microscope will reveal ‘root cause’ of incurable bowel disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:01:15 UTC
08:01:15 KST

The number of young people living with debilitating and incurable bowel conditions worldwide is growing, but researchers now hope a one-of-a-kind microscope will help them understand such diseases and find new treatments.
According to the British Society of Gastroenterology, more than half a million people in the UK are living with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis the two main forms.
While such conditions can develop at any age, experts say they are most often diagnosed between the ages of 15 and 40, blighting lives at a crucial time for education, work and relationships.
Now a new piece of kit could bring fresh hope to those affected by IBD.
“What this microscope technology and what the science we do in the lab can bring is really to understand the mechanism [of IBD] better,” said Dr Karina Pombo-Garcia, a group leader at the Rosalind Franklin Institute at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, Oxfordshire, where the microscope is housed.
“With IBD, and with other many diseases that we collaborate with other groups to study, there [are] some treatments, but maybe those treatments still are not maybe the best or the most targeted that we can do because we … fundamentally don’t understand the disease fully.”
With its black casing, grey hoses and a plethora of wires, the microscope is remarkably unobtrusive.
Yet this is no run-of-the-mill bit of tech: the microscope operates at 10 times the resolution of conventional light microscopy, allowing researchers to see the details down to just 20nm in size.
To do so, the microscope, which researchers have nicknamed “Curie”, uses a two-laser technique known as stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy that scooped its inventors the Nobel prize in physics in 2014.
In this setup, features of interest within cells are labelled with fluorescent tags – these absorb energy from the first laser beam and then emit light, or fluorescence.
A second, doughnut-shaped laser beam overlaps with the area illuminated by the first. Crucially, this second beam “switches off” fluorescence within its outer ring, meaning fluorescence is only detected from the centre of the doughnut – a very small region.
“This allows the microscope to distinguish structures that are much closer together than would be possible using a conventional fluorescence microscope, producing images with exceptionally high resolution,” said Pombo-Garcia.
The microscope also has additional features, making it the only one of its kind in the UK. These, Pombo-Garcia notes, include deformable mirrors that can correct for optical distortions caused by the sample.
“This allows researchers to obtain clear images from deeper within relatively thick tissues and mini-organs,” she said. “It also has a temperature-controlled stage, enabling living cells and mini-organs to be studied under conditions close to normal body temperature.”
Dimitrios Ioannidis, a PhD student, is using the microscope to understand how cells that line our internal organs, including the intestines, come together and create protective barriers.
“For this to happen, we have specific protein complexes, which we hypothesise might change over time. So using this piece of equipment, we are able to visualise these complexes beyond what [we can see with a] conventional microscope,” he said, adding that he was looking at how the structure of these protein complexes changes from foetal development to adulthood. “If the structure changes, so does the function,” he said.
Ioannidis noted that by understanding what healthy tissue should look like, and then comparing and understanding the differences seen in people with disease, there was the potential to shed light on what had gone wrong.
“And then if you work and dig a little bit deeper, you can potentially find the root cause of some of the diseases that are affecting individuals,” he said, noting that this included IBD.
The microscope was unveiled by science minister Chris McDonald, alongside the announcement of £67m of funding for the Rosalind Franklin Institute over the next five years from April 2027, and a further £90m over the same period for the Henry Royce Institute, which focuses on materials research. In both cases, the funding has come from the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council via the core budget of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) set in the 2025 spending review.
The announcement comes at a difficult time for UK science facilities. Earlier this year the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), also part of UKRI, revealed it needs to make £162m in savings by 2030 as a result of factors such as soaring energy costs at its national facilities, increasing staffing costs, an expanded portfolio of activities and “unfavourable movements” in foreign exchange rates.
The situation has put some national facilities at risk of closure, with the Diamond Light Source, Central Laser Facility and ISIS Neutron and Muon Source – all of which sit on the same campus as the Rosalind Franklin Institute – jointly facing a 15% drop in funding, leading to concerns from the scientific community.
However, McDonald maintained such facilities still receive a very high level of funding, and stressed not every project or initiative backed by the STFC will be funded in perpetuity.
“I’m not particularly happy about the characterisation of cuts because that’s not the case at the high-level budget,” he said. “But it is right that STFC live within their means and prioritise their own budget,” he said.

2026-09-13
22:46:29 UTC
07:46:29 KST

Omer Asur Cuhadar and Mohammad Sio
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Syria launched its first locally issued electronic payment card accepted internationally on Sunday, in a move aimed at developing the country’s digital payments system and reconnecting its banking sector with global payment networks.
The card was launched by QNB Syria in cooperation with Mastercard during a meeting attended by Central Bank of Syria Governor Mohammad Safwat Raslan.
The central bank said in a statement that the launch marks “a new milestone in the development of Syria’s electronic payment and transfer system,” ranging from the restoration of acceptance for international cards to the issuance of local cards linked to global payment networks.
The development comes after Syria reconnected its payment system to the Mastercard network and completed its first transaction using an international Mastercard in more than 15 years, according to the bank.
The central bank said it is working on two parallel tracks: developing the national infrastructure for payments and electronic financial services inside Syria and reconnecting the country’s banking and monetary system with global payment networks.
The approach is aimed at expanding payment options and improving interoperability across the system, it added.
The bank said Decision No. 259 established a regulatory framework allowing licensed financial institutions and electronic payment companies to work with international payment companies and systems under requirements covering licensing, compliance, settlement, cybersecurity and data protection.
It added that the framework allows cooperation with qualified global and regional payment networks without limiting financial institutions to a single company or network.
In May, the Central Bank of Syria issued Decision No. 259, which it described as an important step toward modernizing the financial sector.
The decision allowed licensed banks, financial institutions and electronic payment companies operating in Syria to work with international payment providers such as Visa and Mastercard.
The central bank also launched a new electronic payment system in August aimed at expanding payment and transfer options available to individuals and businesses.
It said at the time that the system was designed to make transactions easier, faster and more secure while keeping cash available as an option.

Russian-speaking Ukrainians in Turkey increasingly switch to Ukrainian, says writer

Russian-speaking Ukrainians in Turkey increasingly switch to Ukrainian, says writer
Olena Lytvynenko, a former diplomat and author of the book “The Viburnum Aftertaste of Turkish Tea”, spoke about this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Many of my acquaintances among the Russian-speaking members of the diaspora have already switched to Ukrainian,” Lytvynenko said.
According to her, the Ukrainian diaspora in Turkey is currently strong and united, with both Ukrainians who lived in the country before the start of the full-scale Russian invasion and those who arrived after 2022 acting in concert.
Community representatives organize charity events, collect and send aid to Ukraine, and promote Ukrainian culture, history, and traditions. This also helps popularize the Ukrainian language among the diaspora.
Lytvynenko noted that the active unification and strengthening of the Ukrainian diaspora in Turkey began as early as 2013–2015, when Ukrainian associations began to be established and officially registered in various regions of the country. Later, following the start of the full-scale invasion, many Ukrainians arrived in Turkey, primarily in Istanbul, Ankara, and Antalya. The diaspora provided humanitarian assistance to the new arrivals, offered counseling, and helped with language learning and organizing education for children.
The writer emphasized that Ukrainians in Turkey continue to collectively support Ukraine and represent it within Turkish society.
As reported by Ukrinform, following Russia’s full-scale war, demand for Ukrainian studies in France has surged sharply, and the Ukrainian language is now being studied not only by Slavicists and members of the diaspora but also by French students and researchers.

Yemen’s presidential leadership council chief vows to restore state authority nationwide

Shukri Hussein and Mohammad Sio
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi vowed Sunday to continue efforts to restore state institutions and extend government sovereignty across the country amid rapidly shifting front lines in the conflict with the Houthi group.
Al-Alimi made the remarks during phone calls with several members of the Presidential Leadership Council, Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani, the commander of the Fourth Military Region, governors and military commanders to review the latest field, security, humanitarian and public service developments.
“The course of major national battles is not determined by a temporary change on one front line,” al-Alimi said, stressing that battlefield developments will not undermine the ability of the Yemeni people and armed forces to restore state institutions.
He said the course of the battle will instead be determined by “strength of will, unity of purpose and decision-making, and the ability to learn from challenges and turn them into opportunities to build greater strength and cohesion and regain the initiative.”
He said the strength of the state lies in the “integration of its military, security, political, economic and service fronts.”
The balance of territorial control in Yemen has shifted significantly in recent days, with the Houthis announcing control of several districts in Al Hudaydah and Taiz along the western coast, as well as Red Sea islands, including Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Yemeni government forces, meanwhile, have reported advances in Al-Jawf province along the Saudi border and said they were approaching Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.
Government forces have also reported airstrikes on Houthi targets in Mokha and surrounding areas, as well as locations in Taiz, Lahj and Al-Dhalea provinces, saying military vehicles and weapons were destroyed.
They also said they repelled a major Houthi attack on Marib.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has intensified since early July after years of relative calm.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Three killed in pre-election violence in Philippines' Muslim autonomous region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
22:13:58 UTC
07:13:58 KST

Gunfire has erupted outside a polling station in a semi-autonomous Muslim region of the southern Philippines hours before polls opened, leaving three people dead and 15 others wounded as the region votes to elect its first parliament.
The landmark vote represents the culmination of a protracted peace process that began in the late 1990s and established the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the country's far south.
Cotabato police chief Jibin Bongcayao stated that the shooting occurred shortly before midnight when members of rival political factions jostled for position to cast their ballots first outside a school designated as a polling centre.
Bongcayao noted that the men belonged to rival political parties that emerged from the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), the group that spent decades waging an armed campaign for regional autonomy in the predominantly Catholic country.
Heightened security
In a region long affected by political violence and clan rivalries between influential families, party leaders recently told visiting AFP journalists that a peaceful vote would itself be regarded as a major success.
Security measures have been intensified across the BARMM in recent days, with more than 20,000 security personnel deployed throughout voting areas alongside quick-reaction teams mobilised to counter potential outbreaks of unrest.
Tensions have remained high leading up to the vote; last month, a motorcade transporting the region's interim chief minister—an appointee of President Ferdinand Marcos—was ambushed and struck by gunfire.

Sweden's left-wing opposition leads in first exit poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
22:07:59 UTC
07:07:59 KST

Sweden's 2026 parliamentary election remained too close to call, with only about 20,000 votes separating the left- and right-wing blocs in the latest forecast by public broadcaster SVT.
The Social Democrats, Green Party, Left Party and Centre Party are projected to win a combined 175 seats in the 349-seat parliament, compared with 174 seats for the Moderate Party, Sweden Democrats, Christian Democrats and Liberals.
The razor-thin margin means the balance between the blocs could still change as votes continue to be counted.
According to an exit poll published on Sunday evening, the Social Democrats, Green Party, Left Party, and Centre Party secured a combined 51.3% of the votes, compared with 46.8% for the Moderate Party, Christian Democrats, Liberals, and Sweden Democrats.
The Social Democrats remain the largest party in the exit poll, receiving 27.6%, although this represents a decline from the 30.3% they won in the 2022 parliamentary election.
The Moderates are projected to finish second with 19.8%, narrowly ahead of the Sweden Democrats, who received 17.2%.
In 2022, the Sweden Democrats won 17.7%, while the Moderates received 19.1%.
The Left Party is projected to become Sweden's fourth-largest party with 8.2%, up from 6.8% in 2022.
The Centre Party also appears to have gained ground, reaching 7.2%, compared with 6.7% in 2022.
The Christian Democrats are projected to receive 6.2%, up from 5.3% four years ago.
The Liberals, meanwhile, stand at 5.4%, comfortably above Sweden's 4% parliamentary threshold.
The exit poll is not the final election result, and the balance between the blocs could change as votes are counted.
Late early votes and ballots cast from abroad are expected to be counted Wednesday or Thursday.
'Make Sweden Great Again'
Outgoing prime minister Kristersson meanwhile vowed to focus on improving Swedes' everyday lives now that his government's clampdown on organised crime and immigration was starting to show results.
Deadly shootings and bombings by organised crime networks have fallen sharply in recent years, while asylum applications are at a record low.
"We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people... to make Sweden great again," Kristersson told AFP before the vote, borrowing US President Donald Trump's trademark slogan.
Over the past two decades, far-right leader Jimmie Akesson has steered the party with neo-Nazi roots into the mainstream.
"Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish," Akesson told a campaign rally on Saturday, surrounded by blue-and-yellow "Make Sweden Sweden Again" posters.
At a polling station on Sunday, store manager Linda Eriksson, 48, said she hoped for a change of government.
"Hopefully a lot of people will realise that we have to change course... so that everyone will feel included in society," she said.
Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg had urged voters to "vote out Tido", referring to the right-wing government's alliance with the far-right.
"No fascists in our government. Climate justice now!" she wrote on Instagram.

Tehran and Muscat delay talks, citing regional consensus need
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:50:50 UTC
06:50:50 KST

Tehran and Muscat delay talks, citing regional consensus need
Negotiations in Oman between Iran and Gulf Arab states have been postponed at the request of some regional countries, Iranian media have reported.
The postponement came hours after an attack on an Iranian commercial cargo vessel killed one person in the Strait of Hormuz.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Fighting continues between Yemen gov’t forces, Houthis: What is the latest?
- list 2 of 3A dignified life is a ‘distant dream’ for many Iranian families amid US war
- list 3 of 3BRICS summit: What are the key takeaways?
Iran’s Fars news agency, quoting the director general of the Iranian foreign ministry’s Gulf affairs office, said on Sunday the postponement “was made at the request of some countries in the region and was a joint decision by Tehran and Muscat”.
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on X that the meeting, scheduled for Monday, had been postponed “in the interests of consensus”.
“We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting cooperation in our region,” Albusaidi said.
Oman has emerged as a key mediator in the war, building on its decades-long role as a trusted interlocutor with Tehran. The country is also directly affected by the dispute over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, whose southern shore lies in Omani territory.
In July, Muscat proposed a joint regional mechanism that would split control of the strait 50-50. The proposal also suggested “voluntary fees” from shipping vessels that would go to both countries.
The system is similar to an agreement governing the Strait of Malacca, which asks ships transiting the strait to voluntarily contribute to fund navigation, environmental protection and search-and-rescue operations. Iran rejected the idea of a voluntary fee, insisting instead that payments should be compulsory for vessels transiting the chokepoint.
Tehran has also pushed for vessels to use a route closer to the Iranian coast and has targeted ships travelling closer to the strait’s southern shore. The talks have so far failed to produce a breakthrough.
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which flowed largely unimpeded before Israel and the United States launched their war on Iran on February 28, has become one of the central issues in the conflict. Before the war, about one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies were shipped from Gulf producers via this route.
US President Donald Trump is pushing to restore shipping through the waterway to pre-war levels to bring down energy prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. But Tehran has shown no sign of giving up what it regards as a key source of strategic leverage.
Before Albusaidi’s announcement, Iranian state media reported that an attack off Qeshm Island, about 22km (14 miles) from the port city of Bandar Abbas, had killed one person and wounded four others. The governor of Qeshm reportedly blamed the attack on a “terrorist enemy”.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) monitor separately said a vessel had been hit by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, although it was not immediately clear whether it was referring to the same incident reported by Iran. UKMTO said a severe fire had broken out and local authorities were evacuating those on board.
There was no immediate comment from the US military, which has struck Iranian-flagged vessels during its blockade of Iranian ports and is facing a renewed threat from Iranian ballistic missiles targeting its warships.
Hours before the attack, Iran’s government remained defiant.
“Our people can’t be bullied into submission. Iran won’t surrender,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a social media post.
Trump offered a sharply different assessment on Sunday, saying Iran “wants to make a deal so bad” that “they’re calling constantly”. He spoke at his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, where he was attending a tournament.
Later, when asked by a reporter whether the US had struck the Iranian cargo vessel in the Strait of Hormuz earlier on Sunday, Trump said: “I don’t want to say,” before boarding Air Force One for Washington.

Russian intelligence using fake volunteers to ‘hunt’ Ukrainian troops – SSU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:38:00 UTC
06:38:00 KST

Russian intelligence using fake volunteers to ‘hunt’ Ukrainian troops – SSU
SSU spokesperson Artem Dekhtiarenko said this during a television broadcast, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“We have also recently seen a trend whereby pseudo-volunteers approach military personnel. In other words, the enemy exploits any vulnerabilities that may exist in a serviceman’s psychological profile – this could be a desire for closeness, intimacy and so on. Or a Russian operative may simply approach someone and say: ‘I want to help you as a soldier in a difficult situation. I’m a volunteer, and we have humanitarian aid. Please tell me the address where we can send you a package.’ And instead of food and other supplies, a bomb arrives in that package,” he said.
Dekhtiarenko noted that another continuing trend involves Russians posing as journalists and contacting military personnel through their personal accounts, inviting them to interviews without coordinating with the press services of their respective military units.
“Either they conduct these interviews online and try to obtain sensitive service-related information, or they say: ‘Let’s meet at some location.’ And when the person arrives at that location, everything has already been prepared in terms of a bomb. So, please, remain vigilant,” the spokesperson said.
Asked which Russian institutions are involved in such activities, Dekhtiarenko said that virtually all of Russia’s intelligence and security services are operating against Ukraine, including the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces (GRU), and the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
“They can often carry out similar tasks. If we are talking about a network of bots, other Russian structures that use this method operate in much the same way. They cast a wide net and then work with whoever responds. For example, they send text messages to servicemen saying, ‘Hi, you’re handsome.’ In fact, such messages can be sent to a million service members, and then they respond to whoever engages with them,” the spokesperson explained.
As reported, the SSU has launched a new stage of a nationwide information campaign aimed at countering the recruitment of Ukrainians by Russian intelligence and security services.

United came close shortly before halftime when Marcus Rashford curled a 25-yard free kick beyond the reach of a fully stretched Gianluigi Donnarumma, only for the ball to strike the outside of the left post.
The hosts hit the woodwork again seven minutes after the restart as Kobbie Mainoo's dipping effort from outside the penalty area struck the left post.
City thought they had broken the deadlock on the hour mark when Haaland converted Josko Gvardiol's low cross at the back post, but the goal was initially ruled out for offside.
Following a VAR review, however, the decision was overturned and the goal was awarded in the 63rd minute, with Haaland ruled onside.
City nearly doubled their advantage six minutes later when Enzo Fernandez curled a right-footed effort toward the bottom corner, but United goalkeeper Senne Lammens produced a fine save to tip the ball onto the woodwork.
United continued to push for an equalizer, with Bryan Mbeumo sending a header narrowly wide from Diogo Dalot's cross in the 73rd minute.
The hosts had one final opportunity deep into stoppage time when Fernandes played Mbeumo in behind the City defense, but Donnarumma reacted sharply to turn his effort behind.
City held on, despite playing more than an hour with 10 men to secure their fourth victory from four league matches and move to 12 points.
United, meanwhile, remain on four points after four matches.

Oman has announced the postponement of a high-level regional meeting between Iran and Gulf countries on the future of the Strait of Hormuz, the primary maritime flashpoint in the regional conflict.
The talks were scheduled to take place on Monday in the southern city of Salalah to address transit through the strategic corridor, which remains vital for global oil and gas supplies.
"It has been decided to postpone to a later date the regional meeting that was to be held on Monday in Salalah, in order to create conditions conducive to a constructive dialogue," the state-run Oman News Agency reported on Sunday.
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi posted on the X platform that Muscat remains "determined to promote dialogue that contributes to stability and lasting cooperation in our region."
Iran's Fars news agency, citing the director general of the foreign ministry's Persian Gulf Affairs Office, reported that the postponement "was made at the request of some countries in the region and a joint decision by Tehran and Muscat."
Diplomatic hesitation
Tehran had previously announced that Iraq and Gulf states would participate in the Muscat-hosted negotiations.
However, no regional government formally confirmed attendance, whilst Bahrain explicitly ruled out taking part.
The Strait of Hormuz has been subject to an Iranian blockade—and subsequent US counter-blockades—since February 28, when US and Israeli war against Iran triggered wider regional hostilities.
A June framework accord between Washington and Tehran foundered over unresolved terms regarding the waterway.
More than six months into the conflict, disruptions across the strait have driven international crude oil prices above $100 a barrel.
While the strait operated under free commercial navigation before the war, Tehran now requires transit permits and seeks to impose service levies.
Non-compliant vessels face regular strikes, while US forces have periodically struck targets along the Iranian coastline to challenge Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) control.

‘Sweat the asset’: new development minister plots path to make UK aid count
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:30:14 UTC
06:30:14 KST

The development minister, Kirsty McNeill, has declared herself “a huge believer in aid”, as she reaffirmed Labour’s manifesto pledge to return to a target of 0.7% of national income spending.
McNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown and senior executive at Save the Children, declined to give any timetable, repeating the formula that the government would work towards the target “when fiscal circumstances allow”.
But she made a full-throated argument for the benefits of aid – as well as promising to build new “agile partnerships” to work on development challenges.
“I’m a huge believer in aid; I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact. And I think it’s important that colleagues hear that underscored,” she said.
Repeating the manifesto pledge that Labour made before the 2024 general election to return to 0.7% – instead slashing aid the next year – McNeill insisted that in the Burnham government, “everyone from the prime minister down is a believer in the spirit that animated that manifesto”.
McNeill will be setting out her priorities in a speech to charities and campaigners at the New Economics Foundation thinktank on Monday.
She will announce that the government is making up to £15m available via its humanitarian crisis fund to support preventive action in countries most at risk from El Niño.
“It will just do very practical things like vaccinate livestock and get cash to farmers to provide supplies,” she said. The UN has warned that the climate phenomenon is likely to be the most severe in 1,000 years, exacerbating risks of wildfires and flooding.
The 0.7% aid target was adopted by the Blair government and became a cross-party consensus, until it was set aside by Rishi Sunak in the depths of the Covid pandemic, as the government rapidly stepped up domestic spending.
Charities have warned that Labour’s more recent aid cuts, taking spending to 0.3% of national income, are causing sharp reductions in bilateral UK support to some of the world’s poorest countries. McNeill’s predecessor, Jenny Chapman, took the job after Anneliese Dodds quit over the scale of the cuts.
At the time of Starmer’s decision, some Labour strategists were concerned about what they perceived as the unpopularity of aid spending among voters. But McNeill said Labour should not be afraid to make a straightforward argument for development.
“As we’ve lost our confidence, we started trying to make lots of different arguments for development that go beyond what I believe to be the core one, which is, if you have the capability to save people’s lives and to change people’s lives, you should deploy that capability ambitiously,” she said.
“I think aid is a really good instrument to save children’s lives. And the impacts of British aid, through immunisation, or by feeding children who would otherwise starve, is one that in every conversation with the public I’ve had, whether it’s with a constituent on the doorstep or in my previous job at Save the Children, when you’re saying, ‘Do you think if we can do that, we should do that?’ people say: ‘Yes, we should.’”
Voters’ concerns are more about the value for money and effectiveness of aid spending, she said, promising to “sweat the asset” when it came to getting the best out of the current straitened resources.
She said she saw her role as bringing all the expertise and leverage of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to bear on what she called the “five securities” – “health security, climate security, food security, human security and economic security”.
“The focus on securities is an attempt to recast my job as being about global cooperation and how we get security through solidarity,” she added.
“That will mean pressing for reform of some of the international bodies that spend UK aid, as well as forming ‘bespoke partnerships’, to work on specific issues.”
A veteran of the Make Poverty History campaign in the mid-2000s, McNeill contrasted this approach with that of the Blair government, which used the UK chairing of the G8 group of industrialised countries in 2005 to secure significant debt relief for developing countries.
“Many of us came of age at a time when there were summits with big announcements, and a cheque from the UK government, and actually the thing that I want to be held to account for is have I done the grind, the diplomatic grind, to get the maximum we can out of our relationships?”
McNeill has been the MP for Midlothian, south of Edinburgh, since 2024, winning the constituency from the Scottish National party.
Her boss, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has signalled that he wants development to be a more prominent focus of the FCDO’s work, including by directly taking up the UK’s seat on the World Bank board.
“The foreign secretary’s been very clear that both development and climate are going to be at the heart of British policy: they’re not an addition, they’re right at the beating heart, which I’m obviously absolutely delighted about,” she said.

Babylon, not Egypt: Israel is running on the wrong story about Diaspora Jews - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:23:19 UTC
06:23:19 KST

There is Babylon in the Diaspora.
My father was born in Argentina to Romanian parents; my mother in Shanghai to Russian parents. They met in Israel, where I was born in Beersheba, and we moved to America when I was three.
I grew up in Auburn, Alabama, where there were three Jews in the entire school system. Not my grade. Not my school. The system. My brother and I were two of them. Whatever Jewish life my family had, my parents assembled out of nothing that the town supplied.
Zvika Klein recently argued that Israel does not know how to treat Diaspora Jews as partners. I agree that Diaspora Jews should have a voice on questions that affect the Jewish people. A voice, not a veto. And no vote in Israel’s sovereign decisions. Israelis vote there, serve there, bury their children there, and bear the consequences.
Jewish questions, yes. Whether Israel goes into Gaza, no.
I want to add something. Israel is not only reaching for the wrong tools. It is running on the wrong story.
Klein found his precedent in the Book of Esther, where the rabbis say the Jews of Persia freely accepted a covenant that had once been forced on them. It is the right text, and it proves more than he claimed.
The rabbi who made that argument was living in Babylon, centuries after Persia opened the road back to Jerusalem and most Jews chose not to take it. The classic proof that Jews accept their Judaism freely was itself written by Jews who chose to stay in the Diaspora and built there.
Babylon did not disappear. It became a center. It produced the Talmud, which is to say it produced the operating system of Jewish civilization for the next 1,500 years, and it did so without a state, without sovereignty, and without any expectation of return.
Now go back further. Egypt gives us two stories. The first is the story of those who stayed behind. They disappeared. And it is this lesson that runs deeply through Israeli consciousness: Jews who remain in exile are Jews who eventually will not make it. When Israel looks at a shrinking Diaspora, it instinctively sees the Jews who stayed in Egypt.
But Egypt also gives us the story of the committed minority. Tradition holds that only one in five Israelites left Egypt. The claim is remarkable: from that minority came Sinai and a civilization that changed the world.
The Jewish people did not survive because everyone stayed committed. It survived because enough did. For most of our history, it has been the few leading the few.
For the Diaspora, all three lessons matter. The Jews who stayed in Egypt warn what can happen when commitment disappears. The Jews who left Egypt teach that numbers were never the point: a committed minority can carry the Jewish future. Babylon teaches that a committed minority can build something enduring outside the land.
The Jews who stayed in Egypt warn that Diaspora communities can disappear. Babylon teaches that they do not have to. As Klein put it to me: in Egypt they perish, and in Babylon they write the Talmud. An Israeli hears “fewer” and reaches for Egypt. I hear “fewer, and choosing,” and reach for Babylon.
As Klein wrote, “a smaller Jewish people that chooses is not a weaker one.” In the Diaspora, the Jews who remain actively Jewish when assimilation is easy, particularly after the October 7 Hamas-led massacre, have chosen.
In Israel, Jewish identity is reinforced by language, calendar, geography, culture, and the state itself. In America, nothing requires a Jew to light Shabbat candles, educate a child Jewishly, learn Jewish history, defend Israel publicly, or remain attached to the Jewish people at all. Those who do are making an affirmative choice.
The Diaspora is therefore a test that Israel cannot replicate: whether Jewish civilization contains something compelling enough that people will choose it when they are entirely free not to.
The idea of Jewish peoplehood is coming together
A few weeks ago I had dinner in Tel Aviv with five young Israelis, two of whom had grown up in the Diaspora. One asked me, genuinely and without malice, what Israel actually needs from Diaspora Jews if we are assimilating and evaporating anyway.
Parts of the community are assimilating, and the numbers are real. But something else is growing alongside them: a serious and expanding collective of Jews committed to God, Torah, and Israel, and I mean Israel not only as a place but as the whole idea of Jewish peoplehood.
Many of them are not Orthodox and have no intention of becoming Orthodox. Some are studying with Orthodox teachers, with both sides comfortable that full observance is not the goal. They are learning in their 40s and 50s because nobody handed it to them at 18. Some have moved between communities, looking for depth rather than for a label.
They are not converting to anything. They are refusing to be sorted. Israel produces less of this than it needs.
They are also not sitting quietly. There are Jews here fighting for America, for Israel, and for the Jewish people everywhere. They are fighting on campuses, in city councils, and in their own professional associations.
We are one people, and that carries obligations in both directions. It also means there is something to learn in both directions.
After nearly 2,000 years without Jewish sovereignty, Israel restored self-government, self-defense, sovereignty in the land of Israel, and the capacity to act collectively in history, while building a modern Hebrew civilization.
American Jews built the habit of choosing Jewish life when nothing requires it, and the fluency to engage universal values, translate Jewish particularism into the language of the wider world, and carry the Jewish story into institutions and societies far beyond Israel’s borders.
Neither of those is a favor to the other, and what serious Diaspora Jewish life has developed is not something we offer Israel as supplicants. Both are contributions to the same people.
Neither is sufficient by itself. A Jewish civilization that can explain itself but cannot defend itself will not survive. One that can defend itself but cannot explain itself will not hold. For the first time in 2,000 years, the Jewish people possess both capacities at once. The opportunity of this generation is to use them together.
The best version of this argument I have heard came from an Israeli – a shinshin – who deferred his mandatory military service for a year and spent a year of service in an American community.
He told me what he found there: families lighting candles on Friday night not because the city stopped but because that family decided to stop; mezuzahs on doorposts where the houses on either side had none. He said, I came as an Israeli. I return as a Jew.
He had been sent to teach. He went home having learned something, and what he learned is the thing Israel misses when it looks at us and sees Egypt. We choose. We are building. We are Babylon.
The writer is co-founder of the Zalik Foundation, which has invested more than $200 million in Jewish education, thriving Jewish communities, Israel, and families in need.

Here’s the first riddle. What is the difference between Jews with a State of Israel and Jews without one? That’s easy. It’s the ability to defend ourselves.

Conversely, if their hosts became suspicious of them, to the point of feeling threatened, the fate of Jews became increasingly uncertain. Zionism put an end to that perilous destiny.
By realizing the dream of returning to their ancestral homeland, the Jewish people were finally able to establish their own means of self-defense, guaranteeing their collective survival, no longer dependent upon the benevolence of fickle nations whose mood toward Jews changed like the weather.

US Air Force pilots lack sufficient sortie experience for combat operations - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:22:47 UTC
06:22:47 KST

Many US Air Force (USAF) pilots lack sufficient sortie experience to remain combat-ready, the Military Times reported Sunday.
The report cited John Venable, an expert at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies (MIAS), who said the average USAF pilot currently performs only one sortie a month, down from 5.5 a month in 2023, with the latter still only 60% of the required level.
To be considered combat-ready, USAF pilots need at minimum 9 sorties per month, the Military Times said, citing past service statements.
Venable noted that during Operations Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury, US operations “came on the backs” of the Israel Air Force, whose pilots fly an average of 20 sorties per month.
The report said that, during Operation Epic Fury, the USAF had 25 squadrons with about 325 aircraft, according to the MIAS, out of 1,084 active aircraft, including 634 mission-capable jets as of 2024.
“If you look schematically at the whole picture, 325 aircraft, combat-coded fighter aircraft, is half of what we had in Desert Storm," said Venable. "It’s about all we can muster today.”
Venable: USAF has not released information on pilot sortie rates since 2023
According to Venable, the USAF has not released information on pilot sortie rates since 2023.
He added that the pilot shortage facing the US military stands anecdotally at 4,000 open slots, despite the official number being 2,000.
The Military Times cited the expert as at least partially attributing the issue to the actions of former US Air Force secretary Frank Kendall, who in 2025 reallocated funds away from thousands of aviation maintenance positions while serving under then-US president Joe Biden.

Ratko Mladić is dead. Europe’s genocidal logic lives on

06:21:58 KST

Breadcrumb
Ratko Mladić is dead. Europe’s genocidal logic lives on
Ratko Mladić, convicted of genocide, was buried by a state with full honours. On 7 September in Belgrade, his coffin was wrapped in the flags of both Serbia and Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The genocidaire’s remains had been flown from The Hague on a government plane, and a military commemoration in his honour had been held at an army venue two days earlier.
Soldiers carried the coffin, with an officer’s cap and a sabre placed on top, to a funeral service led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, attended by several thousand, including top officials of Republika Srpska who stood alongside the Russian ambassador.
Aleksandar Vučić, the president of Serbia, was not in attendance. Vučić described the funeral as an “emotional outpouring”, and said it had “nothing to do” with the government approving the event. The honours were military rather than formally state honours, and he made it clear that the state was merely respecting a family’s wishes and providing a dignified burial.
The responsibility of organising the funeral belonged, supposedly, to a grieving public and a private family, despite the aircraft being state-commissioned, as well as the soldiers in attendance, and of course the honours.
Genocidal logic
Anyone who has lived with the enduring ravages of the Bosnian genocide is familiar with this kind of behaviour by the state: the deed is done and simultaneously declared not to have been done, or not to have been done by anyone in particular.
Vučić’s comments and Mladić’s funeral form part of an architecture that I call a genocidal logic. By this I mean it is something far more widespread and pervasive than a set of ideas held by unpleasant men, it’s a structure that organises our world. It organises a politics in which the lives of some are considered targetable for persecution, and it works, subsequently, to control the record of what was done to those who were targeted.
Its instrument is the sowing of doubt and silencing as “every side was guilty”, and it drags with it a silent majority that becomes slightly more visible during events such as the genocidal general’s funeral. The numbers are contested, the historians disagree, and, after all, “nobody can really know”.
This claim, of course, has limits. Contested facts are the ordinary condition of politics, and politics can be cruel and exclusionary without meeting this description. The same institutions that carried out the attempted annihilation manufacture doubt.
The murders, the genocidal rape, the abuse, the destruction, and the forced exile culminate in a destabilising of the facts that establish that these things happened. The negating that accompanies all of this leaves those who survived the violence to reassess what was “real” in the lives and relationships they had before, and has muddied their relationships ever since.
Material for negation
Mladić spent his last years in a cell, partly because the doubt he sowed through his negationism failed him. An International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) courtroom convicted him of genocide for Srebrenica on 11 July 1995, while acquitting him on the count alleging genocide across six municipalities in 1992.
Višegrad, the town in Eastern Bosnia my family fled, was not even among these six. The law drew a line through a continuous project of eradication, named one part of it genocide, and left the rest with “ethnic cleansing”. That judgement has supplied material for negation and obfuscation ever since, and Serbia and Republika Srpska have been living in the space it opened.
My father was on a planned kill list drawn up for the “non-Serb” men of towns and villages in (eastern) Bosnia, most of them Muslim, in the early 1990s. He was pulled out of the car at a checkpoint while we were fleeing. He survived by God’s will, and I say that having engaged with academic explanations available for how a person does or does not survive such a list.
Relatives and friends who had already escaped were told they would be safe if they came home. Some believed it; some of them were subsequently murdered, and some raped. But how many mothers, fathers, aunties, uncles, sisters, and brothers across how many decades and centuries and how many places have been on such enacted lists, and how many were reassured all was fine before the orders were carried out?
So forgive me, or not, for having no tolerance in a politics of appeasement towards fascistic dehumanisers, wherever their racist, anti-Muslim, antisemitic, transphobic and patriarchal exclusions are practised, and whoever is currently supplying their logic.
Having studied the intimate reverberations of mass violence, people’s searches for healing, and perpetrator logics for a living, I am all too familiar with the complexities of the arguments intimately, inside out and outside in.
Fuel for the far-right
The route from Serb Nationalist genocidality into Anders Breivik’s manifesto, and into the song Brenton Tarrant played on his way to the Christchurch mosques, has again been re-traced recently, allowing me the blessing of not having to repeat their words. I would add only what follows. Bosnia was not an analogy for these mass murderers; it was part of their working model, the proof that a European Muslim population could be destroyed, while the rest of the continent was busy elsewhere.
The parliamentary version speaks in slightly more cautious wording when it repeats these same statements, though it is becoming more careless. On 6 September, the day before Mladić’s burial in Belgrade, the AfD took 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, on a record turnout of 77%. It fell three seats short of forming the first single-party majority far-right state government in Germany since the Nazi era.
The AfD’s branch there is classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist organisation by Germany’s domestic intelligence service, while in May 2025, the federal AfD branch was deemed to hold racist and anti-Muslim positions which were incompatible with the constitutional order. The party sits as the second largest in the Bundestag despite a court suspending the racist and anti-Muslim designation in February 2016 pending the party’s challenge.
Viktor Orbán told Brussels a decade ago that Hungary had “a right to decide that we do not want a large number of Muslim people in our country,” and has since said that Hungarians “do not want to become a mixed race”. Six years after Brussels, he was more specific. Asked about Bosnia’s application to join the EU, he said, “The challenge with Bosnia is how to integrate a country with 2 million Muslims,” and that managing the security of such a state mattered to everyone else's security too.
In Northern Belgium, where I work at a university, the separatist Flemish Vlaams Belang was offering one-way plane tickets to Muslims who “yearn for the Islamic caliphate” under the banner of “remigration” as early as 2015.
Remigration is a sanitised word for the removal of populations, which is what the men with the inscribed rifles said when they were doing the dirty work in Serbia.
All of Europe?
None of this is new, and it was made plain while the explicit genociding was still going on. On 3 July 1995, days before Srebrenica, Jean Baudrillard wrote in Libération that “no one dares nor wants to step up to the final analysis” that the Serbs were “our objective allies in this cleansing operation for a future Europe, freed of its bothersome minorities,” and that from “a world perspective, we Westerners, we Europeans, are fighting exactly the same enemies as the Serbs are: Islam, the Muslims. Everywhere.”
Baudrillard was describing rather than applauding, and his “no one” was rhetorical even then, since Bosnians had been saying it into the void for three years. What has changed in 31 years is that the claim no longer needs a European theorist. Parties all over the EU say it themselves while targeting racialised people, and they are winning elections with it.
Read the condemnations that followed Mladić’s triumphalist burial. The European Commissioner for Enlargement cancelled a visit to Belgrade, writing that the glorification surrounding his death was incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built, which “requires confronting the past, genuine reconciliation and respecting victims of war crimes”.
I would ask which Europe(an) is being invoked. This is the union whose own review found indications that Israel had breached Article 2 of their association agreement, the clause making human rights an essential element of the treaty, whose Commission proposed suspending the trade provisions in September 2025, and which has still not assembled the majority to do it.
Berlin and Rome led the refusal, while 20 UN experts call full suspension a legal obligation rather than a political choice.
A visit to Belgrade can be cancelled within a week. A finding the union made about itself has waited more than a year for a vote. The condemnation is not exactly hypocrisy, but the logic recognising itself in a mirror and refusing to witness its reflection.
I have long asked how many people support a genocidal logic, but now I think the question is somewhat misleading. Counting supporters might be the wrong measure, because supporters would be nothing without the architecture which sustains the genocidal logic. It requires functionaries, a securitising vocabulary about identity and threat, and a large number of ‘ordinary’ people who would never attend such a funeral and who will find, when the moment comes, that they are not certain enough to say anything about it. That is perhaps an unwelcome answer, and it implicates Brussels as much as the crowd in Belgrade, differently.
May all the victims of this orchestrated genocide, and of every genocide still underway, have found peace, and may the hearts of their families and their loved ones be held in divine softness.
Rahmet dušama i pokoj svim žrtvama genocida.
Jasmin Emin Tabaković is an anthropologist at KU Leuven with a PhD from the University of Cambridge. He writes on the intimate reverberations of genocidal violence and the search for healing amid its enduring forms, primarily among Bosnians.
