A third person has died of measles in the US, health officials say
Pennsylvania reports that a 40-year-old woman has died from measles, which was declared eliminated in the US in 2000.
A 40-year-old woman in the state of Pennsylvania has died of measles, becoming the third person to die from a rare outbreak of the preventable disease in the United States.
“This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Greg Furlong, the medical examiner for Jefferson County, about 230km (143 miles) northwest of Philadelphia, said in a statement posted online on Sunday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Robert Kennedy Jr expels all 17 members of CDC vaccine panel
- list 2 of 3US health authorities dispute Pennsylvania’s measles-related deaths
- list 3 of 3Two unvaccinated people die of measles in US state of Pennsylvania
Health officials did not identify the woman, but said she died of complications associated with measles on Saturday.
County officials warned residents that measles is a highly contagious and potentially deadly disease, and urged them to “take appropriate steps to protect themselves and their families”.
The Washington Post, citing Furlong, reported that the woman was unvaccinated.
The state of Pennsylvania has also been the site of the other two measles-related deaths to occur this year in the US, reported by authorities to have happened in August. Both were in Lancaster County, a largely rural, agriculture-dependent area home to a large Amish population, a conservative Christian population which has lower vaccination rates than other groups in the US. Those two deaths also involved unvaccinated people, according to state health authorities.
There have been 3,294 cases of measles in the US so far in 2026, according to the Centers for Disease Control, across more than 45 states.
In 2025, there were 2,289 cases in the country and three deaths, according to the agency.
According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, the state has recorded 676 total cases of measles so far this year, with 108 new cases being reported in the last week. Some 124 of these cases involved people having to be hospitalised. Nearly a third were children. Less than 1 percent of all cases in the state were people who were fully vaccinated. Lancaster County, according to the state agency, has accounted for 295 of all cases in Pennsylvania in 2026.
Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, but has made a comeback in recent years, which some experts have linked to a rise in vaccine scepticism.
In recent months, President Donald Trump’s administration has openly clashed with local health authorities, including in Pennsylvania, disputing the state’s characterisation of the deaths earlier this year as being measles-related, and removing them from its national accounting of how the measles outbreak is progressing.
In August, after the state announced the first two measles deaths, US Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F Kennedy Jr, a well-known vaccine sceptic, accused Pennsylvania’s Democrat-led government of “weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain” in a post on X, and raised the possibility the announcement “may even have been altogether fabricated”.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, in turn, has accused Kennedy of spreading conspiracy theories and pointed out that he spoke at an event in Lancaster County several years ago, “downplaying the severity of measles and saying that the cure was ‘chicken soup and vitamin A'”.

The 'authenticity' of Celine Dion: 'She appeals to the Boomers and the Zoomers'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:18:29 UTC
06:18:29 KST

The 'authenticity' of Celine Dion: 'She appeals to the Boomers and the Zoomers'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Nick Rees-Roberts, Professor of Media, Culture and Communication at the Sorbonne Nouvelle University, Paris. According to Roberts, Celine Dion’s extraordinary return to Paris reveals something larger than the enduring popularity of a global pop star. Her appeal lies in an unusual ability to bridge categories that contemporary celebrity and pop culture often keep separate: generations, languages, cultural hierarchies and even the apparent opposition between authenticity and carefully constructed stardom.
Dion’s longevity matters. Audiences have watched her evolve from a young Québécois Eurovision winner into a global superstar whose songs have become part of mass cultural memory. Yet Roberts argues that her continued relevance cannot be explained by the music alone. Her public persona - funny, eccentric and seemingly “unfiltered” - creates an impression of authenticity even as her appearances are embedded within highly sophisticated systems of fashion, branding and celebrity performance. The paradox is central to her appeal: audiences can recognize the machinery of stardom while still experiencing the person behind it as genuine.
Her Paris residency intensifies that dynamic. It transforms the traditional concert tour into a destination experience in which the audience travels to the star, combining fandom with tourism, fashion and the contemporary “experience economy.” At the same time, Dion’s return following her illness activates one of popular culture’s most powerful narratives: the comeback. Her performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics, her association with the Eiffel Tower and now her residency allow Paris itself to become part of that story.
Roberts also identifies a significant shift in Dion’s cultural status. Once dismissed by some critics through associations with sentimentality and kitsch, she has been progressively re-evaluated, with fashion playing an important role in transforming her from commercially successful singer into a figure of broader cultural legitimacy. What emerges is a particularly contemporary form of stardom: globally commercial yet apparently intimate, meticulously constructed yet experienced as authentic, nostalgic yet capable of attracting new generations.
Perhaps most importantly, Dion’s success demonstrates the continuing social power of popular culture. From destination concerts to thousands of people singing together at karaoke, fandom offers something beyond consumption: participation, belonging and collective memory. In Roberts’s analysis, the phenomenon surrounding Celine Dion is ultimately about why, in an increasingly mediated culture, people still want to gather together and feel part of something larger than themselves.

A hard-line faction within Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz in July on its own initiative, without informing senior military and political officials, The New York Times reported Sunday, citing two members of the organization and five Iranian officials familiar with the matter.
The officials said Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was furious over the attack, which had not been authorized by Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, the commander-in-chief of the Revolutionary Guards, the report said. Vahidi himself said the Supreme National Security Council, which is involved in decisions on the war and negotiations, had also been kept in the dark, the sources added.
Iran faced international condemnation following the July 7 attack, in which its forces fired on three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, set fire to a Qatari gas tanker and damaged other vessels. The move effectively derailed efforts by more moderate officials in Tehran to end the confrontation with the United States and revive Iran's economy.
According to the report, when Pezeshkian demanded to know who was responsible for the attack, he was told that commanders on the ground had acted independently under an order allowing them to attack any vessel that violated Iranian control of the strait, without waiting for approval from the central command.
Three Iranian officials told The Times that regime and security-force investigations found that cleric Hossein Taeb ordered the attack. Taeb, who opposed a deal with Washington, was appointed by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to lead the Basij militia. The sources said Taeb told Khamenei that Iran had erred by agreeing to end the war and sign the deal.

Former French Prime Minister and leader of the Horizons party, Édouard Philippe, stated that the drone strike on a civilian train—which occurred after an attempted attack in Leipzig—once again demonstrates the dangerous logic behind the Kremlin’s actions.
“This proves once again that Vladimir Putin believes he can do whatever he wants—whether it comes to military destruction or provocations. Europe must not allow itself to be intimidated and must remain united in its firm response—this is the only way to make Russia understand that it must not go any further,” Philippe wrote.
According to him, it is time for Europe to tighten sanctions against Russia, ensure their enforcement, and increase aid to the Ukrainian resistance.
“Using frozen Russian assets to make Russia pay for the crimes it is committing, and protecting Ukrainian airspace to prevent civilian casualties, without becoming a party to the war ourselves,” he outlined as areas of support.
Another former prime minister, Gabriel Attal, leader of the centrist Renaissance party, emphasized how close the Russian strike was to the European Union’s borders.
“This morning, Russia once again carried out a brutal drone attack on Ukraine’s energy and railway infrastructure. Specifically, in the area of the ‘Yahodyn’ border crossing, two kilometers from Poland. Two kilometers from the borders of the European Union,” Attal noted.
He also pointed out that shortly before the strike, numerous European officials had passed through that station.
“Vladimir Putin wants nothing but war; he seeks only escalation, and this strike on our doorstep must serve as a wake-up call. A wake-up call for new measures to protect Ukraine’s skies, because these are also Europe’s skies. A wake-up call to provide Ukrainians with the means they need to win,” he emphasized.
Attal also reiterated his proposal to use Russia’s frozen assets, stating that they must “finally be confiscated to force the sole culprit—Vladimir Putin and Russia—to pay for this war,” the French presidential candidate said.
As reported by Ukrinform, shortly before the locomotive was struck by Russian forces, a diplomatic train carrying security advisors from several EU countries and former European leaders—including former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson—was at the Yahodyn station.

Nearly 600 illegal Israeli settlers have stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem, as Israeli authorities imposed strict access restrictions on Palestinian worshippers during the Jewish New Year, according to the Jerusalem Governorate.
The governorate stated that 593 illegal settlers entered the holy site through the Moroccan Gate (Bab al-Maghariba) during morning and afternoon sessions under the direct protection of Israeli security forces.
In a separate statement, the governorate reported that Israeli authorities restricted Palestinian access to Al-Aqsa Mosque during dawn prayers on Sunday, funnelling entry exclusively through the Hutta and Chain gates.
Forces also imposed arbitrary age limits, while checkpoint soldiers refused to specify permitted categories, preventing hundreds from reaching the mosque and forcing many to pray at outside gates.
The incursions follow organised calls by Israeli extremist Temple groups to carry out mass visits and perform religious rituals inside the compound during the holiday season.
The governorate warned that illegal settlers are seeking to impose rituals by force to establish a "new reality" and alter the historical and Islamic status of the site, noting that roughly 850 barring orders have been issued against Palestinians since the beginning of the year.
Since 2003, Israeli police have unilaterally facilitated daily illegal settler incursions despite ongoing protests by the Jordan-run Islamic Waqf, which holds exclusive administrative custodianship over the holy site.
Settlement expansion accelerates
The Al-Aqsa incursions coincide with a sharp acceleration in illegal settlement activity.
The Palestinian Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission reported on Sunday that Israeli authorities have advanced 153 plans for illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, since the beginning of 2026, targeting the construction of more than 18,000 housing units.
The commission noted that 100 plans involve 12,300 housing units across the occupied West Bank, while 53 plans target 5,783 units within occupied East Jerusalem.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government has approved 104 new illegal settlements since late 2022, compounding the displacement of Palestinians across territory occupied since 1967.

Yemeni army retakes positions from Houthis, advances in Taiz: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:50:14 UTC
05:50:14 KST

Mohammad Sio
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Yemeni government forces retook positions from the Houthi group and advanced toward new areas in southwestern Taiz province on Sunday, as airstrikes targeted Houthi gatherings and reinforcements across the province, the state-run Saba news agency reported.
A military source in the Taiz Military Axis told Saba that government forces recaptured positions overlooking the Jardad area in Al-Shamayatayn district after the Houthis had infiltrated them.
The forces then advanced toward Ghayl Bani Omar as part of continuing operations aimed at driving the Houthis out of Taiz province, the source said.
Ghayl Bani Omar is a rural area that serves as a front line between government forces and the Houthis.
The military source said government forces seized military equipment during the clashes and inflicted casualties on Houthi fighters, without providing a toll.
Warplanes also carried out a series of strikes targeting Houthi positions, gatherings and vehicles in several parts of Taiz, according to the same source.
The strikes targeted Houthi vehicles and concentrations in Dhubab, Al-Waziiyah and Hayfan districts.
Another strike targeted a gathering of Houthi fighters in the Al-Afirah area of Jabal Habashi district, destroying several military vehicles and causing a stockpile of medium-caliber ammunition to explode, according to the report.
At least 10 Houthi fighters were killed in the strike, the military source said.
The Houthi group has not immediately commented on the report.
The balance of territorial control in Yemen has shifted significantly in recent days, with the Houthis announcing control of several districts in Al Hudaydah and Taiz along the western coast, as well as Red Sea islands, including Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Yemeni government forces, meanwhile, have reported advances in Al-Jawf province along the Saudi border and said they were approaching Al-Hazm, the provincial capital.
Government forces have also reported airstrikes on Houthi targets in Mocha and surrounding areas, as well as locations in Taiz, Lahj and Al-Dhalea provinces, saying military vehicles and weapons were destroyed.
They also said they repelled a major Houthi attack on Marib.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has intensified since early July 2026 after years of relative calm.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Microsoft chief backs pacing AI, independent evaluators for superintelligence

Unknown Publisher

Yasin Gungor
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Advanced artificial intelligence systems must remain firmly under human oversight while developers pursue deliberate pacing to ensure safe deployment, Microsoft Chairman and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Satya Nadella said Sunday.
"Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing," Nadella wrote on US social media company X.
The executive welcomed "deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right" alongside proposals for "embedded evaluators" to monitor systems inside laboratories, urging industry participants to turn safety concepts into concrete operational mechanisms.
He cautioned that governance "cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia." He added that a healthy frontier ecosystem requires "both closed and open-source models" to thrive.
Nadella argued that enterprises must preserve authority over their "unique and tacit knowledge," noting that organizations should run continuous learning architectures with the ability to control their own model weights without becoming reliant on any single model developer.
He announced that Microsoft will release a code of conduct Monday for public consultation to govern its first-party Microsoft AI (MAI) models.
The remarks follow an intensifying industry debate over safety protocols after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed embedding independent reviewers inside laboratories and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman indicated his firm would adopt the practice.

US will scrap Irish whisky tariff, Trump says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:29:57 UTC
05:29:57 KST

US will scrap Irish whisky tariff, Trump says
The announcement comes several months after the United States decreased the tariff by 5 percent.
While in Ireland attending a golf tournament at the golf course he owns in Doonbeg in County Clare, US President Donald Trump said the US will repeal a 10 percent tariff on Irish whisky, a duty that currently falls under those imposed on all European Union wine and spirit exports to the United States.
“Everybody’s been bugging me” to do it, the president said at a trophy ceremony. “And I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off [Irish whisky].'”
Irish whisky producers have been navigating the tariffs levied by the Trump administration on European Union imports for over a year, as part of the administration’s broader trade and import clampdown.
Trump announced a zero-tariff policy for spirits from the United Kingdom in late April, removing duties on Scotch and Northern Irish whisky following a royal visit from the UK’s King Charles III and Queen Camilla.
“The King and Queen got me to do something that nobody else was able to do, without hardly even asking!” Trump posted on social media at the time.
The Scotch Whisky Association said July 24 that the zero-tariff policy had come into effect, calling it “welcome news for businesses on both sides of the Atlantic” that would provide “greater confidence to invest, grow exports, and support jobs and communities”.
In May, the Irish Whiskey Association (IWA) also pressed for tariff elimination to shield US spirit portfolios and consumers from market volatility, while buttressing domestic companies handling Irish brands.
In July, the administration dropped an original 15 percent tariff to 10 percent.
The IWA welcomed the announcement and said it would continue to work with its EU and US counterparts to secure a return to the zero-for-zero tariff arrangement for all drinks exports.
“Nothing exemplifies the US-Ireland trade relationship better than Irish Whiskey,” IWA Director Eoin O Caithain said in a statement, adding that the lobby group looked forward to seeing the announcement fully implemented.
Trump’s sudden announcement at the tournament’s close triggered a chorus of whistles and cheers from the crowd of spectators. Details on how soon the tariff would be lifted were not immediately available.

Sweden election forecast says vote too close to call
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:29:34 UTC
05:29:34 KST

STOCKHOLM — Sweden’s high-stakes general election is too close to call, according to an analysis of early results that suggests a late surge in support for the right.
Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing alliance had been adrift in the polls for most of the past year, only narrowing the gap with the leftwing opposition in the final two weeks of a sometimes bitter and bad-tempered campaign.
If he manages to defy the polls and hold onto power, Kristersson has promised to give ministerial posts to politicians from the Sweden Democrats, a populist-nationalist anti-migrant party, in a first for a country that for decades shunned the far right.
Advertisement
Two exit polls published when voting ended at 8 p.m. local time on Sunday gave the leftwing bloc a clear lead, putting ex-PM Magdalena Andersson on track to return to office.
But public broadcaster SVT’s later analysis of results declared so far suggested the race was far closer, projecting that Kristersson’s right-wing alliance will win 174 seats in the 349-seat parliament, one fewer than the left bloc’s 175 seats.
Swedish broadcaster TV4 produced a separate forecast confirming that the results so far point to a nearly even split: 176 seats for Andersson’s left bloc and 173 for Kristersson’s alliance on the right.
For Andersson, such a close result would be a bitter disappointment. After being ejected from power four years ago, she had been seen as a virtual lock to regain office. But her side’s double-digit poll lead evaporated in the final days of the race.
“Swedish elections are always close,” Andersson told POLITICO earlier on Sunday as she toured the suburbs of Stockholm in her campaign bus. “When I’ve been around Sweden, a lot of people I’ve spoken to said they see things that the government has done that they like but there are also lots of things that they don’t like.”
With the fate of the far right in the balance, the vote is a watershed moment for Sweden and will be watched closely elsewhere in Europe, where other nationalist parties are gaining ground.
Advertisement
Even Andersson accepts that a victory for her leftwing bloc would not consign the Sweden Democrats to history, especially if the final result is a narrow one.
“The hate that they have spread through this election, and if they would become ministers and use their platforms as ministers to spread hate? Well, we’ll see if the Swedish people are very tempted on that,” she said.
For his part, conservative Moderate party leader Kristersson would almost certainly stay on and fight for his job as PM if the SVT forecast proves accurate.
Kristersson insists that the Sweden Democrats can be trusted, having propped up his coalition from the country’s parliament for the past four years, helping drive through hardline policies on immigration and violent crime.
He told POLITICO on Friday that potential ministers from the Sweden Democrats would have limited room to go rogue — because he would remain in charge.
“Since I will be the person that is forming that government, and the person that will appoint every one of them, I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government,” he said.
Advertisement
In the coalition-building efforts that determine which leader gets to run the country, Sweden’s smaller parties often have outsized influence. That will be true again this time, if the projections of a knife-edge finish turn out to be correct.
On the right, Kristersson leads a settled alliance of four parties, including the Sweden Democrats. Andersson’s path to a coalition, meanwhile, is complicated by disagreements among the smaller parties in her bloc. Much may depend on her political skills and her ability to force through a power-sharing deal in the weeks ahead.

Drone attack prompts Poland to evacuate more than 600 people from two border crossings with Ukraine overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:27:00 UTC

Drone attack prompts Poland to evacuate more than 600 people from two border crossings with Ukraine overnight
This was reported during an emergency meeting at the Polish Government Security Center, attended via video conference by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, by representatives of the Nadbużański Division of the Polish Border Guard, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
According to them, starting at 2:00 p.m. on Saturday, vehicle processing was periodically suspended on the Ukrainian side due to the threat of Russian drone attacks. Poland, in response to the situation in Ukraine, also suspended processing at its border crossing points.
Border guards noted that Ukraine had warned for several days in a row about the possible threat of attacks by Russian drones and had asked the Polish side to temporarily suspend processing at certain border crossing points.
Specifically, on September 10, there were three such requests regarding the “Dorohusk-Jagodzin” border crossing and two regarding the “Zosin–Ustyluh” border crossing. On September 11, the Ukrainian side requested once that processing be suspended at the “Dorohusk-Jagodzin” border crossing, and on September 12, twice at the “Dorohusk-Jagodzin” border crossing and twice at the “Zosin–Ustyluh” border crossing. According to Polish border guards, frequent warnings began to arrive following Russian attacks on Ukrainian border crossings on the border with Moldova.
Around 4 a.m. on Sunday, a Russian drone attacked a gas station approximately two kilometers from the “Dorohusk” border crossing. According to Polish border guards, the force of the explosion was such that “the windows in the Border Guard Service building rattled.” An evacuation of the border crossing was immediately ordered. Specifically, 25 Border Guard Service employees, 25 Customs and Tax Administration staff members, and more than 280 other people who were on the border crossing premises were evacuated. Among them were passengers from five buses. Service personnel took shelter in pre-designated shelters, while passengers and other people were led outside the checkpoint.
At approximately the same time, the Polish side received information about an unidentified object moving toward the “Hrebenne–Rava Ruska” checkpoint. A decision to evacuate was also made there. More than 300 people, including over 280 passengers, were evacuated from this border crossing point. Sixty-six employees of the Border Guard Service and the Customs and Tax Administration took shelter in designated safe areas. According to Polish border guards, after consulting with the military, it was determined that the threat of an imminent strike on the “Hrebenne” border crossing had not been confirmed.
At 8:27 a.m., the Polish side recorded another strike on a spur line in Ukraine. According to information received from Ukrainian authorities, a drone struck the locomotive of a freight train consisting of empty tank cars.
According to Polish authorities, following previous incidents at the border, procedures were developed to respond to the threat of drone attacks near border crossing points. In the event of an alert, passenger buses are moved outside the border crossing area, and personnel are directed to shelters. Polish border guards also noted the need to strengthen protection for personnel remaining along the state border, in particular by installing protective structures capable of providing cover while allowing them to monitor the border.
Special attention was paid during the meeting to vehicles transporting hazardous cargo, particularly fuel. As noted, due to long lines at border crossing points, these vehicles could pose an additional danger in the event of an attack.
On Sunday, near the “Dorohusk” border crossing, police and border guards had already begun moving vehicles carrying hazardous cargo further away. According to Polish authorities, these measures are intended to minimize risks to people in the event of possible drone attacks near the border.
As reported by Ukrinform, during an emergency meeting, Tusk stated that Poland must be prepared for increased Russian activity in the coming weeks and months, and that it cannot be ruled out that the escalation could also affect Polish territory.

Israeli Culture Minister Zohar vows to revoke the citizenship of NAZA filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor

Israel's Culture Minister vows to move immediately to revoke NAZA filmmakers’ citizenship
Zohar brands the filmmakers’ work an “act of treason” after NAZA wins the Special Jury Prize
Israeli Culture and Sport Minister Miki Zohar called Sunday for the citizenship of filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor to be revoked after their Gaza war documentary, NAZA, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice International Film Festival.
Zohar denounced the film as “vile” and accused its creators of harming Israel to win international approval. He characterized their work as treason, an allegation that has not been established through judicial proceedings.
“The Venice Film Festival win for the vile film NAZA is shocking,” Zohar said in a statement released by his office. He added that he would act immediately to seek the revocation of the filmmakers’ citizenship.
The culture minister does not possess unilateral authority to revoke Israeli citizenship. Under Israeli law, citizenship revocation on grounds of disloyalty is subject to a formal legal process involving the interior minister and the courts.
Zohar also linked the controversy to his proposed overhaul of public funding for Israeli cinema, saying taxpayers should not be required to finance works he considers attacks on the Israel Defense Forces or the state.
The documentary, directed by Abraham and Szor, is based on interviews conducted over three years with 24 people presented as Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel. Their identities are concealed in the film.
The interviewees describe Israel’s surveillance and target-selection systems in Gaza, as well as the approval of strikes expected to cause civilian casualties. The film alleges that military operations were knowingly authorized despite projections of extensive civilian harm.
The IDF has rejected the documentary’s allegations and questioned its credibility, arguing that anonymous or junior personnel would not necessarily have access to the strategic information discussed.
Accepting the award in Venice, Abraham criticized Israeli politicians and journalists who condemned the documentary without viewing it. He said efforts were being made to avoid confronting the reality portrayed in the film.
Filmed at night on Tel Aviv rooftops, NAZA takes its name from a Hebrew military abbreviation referring to collateral damage. It received a prolonged standing ovation following its festival premiere.
Abraham and Szor were also among the directors of No Other Land, alongside Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. The film, documenting Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank, won the 2025 Academy Award for best documentary feature.

Australia detects H5N1 bird flu in a sea lion for the first time
Kyiv • UNN
A sea lion on Kangaroo Island died from H5N1 after a shark attack. This is the first such case in Australia.
Australia has recorded its first case of a sea lion infected with H5N1 bird flu. According to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), the authorities of South Australia reported that the sea lion, found in the Seal Bay area on Kangaroo Island, was injured in a shark attack and died during its recovery, UNN reports.
An examination showed that the animal's cause of death was not a shark bite but bird flu. The authorities said that the injuries may have made the animal more vulnerable to the disease.
The authorities noted that the state's sea lion population declines by approximately 2 percent annually, emphasizing that bird flu has a "devastating impact" on sea lion and seal populations in various regions of the world.
According to the authorities, bird flu has already been detected in four different mammal species in the state.
On June 19, Australia detected its first case of a disease believed to have been caused by the H5N1 bird flu virus, and on August 3, the first mass die-off among wild birds was recorded.
On August 25, the country's first case of bird flu among mammals was reported—the disease was detected in a long-nosed fur seal in South Australia.

Adolescent narcissism brings brief popularity but not likeability among peers, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
20:00:38 UTC
05:00:38 KST

Teenagers who exhibit narcissistic traits might gain a brief boost in social status, but that dominance does not translate into actually being liked by their peers. While projecting confidence can help adolescents climb the social ladder initially, behaviors like boastfulness predict a decline in popularity over time. These findings were recently published in the Journal of Social and Personal Relationships.
Adolescence is a period defined by shifting social dynamics and a heightened focus on peer relationships. During this time, personality tendencies like egocentrism and narcissism often emerge as teenagers navigate identity formation and separate themselves from their parents. Because these traits are relatively common in youth, they might offer certain social benefits, such as projecting the self-assurance needed to establish independence.
Psychologists categorize narcissism into two main dimensions, known as grandiose and vulnerable narcissism. Grandiose narcissism is characterized by an exaggerated sense of self-importance, a feeling of entitlement, and a tendency to seek admiration through assertiveness or aggression. Vulnerable narcissism involves a more fragile sense of self-worth that depends heavily on social feedback, often leading to hypersensitivity and defensiveness.
Theoretical models suggest that narcissistic individuals use different strategies to navigate social situations. Grandiose narcissism is often linked to overt, status-seeking behaviors like extraversion and social charm. In contrast, vulnerable narcissism is associated with more covert attempts to gain inclusion, which can sometimes manifest as social withdrawal or interpersonal coldness.
In adolescent social circles, there is often a separation between being well-liked and being popular. A teenager might be widely recognized as popular due to their visibility or dominance, even if they are not personally liked by most of their classmates. Christopher Barry, a psychology researcher at Washington State University, led a team to investigate how grandiose and vulnerable narcissism influence these two distinct forms of social status.
The researchers recruited 252 adolescents, aged 15 to 18, who were attending a 22-week residential program for at-risk youth. The participants lived together, attended classes together, and followed a highly structured daily routine. Because the youth entered the program at the same time and were initially unfamiliar with one another, the setting provided a controlled environment to observe how social hierarchies form and evolve.
The residential program incorporated a quasi-military structure, meaning the adolescents wore uniforms, marched in lines, and followed specific behavioral codes. Within this system, the youth were divided into smaller living groups. The peer nomination data were standardized within these specific groups to account for varying group sizes and internal dynamics.
The research team collected data at two distinct points during the program. The first assessment occurred about seven weeks after the youth arrived, giving them time to establish initial impressions of one another. The second assessment took place 15 weeks later, near the end of the program, to capture how these relationships changed over time.
During the assessments, participants completed psychological questionnaires designed to measure their own levels of grandiose and vulnerable narcissism. They also participated in a peer nomination activity. Each adolescent was asked to nominate up to three peers in their living group who fit specific descriptions, such as being popular, well-liked, disliked, confident, boastful, or dominant.
The researchers found that self-reported grandiose narcissism was associated with peer-nominated popularity at the first time point. Adolescents who viewed themselves as highly self-important were initially recognized by their peers as holding high social status. However, this association disappeared by the second assessment near the end of the program.
While grandiose narcissism provided a temporary popularity boost, it did not help adolescents make actual friends. Self-reported grandiose narcissism was not correlated with being well-liked by peers at either the beginning or the end of the study. Similarly, vulnerable narcissism showed almost no relation to social status, aside from a weak association with being disliked during the initial weeks.
The peer nominations provided additional context regarding how specific behaviors influence social standing. When peers rated an adolescent as highly confident or dominant, that individual was generally viewed as popular at both the early and late stages of the program. Displaying dominance also occasionally correlated with being well-liked, suggesting that some group norms might reward assertive behavior.
Boastfulness, however, yielded a different social trajectory. Adolescents who were frequently nominated by their peers as being boastful at the beginning of the program were often viewed as popular at that time. Yet, a follow-up analysis revealed that early bragging predicted a distinct drop in peer-reported popularity by the end of the residential cycle.
The study took place in a quasi-military residential program for at-risk youth, which involves strict routines and specific behavioral expectations. This highly structured environment might foster social norms that reward dominance or confidence differently than a traditional high school setting. As a result, the social dynamics observed here might not perfectly mirror those of a broader community population.
Future investigations will need to explore a wider range of observable narcissistic behaviors, such as manipulation or attention-seeking, to see how they impact long-term friendships. Researchers might also benefit from using larger, unrestricted peer nomination methods, allowing students to rate all of their classmates rather than just a select few. Expanding this research could help educators guide teenagers to project confidence without alienating their peers.
The study, “How Does Narcissism Relate to Popularity and Likeability in an Adolescent Residential Setting?,” was authored by Christopher Barry, Alex C. Yoshizumi, Hyunah Kim, and Paige Yedinak.

Amid Air Raid Sirens and Shelter Shows, Ukrainian Fashion Week ‘Unbreakable’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
19:59:00 UTC
04:59:00 KST

A young woman in a long, red, silk dress, with matching lipstick and a heart-shaped purse with a gold strap, waited to enter the bomb shelter, where a runway show would shortly go on regardless of the air raid sirens sounding overhead.
It was Saturday afternoon, Sept. 5, four days into Ukrainian Fashion Week’s Spring/Summer 2027 season. Just the day before, a Russian drone attack had struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, in downtown Kyiv in the middle of the afternoon, injuring at least a dozen people.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Besides the woman in red, other guests were similarly dressed to the nines – some in heels and silks – all filing underground as the sirens sounded overhead. There was no panic, just the practiced calm of people who have lived with this for years. The woman in red found a seat among rows of folding chairs, and the shelter became, for a couple of hours, a runway: shows by designers Darja Donezz and Vorozhbyt&Zemskova, scheduled back-to-back that day, went on right there, rather than wait out the alert.
Keeping the Bridges Open
                                                                                                                                                                         
It was two of three times this season that Ukrainian Fashion Week moved its runway shows into the shelter at the Mystetskyi Arsenal National Art and Culture Museum Complex – the third was the day before, when an air alert cut into designer Viktor Anisimov’s finale and he chose to keep going underground rather than wait for the all-clear.
According to Ukrainian Fashion Week CEO Yelyzaveta Ushcheka, the increasing number of daytime attacks made holding Fashion Week more challenging.
“Before, we had more attacks at night, and that’s why it didn’t interrupt Fashion Week,” Ushcheka said. “So, it was around… I’d say, 10 air raid alarms in four seasons of Ukrainian Fashion Week. It wasn’t that challenging – well, of course it was – to have the Fashion Week during the full-scale war – but especially this season we faced more challenges.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
This season brought together roughly 50 Ukrainian brands across runway shows, presentations, and a trade show. As Business of Fashion reported, brands participating pointed to gains at home and abroad: stronger domestic sales and an expanding footprint in international retail.
And when the schedule didn’t hold at Fashion Week due to Russian attacks, the audience adapted. One show was delayed by more than two hours, but guests stayed anyway:
“Everyone understands we live in the fifth year of this full-scale war, and we cherish what designers are doing, because they are creating – despite all of this destruction and bad news,” Ushcheka said, adding, “all of the production of these Ukrainian brands is based in Ukraine.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Fashion coordinator Anastasia Kochenko, who has worked with Ukrainian Fashion Week for four years, echoed that sentiment. This season, she said, was especially challenging because of the sirens and the broader security situation, but the team pushed to deliver everything they had planned – not just for clients, but to send “shiny hope” to the wider fashion world that the event still exists and still works.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“The first thing that comes to my mind is the word resilience – because no matter what, no matter the circumstances, we’re still moving forward,” she said. “Regardless of the location, we’ll try to showcase the designers, to bring this energy to the people who are willing to see the show.”
She reflected on the historical significance of holding a fashion show during wartime, saying: “In 20 years, people will be discussing, like, ‘Ukraine did this fashion week, that fashion week’ – and at the end of the day, we managed to do it.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Designer Daria Chuprina, whose eponymous brand Chuprina has shown at Ukrainian Fashion Week for 16 years by her count, said that last September, her show was canceled due to air alarms. But this year it happened, and on the main stage versus the shelter.
“So everything’s great,” she said. Still, “there are very mixed emotions, both for the team and for me. It’s very hard to work in today’s conditions.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
However, Chuprina, who is originally from Donetsk and relocated to Kyiv because of the war, put it simply: “People feel unity – that’s why we’re all here.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Craft, continuity, and a new book on Ukrainian naïve art
This season’s official program placed particular emphasis on craft. At the heart of the season was the “Behind the Craft” exhibition, dedicated to Ukrainian crafts and their contemporary reinterpretation by Ukrainian designers – presenting craftsmanship as a tool for innovation and the preservation of identity.
That theme was echoed by Gunia Project, the Kyiv design house co-founded by Maria Gavryliuk and Natalia Kamenska.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“Today we are re-opening our new store with new reconstruction, and we are also presenting our last project – the book that we have published with Assouline about Ukrainian naïve [art],” Gavryliuk said.
The book, “Naïve My Love: Ukrainian Folk Art of the 20th Century,” written by journalist Anna Lodygina, features roughly 40 self-taught painters and sculptors.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Gavryliuk and Kamenska drew a direct line between that research and Gunia’s design practice. In fact, the word “Gunia” is itself a piece of traditional Ukrainian clothing.
“It’s like a Carpathian woven coat, made with Ukrainian traditional technology, and it was the first item that inspired us to discover Ukrainian artisans and Ukrainian culture and create new objects,” Gavryliuk said. “The main idea is to re-translate our tradition in new design objects.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Kamenska and Gavryliuk were candid about how difficult that work has become.
“We are facing lots of troubles and lots of challenges – with electricity, with logistics, with people going to the army or moving out of Ukraine,” Gavryliuk said. “It’s quite hard to develop your brand right now in Ukraine, but we have our mission, we have our vision, so we’re trying to keep going and keep growing.”
Fashion as rehabilitation: adaptive clothing on the runway
One of the week’s most emotionally charged shows came from designer Yuliia Perekriostova’s label Juliya Kros, whose recent collections include adaptive clothing for people with disabilities, including war veterans. This season’s runway show culminated with two war veterans, each walking with a prosthetic limb, leading the other models down the runway.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“Walking the runway like this, wearing something beautiful and fashionable – that’s a form of rehabilitation,” Perekriostova said. “Fashion reflects what’s happening in society; it plays out on the runway. Fashion can’t be separate from what’s happening around us. Everything going on, we express through clothing, through our brands. Through this show, we’re broadcasting our reality.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Designer Khrystyna Rachytska presented a collection this season titled “Opora/Opir” (Support/Resistance), drawing on more than 20 years of working in Ukrainian ethnic style, a practice that began, she said, when she started collecting traditional Ukrainian embroidered shirts a decade ago.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“It’s only by having that support, having our Ukrainian land beneath us, that we can create anything after everything we’ve been through,” she said. “Our men and women are fighting on the front lines with their bodies and their weapons, while we fight ours through diplomacy and culture.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Getting to Kyiv from Lviv wasn’t simple either, she said – air raid alerts sounded the entire way, and once there, the week’s disruptions meant repeated trips into shelter.
“We’re hostages to the challenges facing Ukraine,” she said, “but we want to show and share as much as we possibly can.”
A win closes the season
The week closed on a triumphant note. Designer Oleksandra Sakhaudinova won the Grand Prix at “Look Into the Future. New Forms of Reality,” the finale of Ukrainian Fashion Week’s 27-year-old young designers’ contest, for a collection titled “Reclaiming the Light,” drawn from Sonia Delaunay, Oleksandr Ekster and Kazimir Malevich.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Getting it to the runway was its own ordeal: days before the show, she shipped her pieces via Nova Poshta – then watched the carrier’s sorting facilities get hit by Russian drone strikes in the Kyiv region and Odesa.
                                                                                                                                                                         
It wasn’t until the day of her show that she found out that her whole collection was safe and that she’d have an opportunity to present it.
On the runway during wartime
Ukrainian model Kateryna Miikluha, who walked in several shows this season for designers including Juliya Kros and Pustovit, said this was the most on edge she had felt at a Ukrainian Fashion Week in some time.
                                                                                                                                                                         
“A few days ago, there was an alarm almost every hour,” she said. Even so: “I’m so excited – it’s an amazing season, amazing moods, so I’m very happy.”
Miikluha modeled in Milan for several seasons starting in 2021, and later in Turkey, before deciding to base her work in Ukraine after the full-scale invasion began.
“I was in Milan when the war started, and I was living with a Russian girl, and I thought something is not right in my life. So, in March, I returned to Ukraine and started to take fewer contracts abroad,” she said. Asked why she chose to keep working in Ukraine rather than abroad, she said: “I can’t leave my country when everyone is suffering – it feels like it’s right.”
Asked what it says about Ukraine and Ukrainians that fashion shows continue, including inside air raid shelters, Miikluha offered a single word: nezlamni – roughly, “unbreakable.”
“It means I don’t know what can break us. Like, nothing,” she said.

Sweden's general election remains too close to call, early results suggest.
With 50% of the votes counted, the two main blocs were separated by only 20,000 votes, Sweden public broadcaster SVT said.
Projected results from Sweden's election authority had given the left-wing political bloc led by the Social Democrats' Magdalena Andersson a one-seat majority over the rival four-party coalition put together by current conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.
Kristersson has been supported in government by the hard-right Sweden Democrats (SD), which have neo-Nazi roots. He has promised cabinet jobs for the SD if he stays in charge.
- Close race in Sweden as hard right eyes role in government 
  - Published1 day ago
But partial results suggest the party was losing support for the first time since 2010 when it entered parliament.
Sweden has two major political blocs featuring four parties on the right and four on the left - meaning coalition and minority governments are relatively common.
On Sunday night, Andersson urged supporters to wait for the final result, but added that if the current results hold, "Sweden will have a new government."
Her party, the Social Democrats, have been a major force in Swedish politics since the end of World War Two.
But SD - founded by Nazi sympathisers in the 1980s - had been shunned for years until 2022 when it became the country's second largest party after campaigning on violent crime and immigration.
After casting her vote on Sunday, Andersson laid out the choice facing the Swedish public: "Should we have a government entirely dominated by the Sweden Democrats, something that has never happened in Sweden before? Or should we have a government led by me, which will steer Sweden in a new spirit of co-operation?"
Kristersson, for his part, said it was important he and his alliance were able to continue their work.
"I think there is a genuine enthusiasm for us being able to continue our important work," he said after casting his ballot in his home municipality of Strangnas.
National security, gang crime and welfare spending dominated the election campaign.

Trump says he will remove all Irish whiskey tariffs as he ends two-day visit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Trump says he will remove all Irish whiskey tariffs as he ends two-day visit
- Published
US President Donald Trump announced he will lift all tariffs on Irish whiskey at the end of his two-day visit to Ireland.
He made the announcement before handing over the winner's trophy at the Trump International golf resort in Doonbeg, Co Clare, to Irish Open winner Shane Lowry.
Whiskey distilled in the Republic of Ireland faces the standard 15% tariff which applies to EU goods entering the US, while whiskey made in Northern Ireland or elsewhere in the UK has no tariff.
It comes after Trump doubled down on his support for a united Ireland and said joining Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland was "one of the naturals of all time".
He spent day two of his visit to Ireland watching the final day of the Irish Open.
On Saturday, Trump was in Dublin where he met with Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin and Irish President Catherine Connolly.
Addressing the crowd before the trophy presentation, Trump said he had discussed whiskey tariffs with Martin and with golfer Lowry.
"Everybody's been bugging me," he said.
"They are saying would you do me a favour? It's so unfair what's going on.
"Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey and I said, on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey."
The presentation ceremony marked the end of Trump's two-day trip to Ireland before boarding Air Force One at Shannon Airport and departing for Washington.
Whiskey tariff analysis - BBC News NI economics and business editor John Campbell:
Assuming the Trump tariffs on Irish whiskey are removed it will end the advantage that some Northern Ireland distillers had over competitors in the Republic of Ireland.
That is because producers north of the border were covered by the removal of tariffs on all UK-made whiskey which Trump announced in May.
All-island supply chains meant that some NI whiskey brands could not benefit from the earlier tariff cut.
Newer distilleries bottle whiskey produced by other companies while they wait for their own product to mature.
This service is dominated by the Great Northern Distillery in Dundalk, County Louth which produces whiskey under licence for brands across the island.
It means the NI distilleries bottling that liquid have been classified as EU rather than UK producers.
Doubling down on united Ireland comments
On Saturday, Trump told reporters he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with Micheál Martin.
Speaking on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort, he said it would be natural to put Ireland and Northern Ireland "together".
He spoke to reporters after watching Lowry tee off.
He described what he said about a united Ireland as "a fairly routine comment".
"I've always loved the people of Ireland. It just seems to me you have Northern Ireland and Ireland," he said
"It seems that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together.
"That's only my opinion, and by the way many people agree."
The president sidestepped a question about Scottish independence.
"I won't talk about Scotland yet I will save that," he said.
Asked about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's remarks that there would be no poll on Irish unity until a majority in Northern Ireland were likely to vote in favour, Trump added: "Everybody says that and then things happen."
- What's next after Donald Trump's united Ireland comments? 
  - Published15 hours ago
The taoiseach said the president's remarks did not come as a "surprise" to him.
"He would make the point this is his view. He believes unity is the logical way for the island to be configured and organised," Martin said.
He added: "I think some of the reaction is an overreaction. It shouldn't be a surprise. He takes a different sort of perspective on things."
Protests continue against Trump visit
More than 10,000 people marched through Dublin on Saturday to show their opposition to the US president.
Others protesting against the visit arrived in buses to Doonbeg on Sunday, with about 100 protesters present.
A small crowd were moved from the president's hotel by Gardai (Irish police), Irish broadcaster RTÉ is reporting.
On Saturday evening, three women were arrested for trespassing on the golf links at Doonbeg and appeared at a special sitting of Ennis District Court.
Rev Steven Foster, a Methodist minister from Galway, attended the anti-Trump protest in Doonbeg.
"I'm here because Trump is the exact opposite of everything I stand for as a follower of Jesus," he told BBC News NI.
Foster added: "As a church leader, it's important for me to be visible, and the church needs to be visible in this regard."
Foster said the "type of welcome he has been given sends out a terrible message".
Golf course is a 'massive employer'
However, others have praised Trump for the benefits and jobs his golf course brings to the local area.
Martin Kelly is a local businessman from Doonbeg and said the village is "very fortunate" to have the Trump International Golf Course.
"It's a massive employer here to be honest with you," he told BBC News NI.
"There's nothing else about here at that scale; they're very decent people to work for, they're very fair."
He said local people are "very proud" that the golf tournament took place there.
Seoirse Comerford owns the Comerford bar in Doonbeg. He described the tournament as "unbelievable".
He said the golf course is a big employer and is keeping Doonbeg "alive".
"Most rural villages in west Clare are all dying a death, young people going away to college, they don't come back.
"Like there's over 300 people employed up there at the golf course , it's a big boost to the local economy. You've got big companies in Dublin, like Intel, the golf course is our Intel down here."

Bodies, remains of 17 missing Palestinians recovered from Gaza rubble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
19:27:09 UTC
04:27:09 KST

Ramzi Mahmud and Mohammad Sio
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Gaza’s civil defense said Sunday that it recovered the bodies and remains of 17 Palestinians who had been missing beneath the rubble of homes destroyed in Israeli attacks during the genocide in the enclave.
 
The recoveries were made as part of the second phase of the “Recovery of Martyrs’ Bodies” project, launched on July 19 to locate Palestinians buried under the rubble of buildings destroyed by Israel, despite limited equipment and machinery available to rescue teams.
 
The second phase includes searches beneath destroyed homes in Gaza City in the north and the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza.
 
The civil defense said in a brief statement that its teams recovered the bodies of 16 missing Palestinians from the rubble of homes belonging to the Hajji and Al-Nadeem families in the Zeitoun and Yarmouk neighborhoods of Gaza City.
The remains of one other missing person were recovered from the rubble of a home belonging to the Al-War family in the Nuseirat refugee camp, it added.
Recovery operations are proceeding slowly because of a shortage of heavy equipment, despite the Gaza ceasefire agreement in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, which Palestinian authorities say provides for the entry of machinery to remove rubble and recover victims.
In October 2025, Gaza’s government media office said around 9,500 Palestinians had been reported missing since the start of the Israeli war, including people whose bodies remain under destroyed buildings and others whose fate is unknown.
 
The second phase of the recovery project is scheduled to involve 800 working hours and searches beneath 147 destroyed homes in the Gaza, North Gaza and Central governorates, where 1,072 bodies are believed to remain buried, according to previous civil defense figures.
 
The first phase began in late November 2025 and resulted in the recovery of around 333 bodies and human remains out of 559 missing people believed to be beneath the rubble of 54 homes and buildings.
Israel’s genocide in Gaza has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 others, while causing widespread destruction to civilian infrastructure.

Centre-left opposition bloc leads in Swedish vote, poll shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
19:25:59 UTC
04:25:59 KST

Centre-left opposition bloc leads in Swedish vote, poll shows
Sweden’s opposition bloc is projected to win the election with a one-seat majority over the ruling coalition.
Swedish Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson has told supporters that the opposition coalition is leading the polls, and if the results stand, “Sweden will get a new government”.
Voting in Sweden’s election ended at 18:00 GMT on Sunday, and officials are counting the results.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3UK, France among 12 states backing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements
- list 2 of 3UK bans goods from Israeli West Bank settlements: What that really means
- list 3 of 3Which countries banned goods from settlements but trade with Israel?
The centre-left opposition was expected to win 175 seats in the 349-seat parliament, the Swedish Election Authority said, based on votes from 4,853 of Sweden’s 6,312 election districts.
The right-wing governing bloc was projected to win 174 seats.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who leads the ruling coalition, said on Monday that he would contact other party leaders after the elections, adding that it remains an open question who will govern Sweden in the coming years.
The centre-left opposition coalition was projected to win 51.3 percent of the vote, ahead of the right-wing bloc’s 46.8 percent, according to an exit poll by public broadcaster SVT.
A separate election-day poll conducted by broadcaster TV4 also showed the centre-left in the lead.
Swedish exit polls, while often indicative of the outcome, have not always proven accurate. In 2022, for example, a poll projected that Andersson’s centre-left bloc would prevail, but a right-wing coalition led by Kristersson ultimately won.
Earlier in this campaign, Sweden’s left-wing bloc appeared headed for a comfortable victory over Kristersson’s four-party alliance, which includes the nationalist Sweden Democrats. But the race tightened steadily in the final weeks of the campaign, turning what had looked like a relatively predictable election into a much closer contest.
Earlier in the year, polls had given the opposition bloc led by Andersson’s Social Democrats a lead of about 10 percentage points. By the final weeks of the campaign, that advantage had collapsed to just two to three points.
A victory for Andersson would provide some respite for left-leaning parties across Europe, where right-wing and far-right parties have been gaining ground. Just last week, Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 44 percent of the vote in a key state election, putting a far-right party within reach of power at the state level in Germany for the first time since World War II.
If the early exit polls are wrong, however, Sweden’s election could instead bring the far-right Sweden Democrats into government for the first time. A party with roots in the neo-Nazi movement, it won 20.5 percent of the vote in the 2022 election, becoming the largest party on the right and a crucial source of parliamentary support for Kristersson’s minority government.
Until now, however, the Sweden Democrats have remained outside government. Kristersson announced in April that his conservative Moderates would be prepared to bring the party into a governing coalition if the right secured a majority, which would give the Sweden Democrats cabinet positions for the first time.
But if the exit-poll lead is confirmed, the Sweden Democrats would be less likely to enter government.

Trump said he would abolish the 10% tariff on Irish whiskey
Kyiv • UNN
Donald Trump announced plans to abolish the 10% tariff on Irish whiskey after the Irish Open tournament. The date of the abolition is currently unknown.
On Sunday, after the conclusion of a golf tournament in Ireland, U.S. President Donald Trump announced plans to cancel the 10% tariff on Irish whiskey, UNN reports, citing AP.
During the awards ceremony at the Irish Open tournament, Trump said that everyone had raised this issue with him, including some golfers.
"Everyone was asking me about it," the Republican president said. "And I responded: 'On behalf of the United States of America, I will cancel the tariffs'" on Irish whiskey.

In May, Trump announced the cancellation of certain tariffs on whiskey from the United Kingdom, including Scotch whisky and spirits produced in Northern Ireland.
Trump's surprise announcement at the end of the tournament prompted loud cheers and applause from spectators.
In May, the Irish Whiskey Association called for the tariffs to be canceled, arguing that such a step would help many American companies whose portfolios include Irish products and would also eliminate uncertainty for consumers.
There is currently no information about when exactly the tariff will be canceled.
On April 30, Trump said he had granted the United Kingdom preferential terms on the whiskey tariff following the visit of King Charles III and Queen Camilla to the White House. "The King and Queen got me to do what no one else could—and they almost didn't even ask!" Trump wrote on social media.
On July 24, the Scotch Whisky Association reported that the zero-tariff policy had already taken effect.

Trump reiterates support for united Ireland, refrains on Scottish independence
US President Donald Trump on Sunday reiterated his support for Northern Ireland breaking from the United Kingdom to unify with the Republic of Ireland, but said he would not talk about Scotland becoming independent "yet".
Trump surprised officials in Dublin and annoyed pro-British politicians in Northern Ireland and London by enthusiastically backing Irish unity during a visit to Dublin on Saturday, saying he would "love" to see it happen sooner rather than later.
"You have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland and it would seem to me that one of the 'naturals' of all time is to put them together," Trump told reporters during a visit to a golf tournament at one of his resorts, doubling down on his initial comments.

Trump made his comments about Irish unity after a meeting with Micheal Martin, the country's prime minister. In his first comments since Trump's remarks, the Irish premier said the response from some unionist politicians was "an overreaction".
"It shouldn't be a surprise. He takes a different sort of perspective on things," Martin told reporters on Sunday after meeting Trump again for lunch at the golf course.
Martin said the pair discussed Northern Ireland and its relationship with the Republic of Ireland and that he also went through with the president how the British-run region achieved peace.
A 1998 peace agreement ended three decades of violence between Irish nationalists seeking a united Ireland and unionists who wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the UK.
"I support unity, I don't see it happening now. I've been very clear about that," Martin told BBC News in a separate interview.
"The chances are if one (vote) was held next week, it would find great difficulty in getting through."

Layan Bsharat and Mohammad Sio
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Nearly 600 Israeli occupiers stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem on Sunday as Israeli authorities imposed restrictions on Palestinian worshippers during the Jewish New Year, according to the Jerusalem Governorate.
The governorate said in a statement that 593 occupiers entered the compound through the Dung Gate (Bab al-Maghariba) on the second day of the Jewish holiday.
The incursions took place in morning and afternoon sessions under the protection of Israeli forces, it added.
The governorate had earlier put the number of those who entered the mosque at 480 before updating the figure to 593.
In a separate statement, it said Israeli authorities restricted access to Al-Aqsa Mosque during dawn prayers Sunday to the Hutta and Chain gates.
Israeli authorities also imposed age restrictions on worshippers, while soldiers stationed at checkpoints refused to disclose which age groups were permitted to enter, according to the governorate.
The measures prevented many worshippers from reaching the mosque, while a small number who managed to reach the area were forced to pray at its gates.
The restrictions coincided with calls by Israeli Temple groups for intensified incursions into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound during the Jewish New Year.
The Jerusalem Governorate said the incursions are part of an ongoing escalation targeting the mosque during the Jewish holiday season, alongside a rise in orders barring Palestinians from entering the site.
It said it had documented around 850 such orders since the beginning of the year.
On Friday, the governorate warned of “growing calls by alleged Israeli Temple groups to impose their religious rituals inside Al-Aqsa Mosque during the Jewish holidays.”
It said Israeli occupiers are seeking to impose their rituals “by force” around the mosque and at its gates, warning of attempts to establish “a new reality” and undermine the site’s Islamic identity.
The Jewish holiday season began with Rosh Hashanah on Sept. 12-13 and continues with Yom Kippur on Sept. 21, followed by Sukkot from Sept. 26 to Oct. 2 and Simchat Torah on Oct. 3.
Since 2003, Israeli police have unilaterally allowed Israeli occupiers to enter the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, despite repeated calls by the Islamic Waqf Department in Jerusalem to halt such incursions.
Palestinians say Israel has for decades intensified efforts to Judaize occupied East Jerusalem, including Al-Aqsa Mosque, and erase its Arab and Islamic identity.
They insist that East Jerusalem should be the capital of a future Palestinian state under international resolutions that do not recognize Israel’s occupation of the city in 1967 or its 1980 annexation.

Russia hits Ukrainian train shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials leave station
- Published
A Russian drone has hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through.
No casualties were reported after the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. All the passengers had been evacuated, Ukrainian authorities said.
Johnson and other European national security advisers, including the UK's Jonathan Powell, had passed along the same line on a different train on their way back from a conference in Kyiv.
Russia said it had struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but Ukraine's state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said that "quite possibly, the target of this drone could have been the diplomatic train".
In a statement, it said the train "had left the station earlier than expected because of the timetable change... due to constant threats of Russian strikes".
It also said an evacuation order for passengers on the hit train had been given "just 15 minutes" before the strike by a Russian jet-propelled drone.
The railway authority also said former CIA chief David Petraeus had been on board another train at Yahodyn station at the time of the drone strike.
Both Ukrainian and Polish authorities said the Russian drone had struck 2km from the Polish border.
Former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, who had also attended the conference in Kyiv, told the BBC passengers on board his train had been told to prepare for evacuation before subsequently being allowed to continue their journey.
"On the train I was on we received order to prepare evacuation after it had stopped. But after a number of minutes we were informed that it was clear and we could proceed," he said.
That train then safely arrived at Poland's border station in Dorohusk.
Some reports have suggested Bildt was on the same train as Johnson, but the former UK prime minister has not confirmed any details.
Johnson wrote on X: "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning.
He said this was "the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day - even on civilian railways" and urged Kyiv's allies to urgently provide Ukrainians "the air defences they need".
Ukraine has made repeated pleas to its allies - particularly the US - to provide more interceptors to defend against daily Russian attacks that increasingly use fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-propelled drones.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric strikes" at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn amounted to "[Russian President Vladimir] Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and Nato" and renewed calls for more sanctions on Moscow.
"Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level. This is the only way to stop him," he said.
In Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk held an emergency meeting to discuss the latest developments.
"The escalation of the actions from the Russian side is becoming a reality, and they are getting closer and closer to our border."
Johnson and other top European security advisers were on their way back from the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv - an annual event that brings together leaders and experts from politics, business, security and mass media.
