Could Iran’s regime collapse? Inside the Israeli assessment of Tehran’s future - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
19:12:40 UTC
04:12:40 KST

What is really happening behind the scenes in Tehran? How close is the collapse of the ayatollah regime, what is going through Mojtaba Khamenei’s mind, and why is Israel’s defense establishment on maximum alert?
Throughout January and February, intelligence agencies closely monitored the Iranian regime’s harsh campaign of retaliation against protesters across the country. Reports collected by officials in Washington and Jerusalem documented arrests, severe torture, and a widespread pattern of citizens disappearing without a trace.
Initially, Israeli and the United States had no plan to launch another operation after Operation Rising Lion. However, as reports emerged of mass killings carried out indiscriminately against men, women, children, and the elderly, Israel’s defense establishment delivered a firm message in closed forums: “The moment for another operation will come; it is inevitable.”
The motivation was not only the growing threat posed by Iran’s nuclear program and former supreme leader Ali Khamenei’s decision to produce thousands of ballistic missiles.
Israeli officials also cited a moral obligation not to stand aside in the face of mass killings. At the same time, they identified a strategic opportunity to advance a process that could ultimately lead to the collapse of the regime.
The White House meeting and the three pillars
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accepted the recommendation of the US administration and traveled to the White House for a critical meeting with US President Donald Trump, accompanied by senior security officials. The goal was to strengthen cooperation and approve a joint strategic plan.
During the closed-door meeting, no explicit commitment was made to overthrow the Iranian regime. One official clarified: “We are going to create the conditions for regime change.”
To advance that goal, the Israeli delegation presented three main pillars: alternative leadership, targeted influence campaigns, and ground operations. The approach was based on the clear understanding that airstrikes alone cannot topple a regime.
Six months after Operation Roaring Lion, Israeli security officials assess that the Iranian regime, despite the aggression it continues to display toward its neighbors, is moving along a path of internal deterioration. The process could take months or even years, but severe economic sanctions and international cooperation could accelerate it significantly.
At present, the regime is struggling to contain unrest in the streets and markets, as well as rising unemployment. Oil exports have been almost completely frozen, and the economic situation continues to worsen.
On the military front, Israeli officials assess that intelligence and operational gains have been preserved. According to security sources, Iran has not resumed uranium enrichment or transferred centrifuges, while most of its infrastructure remains buried deep underground.
“They carried out dilutions and various actions, but they did not transfer anything. Their defense industry has been destroyed,” a senior security official said.
The official added that the Pickaxe Mountain facility remains unchanged due to the lack of aerial munitions capable of destroying it.
The clock game: Fear in Tehran, pressure in Washington
The current situation is being managed under a “clock game,” with the American clock measured by fuel prices and Trump’s patience, and the Iranian clock growing more urgent by the day. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has already publicly recommended reaching a diplomatic agreement “while we are still standing on our feet,” amid growing tensions within the upper levels of the government.
For now, Iran is refusing to consider concessions and believes it can withstand the economic pressure. However, US statements regarding broad sanctions have placed Tehran under unprecedented pressure.
Washington is directing much of that pressure toward the United Arab Emirates and China, which serve as Iran’s main economic lifelines through their purchases of oil on the black market. The goal is to persuade them to stop helping Tehran circumvent sanctions.
Within Israel’s defense establishment, there is growing concern over the possibility of an unexpected Iranian move. The assessment is that Tehran may attempt to escape its economic pressure by attacking Israel in an effort to force limited negotiations and reach new understandings.
The Israeli message conveyed to Tehran has been clear: if Iran attacks, there will be no way back. Israel’s response, officials have indicated, would target critical national infrastructure that a collapsing regime would not be able to rebuild.
At the same time, Iranian officials remain concerned about the possibility of another surprise attack, and the heightened tensions continue to trouble senior figures in Tehran.

Carney is promoting the idea of granting Canada “associate member” status in the EU - media
Kyiv • UNN
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to bring the country closer to the EU amid the trade war with the United States. The sides are discussing trade, visa-free travel and joint projects.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is seeking closer ties with the European Union and is exploring the possibility of Canada acquiring the status of an "associate member" of the bloc, UNN reports, citing The Wall Street Journal and Reuters.
Details
The EU, which previously showed no flexibility on membership rules, is prepared to consider the idea of granting Canada associate-member status — a format that still needs to be developed, WSJ writes, citing unnamed EU and Canadian officials.
The Embassy of Canada in Brussels and representatives of the European Commission did not respond to separate requests for comment.
Canada's escalating trade war with the United States has given additional urgency to the country's strategic pivot toward other trading partners.
Relations between Ottawa and Washington deteriorated sharply after Donald Trump returned to the White House last year due to disagreements over trade and other issues. The trade dispute led to the imposition of tariffs affecting tens of billions of dollars' worth of cross-border trade.
Canada and the EU are discussing measures that would allow the free movement of Canadian goods, services and professionals involved in strategic supply chains — in areas such as energy, artificial intelligence, defense and critical-mineral extraction — which would effectively mean expanding the EU's borders, WSJ notes.
The parties are also negotiating the laying of undersea cables, the joint construction of data centers, the creation of cloud storage facilities and new satellite networks, as well as infrastructure for supplying Canadian energy resources to the EU, the newspaper reports.
Carney regularly discusses with a number of EU leaders, including French President Emmanuel Macron, the possibility of granting Canadians the right to live and work in the European Union without visas, WSJ writes, citing two unnamed officials familiar with the situation.
Macron's press service did not respond to a request for comment.
At the same time, the French president's administration confirmed that on September 20, Macron will meet with Carney in the French territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon — a group of islands off Canada's Atlantic coast.
The visit will be the Canadian prime minister's first official trip to the archipelago and "symbolizes the strength of the ties that bind our two countries," the Élysée Palace said. However, any initiatives to strengthen ties between Canada and the EU will likely face difficulties — as demonstrated by the experience of implementing a more modest trade agreement, which met fierce resistance in Europe.
More than ten years have passed since this agreement was concluded, and nine since its provisional entry into force, yet a number of EU countries have still not ratified it.

In 2022, the Sweden Democrats won 17.7%, while the Moderates received 19.1%.
 
The Left Party is projected to become Sweden's fourth-largest party with 8.2%, up from 6.8% in the 2022 election.
 
The Center Party also appears to have gained ground, reaching 7.2%, compared with 6.7% in 2022.
 
The Christian Democrats are projected to receive 6.2%, up from 5.3% four years ago.
 
The Liberals, meanwhile, stand at 5.4%, comfortably above Sweden's 4% parliamentary threshold.
 
The exit poll is not the final election result, and the balance between the blocs could change as votes are counted.
 
Late early votes and ballots cast from abroad are expected to be counted Wednesday or Thursday.

​Bangsamoro’s parliamentary election is a turning point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:39:28 UTC
03:39:28 KST

Bangsamoro’s parliamentary election is a turning point
It is a milestone of the self-determination struggle in this region of the Philippines. It must be kept peaceful and fair.
On Monday, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the Philippines will hold its first parliamentary election since it was established in 2018. The vote will officially mark the end of the transition period under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA), an interim regional government appointed in 2019.
The election is a significant milestone in the Bangsamoro struggle. It is the outcome of decades of armed conflict and negotiations between the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and the government of the Philippines.
The vote will test the Philippine government’s commitment to the peace process and the MILF’s commitment to the democratic process.
The struggle for self-determination
BARMM is located on Mindanao, the second-largest island in the Philippine Archipelago, and it covers roughly the territories inhabited by the Moro people, a native Muslim-majority group. For centuries, the Moro enjoyed self-governance in independent states and resisted Spanish colonialism. Following the Philippines’s independence in 1946, they continued their struggle for self-determination.
In 1989, the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) was created by Manila to give some devolved rights to the Moro. However, ARMM largely failed to address local grievances and demands due to its weak structural power. It was given limited autonomy in political and fiscal decision-making, but it did not manage to improve socioeconomic conditions in the region. The MILF continued the armed struggle.
In 2012, President Benigno Aquino III recognised the ARMM as a “failed experiment”. Under his administration, the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro was signed between the government and the MILF, paving the way for a new political entity.
Six years later, under President Rodrigo Roa Duterte, the Organic Law for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was promulgated. This legislation granted the region greater fiscal autonomy, a regional government, a parliament, and a justice system.
Then the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro was concluded to outline the mechanism of transition from ARMM to BARMM and set up the MILF-dominated BTA to lead it. All of this is culminating in the parliamentary election, which will determine the makeup of the region’s first legislative body.
A contested election
The vote comes at a time of heightened tensions in BARMM and internal divisions within the MILF. Two camps have emerged within the movement – one loyal to MILF Chair Al Haj Murad Ebrahim and another supporting Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua.
Last month, Macacua joined the newly formed Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), which will compete in the elections against the MILF’s political wing, the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP). Shortly after, his convoy was attacked, but he survived unscathed.
In early September, Macacua and 40 commanders were dismissed from the MILF’s military wing for alleged insubordination.
These tensions have prompted increased public anxiety about possible post-election unrest. There are other factors that could overshadow the vote.
In past elections, vote-buying was widespread, election-related violence was rampant, and electoral fraud and manipulation were pervasive. If these practices repeat at a large scale, the electoral outcome may not necessarily provide a straightforward measure of the will of Bangsamoro’s people. It may also not be an accurate reflection of whether they are satisfied with the transitional government or not.
The MILF presents itself as a champion of moral governance. If it is to retain this label, it should not give in to widespread vote-buying and electoral manipulation. It should also not let internal rivalries turn violent.
But there are already some alarming signs. Prominent MILF figures have conveyed that if the UBJP, the front’s political wing, sees manipulation and fraud, its members are ready to fight. They have also suggested that since the MILF led the transition, it should remain in power. On social media, some citizens have condemned the MILF camp’s threats, calling such tactics un-Islamic.
Before the vote, Manila has deployed military forces in key areas. This has heightened people’s fears that fighting with the MILF may erupt. The tense situation might lead to a low voter turnout.
Under these circumstances, the future of the Bangsamoro is riddled with uncertainties.
Whatever happens in the election, we must remember that the future of BARMM is a shared responsibility. The Philippine government and the Bangsamoro parties are duty-bound to honour the peace agreement. In addition, the people must exercise their civic rights and responsibilities to help sustain the peace achieved after a long and painful armed conflict and to move toward a prosperous Bangsamoro land.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Authorities have evacuated more than 31,000 people have been evacuated in China's southern Hainan province as continued heavy rains battered parts of the island, state media reported on Sunday.

Xi calls on BRICS to act as pioneers of a changing world
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
21:35:38 EEST
03:35:38 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping has placed the idea of BRICS nations acting as “pioneers” at the centre of his message to the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, setting out a programme based on innovation, peace, exchanges between civilisations and reform of global governance.
Addressing the first session of the summit on 12 September, Xi said the BRICS cooperation mechanism had developed over two decades into what he described as the world’s most influential platform for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries.
He presented its growth as evidence that countries of the Global South had built an institution around cooperation, national development choices and common interests.
The summit marks 20 years since the start of BRICS cooperation. Xi used the anniversary to look beyond the organisation’s expansion and set out a role for the grouping in the next phase of international affairs.
His central message was that BRICS members should “strive to be a pioneer of the times” as economic and political weight shifts towards emerging economies and developing states.
The phrase was not presented as a slogan in isolation. Xi linked the idea of pioneering action to four fields in which he wants BRICS members to take a larger role: innovation-driven development, peace and stability, exchanges between civilisations and reform of global governance.
Xi first called on BRICS to pioneer innovation-driven development. His proposal placed artificial intelligence, industrial development and technological cooperation near the centre of the group’s economic agenda.
He urged BRICS members to strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence, support open-source development and pursue greater sharing between members. China also proposed an initiative to promote new industrialisation through artificial intelligence among BRICS countries.
Xi said China wanted to work with other members on research, development and application while strengthening cooperation across industrial and supply chains. He also invited BRICS countries to take part in the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization.
The focus moved from broad principles to a more detailed programme during the second day of the summit on 13 September.
Xi proposed five initiatives for what he called “greater BRICS” cooperation. They cover artificial intelligence, trade and investment facilitation, the digital industry, smart manufacturing and talent development.
He said “greater BRICS” should produce greater impact, pursue greater development and establish a foundation for practical cooperation. He called for members to draw on their position in emerging markets and their links with the Global South while supporting open cooperation, stable industrial and supply chains and more integrated markets.
Xi also called for innovation incubators, the upgrading of traditional industries, the development of emerging sectors and planning for future industries.
Taken together, the proposals give more definition to his call for BRICS members to serve as pioneers. The first part of the programme focuses on moving emerging economies from users of new technologies towards a larger role in research, industrial application and standard-setting.
That approach carries weight because BRICS has expanded far beyond its original format.
BRICS is now an 11-member organisation spanning four continents, with a wider group of partner countries taking part in cooperation. BRICS members now represent close to half of the world’s population.
Expansion has also changed the position of Africa within the organisation. South Africa is joined by Egypt and Ethiopia as full members, giving the continent three seats within the grouping.
This gives African states a larger role in shaping international rules rather than participating only in systems created elsewhere.
Xi’s second call for pioneering action dealt with peace and stability.
He urged BRICS members to support what China describes as common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security. He opposed Cold War thinking, bloc confrontation, interference in other states’ internal affairs and violations of national sovereignty.
He also called for BRICS to take a constructive role in resolving conflicts and disputes.
The Middle East featured directly in his remarks. Xi said the conflict in the region had caused serious losses and ran against the common interests of the international community. He called for political settlement and a permanent and comprehensive ceasefire and said China would work with other BRICS members in support of peace in the region. citeturn463152view0
This part of Xi’s “pioneer” concept gives BRICS a political role alongside its economic work.
The organisation began as a forum centred on emerging economies. Its agenda now extends to questions of security, international institutions, technology, trade and development. Xi’s speech presented that wider agenda as a responsibility that follows from the increased economic and demographic weight of BRICS members.
His third call was for BRICS to become a pioneer in mutual learning between civilisations.
Xi urged the group to support exchanges between countries and societies, expand cooperation in culture, tourism and education and strengthen contact between young people and called on members to exchange experience in governance and use cultural and people-to-people programmes to support stable relations between states.
This part of the speech placed human contact alongside trade, finance and technology.
For a group spanning Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America, internal diversity is one of its defining features. Xi’s approach treats those differences as a basis for exchange rather than an obstacle to cooperation.
His fourth call for pioneering action addressed global governance.
Xi urged BRICS members to support reform of international institutions and push for what he described as a more just and equitable global governance system.
He called for support for the authority of the United Nations, a multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization and opposition to protectionism.
Xi also identified cyberspace, outer space and the deep sea as fields where BRICS members should take a greater part in setting rules and shaping governance. He linked that role to increasing the voice of Global South countries in international decision-making.
The four uses of “pioneer” give Xi’s summit speech a consistent structure.
Pioneering in innovation means building technological capacity. Pioneering in peace means taking a larger role in political settlement and opposing bloc confrontation.
Pioneering in exchanges between civilisations means expanding contact between societies.
Pioneering in global governance means seeking a greater role for emerging and developing countries in international institutions.
The second-day proposals then add an economic mechanism to that framework through AI, trade, digital industry, manufacturing and skills.
A larger membership gives the organisation a broader economic base and wider geographic reach. It also brings together governments with different political systems, economic structures and national priorities.
At the summit, participating leaders also backed a stronger role for BRICS in representing the Global South. Participants supported multilateralism, the central role of the United Nations, sovereign equality, international law and free trade while calling for joint responses to international challenges.
The leaders adopted a joint declaration that set out their shared positions on development, security, economic cooperation and global governance. The declaration reaffirmed support for multilateralism, international law and the central role of the United Nations, while calling for greater representation of emerging markets and developing countries in international institutions. The members backed an open, inclusive and non-discriminatory multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization and opposed protectionism. They also committed to deeper cooperation in areas including trade, investment, finance, technology, artificial intelligence and sustainable development. The declaration reflected the summit’s wider message that BRICS members intend to strengthen coordination among themselves while giving the Global South a larger voice in decisions that shape the international economic and political system.
China will take over the rotating BRICS chair and host the 19th BRICS Summit in 2027. Xi said Beijing wanted to work with all parties to build consensus and begin what he termed BRICS’ third “golden decade”.
That handover gives China responsibility for turning parts of the New Delhi agenda into working programmes.
The five initiatives announced on the second day provide an early indication of where that effort is heading. AI cooperation links research with industrial development. Trade and investment facilitation seeks to strengthen economic connections. Digital industry and smart manufacturing address changes in production. Talent development focuses on the workers and specialists required to support those sectors.
The wider Global South context gives these proposals significance beyond the organisation itself.
For BRICS, the next test is whether expanded membership leads to expanded practical cooperation.
Xi’s speeches in New Delhi set out China’s answer.
BRICS should not limit itself to responding to changes in the international system. Its members should seek to shape those changes.
By repeatedly describing BRICS nations as prospective “pioneers”, Xi assigned the grouping a forward role rather than a defensive one. His four-part framework links that role to technology, security, cultural exchange and institutional reform, while the “greater BRICS” proposals give the programme an economic and industrial base.
As China prepares to assume the BRICS chair, the New Delhi summit has placed that idea at the centre of the organisation’s next phase: emerging and developing countries acting together not only as participants in international affairs, but as states seeking to help set their direction.

Yemen's internationally recognized government decided Sunday to ban the entry and circulation of all Iranian goods and products, according to the state-run Saba news agency.
 
The National Committee for Regulating and Financing Imports approved the measure during a meeting chaired by Central Bank of Yemen Governor Ahmad Ghaleb, who also heads the committee.
 
The committee said the decision was taken “in accordance with the requirements of the higher national interest.”
 
It instructed relevant authorities to take the necessary measures to implement the ban, each within its respective jurisdiction and in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.
The statement did not specify when the ban will take effect or provide further details on the Iranian products affected.
 
The decision comes amid a sharp escalation in fighting between Yemen’s internationally recognized government and the Iran-backed Houthi group.
The Yemeni government accuses Iran of providing military and financial support to the Houthi group while Tehran denies these accusations.
 
The Houthis, who seized Sanaa and large parts of Yemen in 2014, are backed by Iran, while government forces are supported by a Saudi-led coalition. Fighting has intensified since July after a relative lull that had largely held since a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.

Milna Mayor Frane Lozic said the situation changed rapidly after authorities initially believed the fire was under control.
 
Firefighting operations continued Sunday as crews worked to contain the blaze and protect populated areas.

Sweden's centre-left opposition leads election as far-right slips, exit polls show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:25:43 UTC
03:25:43 KST

Sweden's centre-left holds razor-thin edge as exit polls show tight race
Sweden's general election remained too close to call early Monday, with nearly 90% of votes counted. Four opposition parties led by Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson held a one-seat parliamentary lead over Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing bloc, which includes the Sweden Democrats, as both leaders said they were ready to govern.
Sweden's general election was too close to call early Monday, as the incumbent prime minister and the left-wing opposition leader both said they were ready to govern and the far right was seen losing ground.
With almost 90 percent of votes counted, four opposition parties led by Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson, held a one-seat majority in the 349-seat parliament over Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing alliance, which includes the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats.
"For now, we are in the lead. And if that is confirmed, Sweden will have a new government," 59-year-old Andersson, who was Sweden's first woman prime minister in 2021-2022, told her supporters.
But her party -- which ruled the Scandinavian country for most of the 20th century and remains Sweden's largest -- also looked to be heading for its worst score in over a century with 28 percent of the vote.
Outgoing prime minister Kristersson, whose Moderate Party was credited with 19.9 percent of the counted votes, meanwhile said that if the result stood, he would respect Andersson's attempts to try to form a government with the three other parties on the left.
But he noted that the four had irreconcilable differences, primarily between the Left Party and the Centre Party, and were unlikely to agree on a government programme.
Read moreSweden Election Aftermath: A hard night for the hard right?
"I will therefore, even if tonight's result stands, examine whether there are any possibilities within this non-socialist parliamentary majority to find some workable government constellation," Kristersson told his supporters.
"Which government is going to govern Sweden in the coming years is still an open question," Kristersson declared.
In a big surprise, the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, which entered parliament in 2010, lost support for the first time, garnering 17.6 percent of the vote, down from 20.5 percent in 2022.
"We don't yet have the full election result, but it's obvious that we've lost a few percentage points compared with our result four years ago," party leader Jimmie Akesson told an election night watch party.
Now mainstream
But he said it was a success that supporters were no longer afraid to show their support for the party long seen as political pariah.
"There are now so many more people around our country who no longer find it difficult to say that they are Sweden Democrats," Akesson said.
With such a close result, the final outcome might not be clear for a few days, several party leaders said.
Municipal election authorities will start counting votes on Wednesday that had not reached their destination on election night.
In Sweden, all votes are also automatically recounted by the regional county administrative boards, which establishes the final result. This process usually takes a week.
Kristersson has headed a minority coalition backed by the Sweden Democrats for four years, giving the far-right influence over policy in exchange for support in parliament.
Kristersson had promised the Sweden Democrats key cabinet posts if the right-wing won.
Throughout the campaign, opinion polls gave a comfortable lead to the left-wing opposition, but the gap narrowed to a dead heat in the final days.
Much of the campaign focused on healthcare and helping struggling households cope with rising costs.
Andersson, the first woman to head Sweden's government in 2021-2022, has pledged to raise taxes on banks and high incomes, cut healthcare queues, and improve declining school results.
Read moreSweden: Tight election puts all eyes on the far right
'Make Sweden Great Again'
Kristersson meanwhile vowed to focus on improving Swedes' everyday lives now that his government's clampdown on organised crime and immigration was starting to show results.
Deadly shootings and bombings by organised crime networks have fallen sharply in recent years, while asylum applications are at a record low.
"We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people... to make Sweden great again," Kristersson told AFP before the vote, borrowing US President Donald Trump's trademark slogan.
Over the past two decades, far-right leader Jimmie Akesson has steered the party with neo-Nazi roots into the mainstream.
"Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish," Akesson told a campaign rally on Saturday, surrounded by blue-and-yellow "Make Sweden Sweden Again" posters.
At a polling station on Sunday, store manager Linda Eriksson, 48, told AFP she hoped for a change of government.
"Hopefully a lot of people will realise that we have to change course... so that everyone will feel included in society," she said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

White House economic adviser downplays market risks from AI safety warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:24:50 UTC
03:24:50 KST

Yasin Gungor
13 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett dismissed concerns Sunday that recent warnings by technology executives over artificial intelligence (AI) risks would trigger market turmoil.
"I don't expect that that's what's going to happen," Hassett told US broadcaster CNN, describing an essay published by Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei as a "very thoughtful letter" outlining the need to pace developments while ensuring firms demonstrate their systems are safe.
Hassett endorsed Amodei's call to establish independent observers embedded in firms during model training, comparing the proposed inspectors to bank supervisors. While acknowledging risks such as autonomous agents compromising cybersecurity, he cautioned that the "far bigger risk is that a malevolent actor has access to an AI that's better than the one we have that can protect us," specifically warning against foreign development of biological weapons.
US President Donald Trump opposed slowing down the domestic AI industry, arguing Sunday that maintaining a technological advantage over China remains critical for global leadership.
While acknowledging that authorities "can put guardrails" on technological systems, Trump maintained that his primary objective centers on preserving America's edge, because "whoever wins AI wins."
Federal Reserve interest rate decision
Turning to monetary policy, Hassett argued that the Federal Reserve has no compelling reason to raise interest rates despite recent data showing that annual inflation rose 3.4% in August.
"President Trump and I actually think that there isn't a reason right now to raise rates," Hassett said, noting that while oil price surges from hostilities in the Gulf pushed annualized headline numbers higher earlier this year, recent figures show annualized inflation running at “just about 1%.”
Citing historical precedents under former Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, Hassett maintained that central bank officials should leave policy unchanged to protect institutional independence ahead of the November midterm elections.
Hassett affirmed that the administration would support Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh regardless of the outcome while playing down Trump's threats to halt trade with deficit partners if the Fed does not lower interest rates, adding: “I don't expect the trade's going to go to zero.”
Trump confirmed Sunday that he will halt commerce with several trading partners running surpluses against Washington if the Fed does not reduce interest rates.
"Oh yeah, I'm going to do that with some nations," he told reporters upon concluding his visit to Ireland. "I'll have no choice. We don't want to have deficits with nations. We want to have surpluses, or at least break even," he said.
Hassett's remarks came after Trump said the US "should be paying the lowest interest rate in the world" because it “is so strong.”
The next Federal Reserve interest rate decision is scheduled for Wednesday, as the current benchmark rate sits in a target range of 3.50% to 3.75%.

Sweden exit poll: Left on course for election win in blow to far right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:20:49 UTC
03:20:49 KST

Magdalena Andersson arrives at the Social Democrats' election night watch party in Stockholm on Sept. 13, 2026. | Jonas Ekstromer/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images
STOCKHOLM — Former center-left Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson is on course to retake power in Sweden as exit polling suggests a right-wing alliance that includes the far right is falling short.
Andersson, the leader of the Social Democrats, spent much of the election campaign warning voters against handing ministerial posts to what she called an “extremist” party with “neo-Nazi” roots — the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats.
If the surveys prove accurate, it would mean rejection for incumbent PM Ulf Kristersson. The conservative Moderate party leader had decided to work closely with the Sweden Democrats and promised to give them seats in cabinet for the first time if he won.
Advertisement
Two separate exit polls for Sweden’s SVT public broadcaster and TV4 showed Andersson’s left bloc on track to take 51% of the vote. (Sweden’s electoral system is based on proportional representation.) Kristersson’s alliance on the right was projected to win 47%.
Exit polls have not always been accurate in the past, but the picture should become clearer later on Sunday night when broadcasters are expected to announce updated forecasts after a critical mass of districts declare results. Whoever ends up winning, party leaders will take weeks to finalize a new coalition agreement.
“Swedish elections are always close,” Andersson told POLITICO earlier on Sunday as she toured the suburbs of Stockholm in her dark red campaign bus. “When I’ve been around Sweden, a lot of people I’ve spoken to said they see things that the government has done that they like but there are also lots of things that they don’t like. And many people say to me that it’s enough now.”
With the prospect of the far right entering government for the first time, the vote marks a watershed moment for Sweden that will be watched closely elsewhere in Europe, where other populist nationalist parties are gaining ground.
Even Andersson accepts that a victory for her left bloc would not consign the Sweden Democrats to history, especially if the final result is a narrow one.
“The hate that they have spread through this election, and if they would become ministers and use their platforms as ministers to spread hate? Well, we’ll see if the Swedish people are very tempted on that,” she said.
Advertisement
But victory would be a major relief for the Social Democrat leader and her political allies in other parties on the left of Swedish politics. Andersson was thrown out of office in an election four years ago, and spent the intervening period leading the opposition.
For months, her bloc — which includes the Left Party, with its communist roots, as well as the Greens — had enjoyed a comfortable advantage in the polls. But that lead narrowed dramatically in the last two weeks of the campaign, with one poll on the eve of the vote putting the two rival blocs in a dead heat.
Kristersson’s allies on the right may be left wondering whether he made a mistake in seeking to collaborate so closely with such controversial partners in the far-right Sweden Democrats and their leader Jimmie Åkesson.
The PM told POLITICO he trusted Åkesson because the two had worked well together for four years, with the Sweden Democrats supporting the government in parliament without having ministers formally in the cabinet. Kristersson and Åkesson tried to persuade voters they deserved another term to finish the work they started — especially bringing down violent crime and reducing immigration.
But Andersson argued that many voters had balked at moves by the Kristersson government to expel young people from the country who had attended Swedish schools, spoke the language fluently and made their lives in Sweden. “People think that’s stupid and inhumane,” she told POLITICO on Sunday.
It didn’t help Kristersson’s cause that his side was forced to fight claims of Russian infiltration in the final days of the campaign. In an earlier interview with POLITICO, Andersson demanded that Kristersson come clean about allegations that the partner of a senior Sweden Democrats official had promoted pro-Russian narratives and linked up with a Russian state group.
Advertisement
Speaking to POLITICO on Friday, Kristersson argued that the real security risk lay with Andersson’s allies — given that two of the parties she may end up governing with had opposed Sweden’s NATO membership before the country joined the alliance.
Jan Teorell, a professor of political science at Stockholm University, said the center left had tried hard to make the election a referendum on allowing the far right to share power. “This is definitely part of what the Social Democrats in particular want the election to be about,” he said.
The gap between the leftwing camp and Kristersson’s bloc, including the Sweden Democrats, opened up after the latter two agreed to work together in 2022, according to Teorell. That “could be interpreted as dissatisfaction among some center-right voters with either SD, the agreement as such, or both, making them switch to the other side.”
However, it won’t be clear why Sweden turned away from the far right until detailed voter behavior studies are published after the election, he said.

In a first, the US Department of Justice brought a case before a previously unused special court and deported an Afghan woman legally residing in the US after she conceded to being an “alien terrorist,” according to court records.
Prosecutors in the DOJ alleged that Nazira Haji Zada, a 47-year-old mother originally from Afghanistan, supported a plan by her son and son-in-law to commit an ISIS-style mass shooting on America's Election Day in 2024.
Both Haji Zada’s son and son-in-law were charged in the plot and will be deported following their release from prison.
Haji Zada was arrested in July at her home in Fort Worth, Texas. She was tried in the never-before-used Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC), which Congress created in 1996.
The court’s initial purpose was to make it easier for the DOJ to use classified evidence during prosecutions that posed a risk to national security, according to an analysis by NPR.
Afghani woman's deportation not an 'endorsement of this court's legitimacy'
Court records dated August 20 state that Haji Zada waived her right to challenge the detention and agreed to the deportation order; the presiding judge ordered her removal the same day.
Attorney General Todd Blanche stated, “This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law. Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States, and this first-ever case before the ATRC shows how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country.”
Haji Zada’s public defenders contested the legality of the case, arguing they were not permitted to review the evidence because it remained classified.
A statement from the DOJ noted that Haji Zada and her lawyers were provided with almost half a terabyte of evidence supporting the government’s case against her.
Haji Zada’s lawyers stated that their client’s consent to the deportation order “should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy.”
“Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process,” they said.
“We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue.”
The DOJ statement on the case alleged that Haji Zada worked to “radicalize” her family and “formally pledged loyalty to ISIS.”
Assistant Attorney-General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said: "Zada supported her sons’ terrorist plot to attack the United States while she enjoyed the privilege of residing here as a resident alien.”

'Death of a Democracy': Exploring the rise and fall of Weimar Germany - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:16:44 UTC
03:16:44 KST

"Berlin has been defiled – shame on a people that considers itself among the world’s civilized.” This was the editorial in the social democratic daily Vorwärts, commenting on a pogrom enacted in the city against the poor emigrant Ostjuden (Galician Jews). This attack took place 10 years before Hitler rose to power.
Victor Sebestyen’s Weimar Germany: Death of a Democracy paints a graphic picture of a liberating republic after the fall of the Hohenzollern monarchy at the end of World War I.
This interesting book tells a familiar story of Berlin, plagued with hyperinflation, antisemitic nationalists, and blinded Stalinists. A place where famous downtown thoroughfares were lined with prostitutes, and cocaine and opium were easy to obtain.
In 1922, a quarter of all German Jews lived in Berlin. A city where homosexuality was quietly accepted despite its legal ban, where literature, films, and music flourished, and where many Jews felt at home.
The period before the machtergreifung – Hitler’s takeover – was known as the “golden years,” when the currency had finally been stabilized in the Weimar Republic under Germany’s first president (1919-1925), the Catholic-born atheist Friedrich Ebert.
It was a Jewish physician, Magnus Hirschfeld, who established here the first LGBT organization in the world.
The Jewish academic Hugo Preuss drafted the constitution for the new republic.
Weimar created a system of democratic representation that had not existed under Kaiser Wilhelm II.
The Wall Street crash of 1929 hit Germany much harder than other countries – and the rest is a history that no Jew can forget.
Hitler's rise to power was not inevitable
The author argues astutely that Hitler was not inevitable. A combination of unprecedented circumstances, moral weakness, political opportunism, and bad luck all played a part.
He tells how Germany by 1916 had become “a silent dictatorship” – a military regime, overseen by Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Friedrich Wilhelm Ludendorff, that preached “final and total victory” in the war against the Allies.
No one – least of all the kaiser – expected a sudden end to the conflict. He blamed the Jews for his eventual abdication.
The war had cost $1.45 trillion in 2025 values. In the summer of 1917, the three democratic parties in the Reichstag had called for a ceasefire in the war.
The generals reacted by forming “the Fatherland Party” and began deflecting responsibility away from themselves. The Jews were blamed for “the stab in the back.”
Already by 1916, Hindenburg and Ludendorff had initiated an inquiry to demonstrate that Jews were underrepresented in the German armed forces. Yet the inquiry proved the opposite: 12,500 German Jews perished in the trenches.
Within weeks of the kaiser’s departure, there was a botched attempt by the Spartacus League to overthrow the republic, led by the Polish-born Jewish revolutionary Rosa Luxemburg.
This was followed by other attempts in which Jews played a prominent part to create a different type of society: Politician, journalist, and revolutionary Kurt Eisner declared a Bavarian Workers and Soldiers Council. The anarchist Gustav Landauer, whose writings influenced Martin Buber, was murdered in Stadelheim prison. German-Russian Communist revolutionary Eugen Leviné headed the second Bavarian Soviet republic.
ALL MET untimely deaths at the hands of the Freikorps, embittered antisemitic nationalists who could not understand why the war had ended so abruptly, why the monarchy had disappeared, and why there had been a challenge to traditional Prussian norms.
Ebert willingly used the Freikorps as well as the army to crush any challenge to the Weimar Republic.
The exhausted returning soldiers proved willing recruits for the Freikorps. The author writes: “Their eyes were hidden in the shadow, thrown by the peaks of their caps, sunk in dark hollows, gray and sharp.”
The Bolsheviks in Soviet Russia desperately hoped that revolution would also break out in industrialized Germany and save them from isolation.
Lenin, however, was in despair at all these failed attempts and berated the German revolutionaries, noting: “when the moment may come to storm the railway stations, they would line up in a queue and buy platform tickets.”
Weimar labeled as 'the Jew republic'
The nationalists called Weimar “the Jew republic” and celebrated when the Jewish foreign minister, Walter Rathenau, was assassinated in 1922. He was accused of being one of 300 “Elders of Zion” bent on world domination.
The author argues that the repeated attempts by the Left to gain power by undemocratic means diverted attention from the threat of the Right.
While Berliners had little sympathy for the attempts to establish a Soviet republic in Germany, they were appalled at the violence and thuggery of the Freikorps.
Albert Einstein was on a Freikorps hit list and, like Rathenau, feared assassination. Nationalists demonstrated outside his home and outside his office at the Prussian Academy of Science.
The Nobel Prize winner Philipp Leonard and his colleague Johannes Stark were brilliant thinkers but devout antisemites. They railed against Einstein and “the Jewish style of physics.”
The Bauhaus ideas of Walter Gropius were regarded as “Bolshevist architecture.” Braided hair was “Aryan”; bobbed hair was “Jewish.”
A DISQUIETING conclusion from this work is that if events had taken another course, any mention of Adolf Hitler would today have gained a mere footnote in a history book.
During the Beer Hall putsch in 1923, Hitler and his followers marched to the center of Munich. They refused to obey police warnings and were then fired on. Max Scheuber-Richter, who had linked arms with Hitler, fell dead.
At Hitler’s subsequent trial, the judge, well-known for his hardline nationalism, allowed the future fuhrer full rein to theatrically perform in the courtroom. He received a six-month jail sentence instead of deportation to his home in Austria.
Stalin directed the German Communists to challenge the social democrats and thereby split the vote at every turn. The split allowed Hindenburg to win the presidency on the second vote in 1925. As a committed monarchist, he was determined to destroy the republic.
Hitler's electoral breakthrough
In the early days, the Nazis could not have advanced without generous financial donations to the party coffers. Hitler was funded by the piano manufacturer Carl Bechstein and the Ruhr steel magnate Fritz Thyssen.
All this allowed Hitler to make an electoral breakthrough due to soaring unemployment. Six million were unemployed by mid-1932. Hitler stood against Hindenburg in the presidential election that year and lost. He claimed that the election had been stolen and continued to do so even after a German court ruled that Hindenburg was indeed the victor.
The Berlin correspondent of the British Daily Mail wrote that he saw Hitler as “a man whose power lies not... in his eloquence and his ability to hold the attention of the crowd but in his convictions.”
The aged Hindenburg similarly came around to “understanding” Hitler. He was egged on by his son, Oskar, by Franz von Papen (German chancellor in 1932 and vice chancellor 1933-1934), by the leader of the monarchist German National People’s Party Alfred Ernst Christian Alexander Hugenberg, and by many political notables, in the belief that they would easily be able to control the Nazi leader.
The story of Germany between 1918 and 1933 is painful to contemplate amid a plethora of what-ifs. What if the police bullet had hit Hitler during the Beer Hall putsch and not the man standing next to him?
Sebestyen has painted a vivid picture of the life and eventual death of Weimar Germany. It is an important and illustrative rendition of the events which defined this transient republic.
As the Austrian writer Peter Drucker noted before escaping to the US: “Fascist ideas spread when people refuse to believe in anything.”■
WEIMAR GERMANY: DEATH OF A DEMOCRACY
By Victor Sebestyen 
Pantheon
480 pages; $35

“The disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the agency said.

Andrei Rublev’s 15th-century ‘Trinity’ icon is reportedly warping after its climate-control chamber broke. A German specialist fixed it once but couldn’t return when it failed again.

Andrei Rublev’s 15th-century ‘Trinity’ icon is reportedly warping after its climate-control chamber broke. A German specialist fixed it once but couldn’t return when it failed again.
The special climate-controlled chamber housing the Trinity icon, which was transferred to the Russian Orthodox Church in 2023, broke down several months ago, Ekho and religious affairs researcher Ksenia Luchenko said, citing sources.
Ekho’s source said a specialist from Germany was called in to repair the chamber. He fixed it, but it broke down again immediately after he left — and they were unable to bring him back “because of difficulties in international relations.”
The icon is now being kept at 80% humidity, although experts insist it should be stored at 50% to 55% humidity.
Ekho said Trinity was painted on three wooden panels. High humidity causes the panels to absorb moisture and swell, narrowing the gaps between them. This warps the icon, effectively “curling into a tube.”
Luchenko’s source said the leadership of the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius “was afraid for some time to tell the Tretyakov Gallery after realizing that the icon was in bad shape.” Luchenko said the icon is now in the monastery’s restoration workshop.
Trinity was housed at the Tretyakov Gallery for nearly 100 years. Russian President Vladimir Putin transferred it to the Russian Orthodox Church by decree in the spring of 2023, after which it was taken to the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius.
Art historians opposed the transfer from the outset, warning that improper storage conditions could damage or destroy the icon.

Unintentional mind wandering disrupts attention in ADHD through two different mechanisms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
18:00:36 UTC
03:00:36 KST

New research suggests that unintentionally losing focus, known as spontaneous mind wandering, predicts distinct aspects of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in adults. The findings indicate that both a general tendency to experience unintentional mind wandering and real-time performance drops during these episodes are linked to higher levels of inattentive and hyperactive traits. The study was published in Journal of Attention Disorders.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsive behaviors that interfere with daily functioning. To understand how attention lapses happen, scientists often look at the default mode network. This is a network of brain regions that typically becomes active during rest or internal thought and tends to decrease in activity when a person engages in a demanding task requiring focus on the outside world.
Mind wandering occurs when a person’s attention shifts away from the task at hand and turns toward internal, unrelated thoughts. Historically, mind wandering was treated as a single concept, but recent evidence suggests it is multidimensional. Deliberate mind wandering is an intentional shift of thought, which can be adaptive for planning, recalling past experiences, or creative problem-solving. Spontaneous mind wandering is an intrusive, unintentional drift of thought that frequently disrupts a person’s ability to complete ongoing tasks.
The distinction between intentional and unintentional focus loss is a growing area of psychological research. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2016 demonstrated that people tend to engage in intentional mind wandering during easy tasks but experience higher levels of unintentional mind wandering during difficult tasks. Another study covered by PsyPost in 2016 proposed that spontaneous thought is linked to reduced activity in cognitive control networks. This provides a theoretical framework for viewing conditions like ADHD as natural extensions of standard variations in spontaneous thinking.
In addition, a 2026 study of adults with ADHD found that a subjective feeling that one’s attention has drifted off task, even without remembering the specific thoughts, is associated with poorer attention and lower well-being. This highlights the complex ways off-task thoughts interfere with daily life.
“Executive function deficits have long been considered a core mechanism underlying the symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), including inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity,” Takehiro Minamoto, an associate professor of psychology at Shimane University, told PsyPost. “However, emerging evidence suggests that spontaneous mind wandering, the unintentional intrusion of task-unrelated thoughts, may also play a critical role in ADHD symptomatology.”
“This raised an important question about how spontaneous mind wandering contributes to ADHD symptoms, prompting us to investigate the underlying mechanisms using methods developed in psychological research,” Minamoto explained. Building on this background, the research team sought to examine how intentional and unintentional mind wandering relate to ADHD symptoms by directly measuring people’s performance during these specific mental states.
The research team recruited 67 university students. Several days before the main experiment, the participants completed self-report questionnaires to measure their ADHD symptoms and their general tendencies to engage in both deliberate and spontaneous mind wandering in daily life. The participants also completed a working memory test to ensure general intellectual ability was accounted for and did not skew the results.
During a later session, the participants completed a modified counting Stroop task on a computer. In this test, participants saw groups of Japanese words that spelled out numbers, but the meaning of the word never matched the actual number of words shown on the screen. For example, the word “four” might be written two times. Participants had to press a keyboard key corresponding to the number of words, ignoring what the text actually said. The task was long and demanding, consisting of 1,152 trials. To prevent participants from guessing or falling into a physical rhythm, the correct response key changed on every single trial.
To track mind wandering, the researchers randomly paused the task 40 times. During these pauses, they presented a prompt asking participants to classify their attention at that exact moment. Participants could report being fully concentrated, engaging in deliberate mind wandering, experiencing spontaneous mind wandering, or dealing with other distractions.
Deliberate mind wandering was defined as thinking of a strategy or intentionally thinking about unrelated things without affecting performance. Spontaneous mind wandering was defined as unintentional thoughts that affected performance or the mind simply wandering off. Eight participants were excluded for various reasons, such as not reporting any mind wandering at all, leaving 59 participants in the final analysis.
The researchers found that participants engaged in deliberate mind wandering more frequently than spontaneous mind wandering. Despite being less frequent, spontaneous mind wandering had a much more negative impact on task performance. When participants reported spontaneous mind wandering, their accuracy was lower, their response times were slower, and their reaction times varied more wildly compared to periods when they reported deliberate mind wandering. The drop in accuracy during spontaneous mind wandering showed a moderate effect size, highlighting a distinct behavioral difference between intentional and unintentional attention shifts.
When looking at ADHD traits, the data indicated that two different measures of spontaneous mind wandering independently predicted higher ADHD symptom scores. First, participants who scored higher on the self-report scale for spontaneous mind wandering in daily life tended to have higher ADHD symptom scores. Second, participants who had poorer real-time accuracy specifically during spontaneous mind wandering episodes in the counting task also tended to have higher ADHD symptom scores. The deliberate mind wandering scale and accuracy during deliberate mind wandering did not predict ADHD scores at all.
Because the self-report scale and the real-time accuracy metric did not overlap in their predictive power, the authors propose that people with ADHD traits might suffer from two different types of interference. The self-report scale captures macroscopic interference, where individuals struggle generally in daily life because they are frequently distracted by unrelated thoughts. The task accuracy metric captures microscopic interference, meaning that when these individuals do experience a spontaneous thought, they have a much harder time coping with the immediate distraction and making the correct decision in the moment.
“Our findings suggest that spontaneous mind wandering may contribute to ADHD symptoms through at least two distinct mechanisms,” Minamoto noted. “One appears to reflect a persistent tendency for task-unrelated thoughts to interfere with attention and self-regulation, while the other reflects momentary disruptions in the ability to switch between mental states and maintain focus.”
“This highlights that attentional difficulties in ADHD may not arise from a single underlying process, but from multiple forms of cognitive interference that affect everyday functioning,” he added.
These results align with research covered by PsyPost in 2022, which found that mind wandering heavily disrupts attention and productivity in children with ADHD, though the new study specifically utilized adult self-reports and real-time cognitive testing rather than childhood classroom observations. The findings are also in line with a 2024 study covered by PsyPost indicating that excessive mind wandering is linked to ADHD symptoms in adults. It is worth noting that the earlier research focused on clinically diagnosed patients rather than a general student sample.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The sample consisted entirely of university students, none of whom had a formal clinical diagnosis of ADHD. While a portion of the participants scored high enough on the symptom scale to warrant clinical evaluation, the results might look different in a formally diagnosed population.
Additionally, the structure of the counting Stroop task required participants to use different fingers to press alternating keys. The physical distance between these keys varied randomly on the keyboard, which might have obscured deeper connections between mind wandering and the raw speed of response times. Future studies could use tasks with simpler motor requirements to better capture how reaction speeds relate to attention lapses. Because the study measured traits at a single point in time, it cannot determine whether spontaneous mind wandering directly causes ADHD symptoms or if the condition leads to a higher frequency of mind wandering.
“Our next step is to conduct further studies to confirm the two potential forms of interference associated with spontaneous mind wandering and to better understand their underlying neural mechanisms,” Minamoto said. “In the long term, we hope this line of research will inform the development of more targeted behavioral, cognitive, and pharmacological interventions to help alleviate the challenges experienced by people with ADHD.”
The study, “Behavioral and Self-Report Measures of Spontaneous Mind Wandering Predict Different Aspects of ADHD in Adults,” was authored by Takehiro Minamoto, Takuma Hayashi, and Md Abdullah Al-Mamun.

Ukraine's missile gap — Kyiv's struggle to close the ballistic divide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
17:51:12 UTC
02:51:12 KST

Ukraine's race for its own ballistic missile
Screenshot from a video showing a test launch of the FP-7 ballistic missile, published on Feb. 27, 2026. (Denys Shtilierman / X)
Incredibly fast and destructive, ballistic missiles have become a key feature of Russia's continuing long-range assault against Ukrainian cities. And while Kyiv has built world-leading drone technology, when it comes to producing ballistic missiles, a key capability in modern warfare, Ukraine still decisively lags behind Russia.
This could soon change, as Kyiv seeks to close the gap by mass-producing its own ballistic missiles, two of which are scheduled to enter service in the coming months.
Fire Point's new FP-7 short-range ballistic missile is due to enter service with the Ukrainian military within "weeks," with the longer-ranged FP-9 "currently undergoing flight tests," according to Fire Point's CEO, Iryna Terekh, speaking at a defense conference in Poland on Sept. 10.
"Ukraine’s new ballistic missiles could have a significant impact on the outcome of the war if they enter service in meaningful numbers," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
A battle of ballistics
Hoffmann said a ballistic missiles would give Ukraine the ability to quickly launch devastating missile strikes against valuable, time-sensitive military targets, such as Russian ballistic missile launchers — a capability Ukraine currently lacks, though one it desperately needs.
Broadly speaking, ballistic missiles fly in high arcs at hypersonic speeds and only a handful of air defense systems can intercept them. Cruise missiles fly significantly slower and lower to the ground, and are generally easier to intercept.
Ukraine relies on American-made Patriot PAC-3 air defense systems to defend itself against ballistic missiles and a chronic shortage of Patriot interceptors has left cities highly vulnerable ahead of winter.
Russia currently produces the munitions at a rate of "about 120 ballistic missiles every month."
Russia currently produces the munitions at a rate of "about 120 ballistic missiles every month", Ukrainian President Zelensky told a NATO-Ukraine Council meeting in Kyiv on June 3, a tempo of production that allows for sustained and deadly missile barrages against Ukrainian cities.
Unfortunately for Ukraine, Russian production of ballistic missiles far outpaces Western production of Patriot ballistic missile interceptors — which Lockheed Martin currently produces at a rate of around 50 per month — let alone Ukraine's ability to acquire the costly and in-demand missiles.
When Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022, Ukraine possessed around 500 OTR-21 Tochka short-range ballistic missiles for around 90 launchers, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), with no ability to produce more. These Soviet-legacy missiles were both limited by range of a maximum of 120 kilometers (75 miles) and were relatively inaccurate compared to modern precision weapons.
In comparison, Russia fielded 900 modern and longer-ranged Iskander-M ballistic missiles in February 2022, according to the IISS, along with significant numbers of Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles, 3M22 Zircon quasiballistic missiles, and a large number of S-300 and S-400 surface-to-air missiles with a secondary land attack role.
By ramping up domestic production, as well as by sourcing supplies of munitions from North Korea, Russia has been able to maintain a stockpile of ballistic missiles while routinely subjecting Ukrainian cities to mass barrages.
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) assessed that by mid-2026, Russian stockpiles still held 130 Iskander ballistic missiles, 400 RM-48U ballistic missiles for the S-400 system, 120 Zircon quasiballistic missiles, 50 Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles, and 50 North Korean ballistic missiles of various types.
In comparison, Ukraine currently has little to no serial domestic ballistic missile production. While President Zelensky claimed Ukraine had "begun using" the 1KR1 Sapsan short-range ballistic missile on Dec. 9, 2025, evidence of it entering widespread production has remained elusive. If the weapon system had indeed entered Ukrainian service, it did so in extremely small numbers.
read also
Limited supplies
With such limited domestic production, Ukraine has relied on foreign allies for an extremely limited supply of replacement ballistic missiles — the American-made ATACMS. Ukraine officially received its first consignment of these older American missiles in October 2023. Unofficial reports suggested Ukraine received between 40 to 50 of the missiles.
Upon arrival, Ukraine immediately put them to use. On Oct. 17, 2023, Ukraine used M39 ATACMS to strike two helicopter forward operating bases in occupied Luhansk and Berdyansk, destroying 14 Russian helicopters, according to a British Defence Intelligence assessment — including eight Ka-52 attack helicopters — approximately 11% of Russia's entire fleet of that type.
Ukraine had to use its small stockpile of ATACMS sparingly, as opportunities to replenish stocks were extremely limited. The most significant replenishment came in August 2026, when Ukraine signed an agreement to purchase 70 M39 ATACMS missiles from Turkey as part of a wider arms deal.
This reliance on external supply from often unreliable foreign partners has created a key strategic vulnerability Ukraine has sought to address with domestic ballistic missile production. As part of this, leading Ukrainian defense company Fire Point spent 150 million euros to construct a solid rocket fuel plant in Denmark to support the development of Ukraine's new FP-7 and FP-9 missiles.
Ukraine's ballistic hopefuls
Fire Point has become an important domestic defense manufacturer since its founding in 2022, manufacturing a series of highly effective long-range drones, yet corruption allegations and questions about the ultimate ownership of the company have accompanied its rise.
Despite the allegations, Fire Point's FP-1 long-range drone has become a key part of Ukraine's deep strike campaign, while the FP-2 medium-range drone — which sacrifices range for a larger warhead — has become a mainstay of Ukraine's increasingly successful mid-range strike campaign.
"The development of Ukraine's drone program has demonstrated that, with sufficient funding and prioritization, significant results can be achieved in the production of long-range weapons," Nazarii Barchuk, an analyst at the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, told the Kyiv Independent, while noting that "ballistic missiles are a more complex type of weapon to manufacture."
Barchuk believes the critical factor will be ensuring "adequate funding for the program," including investment from foreign partners, as well as the "preservation and expansion of component production chains."
Although Ukraine's various domestic long-range drone programs have matured into a successful capability that frequently inflicts severe damage on Russian military and economic infrastructure, they have been less able to deal with more mobile military targets. Russian forces have frequently mitigated the damage of Ukrainian drone raids against military airfields by flying valuable aircraft away from incoming slow-flying drones.
read also
A learning curve
Fire Point also manufactures the FP-5 Flamingo heavy cruise missile, and while the first few operational uses saw the missiles fall short of their intended targets, recent Flamingo launches have been far more successful. In June 2026, three of the large cruise missiles struck the Titan-Barrikady manufacturing plant in Volgograd, damaging the facility.
"The Flamingo was fairly inaccurate in the beginning," Hoffmann told the Kyiv Independent, explaining that Fire Point has since modified and upgraded its missile.
"The FP-5 Flamingo is now operationally more useful and I could see the same process taking place with the FP-7 and the FP-9," Hoffmann said.
The new FP-7 ballistic missile is designed with a claimed range of 200 kilometers (124 miles), a top speed of 1,500 meters per second (3,355 mph), and a 150-kilogram warhead. The missile is based on the Soviet-era 48N6 interceptor used in the S-300 and S-400 air defense systems, but uses modern components and manufacturing techniques.
"This will be an analog of ATACMS, probably even with a larger warhead. But it will cost at least twice as little," Denys Shtilerman, chief designer and co-founder of Fire Point, said in an interview in March. Shtilerman emphasized the goal was to produce the system en masse. "If you produce two or three ballistic missiles a month, it makes no sense. It will not affect the front," he said.
read also
Likely targets
"There will be different targets for each type of missile," Barchuk told the Kyiv Independent. "The FP-7 is designed for targets at the front line and in the immediate rear, such as headquarters and command posts, weapons storage facilities, military equipment (radar stations, electronic warfare systems, air defense systems, and missile launchers), drone launch sites and military infrastructure, including airfields within the missile’s range," he said.
The larger and more complex FP-9 is due to enter service "by the end of the year," according to Terekh.
The FP-9 is a significantly larger, faster, and longer-ranged missile, with a range of 855 kilometers (531 miles), a top speed of 2,200 meters per second (4,920 mph), and the ability to carry an 800-kilogram warhead.
Besides enabling strikes on a huge number of military facilities and important industrial sites, the missile also puts Moscow, as well as other Russian cities, within range.
"If Ukraine is able to mass produce around 50 FP-9 missiles per month, and if they're reasonably accurate so they can go after high-value military assets, as well as larger infrastructure targets, then it's going to get much more uncomfortable for the Russians," Hoffmann told the Kyiv Independent. "That would be really significant, I would say, but we have to get there first."
"The FP-9 has a longer range and a larger warhead," Barchuk said. "This missile is intended to strike targets deep in the rear, specifically on Russian territory. Their targets may vary, but priority is likely to be given to military-industrial facilities, protected weapons arsenals, critical communications nodes (including satellite communications), military installations and airfields from which Russian tactical aircraft take off to carry out strikes against Ukraine," he said.
The successful introduction of the FP-9 could be a significant upgrade of Ukraine's capabilities, Hoffmann said. "Within minutes you could strike, 600, 700, 800 kilometers deep into Russia, which could make ballistic missile launcher hunting or air defense suppression and destruction a lot more successful."

Adel Abdelrheem and Mohammad Sio

Nearly 100,000 people have been displaced in Sudan’s southeastern Blue Nile state since January amid escalating fighting between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Sunday.
The IOM said an estimated 99,277 people, representing 19,497 families, were displaced from different parts of Blue Nile state between Jan. 11 and Aug. 23, 2026.
The figure represents a 66% increase from the agency’s previous update on May 21, when 59,742 displaced people were recorded.
Nearly half of those displaced, or 47%, are children under the age of 18, the agency said.
The IOM said 39,570 people were displaced from Geissan locality, 32,515 from Kurmuk and 27,192 from Bau.
The displaced population moved to seven locations across Blue Nile state, including Damazin, which received 45,740 people, and Geissan, which received 15,735.
The agency said 58% of the displaced are staying at informal gathering sites, while 9% are living with host families and 33% are sheltering in schools and other public buildings.
Blue Nile state has seen intensified fighting in recent days amid attacks by the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, on several areas.
Sudan’s humanitarian crisis has continued to worsen since fighting erupted between the army and the RSF in April 2023 over disagreements related to the integration of the paramilitary force into the military.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

German lawmaker Robin Wagener also said he had been traveling by train on the same line hit by a Russian drone attack near the Polish border, warning that Russia was an “immense danger to Europe’s security.”
‘Chance decided survival’
In a social media post, the Green lawmaker said he had just come from Kiev, where air defence fire and drone attacks were more intense than on previous visits. “And this morning I traveled by train on the same route where this attack happened,” he wrote, sharing a video of the strike. “Sometimes chance decides whether you get through safely — after Russian terrorists have already decided on the attack.”
“Russia is an immense danger to Europe’s security. Too many of us have still not realised that,” Wagener wrote. “Our support for Ukraine in defending against it is still too hesitant.”
In the German parliament, Wagener serves on the Foreign Affairs and European Affairs Committees and is the Green group’s spokesperson on Eastern Europe. He also chairs the German-Ukrainian parliamentary friendship group.
Der Spiegel reported that the special train was later stopped over a drone threat and partly evacuated after strikes in the area. Guenter Sautter, one of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s closest advisers, was among those on board.
The security measure followed an attack on the same railway line. Early Sunday, a drone struck a passenger train traveling from Kiev to Warsaw near the Polish border. The operator said the locomotive was hit. No one was injured.
Sautter, a foreign and security policy adviser at the Chancellery, had been in Kiev with security advisers from Britain, France and Italy for talks with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s government on possible peace negotiations with Russia. He also attended the Yalta European Strategy conference on Saturday.

Sobh-e-No: BRICS; from potential cooperation to operational implementation
Sobh-e-No analyzed President Pezeshkian’s trip to New Delhi for the BRICS summit. The visit has two main dimensions. First, bilateral relations between Iran and India. Javan discussed the recent understanding reached between Tehran and Muscat, with Persian Gulf foreign ministers present. According to the paper, the agreement is strictly technical, concerning the details of new entry and exit routes in the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman. Other Persian Gulf states are attending the meeting only to signal their implicit non‑objection to the international community. Javan emphasizes that this understanding does not mean the Strait of Hormuz will reopen. Iran has delivered seven conditions to the United States through intermediaries. These conditions have been approved by Iran’s highest authorities, and until they are fully implemented, the strait will remain closed. Thus, the Iran–Oman agreement does not signify reopening; rather, it establishes that if the strait is eventually reopened, it will be done under this specific framework, which the paper describes as a major step in asserting Iran’s sovereignty. Any reopening depends entirely on US compliance with Iran’s conditions.
Ham‑Mihan: Why has Iran’s nuclear file returned to the UN Security Council?
Ham‑Mihan explains that Western governments are trying to move Iran’s nuclear issue from the IAEA Board of Governors back to the UN Security Council to create a “two‑track process.” Track One is the JCPOA & Snapback Mechanism. This track is based on alleged Iranian violations of the JCPOA. However, China and Russia opposed this path in the Security Council, preventing it from gaining full legal legitimacy. Track Two is Safeguards Non‑Compliance Referral. This new track focuses on alleged Iranian non‑compliance with its IAEA safeguards agreement. The key difference of the second track is that because in the Board of Governors, there is no veto, so a resolution can be passed and the case referred to the Security Council. Once referred, China and Russia cannot easily dismiss the IAEA’s findings and will face a more difficult diplomatic position. Ham‑Mihan argues that the Western goal is for these two tracks to reinforce each other, increasing pressure on Iran.
