Former hostage Omer Shem Tov recalls loneliness, hunger, abuse during Hamas captivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:23:58 UTC
23:23:58 KST

Former hostage Omer Shem Tov described the prolonged loneliness, intense hunger, and physical abuse he endured during 505 days in Hamas captivity, as well as his life after release, in a wide-ranging interview with Maariv last week.
Shem Tov was abducted from the Nova music festival on October 7, 2023, and held in Gaza for 505 days before being released in February 2025. His comments came following the launch of his first book, Meeting Myself in Hell, which was published last month and reveals details of his 16 months of captivity.
“For me, loneliness was the hardest thing,” Shem Tov said in the interview. He noted, though, that there were difficult aspects of his captivity, including abuse at the hands of the terrorists who held him, that he has not spoken about.
At first, Shem Tov recounted, he was held together with Itay Regev, who, along with his sister Maya, was released during the November 2023 hostage-prisoner exchanges.
“When they separated us, it was one of the hardest moments of captivity, because by then we had grown accustomed to sharing the hardship, hunger and fear together,” Shem Tov said. “I think the period alone after being separated from Itay was one of the hardest periods of captivity.”
Omer Shem Tov’s 50 days of cramped darkness in Gaza
The time following Regev’s release made up the bulk of Shem Tov’s captivity. During this time, he recounted, he spent 50 days isolated and in complete darkness in a cell so small that he could not stand upright.
“In the first few days, it suffocated me. I couldn’t breathe because of the anxiety,” he said. “Slowly, I got used to the darkness. I started imagining things, shapes. My imagination developed tremendously during that period.”
At one point, he said, a small flashlight fell from a terrorist’s pocket. Shem Tov hid it and would switch it on briefly each day “to check that my eye could still see.”
After his release, he said he realized that he sometimes missed “the absolute darkness,” because despite his suffering at the time, it was also when he felt “most connected to myself and to God.”
Hunger was another challenge.
“We were very hungry, because we got very little bread — half a pita, sometimes less. A little canned meat,” he recalled. “We talked about meat. We dreamed about meat.”
This was exacerbated at times, he added, when, while hungry, he could smell Gazans cooking food nearby.
“Sometimes they would grill behind the room where we were being held. We would smell the kebab and hear the voices of the women and children,” he said. “I would tell Itay to smell the smoke so the smell would remind us of the taste of meat.”
Shem Tov added that they would pretend that the bits of food they received were actually meat.
“We would bite into the pita, close our eyes, and imagine it was meat. A bite of pita — chicken thigh. A bite of pita — kebab. A bite of pita — shishlik.”
He also spoke briefly about some of the physical abuse he received, including one incident in which a terrorist beat him after telling him that his friend had been killed.
“I remember that one day, when I was in a tunnel, a terrorist came in and told me, ‘Today you killed my best friend,’” he said. “I immediately told him I was very sorry, but he picked up a broomstick and started hitting me extremely hard on the legs.”
Shem Tov was ultimately released alongside Eliya Cohen and Omer Wenkert in February 2025.
Before his transfer to the Red Cross, however, Hamas forced the three men to participate in a staged release ceremony. Shem Tov said that minutes beforehand, one of the terrorists instructed him to kiss the head of Sabai Abu Hasna, one of the terrorists who had taken part in holding him captive and who was standing beside him on stage.
Shem Tov initially refused, but said he feared angering his captors with freedom so close.
“Suddenly I told myself, fine, I’ll kiss him on the head, I’ll go home, he’ll stay there, and that’s it,” he recalled.
After reaching the Re’im base and reuniting with his parents, Shem Tov said one of the first things he told them was that he was ashamed of what he had done and feared Israelis would think he was a “traitor.”
He only understood later, after meeting members of the public, that people recognized he had been coerced.
Abu Hasna, a member of Hamas’s Nukhba unit, was later killed by the IDF and Shin Bet in June of this year in northern Gaza.
After getting a call from the Shin Bet informing him of Abu Hasna’s death, Shem Tov said he was glad, “because he was an evil person who caused me a great deal of suffering and did other terrible things,” but that, for him, it wasn’t life-changing.
“I think that from the moment I left him and was transferred by the Red Cross to the IDF, I left him and his evil behind,” Shem Tov said.
Still, he said, his freedom didn’t bring him immediate peace.
Shem Tov said captivity continues to intrude on his life, with certain things triggering intense emotional responses.
He said the sounds of fighter jets, fireworks, and loud explosions can trigger memories of Gaza. Sometimes, seeing someone who resembles one of the terrorists who held him can also throw him back into his experiences there.
At the same time, he has resisted allowing captivity to define his identity.
Since his release, Shem Tov has traveled, lectured, and studied. Recently, he completed an acting course in New York and published his book.
He said he initially rejected the idea of writing the book because he did not want his identity to be defined by having been a hostage, but ultimately decided his experience could offer others “tools and guidance, light and hope” in confronting their own crises.
At the same time, he said, he feels deep gratitude for the soldiers who fought for Israel.
“It bothers me when people tell me I’m a hero,” Shem Tov said. “I don’t think I’m a hero. This was a reality that was forced on me. The soldiers are heroes, the reservists, everyone who fought for me at home is a hero.”

Hegseth, Pentagon pressured F-15 crew to appear in '60 Minutes' Iran rescue story, CNN reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:23:58 UTC
23:23:58 KST

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and political officials in his office pressured two crew members from an F-15 jet shot down over Iran in April to participate in a special 60 Minutes episode on CBS about their rescue operation, CNN reported on Sunday.
The two crew members were initially reluctant to be interviewed. One of them reportedly raised concerns that he could be ordered to take part in the program, while military officials expressed concern that the interview could expose classified details about the rescue operation while fighting with Iran was still ongoing.
Two sources told CNN that political officials in Hegseth's office initially insisted that both crew members participate in the interview.
After the two expressed their reservations, Hegseth met with them privately and asked whether they wanted to participate rather than forcing them to appear on the program. Following the meeting, one crew member, identified in the report by the nickname "Bravo," agreed to appear on camera and discuss his experience. The second, identified as "Alpha," decided not to take part.
Concerns over Hegseth's security and political messaging
The episode went beyond a routine dispute over a television interview, CNN said. The network described the affair as an example of how Hegseth's office has sought to shape the public narrative surrounding the war with Iran, which CNN reported has become less popular among the public and has increased pressure on the defense secretary to highlight successes and declare achievements.
The report said Hegseth was unusually involved in the production details of the segment, far more than is customary for a US defense secretary. He and his staff were eager to present a dramatic reconstruction of the incident on 60 Minutes, particularly the rescue operation.
The event provided material for a television feature almost on its own. The F-15 pilot was located within hours after the aircraft was shot down by Iranian forces. The second crew member, a weapons systems officer, spent more than a day evading approaching Iranian forces. At one point, he climbed through difficult terrain to a ridge about 7,000 feet high, carrying mainly a pistol, communications equipment, and a locator beacon.
He was eventually rescued by a US commando force, while American aircraft bombed targets in the area to enable the extraction. Despite experiencing the longer and more dramatic ordeal, the weapons systems officer was the one who ultimately agreed to be interviewed, while the pilot declined.
CNN reported that military officials were concerned not only about the pressure placed on the crew members, but also about the possibility that the White House and the Pentagon would use the soldiers' heroism and the rescue operation for political purposes. Two sources told the network that military personnel feared the segment was intended to turn the successful rescue into a public relations tool for Hegseth and the Trump administration.
Pentagon rejects CNN account
Security concerns were another factor. Military officials feared that a detailed account of the rescue mission could expose methods and tactics to Iran while the war was still underway. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine was involved in some of the discussions over the possibility that the program could unintentionally reveal military tactics to an adversary. Despite those concerns, he decided to participate in the program.
The Pentagon rejected CNN's account entirely.
"This entire story is completely false." The department's chief spokesman, Sean Parnell, said.
"The decision to participate in the interview was solely up to each of the pilots, because this is their story."
Parnell said one crew member decided to participate while the other did not, adding that the Pentagon took precautions to protect operational security, sources, and methods.
CBS also conducted an intensive effort to secure the interview. CNN reported that executive producer Bari Weiss considered access to the crew members one of the network's top priorities and personally contacted Hegseth to secure exclusive access for CBS. She also approached additional officials in the Trump administration.
The segment took on particular importance for 60 Minutes ahead of the launch of its new season, after months of internal turmoil at the network. The interview was approved only in mid-July and filmed in mid-August.
Within the Pentagon, Tammy Radabaugh, who previously worked as Hegseth's producer at Fox News and moved with him to the Defense Department as a senior adviser, played a significant role in coordinating the appearance. Hegseth himself had previously given a rare interview to the program.
In a CBS promo, "Bravo" is seen sitting across from correspondent and morning show host Norah O'Donnell, who asks him: "Did you ever doubt that the US military was going to come rescue you?"
The full interview is scheduled to air Sunday night in the US. Before it was broadcast, however, it had already become part of a broader debate in Washington over where the line lies between presenting military heroism to the public and using a dramatic rescue operation as a tool in the battle for public opinion surrounding the war with Iran.

How can BRICS help Iran’s trade get past sanctions, dollar?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:18:32 UTC
23:18:32 KST

How can BRICS help Iran’s trade get past sanctions, dollar?
TEHRAN- For Iran, BRICS is not merely an economic pact; it is a large market and a set of financial, commercial, and transit routes that, if their capacities are activated, can open a new chapter in the country’s foreign trade.
According to Mehr News Agency, Iran attends the BRICS summit in India at a time when the group has become one of the most important centers of Global South trade. According to the UN Conference on Trade and Development, BRICS members’ merchandise exports reached about $6 trillion in 2024 and their imports about $5 trillion, while intra-group trade rose to about $1.2 trillion.
These figures show that for Iran, BRICS is not merely a political coalition; rather, it encompasses a set of major consumer, producer, energy-exporting economies and capital-market owners. Iran also became a full member of the group in 2024, alongside China, India, Russia, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Brazil, and South Africa.
* Iran’s trade with BRICS; a number more important than membership itself
The reality is that even before its official membership, Iran conducted a significant portion of its foreign trade with BRICS member states. Data published in the BRICS economic bulletin show that Iran’s customs exports to BRICS countries reached about $23.7 billion in the Iranian year 1403 (ended in March 2025) while Iran’s imports from these countries in the same period were about $38.8 billion.
Thus, Iran’s trade with BRICS, before being a potential opportunity, is already an important part of the country’s foreign trade reality. The main question begins here: to what extent can Iran’s membership in this group change the quality of this trade?
The challenge of Iran’s trade with BRICS member states is not merely finding a buyer or seller; in many cases, the main problem goes back to money transfers, transaction costs, insurance, transportation, banking restrictions, and sanctions risk.
From this perspective, the importance of BRICS’s financial track for Iran is no less than increasing trade volume itself.
One of the most important economic topics at this year’s BRICS summit was developing payment mechanisms and reducing friction in exchanges among members. India, as BRICS chair in 2026, is now pursuing a proposal to connect the central bank digital currencies of the group’s members to facilitate cross-border payments. This plan continues BRICS efforts to increase interoperability of members’ payment systems.
For Iran, the importance of this issue is clear. Any mechanism that can reduce the cost and time of foreign trade settlement can directly affect the possibility of expanding exports and imports.
Of course, this path still faces serious obstacles. Reuters has reported that geopolitical disagreements among members and even the severing of financial relations between Iran and the UAE, along with the need for currency swap mechanisms to manage trade imbalances, have made implementing such plans difficult.
Therefore, expectations from BRICS should not be the creation of a “common currency” or the overnight elimination of the dollar; rather, in the short term, reducing settlement costs, greater use of local currencies, and connecting payment systems can be a more practical achievement for members’ trade.
Expectations from BRICS should not be the creation of a “common currency” or the overnight elimination of the dollar; rather, in the short term, reducing settlement costs, greater use of local currencies, and connecting payment systems can be a more practical achievement for members’ trade.
Among BRICS members, China remains Iran’s most important trading partner. World Trade Organization data show that in 2024, China accounted for 26 percent of Iran’s imports and 26 percent of Iran’s exports.
But this high concentration has another side; if BRICS is to become a tool for diversifying Iran’s foreign trade, merely increasing exchanges with China is not enough.
India, Russia, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and other members of the group each have different markets and capacities, and expanding trade with them can reduce the excessive concentration of Iran’s trade on a few limited partners.
Of course, India’s situation is different from China’s. Trade between Iran and India in recent years has been limited under the influence of sanctions and secondary pressure from the United States, and bilateral trade, compared with the capacity of the two economies, is far below the expected level. Reuters, in an August report, also reported a decline in India-Iran trade under US pressure and described India’s trade with Iran as mainly limited to certain food and pharmaceutical items.
From this perspective, Iran’s presence at the India summit was an opportunity to redefine this very trade relationship—not only at the Tehran–Delhi level, but within the broader BRICS framework.
* Iran can turn from a “Market” into a “Trade Route”
Iran’s capacity within BRICS is not limited to goods exports. The country’s geographical position, especially in connecting Russia and northern Eurasia to southern waters and the Indian market, is another important advantage.
Before the trip to India, too, the economy minister had described strengthening the North–South Corridor, along with developing financial and trade cooperation with Russia, as among the axes of the government’s economic diplomacy.
The Mehr reporter’s conversation with economic actors confirmed this point: this issue is particularly important from a trade perspective, because if Iran can simultaneously be a producer, exporter, and transit route, the economic value of BRICS membership for the country will multiply.
If Iran can simultaneously be a producer, exporter, and transit route, the economic value of BRICS membership for the country will multiply.
According to economic actors, in such a model, goods are not only exported from Iran to a BRICS member state; rather, part of the trade among BRICS members can also pass through Iran.
The North–South Corridor gains particular importance here, because India, as one of BRICS’s major economies, needs diverse routes to access the Russian and Eurasian markets, and Iran enjoys a privileged geographical position in this regard.
Despite all these capacities, one reality should not be overlooked: BRICS membership does not by itself create trade.
The experience of other members also shows that even trade among BRICS countries, despite notable growth, faces structural obstacles; for example, India’s trade with BRICS has grown in recent years, but India’s trade deficit with the group reached about $226 billion in fiscal year 2026—a matter showing that increased trade does not necessarily mean balanced trade or equal benefits for members.
Economic actors believe that for Iran, too, the issue is not only increasing the trade figure; rather, it must be seen what effect this trade will have on non-oil exports, imports of raw materials and machinery, investment, technology transfer, and foreign exchange income.
In this framework, if BRICS merely leads to an increase in Iran’s imports from member states, it cannot be considered a trade success. The main goal should be creating greater balance, increasing exports with higher added value, and attracting capital for export-oriented production.
If BRICS merely leads to an increase in Iran’s imports from member states, it cannot be considered a trade success. The main goal should be creating greater balance, increasing exports with higher added value, and attracting capital for export-oriented production.
Iran’s presence at this year’s BRICS summit came as the global economic atmosphere is more than ever affected by sanctions, trade war, financial restrictions, and disruption of transportation routes.
At the same time, the Iran–US war and developments in the Strait of Hormuz have confronted BRICS itself with an unprecedented test. Reuters has reported that the current crisis has even affected trade relations between two BRICS members, Iran and the UAE, and that the UAE has halted trade with Iran since August.
This development makes one important point clear to Iran: BRICS is not yet a free trade area or an integrated economic union. Its members have different and sometimes conflicting interests, and it cannot be expected that mere membership in this group will remove Iran’s trade restrictions.
But this very reality makes the importance of Iran’s economic negotiations within this framework greater.
If Iran can use BRICS’s capacity to create payment routes, use local currencies, finance projects, develop transit corridors, and expand trade agreements, membership in this group can turn from a diplomatic achievement into a real tool of foreign trade.
Otherwise, despite BRICS’s multi-trillion-dollar market, an important part of the capacity of this membership will remain on paper.
Therefore, merely being large cannot by itself help improve Iran’s trade process; rather, it must be seen what share of this bloc’s trade Iran can obtain and, more importantly, through what mechanism it can move the money generated by this trade, and even more importantly, that BRICS moves from the level of political statements to the level of contracts, payments, investment, and the real flow of goods.

‘The best friend in the world’: Loved ones mourn police commando after deadly diving accident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:16:23 UTC
23:16:23 KST

Relatives, friends and acquaintances gathered over the holiday at the Haifa home of 23-year-old Itai Parson, an officer in Yamam, Israel Police’s elite counterterrorism unit, who drowned while diving off the northern city last week. His body was found Saturday after an intensive three-day search.
“Itai was the best friend in the world — always smiling, devoted, gifted and, above all, the person who always gave good advice and helped,” his friends told Ynet. “His death is impossible to comprehend. We are shocked and still can’t process this tragedy.”
Parson’s funeral is expected to be held Monday at Haifa’s military cemetery.
At the family home, his parents were joined by his siblings and Parson’s longtime girlfriend, Nicole, who attended Haifa’s Hebrew Reali School with him. His mother, Rona Parson, is a Haifa Magistrate’s Court judge, while his father, Alex, is a dentist. His brother Yair returned from a trip to Thailand following the tragedy. Parson is also survived by his brother Yoav and two younger sisters.
Parson went freediving Thursday at Student Beach in Haifa. A relative accompanied him on a kayak and remained about 1.3 kilometers (0.8 miles) offshore while Parson entered the water. When he failed to return, the relative alerted rescue services.
His body was found Saturday on the seabed about 800 meters (half a mile) from shore. The circumstances that led to his drowning remain unclear.
The discovery ended a massive three-day search involving hundreds of police officers, rescue workers, military personnel and volunteers. Authorities deployed drones, a police helicopter, light aircraft, boats, jet skis and other equipment.
The Navy joined the operation, deploying personnel from Shayetet 13, its elite naval commando unit, and Yaltam, the Navy’s specialized underwater missions unit. Parson had been freediving without breathing equipment. Border Police, marine police, canine and mounted units, firefighters, volunteer divers, lifeguards and several Israeli emergency and rescue organizations also took part.
“From the moment the report was received, Israel Police deployed hundreds of officers, fighters and volunteers who worked without interruption day and night, at sea, in the air and along the coastline,” Carmel District Commander Brig. Gen. Boaz Samucha said after Parson was found.
From pilot training to an elite police unit
Parson enlisted in the IDF in January 2023 and initially entered the Air Force’s prestigious pilot training course. He later transferred to the Border Police, where he served in an undercover combat unit.
Police said Parson transferred to compulsory service in the Border Police in August 2023, completed combat training and entered a specialized undercover training track. After completing his military service, he joined Yamam as a career officer in December 2025, serving on its observation and drone team.
He would have celebrated his 24th birthday in three months and had been expected to leave police service later.
Friends described Parson as charismatic, talented and striking, with a memorable sense of humor and an appetite for challenges.
“He loved challenges and took part in ‘Ninja Israel’ a few years ago,” they said, referring to the Israeli version of the obstacle-course television competition “Ninja Warrior.” “He injured his shoulder there. He didn’t talk much about his service in the military and police, but we knew he was one of the best and most talented in the group.”
Riki Rosenthal, who was Parson’s homeroom teacher during his three years at the Hebrew Reali School’s Beit Biram high school campus, remembered him as an exceptional student with a deep attachment to those closest to him.
“He was a people person, with a warm smile, handsome, sensitive and empathetic,” Rosenthal said. “He loved challenges, but he was levelheaded, thoughtful and goal-oriented, and he excelled in his studies.”
“He was very close to his parents, his sisters, his brothers and Nicole,” she added. “It is an enormous tragedy that the heart refuses to comprehend. The Reali School family shares in the profound grief of his family and friends.”
The school also mourned its 2022 graduate in a Facebook post, saying it had learned “with great sorrow and grief” of the death of Yamam officer Master Sgt. Itai Parson in a diving accident.
Haifa Mayor Yona Yahav offered condolences to the family, saying the entire city was mourning with them.
“Our hearts broke upon receiving the terrible news,” Yahav wrote on Facebook. “At this painful hour, all of Haifa embraces his parents, brothers and sisters, his partner, his friends and everyone who loved him.”
“On behalf of the city of Haifa and its residents, I send the Parson family our deepest condolences and the embrace of an entire city,” he added. “May Itai’s memory be a blessing.”

Sudan famine fears grow as hunger grips West Kordofan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:06:13 UTC
23:06:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan famine fears grow as hunger grips West Kordofan
Fears of famine are growing across Sudan's West Kordofan state, where local aid workers have warned that worsening hunger, failed harvests and the continuing war are pushing communities towards catastrophe.
The Dar Hamar Emergency Room, an informal volunteer-led aid group, warned on Saturday that an "imminent famine" threatened six localities in West Kordofan following poor rainfall, damaged harvests and soaring food prices.
The group said conditions had deteriorated sharply across areas largely controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), with widespread looting and the destruction of livelihoods exacerbating the food crisis, according to Sudan Tribune.
The warning comes just days after reports that families in the town of Al-Odaya had resorted to eating umbaz, the residue left after oilseeds are pressed and normally used as animal feed, because of severe food shortages.
The Dar Hamar Emergency Room said residents were also facing disrupted transport, shortages of medicines and an outbreak of cholera, compounding the effects of malnutrition.
The latest warning adds West Kordofan to other areas of Sudan affected by severe hunger.
The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) has warned of a credible risk of famine through January in seven areas of North Darfur, as well as Dilling and Kadugli in South Kordofan.
The organisation said worsening conflict or renewed sieges, combined with marginal or almost non-existent crop production, could push affected communities into famine conditions.
Sudan's annual harvest season normally begins in October and runs until the end of the year, typically increasing food availability and helping reduce market prices.
However, more than three years of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF has devastated agricultural production and disrupted markets and humanitarian access across large parts of the country.
The World Food Programme says it is currently reaching more than four million people each month, including around 825,000 people in Kordofan, but has warned that a huge gap remains between humanitarian needs and available resources.
The deepening hunger crisis comes as weapons become increasingly available throughout Sudan despite international attempts to curb the flow of arms into the conflict.
Sudanese authorities said on Saturday that customs and intelligence forces had intercepted a cache of weapons and military equipment being smuggled along the Red Sea coast.
Sudan's Customs Police said the seizure, in the south of Red Sea State, included a Kornet anti-tank missile launcher, 595 empty Kalashnikov magazines and another 595 G4 magazines, as well as 15 US-made pistols and three Brazilian-made pistols.
The operation was carried out jointly by the state's anti-smuggling department and Sudan's General Intelligence Service.
Authorities did not identify the origin of the shipment or its intended recipient, and did not announce any arrests in connection with the seizure.
Sudan has been engulfed in war since April 2023, when tensions between army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and his former deputy, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into open conflict.
The fighting has since displaced millions of people and created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises, with famine or the risk of famine affecting communities across several regions of the country.

Former Czech FM: Europe must stop believing it can reach deal with Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

Former Czech FM: Europe must stop believing it can reach deal with Putin
Czech MP and former Foreign Minister Jan Lipavský wrote this on X while returning from Kyiv, where he attended the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference, according to Ukrinform.
“Russia is mobilizing hundreds of thousands of people, producing thousands of drones, missiles and munitions, and preparing for a prolonged war. Meanwhile, in Europe, we keep telling ourselves that somehow we can reach a deal with Putin. But there will be no peace if we want it more than Putin does. We must also consider that one day hundreds of thousands of Russian soldiers, thousands of drones and hundreds of missiles could be turned not against Ukraine, but against another European country. Ukraine is showing us today what that would mean,” the politician said.
Lipavský, who has visited Ukraine several times since 2022, noted that despite their exhaustion, Ukrainians have no intention of giving up their freedoms and continue to fight.
He stressed that Europe must prepare by strengthening its air and missile defenses, counter-drone capabilities, civil protection and ability to withstand mass attacks.
“We need to get rid of the Russian fifth column. We need to gain the upper hand in the information war. We need to prevent Russian sabotage,” Lipavský added.
He also said that the Czech Republic and Europe need Ukraine as an ally with valuable lessons to offer: Ukrainians have wartime experience that no one else in Europe currently possesses, including in countering drones, protecting energy and critical infrastructure, and keeping the state functioning under daily attacks.
“We must bring this experience into the Czech army, Czech companies and our civil protection system. Our soldiers should go to Ukraine, while Ukrainian soldiers should come to us. Our companies should develop and produce weapons together with Ukrainian companies. We should jointly test technologies against drones and missiles. We should participate in European air and missile defense projects. And we must start supplying weapons to Ukraine again: ammunition, aircraft, missiles, drones and everything that can genuinely help it stop the Russian war machine before it can be turned against someone else. If our L-159s can help Ukraine counter Russian drones, we must find a way to get them there,” Lipavský stressed.
He believes that helping Ukraine and protecting the Czech Republic are one and the same thing: every Russian drone shot down over Ukraine is a drone that will never fly anywhere else, while every Russian tank destroyed is a tank that will not appear on another European border. Every lesson learned through cooperation with Ukrainians could one day save European lives.
“Putin will not be stopped by our desire for peace. He will be stopped by the conviction that he cannot win another war,” the MP wrote.
Lipavský spent the past four days in Kyiv, where, in addition to attending the Conference, he held numerous meetings.
As reported, the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference was held in Kyiv on September 11–12, 2026, under the slogan “Peace Through Strength NOW.” The event, organized by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation, brought together 700 leading politicians, diplomats, businesspeople, Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel, veterans, civil society activists and experts from 28 countries.

Mohamed Al Fayed abuse compensation claims could reach £150m, says law firm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:03:43 UTC
23:03:43 KST

Compensation claims by 275 survivors of alleged sexual abuse by the former owner of Harrods Mohamed Al Fayed could reach between £100m and £150m, according to a law firm representing the women.
The combined value of their claims, calculated by KP Law (KPL), which represents more than half of known survivors, is around two to three times greater than the amount the luxury department store has set aside for all abuse payouts.
This suggests that Harrods and the late billionaire’s estate together could face a combined compensation bill of more than £200m.
Harrods’ latest annual report, published in August, showed it had paid out only £4.1m from the £57m it set aside for compensation in 2025, excluding legal and administration costs. The accounts also showed that the retailer reduced the amount set aside by £1.1m, leaving a compensation pot worth £51.8m in January 2026.
Lucy Traynor, a senior associate at KPL, said Harrods’ own compensation scheme, which stopped accepting claims on 31 March, was “not fit for purpose” and underestimated the impact of the alleged abuse on survivors’ lives and careers.
She added: “The evidence available to us indicates that the average value of the claims being pursued is likely to be hundreds of thousand pounds higher than the apparent average payment under the Harrods scheme. We’re seeing figures in the millions for [a client’s] loss of earnings and future loss of earnings.”
Harrods said it had made settlements with 113 women through its redress scheme to date. The store did not clarify how many settlements were covered by the £4.1m paid out last year, but noted that more than 50 were made by mid-February this year.
Traynor said this suggested that the average payout to survivors under the redress scheme would be approximately £82,000. “As Harrods say that payments were made to more than 50 survivors, the actual average would be lower still,” she added.
This estimate is also significantly lower than the maximum payout of £385,000 under the Harrods scheme, which includes general damages of up to £200,000 and a work impact payment of up to £150,000, as well as payments for treatment costs and “wrongful” medical tests for sexually transmitted diseases.
A Harrods spokesperson said the store did not “provide ongoing commentary on settlement values”, but that it was “committed to ensuring all eligible survivors receive compensation for the appalling abuse they suffered”.
More than 400 allegations including rape, sexual assault, sexual exploitation and human trafficking have been made against Fayed, who died three years ago.
One of KPL’s clients, Carrie Lazell, from Norfolk, said her nascent career as a designer ended after she was groomed and sexually assaulted by the former Harrods boss.
Lazell, who worked as a designer at the luxury store in her early 20s, said: “I lost a career, and I’ve gone through a whole load of very unpleasant, unnecessary trauma with a man I did not want to engage sexually with at all. I was really enjoying work [at Harrods]. I think I was set to become a successful designer.”
But she said her performance suffered as a result of the alleged abuse. Lazell added: “I couldn’t say it’s because every day the chairman of Harrods is abusing me. And I was threatened that I should never tell anybody because bad things would happen to me or my family.”
KPL said it had begun issuing settlement formal offers against Harrods and the estate.
The law firm said its negotiations with Harrods and the estate halted earlier this summer. Traynor said this delay was due to the department store’s action to replace the executors of estate – believed to be Fayed’s close relatives. But Harrods denied this had any bearing on survivors accessing compensation.
Sarah Savogi, another KPL client, who says she was sexually assaulted by Fayed in a restaurant, said only once her claim was settled could she fully lead her life.
“I have severe PTSD and relapses of what happened and sometimes I wake up in the night, I think I can’t breathe, I have awful nightmares about Al Fayed,” she said.
“Sometimes I’ll see a man and he looks like him and it will all come back to me again. There’s only so much that a therapist and counselling session can do, and I feel like I’ve reached the end of everything they can do to help me.”
Holly Johnson and Heidi Givens, KPL clients and sisters from Texas, said the delay to reaching a settlement was aggravating their distress.
The twins, who say they were sexually abused by Fayed when they worked at Harrods and Fayed’s Park Lane offices, said they felt unable to move on in their lives.
Givens said: “I don’t think that the estate or Harrods understand what it feels like for all of us to just keep going. Right now it’s like an open wound that can’t heal.”
Harrods said it “continues to work at a pace dictated by survivors and their legal representatives towards redress through the route of their choice. However, the timely progression of claims was only possible where the information required is made available, in line with established legal principles.”
It added that any suggestion to survivors that Harrods was preventing access to compensation was a misrepresentation, and harmful to survivors’ trust in the process.
The survivors also criticised Harrods for closing its redress scheme before recent significant developments in the police investigation, which suggested the scandal was greater and more complex than previously thought.
This includes several women being recognised as trafficking victims, the Met police interviewing seven suspects under caution, including one who was a Harrods employee until 2025, and a file being sent to the Crown Prosecution Service for charge advice about a man in his 80s over indecent assaults on two women.
In response Harrods said: “Harrods has reiterated that the scheme is one route to redress and compensation open to survivors. We support all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continue to work closely with the Met police on its investigation.”
Shanta Sundarason, another of KPL’s clients, said: “I don’t even know if [Harrods] really cared to truly understand the scale of the abuse. I think what they were trying to do was to pay off as many women as they possibly could as quickly as possible.”
In a statement, Harrods said it was “committed to ensuring all eligible survivors receive compensation for the appalling abuse they suffered”.
It added: “More than 260 survivors have engaged with the Harrods redress scheme, with 113 claims settled to date. Any suggestion to survivors by their legal representatives that Harrods is preventing survivors from accessing compensation is a misrepresentation of the facts, and harmful to survivors’ trust in this process.
“Harrods continues to work at a pace dictated by survivors and their legal representatives towards redress through the route of their choice.”
The statement added that Harrods believed the appointment of new executors to the Fayed estate was for the benefit of all survivors
“We have continued concerns over the solvency of the estate and its ability to pay all survivors in a timely and appropriate manner,” it stated.
The estate was approached for comment.

OpenAI boss and Elon Musk back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:02:24 UTC
23:02:24 KST

Sam Altman and Elon Musk have backed a call from the head of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, to “slow the pace” of AI development after he warned that an AI swarm could otherwise become capable of “taking over the entire internet” within a year.
In a rare show of unity, the rival technology leaders threw their weight behind the appeal from the founder and chief executive of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, which came after a series of warnings from AI researchers last week. Amodei also called for safety coordination with China.
But the US president, Donald Trump, on a visit to his golf course in Ireland, played down the warnings and said “very negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”.
“We’re leading China in AI,” he said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.
Amodei laid out his thoughts on “why the AI industry should slow down”, in an essay with a three-part plan for doing so, starting with giving independent monitors constant access to developers’ research processes. Amodei said “building [AI] too fast is reckless” and he feared that after hundreds of OpenAI agents hacked into the Hugging Face website this summer, a swarm with greater capabilities but similarly misaligned could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet”. This was disputed by some AI experts as not particularly plausible and to be treated with scepticism.
Musk, the founder of Tesla and SpaceX, responded to Amodei’s slowdown plan with a series of posts on X: “Dario is right.”
He said: “I’ve been sounding the alarm on AI for a long time,” and referred to a 2014 post where he said: “We need to be super careful with AI. Potentially more dangerous than nukes.”
Amodei’s call comes as Anthropic prepares to float on the US stock market, in what is expected to be the biggest initial public offering of all time. It is expected to start marketing its planned $2tn-plus (£1.5tn) IPO soon.
Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, responded to Amodei’s comments on Saturday. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” he said in a post on X. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.”
He also said OpenAI would not go public in 2026, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence.
“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman told Fortune. Asked why he, Amodei, Musk, and the chief executives of Meta and Google did not sit down and “get on the same page” about a collective slowdown, he said: “I think that will happen.”
Demis Hassabis, a co-founder and chair of Google Deep Mind, also said: “The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.”
But some safety experts questioned whether Amodei’s plan went far enough. David Krueger, an AI professor, safety campaigner and former founding director of the UK government’s AI Security Institute, said: “We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”
Amodei’s plan seeks a waiver from the US government to allow the frontier AI companies to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. But David Sacks, a co-chair of Donald Trump’s council of advisers on science and technology, said: “Stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission … Stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyber-attack.”
Meanwhile, King Charles is preparing to meet leading figures from the most prominent AI companies on Thursday to ask them how the technology can be developed under the theme “AI for good”. One session is set to be called “prudence at the frontier”, which is expected to explore the possibility for clear red lines on the uses of AI to create bioweapons and launch cyber-attacks on critical systems.
Those expected to attend the event overseen by the Ditchley Foundation, which has drawn up a draft charter for AI leaders, include: senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic; the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang; Hassabis; Niccolo de Masi, the chair and chief executive of IonQ,; and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the pope on issues of AI and technology ethics
The OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin called Amodei’s essay “excellent” and said he agreed “with basically every word”.
Amodei said his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps, saying Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”.
Growing numbers of US lawmakers are calling for new rules to govern AI systems after cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies over concerns about the technology’s risks.
Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action. At the weekend the New York Times reported that Barack Obama on Thursday privately urged the Democrats to prioritise AI oversight in their agenda, telling party leaders on Thursday: “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous.”
The former British prime minister Rishi Sunak, who advises Anthropic, wrote on Sunday: “We have had a wake-up call to take AI safety more seriously, to work out how to set limits on research. If governments don’t heed this, the risk of a serious accident will become unacceptably high.”
On Wednesday, a former Anthropic employee had warned that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. The researcher, Jacob Coxon, said in a series of posts that he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed.
Asked to comment on his former employee’s view, Amodei said: “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him … I think there’s some chance that things go wrong but it’s not all that high.”
“I am not a doomer about this,” he told CNN. “I think this technology can be built safely.”

A 20-minute workout protects memory after sleep loss just as well as a 90-minute nap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
14:00:31 UTC
23:00:31 KST

Experiencing a sleepless night often makes it difficult to absorb and retain new information. A recent study suggests that engaging in a short bout of physical activity or taking a long nap can both protect the brain’s ability to form fresh memories after heavy sleep loss. The findings, published in PNAS, indicate that while these two strategies help memory in similar amounts, they rely on entirely different internal brain mechanisms to achieve that benefit.
Episodic memory allows people to consciously recall past events along with the specific time and place they occurred. This type of memory is essential for daily life, helping people navigate their environment, learn from past experiences, and make informed decisions about the future. When people do not get enough sleep, their capacity to record these episodic memories drops noticeably. In fact, a 2017 review explained how missing sleep directly disrupts the specific brain networks required to absorb and file away new information.
Because sleep loss is common among shift workers and medical professionals, scientists have been looking for accessible ways to shield the brain from its cognitive toll. At the same time, researchers have documented that movement benefits the brain under normal resting conditions. For instance, a 2019 meta-analysis demonstrated that a single short session of physical activity just before learning strongly improves memory performance.
Building on these separate lines of evidence, the authors of a 2021 review advanced the theory that exercise might act as a buffer to counteract the specific memory deficits caused by sleep deprivation. The current research, led by Madhura S. Lotlikar, was designed to test this idea directly by comparing the effects of exercise against the effects of a long nap. To understand what happens beneath the surface, the research team used electroencephalography, or EEG, a technique that involves placing small sensors on the scalp to measure the brain’s electrical waves.
To conduct the study, the researchers recruited 53 healthy young adults and kept them awake in a laboratory for 30 consecutive hours. After the sleep deprivation period, the participants were randomly split into three groups to undergo a specific intervention. One group exercised for 20 minutes on a stationary bicycle at a moderately intense pace, reaching 80 percent of their maximum heart rate. A second group was given a 90-minute opportunity to nap in a quiet, dark room. A third group, acting as a control, sat on a stationary bicycle for 20 minutes without pedaling.
Following their respective interventions, all participants waited for about 30 minutes. This interval ensured that the napping group had time to shake off any grogginess from waking up. Next, the participants completed a memory task while wearing EEG caps. They viewed 150 distinct images on a screen and rated the emotional intensity of each picture to ensure they were paying attention. Three days later, the participants returned for a surprise memory test where they were shown a mix of the original 150 images and 75 new ones, and they had to indicate whether they recognized each picture.
The results showed that both exercise and napping protected the participants’ memory capacities. The exercise and nap groups successfully identified 56 percent and 57 percent of the original images, respectively, compared to a base rate of 46 percent in the control group. This amounts to an average relative increase of 22 percent in memory performance for those who exercised or rested compared to those who did nothing. The researchers noted that these improvements were not due to participants simply guessing “yes” more often, but reflected a genuine boost in their ability to remember the specific items.
The EEG recordings indicated that the two interventions achieved this memory preservation through distinct brain pathways. For the napping group, sleeping successfully reduced markers of neural fatigue and sleep pressure in the brain before the memory task even began. By downscaling these exhausted neural networks, the nap placed the brain into an optimal state to receive and hold onto new information. In this group, the baseline state of the brain was the strongest predictor of how well a person would perform on the memory test three days later.
The exercise group displayed a different internal response. Before the memory task, their EEG markers showed the same high levels of neural fatigue and sleep pressure as the control group. However, exercise appeared to prime the brain to process information more efficiently once a new image appeared. When a picture was shown, the brains of the exercising participants successfully engaged specific electrical rhythms associated with active learning and attention allocation. This allowed the participants to mobilize their available mental resources without needing to exert extra compensatory effort.
In contrast, the sleep-deprived control group struggled to encode the memories. Their brainwaves indicated high levels of fatigue, and when they tried to process the new images, their brains showed signs of elevated effort. Unlike in the exercise group, this extra mental strain did not translate to better memory performance, suggesting that the sleep-deprived brain was attempting to compensate for its exhaustion but failing to store the new information effectively.
The new findings are in line with a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that a two-hour nighttime nap during a 24-hour shift improved nurses’ visual and verbal memory performance and restored disrupted resting brain connectivity. The results also align with another study covered by PsyPost, which found that engaging in moderate physical activity is associated with better episodic memory performance the following day, though that study tracked everyday activity in middle-aged adults rather than testing an acute workout as a buffer against total sleep deprivation.
As with all research, there are a few caveats to consider. First, the laboratory setting involved a single bout of extreme sleep deprivation, which might not fully mirror the ongoing sleep loss that many shift workers experience in the real world. Additionally, the durations of the two interventions did not match, with exercise lasting 20 minutes and the nap lasting 90 minutes. The researchers intentionally designed it this way to mimic practical real-world options, as exercising for 90 minutes would be physically exhausting and napping for only 20 minutes might not provide enough deep sleep to restore brain function.
Future research could look into how these interventions affect occupation-specific tasks, such as medication administration for nurses or lane tracking for truck drivers. Scientists are also interested in whether combining these strategies, such as taking a nap and then exercising, might offer even greater benefits for the exhausted brain.
The study, “Protecting episodic memory after sleep loss: Similar benefits of exercise and naps via distinct neural contributions,” was authored by Madhura S. Lotlikar, Beatrice Ayotte, Amy Choi, Freddie Seo, Edwin M. Robertson, Fabien Dal Maso, and Marc Roig.

Iran-GCC summit: What’s behind the meeting, why is Bahrain not attending?

Iran-GCC summit: What’s behind the meeting, why is Bahrain not attending?
Iran says it plans to hold talks with Iraq and Gulf nations in Oman to help strengthen shared regional security.
Iran says a meeting between Iraq and the Gulf countries will be held in Oman on Monday to discuss the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under Tehran’s blockade amid the diplomatic deadlock with the United States.
Global energy supplies have been disrupted due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, impacting countries around the world. The blockade has particularly affected Gulf countries, which depend on oil and gas for vast majority of their budgets.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why US-Iran war over Hormuz is threatening the Gulf’s waters
- list 2 of 3Houthis, Yemeni forces engaged in fierce battles: Why each front matters
- list 3 of 3Iran claims to have captured a US ‘sail drone’ near Hormuz Strait
In a statement on Friday, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the meeting is intended to “promote better understanding among the countries of the region and help strengthen shared regional security”.
But Bahrain, a member of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), has said it will not participate in the planned meeting. Bahrain has borne the brunt of Iranian attacks since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February.
So what’s behind the meeting and why won’t Bahrain participate?
Here’s what we know:
What has Iran said about the meeting?
On Saturday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, told Al Jazeera that the meeting is “a sign of Iran’s good intention because we have said all along that the security of the region must be guaranteed by the countries of the region, without intervention by the foreigners, without intervention by the outside powers”.
“This is a sign we will talk to our neighbours, despite the fact that their territories, their military bases or the military bases of the United States, were used to attack Iran,” he said.
Gulf nations have accused Tehran of attacking civilian targets, including airports and desalination plants.
Baghaei added that Tehran would “brief the delegations about the results of the Iran and Oman consultations regarding the safe passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz”.
Moreover, on Sunday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned that Tehran’s expected agreement with Muscat to govern the Strait of Hormuz will not trigger a reopening of the waterway.
In comments to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, Araghchi said Iran will “provide the participating countries with the details of the agreement with Oman and the maps related to the new route” during the meeting.
But the agreement does not “in any way” signal that the strait will reopen, with Tehran still expecting the US to honour the commitments of the June 60-day memorandum of understanding signed in June, he said. The MoU collapsed in July after the US tried to push for an alternative route closer to Omani territory, drawing Iranian attacks.
On Sunday, at least one person was killed and four others wounded after an Iranian commercial vessel was attacked near Qeshm Island in the strait, with attacks on ships escalating in recent weeks.
“Iran believes that the responsibility for ensuring security and stability in the region lies solely with the countries of the region,” Araghchi added.
Who is planning to attend the meeting?
Iraq and most of the Gulf nations have not yet responded whether they will attend the planned meeting.
However, Bahrain has said it will not be participating in the proposed meeting.
“In light of what has been circulated … the Kingdom of Bahrain will not participate in it,” Bahrain’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Saturday.
Pointing to attacks on infrastructure across the Gulf, Bahrain said that security and stability in the region “cannot be preserved through a policy of appeasement” and called for Hormuz to be open without “discrimination, fees or permits”.
Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry said it maintains its commitment to dialogue, but “will not be a party to any collective meeting that includes Iran before the resumption of diplomatic relations between the two countries”.
Bahrain cut diplomatic ties with Iran in 2016 alongside Saudi Arabia during an earlier crisis between the regional rivals. While Riyadh restored ties in 2023, Manama is yet to do so.
What is behind the meeting between the GCC and Iran?
Indirect talks mediated by Oman are continuing between regional actors regarding safe passage and temporary shipping lanes, even as recent attacks on commercial vessels highlight the ongoing danger in the waterway through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes.
Top officials from Iran and the Gulf countries have held calls in an effort to resolve the conflict. Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani visited Tehran late last month, aimed at de-escalating tensions and helping break the diplomatic deadlock between Iran and the United States.
A source familiar with Monday’s meeting told Iran’s Tasnim news agency that an agreement on routes through the strait between Iran and Oman will be presented at the meeting, but the strait will not reopen unless the US meets Iran’s conditions on the waterway.
Iran wants its control of the Strait of Hormuz to be recognised, allowing it to collect fees from ships that use it, which Washington rejects. Oman, which controls the opposite bank of the strait, says it is negotiating with the agreement of other regional states.
What is the current situation at the Strait of Hormuz?
The status of the Strait of Hormuz is contested and restricted more than six months into the US and Israel’s war on Iran.
Iran maintains restrictions and considers the strait largely closed or tightly controlled amid ongoing conflict.
Tehran has also been pushing to formalise its control over the waterway, including potentially charging fees for passage, and has been in negotiations with Muscat, as Oman’s territorial waters also cover Hormuz.
Tehran has also insisted that normal transit will not resume until the US lifts the naval blockades on its ports and removes sanctions.
The strait was free to use by shipping from all nations before the US and Israel attacked Iran late in February, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Daily shipping traffic through the strait has plummeted by about 95 percent since the start of the war on Iran, dropping from a pre-war average of roughly 130–140 ships per day down to an average of about five to seven vessels a day.
US President Donald Trump has, however, said it is in total control of the waterway.
Meanwhile, on Sunday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a vessel has been struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
In another incident on Sunday, at least one person was killed and four others were wounded in an attack on an Iranian commercial vessel near Hengam Island and the Shib Deraz coast of Qeshm Island, Qeshm Governor Hossein Amir Teymouri said, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB.
Teymouri described the incident as an attack by the “US terrorist enemy”.
A senior Iranian Revolutionary Guard Navy official has also warned US naval vessels against approaching the Strait of Hormuz, challenging Trump’s claims that Washington controls the waterway.
“If the Strait of Hormuz is under American control, then go ahead – bring one of your warships within 100km [62 miles],” the deputy political commander of the IRGC Navy said, according to Iran’s Fars news agency.
He said US forces know that any vessels approaching the area would face a response from Iranian forces, adding that similar incidents had occurred in recent days.
The US has not yet commented on this incident.

Keeping the Bridges Open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:58:00 UTC
22:58:00 KST

One afternoon recently, I took my car to a service station to the “left bank” of the Dnipro river. With a meeting to attend near Zoloti Vorota (Golden Gate) on the right bank, I was planning to take the Metro back across the river and return for my car in the evening. The metro ride would have taken no more than 40 minutes, but there was an air raid alert and, as usual during alerts, the metro trains stopped crossing the river.
I got as far as Osokorki metro station – the last one before the bridge – and booked an Uber, thinking I could cross the river that way. But they couldn’t find a car for me. For half an hour I stood at the edge of Mykola Bazhan Avenue, looking toward the bridge which I very much wanted to cross. Then, just as I was cancelling my Uber request, for the first time since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion I saw a Russian drone dive onto a car-filled avenue and explode on the road, next to a huge NOVUS supermarket.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
I’ve often seen Russian drones in the sky above me. I’ve seen missiles flying overhead several times, and I’ve heard explosions from drones and missiles hundreds of times, but I’ve never seen a drone dive toward its chosen target.
Half an hour later, still standing there, I learned from one of Kyiv’s many air raid information sites that, miraculously, no one had been killed in the attack. However, several people were injured, and shrapnel destroyed some cars and damaged others.
Drones Target Nizhnekamsk Hub and Slavyansk Refinery in Russia
Most likely, the drone’s target wasn’t the road, but the NOVUS supermarket nearby. Russia has already destroyed several warehouses of this Lithuanian chain, as well as some of their stores. If the “Shahed” had reached the supermarket, there would have been many casualties. It missed by a mere 100 meters, leaving a meter-deep crater on the road. Traffic on the avenue came to a halt. Ambulances, police, firefighters, and road maintenance vehicles arrived very quickly.
An hour and a half later, the injured had been evacuated, and the hole created by the explosion had been repaired. The police finished drawing up a report on yet another Russian war crime, and traffic on the avenue was restored. Only one burned-out car remained stranded on edge of the road.
Since drones were still flying over Kyiv, the Metro bridges remained closed. I cancelled my meeting in central Kyiv and returned to the service station, where I waited for my car.
Russia’s new tactics, which keep drones in the skies over the capital almost constantly, have further divided Kyiv into two “cities” – the “left bank” – a “dormitory” town with plenty of amenities of its own, and the “right bank,” with its ancient city center, the government quarter, and residential areas with older buildings and a buzzing café and restaurant culture that defies the air raid warnings.
The left and right banks of the Ukrainian capital are connected by eight bridges. Two of them support railways, and two are combined metro/road bridges. Two million residents live on each side of the Dnipro River, and hundreds of thousands commute to the other bank every day. It’s therefore not surprising that residents are increasingly concerned about Russian attempts to disrupt communication between Kyiv’s left and right banks.
The bridge debate was recently fueled by Denis Yaroslavsky – an officer in the Assault Troops Command. He stated that Russia plans to attack Kyiv’s bridges in order to paralyze the capital. Other experts were more reassuring, arguing that drones or conventional missiles could not destroy powerful structures like bridges. They could only damage them. Destroying a bridge would require multiple, well-aimed hits from heavy missiles on its supports, which the Russians are unlikely to be able to pull off.
However, Russia has destroyed or seriously damaged approximately 350 Ukrainian bridges. Last Sunday, Russia bombed and made impassable one of the two bridges over the Kazennyi Donets River in Kramatorsk, an industrial city in Ukraine-controlled Donbas, only 10 kilometers from the front line. The destruction of this bridge will weaken the ability of Ukrainian troops to defend the front line.
While there’s some good news on the military and anti-corruption fronts, with no comprehensive victory in sight, the home front is growing fragile. The recent uncovering of racketeering and fraud protection at the General Procurator’s Office, cause tremendous angst among the population and damaged a sense of unity.
Meanwhile, bridges between Ukraine’s many and varied social groups need constant attention and support. I was impressed by efforts in this direction coming from civil servants responsible for culture in Zhytomyr region. They recently organized a day of exploration and networking for the region’s librarians.
The day’s events brought the librarians together with representatives of the region’s agricultural and food processing industries, as well as cultural personalities with links to the local area – including myself and the well-known actor Bohdan Beniuk.
A few days before the event, copies of my recently published novel, which were to be presented to the librarians, had been destroyed in a missile attack on a Zhytomyr Nova Poshta (New Post company) warehouse, but, immediately, a local businessman offered to fund the procurement of replacement stock.
Perhaps it is easier to build bridges in smaller communities inside one region, but bridges of all kinds in Ukraine’s big cities will need special attention as winter approaches and US peace missions fade into the sunset.

The Ministry of Energy has drafted a bill on transferring the property of liquidated mines to municipalities
Kyiv • UNN
The transfer of property will take place subject to a corresponding initiative by local self-government bodies. This is intended to attract business and reduce budget expenditures, Denys Shmyhal said.
The Ministry of Energy has prepared a bill that would allow the free transfer from state to municipal ownership of the above-ground property of coal and uranium mines undergoing liquidation. The document is planned to be submitted to the government for consideration and to the Verkhovna Rada within a week. This was reported by First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy of Ukraine Denys Shmyhal, reports UNN.
Details
The transfer of the property will take place subject to a corresponding initiative by local self-government bodies. This is expected to enable communities to attract businesses and use the sites of former mines as industrial parks.
Implementation of the bill will also make it possible to reduce the amount of budget funds allocated for the implementation of liquidation projects and ensure the rational use of existing mine infrastructure. At the same time, the Ministry of Energy, together with the communities, is working on a strategy for the just transformation of the territories of former mines
In addition, according to the minister, as part of a Memorandum of Cooperation between the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH and the Ministry of Energy, a prospective development plan is being drawn up for one of the mines that is currently undergoing liquidation.
This is a pilot project that will result in a development plan for the territory of the former mine and an analysis of its investment potential, with an estimated cost of the necessary work. The plan developed will serve as a roadmap for attracting donors and potential investors to develop the territories of former mines

Prabowo made the remarks at the opening session of the BRICS Leaders' Summit in the Indian capital New Delhi, local English daily Tempo reported, citing the Presidential Secretariat's Media and Information Bureau.
Prabowo said that strengthening the voice of the Global South was important to give developing countries a greater role in determining the direction of global development.
Noting that the international community is approaching 2030, the target year for achieving the 2030 Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), he said countries had made various commitments to eradicate poverty, protect the planet and build stronger institutions.
“These commitments remain firm. We must continue moving beyond 2030,” he said.
Prabowo said that instead of viewing the 2030 Agenda simply as a set of targets to be achieved within a specific timeframe, it should also help put developing countries in a stronger position in the global system.
“This agenda aims to bring developing countries to where they rightly belong, to realize peace and prosperity for our people, and to give developing countries a greater role in shaping the global order,” he said.
The voices of the Global South, he went on to say, should be heard both in accelerating implementation of the 2030 Agenda and in determining the direction of the world after 2030.

Interview: Iran's Araghchi to brief Gulf states on Hormuz route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:49:37 UTC
22:49:37 KST

Breadcrumb
Interview: Araghchi says Iran will present Hormuz route at meeting with Gulf states
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said that there will be a meeting between Iran, Iraq and five Gulf states on Monday in Oman. He added that participating countries will be briefed on the details of a new maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz agreed upon between Tehran and Muscat.
Araghchi said that if there is sufficient political will, the meeting could pave the way for future consultations on other issues of concern to the countries of the region.
He sat down with The New Arab’s Saber Gul Anbari in Tehran for an interview.
Q: For the first time, amid continuing tensions in the region, a joint meeting between Iran, the Gulf states, and Iraq is being held tomorrow in Oman. What are the most important items on the agenda, and what are the objectives of this meeting? How did the idea of holding it come about?
First, I would like to clarify an important point about this meeting. In fact, it is a meeting of the eight countries bordering the Persian Gulf. However, Bahrain, for reasons it has announced itself, did not wish to participate. Accordingly, the meeting will be held with the participation of seven countries.
The most important item on the agenda - in fact, the only item - is the issue of the new maritime route in the Strait of Hormuz.
As you know, an agreement has been reached between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Sultanate of Oman regarding its establishment.
The maps relating to this route have also been prepared, and a joint statement has been drafted on the matter.
At this meeting, the participating countries are to be briefed on the details of the agreement, the relevant maps, and the joint statement. 
Ultimately, these documents will be submitted to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) for registration within the organization’s mechanisms.
Therefore, the meeting’s agenda is very clearly defined, and other subjects should not be presented as formal agenda items. Of course, this is the first time that such discussions have taken place among the Persian Gulf states in this format.
From this perspective, there is hope that, if the political will exists, these discussions could pave the way for future consultations on other issues of concern to the countries of the region. But I emphasize that these are not the current objectives or agenda of the meeting. Its agenda is exclusively and specifically focused on the new maritime arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz.
Q: Given that the Iranian and Omani sides proposed the initiative to hold the meeting, what does Iran hope to achieve through it?
Iran fundamentally believes that the countries of the region themselves are solely responsible for their security and stability. It is therefore natural for them to engage in dialogue and consultations with one another regarding the region’s issues and challenges.
For many years, we have emphasized dialogue, confidence-building, and cooperation among the countries of the region. We believe that sustainable security is achieved when the countries of the region are able to reach an understanding on their common issues without interference or disruptive interventions by actors from outside the region.
Q: Are you seeking, through this meeting, a mechanism for regional security without the presence of the United States?
The objective of this meeting is not to establish a new security mechanism for the region, and there is no such issue on the meeting’s agenda.
Nevertheless, the fact that the countries of the region are meeting for the first time at this level around a single table, and engaging in dialogue on a specific issue related to maritime security in the region, is an important event and can be regarded as a confidence-building step.
We hope that, if this process continues, conditions will eventually emerge for dialogue and cooperation on other issues.
We believe that regional issues should be managed solely by the countries of the region themselves. The more dialogue and cooperation there is among neighbouring countries, the less room there will naturally be for interference and arrangements imposed from outside the region.
Q: This meeting is taking place at a time when the Houthis in Yemen have taken control of Bab al-Mandab, and conflict between them and Saudi Arabia has intensified. What can this meeting contribute toward easing the current tensions between Iran and Gulf countries and resolving regional issues such as Yemen?
We must distinguish between these two issues.
This meeting is not being held to discuss the Yemen issue or to resolve disputes between the countries of the region. As I mentioned, the meeting’s specific agenda is the new maritime arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz and briefing the parties on the agreement and the relevant documents.
However, the fact that this dialogue is taking place amid the current circumstances in the region is itself significant.
Today, we are facing a series of interconnected crises and tensions in the region. The experience of recent years has demonstrated that these issues cannot be resolved through confrontation, pressure, or the involvement of actors from outside the region.
The more the countries of the region engage in dialogue with one another, the greater their mutual understanding of each other’s concerns, interests, and priorities. This process can help reduce misunderstandings and manage tensions.
With regard to Yemen, the position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is clear. We believe that there is no military solution to the Yemen issue, and that the future of the country must be determined by the Yemenis themselves through dialogue and an inclusive political process.
Q: Given that the agreement between Iran and Oman regarding the Strait of Hormuz is expected to be signed and announced at this meeting, can you explain its contents and the extent to which Tehran is counting on these countries’ support for moving forward with the agreement and putting pressure on Washington to accept the new maritime route?
Regarding the content of this agreement, I should clarify one point from the outset: this understanding does not in any way mean opening the Strait of Hormuz.
The understanding between Iran and Oman actually establishes the framework and arrangements under which maritime traffic would operate if the conditions for reopening the strait are met.
The details and specifications of the new entry and exit routes through the Strait of Hormuz have been determined.
Iran’s condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz is for the United States to return to its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.
Q: Tehran has repeatedly stated that the agreement with Oman does not mean reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as you have also indicated, and has linked reopening it to the fulfillment of certain conditions. Can you specify these conditions precisely, and to what extent could such an agreement pave the way toward meeting them and resuming negotiations with the United States?
To answer with complete clarity, Iran’s condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz is neither complicated nor a new list of conditions.
If the United States returns to the commitments it accepted and signed under the Islamabad MoU, and acts in accordance with them, the conditions will be created for the situation in the Strait of Hormuz to return to normal.
The Islamic Republic of Iran is committed to its responsibility to seek to ensure navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. However, naturally, US aggressive actions and illegal interventions - including the naval blockade and economic warfare - are the main factor behind the lack of maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Iran-Oman understanding should also be viewed within this framework.
This understanding establishes new arrangements and routes for navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, but it does not itself mean that the strait has been reopened.
If the United States honors its commitments under the Islamabad MoU, then the framework designed by Iran and Oman concerning how maritime traffic should operate could serve as the basis for returning maritime traffic to normal.
