Solving the ‘what now?’ dilemma at Kfar Maccabiah Hotel - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:45:41 UTC
22:45:41 KST

There are hotels that welcome children, and then there are hotels where children immediately realize they have struck gold.
Kfar Maccabiah, tucked away amid the greenery of Ramat Gan, falls very much into the latter category.
For families, particularly those with younger children, its great advantage is that there is simply so much to do. Our children had the best time, and it was easy to see why.
Between several swimming pools, multiple water slides, large outdoor playground spaces, and a seemingly endless choice of sporting activities, there was little chance of hearing the dreaded question that accompanies so many family holidays: “What are we doing now?”
The pools alone can occupy much of a day. For children, the water slides are inevitably the main attraction, and ours would happily have spent hours going up and down them. For parents, meanwhile, there is something particularly appealing about settling into a resort for the day without constantly bundling everyone into a car to find the next activity.
Complete with lawns and green spaces, Kfar Maccabiah feels removed from the city
That is probably Kfar Maccabiah’s greatest strength. Although it sits in the middle of the Tel Aviv metropolitan area, the hotel feels removed from the city surrounding it. The lawns and green spaces give it more of a family-resort feel than a conventional city hotel.
The scale of the wider Kfar Maccabiah complex also means that guests have access to far more than one would normally expect from a hotel.
There is a smaller fitness room within the hotel itself, but guests can also use the gym in the main sports complex – a serious, fully equipped sports facility rather than the handful of machines that too often constitute a hotel fitness center.
The hotel also offers studio classes, including Pilates, giving adults the chance to exercise properly during a stay rather than simply promising themselves they will use the treadmill once before breakfast. Guests can use all these facilities and classes for free.
The wider sporting complex includes indoor and outdoor basketball facilities and swimming pools, while the hotel’s program gives guests access to a range of activities during the week. It is one of the relatively rare Israeli hotels where sport feels integral to the place, rather than an afterthought.
In many ways, that is the whole essence of Kfar Maccabiah.
Next to the hotel is the headquarters of the Maccabi World Union, which organizes the Maccabiah Games and, alongside it, the World Jewish Sports Museum, which is well worth setting aside time to visit. The museum explores the history of Jewish and Israeli sport, but it does so within the much broader story of Jewish history, Zionism, and identity.
Its collection combines memorabilia and historical objects with interactive exhibits and the stories of Jewish sportsmen and women from around the world. That makes it considerably more interesting than the name “sports museum” might initially suggest, even for visitors who are not particularly devoted sports fans.
Its proximity to the hotel is another advantage. No journey is involved and no need to devote an entire day to it; you can simply walk over from the hotel and include the museum in your stay.
That ease is a recurring feature of Kfar Maccabiah.
The hotel is also close to the Ramat Gan Safari, the National Park, and a number of other family attractions, so anyone staying for several days has plenty of options nearby. Yet the point is that you do not actually have to leave. There is enough happening inside the complex to make staying put perfectly viable.
The accommodation also works particularly well for families. Kfar Maccabiah has family suites large enough to accommodate five people together, including a 57-square-meter suite with a bedroom and living room and a larger 72-square-meter option with two bedrooms and a living room.
For parents used to squeezing children, bags, toys, and assorted holiday paraphernalia into a standard hotel room, the extra space makes a considerable difference.
The hotel also has a spa for anyone fortunate enough to find some child-free time, with treatments, massages, and relaxation areas available on site.
For couples looking exclusively for a boutique city break, there may be more obvious choices, but for families – particularly families with energetic children – what Kfar Maccabiah offers is difficult to beat.
The children can swim, race down the slides, play and explore; parents can use a proper gym or take a class; everyone can eat extremely well; and there is even an excellent museum a few minutes’ walk from the room.
Most tellingly, our children did not need persuading to enjoy themselves; quite the opposite. The difficult part was getting them to leave.
The writer was a guest of the hotel.

Israel’s survival story inspires vision for Republika Srpska’s future, Milorad Dodik tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:45:26 UTC
22:45:26 KST

BANJA LUKA, Bosnia and Herzegovina – Sitting in Banja Luka last week, there was little ambiguity about where Milorad Dodik would like the future to lead.
Eight months after we first met in Jerusalem, the longtime dominant figure in Republika Srpska spoke with The Jerusalem Post about Israel, Europe, Islam, the breakup of Yugoslavia, the Bosnian War, and the grievances that have shaped Serbian politics for more than three decades.
Dodik has been around the block in the great game of geopolitics, and in a region where borders, identities, and nationalities have shifted repeatedly within living memory, he has learned to think less in terms of permanence than opportunity.
If the people of Republika Srpska were one day given the opportunity to vote in a referendum on leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina and ultimately joining Serbia, was that a future he thought about, the longtime leader was asked.
“Do I think about it?” Dodik replied. “I dream about it. Absolutely.”
To understand his answer, it helps to first understand the unusual country in which he gave it.
Before the Bosnian War, Bosnia and Herzegovina was one of six republics within socialist Yugoslavia, a federation that for decades held together Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, Bosnian Muslims, and others under Josip Broz Tito.
For nearly four decades, Tito was the only man who could hold the system together, suppressing any scent of nationalism among the constituent republics for the good of Yugoslavia.
But after his death in 1980 and the collapse of Communism later that decade, Yugoslavia began to unravel, as each of the republics sought independence.
Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, nationalism surged across the federation, and Bosnia – where Bosniak Muslim, Serb, and Croat communities were far more geographically intertwined – became the most dangerous piece of the Yugoslav puzzle.
When Bosnia held an independence referendum in 1992, Bosnian Serbs overwhelmingly boycotted it. Independence nevertheless passed, and within weeks the country descended into war.
Bosnian Serb leaders, backed militarily and financially by Belgrade, established their own republic and army (Republika Srpska), while the Bosnian government fought to preserve an independent state and Bosnian Croat forces pursued their own territorial ambitions.
What followed between 1992 and 1995 devastated the country. More than 100,000 people were killed, and around two million were driven from their homes on all sides of the conflict. Cities were besieged, communities that had lived alongside one another for generations were torn apart, and ethnic cleansing changed the demographic map of Bosnia.
Crimes were committed by all sides, although international courts subsequently established that extensive campaigns of persecution and ethnic cleansing were carried out by Bosnian Serb forces.
The Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war in late 1995, keeping Bosnia and Herzegovina intact while dividing it internally. Republika Srpska received just under half the country’s territory, with most of the remainder forming the predominantly Bosniak-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. To this day, Bosnia still has three members of its presidency to give all factions representation.
Three decades later, Republika Srpska has its own president, government, parliament, police, and public institutions. Serbian flags are ubiquitous, and many of its residents regard Serbia as their national homeland.
It is not, however, a sovereign state. For Dodik, that remains unfinished business, and that is where Israel enters his thinking.
From Jerusalem to Banja Luka
The immediate reason for the Post’s visit was considerably less dramatic than the future of Bosnia.
Israeli and Republika Srpska officials had gathered in Banja Luka to inaugurate the representative office of the Israel Chamber of Commerce, intended to turn a relationship that has grown increasingly warm in recent years into economic cooperation.
Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Minister Amichai Chikli traveled from Israel for the occasion. Galit Peleg, completing her term as Israel’s nonresident ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, was also there, along with Zeljka Cvijanovic, the Serb representative of the Bosnian Presidency, and local political and business leaders.
Amir Gross Kabiri, one of the initiative’s driving forces, will head the office.
While it is intended to boost trade, technology and investment, its opening also showcased the increasingly close political relationship between Israel and Republika Srpska – one that has reached unprecedented levels in recent years.
Dodik has deliberately cultivated ties with Jerusalem and told the Post that the idea of establishing the chamber office emerged during his meeting with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu earlier this year, when the Balkan politician was in town for Chikli’s “Generation Truth” conference.
“We maintain a high degree of understanding and support for Israel and, of course, for the Jewish people as a whole,” Dodik told the Post. “We wholeheartedly want to raise those relations to the highest possible level.”
Yet something deeper lies behind Dodik’s attachment to Israel. He sees parallels between Jewish and Serbian history – peoples repeatedly subjected to persecution and both, in his interpretation, learning the consequences of being unable to defend themselves.
That history is particularly powerful in this part of the Balkans. During World War II, much of modern-day Croatia and Bosnia fell under the fascist Ustaše-run Independent State of Croatia, an Axis puppet state that murdered Serbs, Jews, Roma, and political opponents. Jasenovac, its largest concentration camp complex, remains central to Serbian national memory. Of all the nations to suffer during World War II in the Balkans, the Serbs lost the largest percentage of their population.
Dodik believes Israel understands that history and the instinct it created better than most. He visited Kibbutz Be’eri following the October 7 massacre and said the destruction he witnessed there resonated with Serbian historical experience.
“We stood in solidarity over the suffering that occurred in October,” he said, reminding the Post that after October 7, the presidential palace in Banja Luka was emblazoned with the Israeli flag.
“Israel is waging a decisive struggle for its status and for a peaceful and stable environment,” he added. “And, to the extent that we are able, we will support all the efforts Israel undertakes in that regard.
“Israel is fighting to preserve its state and its people,” he told the Post. “Republika Srpska is doing the same.”
The comparison is not without contentious points, however.
Israel is a sovereign state. Republika Srpska is an autonomous entity created within the internationally recognized borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Moreover, the history surrounding Republika Srpska’s creation cannot be separated from the crimes that were committed in establishing and consolidating Bosnian Serb-controlled territory, which are a matter of legal history. International courts found that Bosnian Serb forces carried out systematic campaigns to remove Bosniaks and Croats from areas claimed for a Serbian state through killings, imprisonment, deportation, sexual violence, and the destruction of homes and religious buildings.
For many Bosniaks, therefore, Republika Srpska cannot be viewed simply as the realization of Serbian self-determination. Its territory also carries the memory of those expelled or killed during its creation.
Many Serbs tell the story from the opposite viewpoint. They remember Serbian civilians killed, villages attacked, and families displaced, and point to atrocities committed by Bosniak and Croat forces. There is no doubt crimes were committed by Bosniak and Croat forces, and many Serbs in Bosnia believe international institutions subsequently allowed Serbian crimes to define the war while reducing Serbian victims to an afterthought.
More than 30 years after Dayton, Bosnia has peace, but reconciliation remains another question, and Dodik’s language shows how wide that divide is.
He accused Bosniaks in Sarajevo of harboring a “systemic hatred” toward Jews and Israel, as well as toward Serbs, and his argument widened into a broader criticism of Muslim immigration into Western Europe and what he considers liberal Europe’s failure to defend its own civilization.
His characterization of Muslims is sweeping and, for Bosniaks who themselves suffered mass killing and ethnic cleansing during the war, deeply inflammatory. Yet it offers one of the clearest explanations Dodik gave for why he rejects Bosnia in its present form.
“Bosnia and Herzegovina does not work,” he said. “It would be the same as if you took Israel now and put it into a common state with Iraq, Syria, and Egypt and told [everyone] that you were all one country.
“Is that possible? Of course it isn’t. So why are you doing it to us?”
The shadow of Ratko Mladic
During the Post’s days in Banja Luka, those arguments about history were impossible to separate from something happening around us. Gen. Ratko Mladic, one of the Bosnian Serbs’ most identifiable figures, had only recently died.
As commander of the Army of Republika Srpska during the Bosnian War, Mladic oversaw the forces that captured the UN-declared safe area of Srebrenica in July 1995. In the days that followed, more than 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed.
Judges at the International Criminal Tribunal for Yugoslavia based in The Hague convicted Mladic of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, as well as persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, and forcible transfer.
Alongside political leader Radovan Karadzic, Mladic became the international face of the Bosnian Serbs during the ’90s.
Mladić was also convicted of crimes connected to the campaign of sniping and shelling against civilians during the siege of Sarajevo and the taking hostage of UN personnel. His life sentence was upheld on appeal in 2021. He died in The Hague on August 27 while serving a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes.
But walk through Banja Luka after his death, and another Mladic is visible.
At a makeshift memorial in the city, candles and flowers sat beside his photograph. Residents who spoke to the Post described not the commander portrayed in the judgments from The Hague, but a soldier who had defended them.
“Mladic defended us when we were under attack,” one resident said. “He fought for Serb rights.”
Some of those honoring him were not even alive during the war.
“Today, these people – young people born after the war – are going into the streets and paying tribute to Gen. Mladic,” Dodik said. “Excuse me, how am I supposed to prohibit that?”
He argues that international condemnation and attempts to criminalize the glorification of convicted war criminals have instead strengthened Mladic’s symbolic importance.
“What the West and the Muslims have done is turn Gen. Mladic into an icon of identification for the Serbs, whatever anyone may think about him,” he said.
The gulf is extraordinary.
The international judicial record describes a commander convicted of genocide and of participating in campaigns of terror and persecution. In Banja Luka, the Post encountered people mourning a general they believed had protected them.
Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade this week demonstrated the power of that competing memory, with thousands turning out for his burial, and the honors afforded him producing outrage in Bosnia and across Europe.
More than three decades after the wars of the Balkans, the dead are still shaping the politics of the living.
Against that historical backdrop, the warmth toward Israel visible in Republika Srpska takes on greater significance.
Peleg, speaking at the opening of the chamber of commerce, recalled that after October 7, the Israeli Embassy wanted to hold a memorial for the massacre victims in Sarajevo but was unable to find a venue willing to host it. Republika Srpska officials stepped in and offered a theater in East Sarajevo.
“From that moment we knew that we could commemorate our loved ones and get all the respect,” she told those gathered.
Here, yet again, is where the intricacies of Balkan politics come into play. Israel maintains diplomatic relations with Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state. Yet some of its warmest political relationships within Bosnia are increasingly found among leaders in an entity whose dominant political movement has spent years questioning whether that state should continue to exist in its current form.
For Dodik, there is no contradiction.
For Dodik, Israel is a strong example of the kind of relationship he wants Republika Srpska to build abroad – that of close political ties, stronger economic links, and direct engagement with countries he regards as natural partners.
Which brings the conversation back to Serbia.
The people of Republika Srpska are overwhelmingly Serb. They share their language, Orthodox Christianity, cultural traditions, and much of their national history with Serbia. Serbian television is watched, Serbian politics followed, and Serbian sporting victories celebrated. One Banja Luka resident told the Post how Bosnian Serbs always support Serbia over Bosnia in any sporting event where the two may meet.
Yet an international border separates Bosnian Serbs from Serbia. Dodik would like that to change.
His argument, and that of the Bosnian Serbs, rests partly on Kosovo, the southern region, which declared independence from Serbia in 2008. For Serbian nationalists, it created an obvious question: if self-determination permitted Kosovo Albanians to separate from Serbia, why could Bosnian Serbs not choose to separate from Bosnia?
Western governments reject the equivalence, arguing that Kosovo emerged from a different legal and historical process and that Dayton established Republika Srpska as an entity within sovereign Bosnia rather than a state possessing a unilateral right to secession.
For Dodik, this amounts to different rules for different peoples.
“Why can’t we do it if Kosovo can, according to your rules?” he asked.
And then came perhaps the most consequential part of his answer.
“Serbs are aware that if even a small opportunity arose, they would take advantage of it,” Dodik said. “We are preparing for that because nobody knows what will happen.”
For now, no internationally accepted route exists by which such a referendum could produce an independent Republika Srpska, much less union with Serbia, but the aspiration has not disappeared.
After several days in Banja Luka, it became easier to understand why.
Republika Srpska is simultaneously a product of war, a component of a peace agreement and, for many of the Serbs who live there, the closest thing they have had in modern Bosnia to a state of their own.
Its creation is inseparable from some of the darkest crimes of the Yugoslav wars. Its people also carry their own memories of Serbian suffering and displacement. Its institutions emerged from Dayton, but the national aspirations that preceded Dayton did not simply vanish when the agreement was signed.
That is the world in which Dodik’s admiration for Israel makes sense.
He looks at the Jewish state and sees a people that learned through catastrophe that survival cannot be entrusted to others. He looks at Republika Srpska and believes Serbs learned the same lesson.
His critics see nationalism that threatens the peace settlement that ended Europe’s bloodiest conflict since 1945, historical revisionism surrounding the crimes committed by Bosnian Serb forces, and rhetoric toward Muslims that makes reconciliation more difficult with every generation. Dodik sees a people whose statehood remains incomplete.
The chamber of commerce office inaugurated in Banja Luka last week is a small institution against that enormous historical backdrop. It may bring Israeli businesses, investment, tourists and technology to Republika Srpska, but it also gives Banja Luka another tangible connection with the country Dodik repeatedly invokes as an example of national survival.
The question that has followed Republika Srpska from the battlefield to Dayton and through the three decades since is whether Bosnia’s Serbs ultimately see their future inside Bosnia – or whether, given the opportunity, they would choose another one.
For Dodik, at least, there is no uncertainty. He is just waiting for the opportunity

Saudi pipeline outage threatens loss of 4% of global oil supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:45:08 UTC
22:45:08 KST

Saudi Arabia will run out of oil stocks for exports if it doesn't restart its major pipeline to the Red Sea within days, leading to a loss of up to 4% of global supply, Saudi oil buyers and traders said.
A further decline in Saudi flows will worsen the global supply crunch, which has already pushed global fuel prices to record highs, spurred inflation around the world and sent US bond yields to the highest levels since the 2008 financial crisis.
Since drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to shut its huge east-west oil pipeline on Friday, Riyadh has not given full details about the extent of the damage or how long the route will stay offline.
Sources that spoke to Reuters gave varying estimates, with one saying the damage could take as long as five to six weeks to repair, while another said it could be fixed sooner and could resume pumping partially while repairs are ongoing.
Saudi Arabia's government media office and energy ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. For the past six months, the pipeline running through the desert across the Arabian Peninsula has spared Saudi Arabia from the brunt of the impact of the wartime shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz that has crippled exports from its neighbors.
4% of global supply rerouted using the damaged pipeline
The world's biggest exporter has used the pipeline to reroute around 4 million barrels per day — around 4% of global supply — to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. But with the pipeline out of service, Yanbu now has stocks to maintain exports for just five to seven days, according to three industry sources familiar with Saudi exports.
Saudi Arabia also has stocks to supply customers for several days from Egypt's ports of Ain Sukhna on the Red Sea and Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean, a fourth source said.
Yanbu storage capacity stands at around 35 million barrels, according to industry estimates, with Ain Sukhna and Sidi Kerir able to store 18 million and 20 million barrels respectively. Stocks are not full and will ultimately run out without the east-west pipeline resuming operations, the four sources said.
Saudi oil supply fell to a more than three-decade low in August on reduced flows via Hormuz and the Red Sea, the International Energy Agency said on Friday. World oil supply will decline this year by 5.7 million bpd, or about 6%, the IEA, which coordinates Western energy policies, said. In addition to the attack on the pipeline, Houthi fighters in Yemen, who have threatened Saudi oil shipments, seized an island on Friday in the mouth of the Red Sea.
The Middle East supplied around 22 million barrels of oil per day before the war. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz have slowed to just 6 million to 9 million bpd, industry sources say.
Saudi Arabia told OPEC last week that its oil production had dropped to just 6.2 million bpd in August from 10.9 million bpd in February before the start of the war.

A different way to travel: Azadeh Abedinzadeh explains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:44:36 UTC
22:44:36 KST

A different way to travel: Azadeh Abedinzadeh explains
TEHRAN - Tourism is often measured by the visitors it attracts and the income they generate. But what if its success could also be measured by the forests it helps protect, the traditions it keeps alive and the opportunities it creates for local communities? This is the thinking behind regenerative tourism, an approach that seeks to move beyond reducing tourism’s negative impacts and toward restoring and strengthening the places people visit.
In Iran, the idea is finding relevance in rural destinations where nature, cultural heritage and local livelihoods are closely intertwined. Soheili Village on Qeshm Island offers one example, where mangrove conservation, community-based tourism and local enterprise have developed alongside one another. To explore the meaning and potential of regenerative tourism, we spoke with Dr. Azadeh Abedinzadeh, a tourism expert who has worked with rural communities in Iran and was involved in preparing Soheili’s application for the UN Tourism Best Tourism Villages initiative.
The full text of the interview is as follows:
First of all, I would like to ask you about Soheili Village. You played a major role in Soheili, which, along with several other villages in Iran, was recently named one of the Best Tourism Villages in the world.
Soheili is like a star shining in the sky, if we may put it that way. At the beginning of our discussion, we came across a story or legend about the name “Soheili.” When I first entered the village in 2018, I observed all the tourism activities taking place there and joined a group of local residents who were working in tourism.
I joined them as a facilitator--someone who could work alongside them, bringing the knowledge we had acquired at university and the experience we had gained in the professional field to help develop a marine tourism destination. It was a great opportunity for me to take part in preparing the dossier for the Best Tourism Villages of the world initiative, as one of the people responsible for compiling the application.
How much did the local community support the initiative? How involved were they, and how much did they want this to happen for Soheili?
When we talk about the rural lifestyle in southern Iran, we see a value chain--a table, so to speak. Unlike the familiar slogan of “from farm to table,” here it is “from the sea to the table.” َA table that is adorned with a woven mat called Badil.
These people had been continuously hosting domestic and foreign tourists for at least 10 years, so they had come to understand the economic benefits of tourism. They had also taken an important step back in 1385 [2006–07], when they secured a presence and equipment for a tourist jetty in the mangrove forest.
But what fascinated me even more was the way this community behaved. Whenever I went into the village, I saw that people in this southern region were hosting migratory birds. When the tide goes out in the mangrove forest and the water level drops, the people go fishing, while the birds around them also feed on the fish.
I never saw birds being hunted in southern Iran. When I asked them, “Well, these birds are eating the fish you catch. Why don’t you keep them away, perhaps like a scarecrow in a field?” they would say, “Just as we benefit from the sea, this is the birds’ share of it.”
This broad-minded attitude toward nature really impressed me. During the Kong-e Harra season--the young mangrove shoots, which are being collected at this time of year--they gather them, and their children take responsibility at home for growing mangrove seedlings and saplings.
In other words, they are taking care of their own environment. I believe this reflects a form of social and intellectual maturity that has developed within the community: they benefit from nature, but they also take responsibility for protecting it. That was the most beautiful thing I experienced in Soheili.
Tell us about the mangrove forests. Perhaps some of our readers are not very familiar with them.
Mangrove forests are forests that grow and develop in tropical regions. They are not unique to Iran. Their roots are adapted to being submerged, and the roots of these trees filter water. They desalinate seawater through three layers found on their roots, producing fresh water that the trees can then use.
Within the tangled roots of the mangrove forests, which are said to have inspired the design of industrial desalination systems, we can observe a wide variety of aquatic creatures. We see crabs and mudskippers, for example. The mudskipper is an interesting fish with a distinctive and attractive appearance. It burrows into the mud, loosening it in a way that is almost like ploughing the soil, allowing air to move through the mud.
So, we have a unique ecosystem in the mangrove forest. There are shrimp, Gariz fish and Jahro fish. It is an ecosystem that has been building and regenerating itself for thousands of years, while humans also benefit from it.
So, the wonder is that you have a forest growing and thriving in salt water, which is something truly remarkable and extraordinary in its own right.
Yes. Interestingly, this mangrove forest has been designated as a biosphere reserve. When we talk about a reserve in the context of natural sites, it means that the people living around the mangrove forests are custodians on behalf of the world. They are expected to use these resources responsibly, so that future generations can also benefit from them and their quality of life is not diminished.
At the same time, they are accountable to the world for how they protect these forests. These forests are registered within Qeshm Geopark. Qeshm Geopark was the first geopark in West Asia, and today we have three geoparks in Iran that are registered with UNESCO.
Let me start questions about regenerative tourism with one of the most fundamental questions. What is that type of traveling and how does it differ from sustainable tourism? And was sustainable tourism not enough in itself?
Sustainable tourism emerged from CoP20, with the collective resolve to forge a more sustainable future for the world's natural heritage.
At one point, we needed that concept. What it basically means is that we examine the impacts of tourism, identify them, and try to reduce the negative impacts. But, as has been demonstrated by experience around the world, negative impacts can never be reduced to zero. The aim in sustainable tourism is therefore to further develop and increase the positive impacts of tourism.
But regenerative tourism has a difference from sustainable tourism.
In a way, regenerative tourism represents a new paradigm in global tourism. It means working alongside the local community through participatory approaches, so that while they are managing the impacts, they are also able to do what is truly the right thing to do. Tourism is approached with a forward-looking perspective. It is not simply about tourists coming to a village.
In the context of sustainable tourism, we have always opposed mass tourism. But now, in regenerative tourism, we say that perhaps 10 tourists who behave destructively and damage the environment can cause more harm than 100 tourists who understand nature tourism and appreciate and respect the local community.
These distinctions have emerged in the definitions because the economic and social impacts that tourism should have on a village cannot simply be defined or achieved through restrictions alone.
You said that regenerative tourism is a new paradigm. I want to ask you about a possible paradox. A tourist comes into a village, consumes water and spends money. We want to know what that tourist can actually do for the environment so that, when they leave the village, they have left something behind--that the environment is better, the local community has earned more income, young people in the village become interested in staying there, and traditions or even foods that are at risk of disappearing are revived. What can happen to create these positive impacts?
In regenerative tourism, we are making a transition from sustainable tourism, in a sense. We are not rejecting sustainable tourism; rather, we are going beyond it and adding another dimension.
For example, when a tourist visits Soheili Village during the season for planting Kong-e Harra, the local community involves the tourist in the process and the event. Chichak-haye Harraye Soheili is an event during which children go into the mangrove forest and collect mangrove seeds themselves.
The child who is being educated and raised in this way is learning in front of the tourist. The children draw pictures there and explain the process of growing the seedlings to visitors. In this way, the tourist sees the next generation. If the tourist is interested, they are given the opportunity to plant 10 mangrove seedlings of their own.
Each tourist becomes, in a way, a cultural ambassador for the village they have visited. They see that, with the growth of tourism, young people in the village are becoming interested in staying there.
For example, we had someone from Qeshm city who had a real-estate office there. He has now returned to the village, established an eco-lodge and is living in the village.
What could be more beautiful than creating entrepreneurship in this way? A person can earn a living while remaining connected to their identity and taking pride in it. This is social capital. They explain, introduce and describe this to their guests, and tourists can easily understand the flow of tourism and the local economy.
Another example of local community participation is the fish caught that same day. The fresh fish is cooked by village women in the kitchens of the local restaurants, so the food still retains its homemade taste.
So regenerative tourism is not simply about tourists coming to a village, taking a few photographs and leaving with nothing more than images of the place.
Rather, the tourist creates a deep memory of the village with the help of local people. For example, the local Nan-e to-mushi bread is prepared for them early in the morning. And if they want to participate and bake it themselves, they are given the opportunity to do so.
These are the truly deep experiences that regenerative tourism offers.
When we talk about tourism in Iran in broader terms, both for international and domestic tourists, cities such as the lush cities of northern Iran in Gilan and Mazandaran provinces, as well as historic cities such as Isfahan, Shiraz, Yazd, Tabriz, Qazvin and Kerman, have traditionally been viewed as tourism destinations. But over the past few years, there has been a greater focus on Iran’s villages. How do you see this shift, and what capabilities and potential do you think Iran’s villages have for tourism? And how much could they actually contribute to attracting tourists in the future?
One of the very positive developments is that, if we look back, whenever we talked to travel agencies or did a quick search on various platforms, we would see the classic tourism route in Iran. It would generally start in Tabriz, then continue through Qazvin, Tehran, Kashan, Isfahan, Yazd, Kerman and Shiraz, and sometimes eventually end in Bandar Abbas or Bushehr.
But over the past few years, particularly from around 2017 onward, we can say that rural tourism in Iran has gained momentum. Some people become tired of their mechanical, urban lifestyles and of modern life, and they want to go and stay with a rural family, surrounded by nature, in search of something they feel they have lost.
And what is that something? It is an authentic Iranian culture that they have continually heard stories and narratives about. When we want to talk about tradition and authenticity, the village is still one of the places where we can find these things.
In a village, you have nature; you can see authentic, traditional architecture. In most villages, traditional clothing still exists, as do traditional foods and cuisine.
Today, whenever we buy something, if it carries a “healthy” label, it attracts more customers. Tourists, too, know that they are making a choice that will give them the greatest return--not only in terms of the money they spend, but also in terms of the time they devote to the trip. They want that time to create the greatest possible value for them.
Q: So, in order to reach this desirable point, what challenges do you think we face?
When a tourist enters a village, they have certain expectations. The most important thing that needs to happen is education.
When we talk about education, we are not simply saying that tourists need to know what behavioral guidelines they should follow and what boundaries they should respect. The local community, on the other hand, also needs to be aware of these issues.
One of the most important aspects is intercultural communication. A villager who has previously interacted with people in their own ethnic and cultural community, using the simple language of everyday life, may suddenly find themselves hosting people from different ethnic backgrounds and tourists of different nationalities.
They therefore need training. And one of the most important pillars of tourism and hospitality is health and safety, which they need to learn about. They must also be able to introduce the ancient culture inherited from their ancestors to tourists in a clear, fluent and engaging way.
Q: Who is responsible for providing this training?
When we look at the stakeholders involved in tourism, the first responsible body is naturally the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts.
On the other hand, if we are talking specifically about villages, the largest number of tourism establishments found in Iran’s villages are eco-lodges. We have a professional community of eco-lodge operators, while educational institutions can serve as the implementers of training programs.
But we should not look at this phenomenon from only one dimension. The village head, for example, needs to receive appropriate training, with the Ministry of Interior responsible for that area. The village council also needs its own training, while people working in tourism establishments need specialized training relevant to their activities.
And the most important group that we focus on in rural tourism and, particularly, regenerative tourism is children and adolescents.
They need to be educated in a way that helps them understand the value of their authenticity and traditional clothing. They should recognize their traditional dress as something valuable--not merely as something being presented to tourists--and understand that tourists have traveled there to experience the tangible and intangible cultural heritage of the village.
Q: As a final question, I’d like to ask you to share some of your experiences of the villages you have visited and, in a way, encourage our audience to travel to rural areas.
Based on my experience, I believe that what is particularly valuable is the fact that Iran now has five villages that have managed to join the Best Tourism Villages network. Each of these villages has its own very distinctive and unique character and is shaped by a particular climate and geographical environment.
When we talk about Kandovan, for example, we are talking about a terraced village nestled in the heart of the mountains, with its beautiful traditional houses. Tourists have the opportunity to stay in this authentic architectural setting and enjoy foods that are naturally produced and processed in the village.
From there, let’s move toward Esfahak, a village in South Khorasan province. This village was destroyed by an earthquake, and its people came together and rebuilt it from the ground up. Here, we can see a kind of translation of resilience into practice. This is also a clear example of regeneration: the villagers have revived even the traditional mud bricks, restoring the way these houses were originally built and the standards and characteristics of the bricks that were used.
Then there is Kandelous, which is now among the world’s Best Tourism Villages. The village has the legend of Mina and the Leopard. I think it is very interesting when this story is told to us in that setting, together with the Mina and Leopard dolls. It raises the question of how human beings can interact with wildlife without causing it harm.
Then we come to Shafiabad, where women are actively involved in tourism. Through regenerative tourism there, visitors realize that part of the money they spend on purchases in the village goes toward restoring the qanats.
These women have reached a level of vision and empowerment that allows them to set aside part of their income to restore the qanats, despite the very high cost of doing so. Life in the desert depends on water, and a qanat is essentially a source of life in the desert.
And then we come back to Soheili, where wetland tourism, culinary tourism and the conservation-oriented use of the mangrove forests create a very different experience. A tourist can take a wooden boat into the mangrove forest, catch a fish and have that same fish cooked for them. They can also learn how the food is prepared. At some of the eco-lodges, visitors are even taught how to weave mats.
When a tourist comes and learns a skill, they are acquiring something new. Human beings are naturally inclined to learn and develop, to keep their minds active and prevent them from becoming stagnant. And this is done through the hands, through developing practical skills and becoming capable with one's own hands.
These five villages have five different stories to tell. Anyone who plans a journey through Kandovan and Kandelous and then continues to Shafiabad, Esfahak and Soheili will encounter an authentic culture at the heart of Iran.
These villages have earned recognition through the UN Tourism’s rigorous evaluation process, and the people of these villages are waiting to welcome you, the tourists, with the doors of their homes open.

Defence spending has exposed tensions within Italy’s governing coalition, including with Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini’s League.

Syria demands Israeli withdrawal after attack on Abu al-Duhur Airport
Damascus says the August 18 strike was intended to disrupt Syria’s recovery and has called for the restoration of the military lines that existed before December 8, 2024
Syria has accused Israel of carrying out an attack on Abu al-Duhur Airport on August 18, describing the strike as part of a wider effort to destabilize the country and obstruct its state-building process.
In a statement carried by Syrian state media, Damascus argued that the significance of the attack went beyond any immediate damage to the airport. Syrian authorities said it sent a political and security message intended to weaken the state as it works to restore its institutions, rebuild the economy and attract international investment.
Damascus also renewed its demand for Israeli forces to withdraw to the positions they held before December 8, 2024. It also called for full compliance with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement, the framework governing the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces.
Syrian authorities presented adherence to that agreement as an essential step toward preventing further military escalation. They argued that Israel’s continued operations threaten both Syria’s sovereignty and broader regional stability.
Despite its strong language, Damascus said it intends to address the dispute through diplomatic and political channels rather than enter another direct conflict.
The Syrian statement acknowledged the devastating consequences that renewed warfare could have for a country already facing major reconstruction and development challenges. It said the government would pursue what it described as “diplomatic confrontation” while avoiding actions that could be used to justify additional Israeli strikes.
That position reflects an attempt to balance two priorities: maintaining Syria’s territorial demands while limiting the risk of a wider war.
Damascus also praised Türkiye for condemning the attacks and supporting Syria’s call for the implementation of the 1974 agreement.
By emphasizing Turkish support, Syrian authorities appeared to signal that they are seeking broader diplomatic pressure on Israel rather than responding through military escalation.
Syrian authorities portrayed the country as entering a new period of sovereign decision-making in which outside military action would not be allowed to dictate its alliances or development plans.
Damascus also did not identify the specific diplomatic measures it plans to pursue.
Nevertheless, the government’s demands were explicit: a return to the military positions that existed before December 8, 2024, renewed observance of the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and an end to attacks on Syrian territory.

US President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Tehran "wants to make a deal" to end the war, forecasting a rapid decline in domestic fuel costs once hostilities cease.
 
"Look, it could end before the midterms, but it'll end after the midterms," Trump told reporters in Ireland, where he attended the Amgen Irish Open golf tournament hosted at his Trump International Golf Links resort.

"We will ultimately get out unless we decide to stay and keep the oil, like Venezuela," he added.
 
The ongoing Iran war, now in its seventh month, has claimed the lives of 18 US servicemembers and triggered sustained volatility across global energy routes.

Boris Johnson and Merz adviser's train stopped near Polish border for evacuation due to drone attack, but all-clear given
German newspaper Der Spiegel has learned that passengers on a train carrying Günter Sautter, one of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's closest advisers, security advisers from other European countries and former UK prime minister Boris Johnson were woken and prepared for evacuation near the Polish border following an attack on another Ukrainian train. The evacuation did not take place, however, as the all-clear was given after no further drones were detected.
Source: Spiegel, citing sources; Carl Bildt, former Swedish prime minister, on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to information obtained by Spiegel, Sautter was travelling by train from Kyiv to Poland on the night of 12-13 September. At around 05:00, the train stopped near the Polish border; some passengers were evacuated from the train due to drone strikes in the border region.
The security measures were prompted by an incident on the same railway line, where a Kyiv-Warsaw train was also targeted by a drone near the Polish border in the early morning. The state-run railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) reported that the locomotive of the train was struck, but no one was injured.
Sautter was in the Ukrainian capital alongside security advisers from the UK, France and Italy, as well as representatives of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's government, to discuss possible peace negotiations with Russia. On 13 September, he attended the international YES conference on security.
In addition to Sautter, the train also carried security advisers from other European governments, members of the German Bundestag, diplomats and academics.
Former UK prime minister Boris Johnson also travelled to Poland on this special train after the conference.
No passengers were injured. The train stopped after a drone alert, prompting conductors to wake passengers and evacuate them. The all-clear was given shortly afterwards after no further drones were detected.
Bildt explained that passengers were instructed to evacuate, but the order was cancelled and the train was able to continue its journey.
Robin Wagener, a member of the Green Party in the Bundestag, was also on board the special train. The MP expressed his outrage following the attacks.
"These drone attacks are blind terror against the Ukrainian civilian population and a dangerous escalation of Putin's war," Wagener told Spiegel.
The parliamentarian views the attacks as a provocation against Ukraine's supporters.
"Russia is becoming increasingly unprincipled and is playing with fire right on the border of the European Union and NATO; we must finally put a clear end to this terror," Wagener stressed.
Background:
- Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stated that the Russian attack complicated his team's crossing of the Ukrainian-Polish border.
- Dariusz Sinecki, spokesperson for the Nadbużański Border Guard Unit in Poland, said that a drone hit a lorry near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing on the night of 12-13 September.
- Earlier, Andrii Demchenko, spokesperson for Ukraine's State Border Guard Service, said that the Yahodyn border crossing itself on the border with Poland had not been hit.
- Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that there had been no violation of the country's airspace.
- Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this was Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin's terrorism, which is "knocking directly on the doors" of the EU and NATO.
- Ukrzaliznytsia reported that Russia had struck the locomotive of a passenger train near the border with Poland.

Norman Finkelstein’s latest book indicts those ‘in high places’ for genocide in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

GAZA’S GRAVEDIGGERS
An Inquiry Into Corruption in High Places
by Norman G. Finkelstein
409 pp; OR Books; $34.95
This is a hard book to read. Norman Finkelstein looks closely at Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and over 409 densely written pages, he is unsparing about some of the high-ranking and influential people who let it happen.
Finkelstein needs no introduction. He’s now in his 70s, the son of Holocaust survivors, and he’s spent 50 years chronicling Israel’s murderous apartheid policy toward Palestinians. He’s written 17 books, most of them about Israel/Palestine, and he sacrificed his academic career as the penalty for telling hard truths. He has never been successfully challenged on his major findings of fact. He is first and foremost a scholar, rigorous in his attention to detail, and this latest book is stuffed with evidence: hundreds of references and long, detailed, numbing-but-important documents.
In Gaza’s Gravediggers, he focuses not on the Israelis who actually carried out the mass killings, but on those “in high places” around the globe who enabled and continue to enable the genocide. He says at the beginning, “… this volume documents the complicity, born of cupidity and corruption, cowardice and careerism — of officials in high places. Its purpose is to send a firm warning to those occupying positions of public trust: We are watching you.”
Four detailed case studies illustrate his argument.
Charge Number 1 in Finkelstein’s indictment is demolishing the allegation that Hamas committed mass rape as a “weapon of war,” starting on October 7, 2023. He spends 52 pages scrutinizing and refuting the widely publicized rape allegations, such as the notorious New York Times article, “Screams Without Words,” and the subsequent documentary film hosted by Sheryl Sandberg, the former Facebook top executive, titled “Screams Before Silence,” which has 1.5 million views on YouTube.
Finkelstein’s summary and interpretation of the motives for the dishonesty are important. He does not deny that Palestinian armed groups committed certain war crimes on October 7, including killing civilians and taking hostages. So why manufacture the charge of widespread rape? He points out that “the target audience of Israeli hasbara has always been U.S. public opinion.” In other words, eliminate the false charges of systematic rape, and American opinion would probably have turned even more promptly and decisively against Israel’s genocide.
Finkelstein next indicts the United Nations Human Rights Council for issuing a report that he charges “watered down Israeli crimes.” The Council, in May 2021, had created an “Independent International Commission of Inquiry,” headed by Navi Pillay, a former United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. He looked closely at the Pillay Commission’s findings after October 7, and concluded that it had downplayed Israel’s crimes. He contrasted its findings with Amnesty International’s verdict, which said straightforwardly that Israel was committing a “genocide.”
Finkelstein’s third charge focuses on the International Court of Justice. First, after the Israeli onslaught started, South Africa immediately brought a case before the court, which promptly, in January 2024, issued an “Order” that found that “Israel was plausibly committing genocide and indicated provisional measures.” Of the court’s 17 voting judges, only one voted against the entire Order: Judge Julia Sebutinde, from Uganda.
He scrutinized Sebutinde’s opinion at enormous length, and concluded that “huge swaths” of her legal reasoning “were demonstrably plagiarized from publications by Israel’s stalwarts, [which] posed in stark form the question whether she was being bribed or blackmailed by Israel.” He substantiated his charge with a 48-page appendix, which lists long excerpts of Judge Sebutinde’s opinions alongside the sources that she all-too-apparently plagiarized from.
His zeal in this instance may at first seem somewhat excessive. After all, the overwhelming majority of the Court’s judges did find that Israel was plausibly committing genocide. But Finkelstein is understandably enraged that Israel and its sympathizers could apparently even reach into the Court and try to tarnish its findings. Again, his aim in this particular book is not to indict the Israeli military and the Netanyahu government directly, but to focus on the global figures and institutions that let them get away with the mass killings. (What’s more, if Americans learned that even a single Justice on our Supreme Court had been “bribed or blackmailed,” we would, of course, demand an investigation.)
Finkelstein’s last charge is briefer but still important. We’ve already seen how the International Court of Justice in January 2024 started issuing Orders that found that “Israel was plausibly committing genocide.” But then, on April 24 that same year, Joan Donaghue, the Court’s former president who had just stepped down, “dropped a bombshell” during an interview on the BBC. Donaghue off-handedly made comments that undermined the decision the Court had just reached. As Finkelstein points out, the pro-Israel media immediately jumped on her “off-the-cuff” remarkss to tarnish the Court’s finding of genocide. He painstakingly dissects the contortions in her television interview and charges that she had uttered “a shameful and shameless lie.”
On balance, Finkelstein’s intense scrutiny may seem excessive. After all, in this book he is not indicting Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s military leaders, or Israeli warplane pilots. Nor is he exposing President Biden, former Secretary of State Anthony Blinken, or Biden’s National Security Advisor, Jake Sullivan — people whose responsibility for the mass killings in Gaza is also clear.
Norman Finkelstein again explains what motivated him to research this enormous indictment. Here is part of his Epilogue:
This book was written to expose lies and restore Truth. It will not save lives. The genocide in Gaza is too far gone. Is the book then pointless? For the dead, yes. But for the living, no. The demand sounded in the Book’s Prologue stands: not just the perpetuators in Israel but also their accomplices in high places — blood-soaked, all — must be held accountable.”

Germany Weighs Restricting NATO Defense Plans if AfD Governs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

German defense officials are weighing procedural measures to bar regional administrations from accessing confidential national and NATO defense plans if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) enters government following state elections, Bloomberg reported.
The security contingency discussions were prompted by regional voting in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD secured 44% of the vote, capturing 39 of 83 seats in the state parliament and falling just three seats short of an outright majority.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius aims to ensure that any state administration led or influenced by the pro-Russian AfD would be legally and operationally prevented from accessing sensitive defense documentation that could be shared with Moscow.
At the center of the security review is Germany’s Operational Plan (OPLAN), a confidential, 1,000-page defense blueprint drafted by German authorities alongside NATO planners.
The document coordinates joint defense responses, military mobility, and emergency protocols between federal authorities and regional governments during a conventional military crisis or allied defense emergency.
According to an insider familiar with the discussions, Pistorius outlined the security initiatives during a closed-door consultation with defense policy experts from governing coalition parliamentary groups.
German defense planners operate under the working assumption that OPLAN protocols could be activated in the event of open escalation between NATO and Russia.
Budanov Eyes Trilateral Ukraine Peace Talks in October
Regional access controls
OPLAN relies heavily on Germany’s central geographic location within Europe, where the country functions as the primary logistical transit corridor and rear operational staging area for allied NATO forces advancing toward eastern positions during an Article 5 contingency.
Under standard operational protocols, the comprehensive version of OPLAN is provided directly to the heads of all 16 German federal states, while regional administrative bodies and interior ministries receive access to specific annexes and logistical chapters pertinent to their geographic territory.
Over recent months, German officials have debated legal and administrative mechanisms to safeguard military intelligence in the event that the AfD takes control of regional interior ministries or state police forces.
Proposals under review include redacting specific logistical chapters, compartmentalizing infrastructure data, or reclassifying regional transit schedules to restrict access exclusively to vetted federal personnel.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), classifies the AfD’s regional branches in Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, and Saxony as confirmed right-wing extremist entities deemed hostile to the country’s free democratic basic order.
Political fallout in Berlin
The debate over military intelligence arrives amid political reverberations across Berlin following the Saxony-Anhalt election, where the AfD achieved its strongest regional result to date. The governing Christian Democratic Union (CDU), led in the state by incumbent Minister-President Sven Schulze, dropped to roughly 18% of the vote.
The electoral triumph placed the AfD – led in the state by 35-year-old Ullrich Siegmund – within reach of attempting to assemble a governing cabinet. National co-leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla hailed the outcome as a historic turning point and a strategic template for federal parliamentary elections in 2029.
In Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faced mounting internal party pressure over the scale of the defeat, with CDU employee wing chairman Dennis Radtke describing the result as a “watershed moment” that demands a fundamental reassessment of the party’s containment strategy.
Although the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority in Magdeburg, forming an alternative governing coalition remains mathematically fraught.
The traditional cross-party cordon sanitaire against the AfD would require complex negotiations among the CDU, Social Democrats (SPD), Greens, and the socialist Left Party, while the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could emerge as a potential kingmaker if it clears the 5% parliamentary threshold.

NEW DELHI, September 13. /TASS/. Russia will keep a close eye on the situation in Yemen, which is fraught with a major escalation, Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov said.

The armed confrontation between the Saudi-backed government forces and Houthi rebels has been continuing in Yemen since August 2014. The situation deteriorated dramatically this summer. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saria said on Friday that on September 3, the rebel movement Ansar Allah has launched an operation on Yemen’s western coast to push Saudi forces out of the region. In his words, it was prompted by "Saudi-backed attacks on people and villages on the western coast that have been continuing for years." The operation resulted in the Saudi forces being squeezed out of the Taiz and Hodeida governorates, from an area of 5,400 square kilometers, Saria stated.

Global interest in BRICS keeps growing – Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:23:13 UTC
22:23:13 KST

Global interest in BRICS keeps growing – Putin
International interest in BRICS “continues to grow” as the group’s values and independent approach attract countries around the world, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Sunday.
Speaking at a BRICS Outreach/BRICS Plus session that concluded its 18th summit in New Delhi, Putin pointed to the broad participation in the meeting as evidence of its growing appeal.
“Our basic values and ideals, such as commitment to an independent and autonomous course and the desire to resolve problems collectively based on international law and the key provisions of the UN Charter, appeal to many around the world,” he said.
BRICS has expanded significantly beyond its original five members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – in recent years and introduced a partner-country category for states seeking closer cooperation without full membership.
Putin described the organization as “one of the powerful driving forces” behind strengthening “genuine multilateralism” and forming a “new, fairer multipolar world order.”
Trade among BRICS members has reached $1.2 trillion, and they account for almost a quarter of global exports and 49% of global GDP growth, according to Putin.
“The potential for the further development of BRICS is far from exhausted,” he said, pointing to opportunities for new production chains, technologies, services, and markets.
BRICS countries have also developed their own channels for moving goods, services, and capital, allowing financial and commercial operations to be conducted “without paying attention to external pressure,” Putin said.
He urged participants to consider Russian proposals for “building BRICS payment and settlement-depository infrastructure,” as well as establishing a reinsurance mechanism and a grain exchange.
Practical steps have already been taken. On the eve of the summit, the Russian Direct Investment Fund, BRICS Pay and BRICS Pay India agreed to explore integrating the payment platform with India’s existing infrastructure and to prepare pilot cross-border payment projects.
A group-wide payment mechanism has yet to be launched, however. The New Delhi Declaration said the BRICS Payment Task Force would continue seeking practical solutions for cross-border transactions.

Children are disappearing, while the number of pensioners is growing: Russia’s demographic crisis is worsening
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
16:22:34 EEST
22:22:34 KST

Children are disappearing, while the number of pensioners is growing: Russia’s demographic crisis is worsening
Kyiv • UNN
The number of children under five in Russia has fallen to 6.5 million, while the number of people aged over 65 has risen to 23.7 million. Intelligence services forecast a shortage of young professionals.
Russia is facing a deep demographic crisis that began as early as the beginning of the 1990s. Over the past decades, the number of young children in the country has more than halved, while the number of people over the age of 65 has increased significantly. This is reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, as reported by UNN.
Details
While the global community is only now beginning to record the global aging of the population, Russia plunged into a deep demographic crisis as early as the beginning of the 1990s. The number of elderly people in the Russian Federation has long exceeded the number of young children, and the gap between generations is deepening every year, leaving the country without a demographic future. The catastrophic trends are evidenced by the inverted age structure of the population. If, at the end of the 1980s, the number of children under the age of five and people over 65 was approximately the same—about 14.5 million people—then over the past decades the situation has become critical
According to the agency, the number of infants has more than halved—to 6.5 million, while the number of pensioners has risen to 23.7 million.
The intelligence service cites chronically low birth rates, which remain below the level necessary even for simple population replacement, as one of the main causes of the demographic changes.
Despite regular statements by pro-government experts about the country's "relative youth" compared with Japan or the EU, the real figures point to a severe reduction in the working-age population and an unbearable burden on the social system. Russians are not merely aging; they are also being left without prospects for replenishing the human resources
In addition, according to available data, the continued decline in the proportion of children means that within one or two decades the country will face an acute shortage of young specialists, and there will simply be no one to give birth to a new generation.
Russia has effectively led the negative global trend, overtaking the global demographic turning point by almost 30 years. Against the backdrop of economic and social problems, the country is confidently moving along the path of depopulation, transforming into a state with fading demographic potential
Let us recall
In 26 regions of Russia, 165 abandoned settlements were eliminated in less than eight months of 2026. According to Ukrainian intelligence, the leaders in the rate of depopulation and legal liquidation of villages were Novgorod region (according to various data, from 21 to 35 villages erased from the map) and Kostroma region (from 21 to 23 settlements).

Kremlin foreign policy aide says territorial issue remains key to Ukraine settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:21:17 UTC
22:21:17 KST

Elena Teslova
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said on Sunday that resolving the territorial issue remains the main task in efforts to settle the Ukraine conflict.
Speaking in an interview with Russian media, Ushakov said each side of the conflict has its own view of what it could seek to advance in negotiations.
“One of the main issues is the territorial one. That is true. There is undoubtedly a lot of work still to be done,” he said.
Asked if the Ukraine issue was discussed at the BRICS summit in New Delhi, Ushakov said only Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira mentioned the issue in his speech.
“I noticed yesterday that during the leaders’ speeches at the summit, only one — the Brazilian foreign minister — mentioned Ukraine, while all the other leaders simply left it aside,” he said.
Asked whether this indicated solidarity within BRICS over the Ukraine conflict, Ushakov said he believed it reflected an understanding of Russia’s position.
“In my view, this speaks of an understanding of our position. And what our president explained during his conversations with individual leaders is, of course, going into our asset column,” he said.
Meanwhile, the Ukraine issue was among the main topics during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in India, Ushakov said.
Moscow hopes the peace process regarding Ukraine will eventually produce a positive result, he added.
“The peace process on Ukraine is continuing. And we hope that sooner or later it will lead to a positive result,” he said.
According to Ushakov, agreements reached by Russia and the US during the Aug. 15, 2025, presidential meeting in Anchorage, Alaska, form the basis of the Ukraine peace process, which he described as “lengthy and complicated.”
“The negotiating process does not start from scratch. All this — the Anchorage agreements — constitutes the essence of a process that is lengthy, of course, but at the same time complicated,” he said.
Russia’s demands for a settlement remain unchanged, with no tightening of its position, Ushakov said.
“I would say that the demands remain the same, there has been no tightening. We simply would like these demands to be fulfilled sooner or later — preferably sooner,” he said.
Abu Dhabi has been discussed as one possible venue for trilateral Russia-US-Ukraine talks, while Türkiye and other countries also confirmed their readiness to host the negotiations, Ushakov said.
“Abu Dhabi was discussed as an option,” Ushakov said when asked whether the UAE capital had been considered during Putin’s meeting with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Ushakov described Abu Dhabi as “a suitable place” for the talks, and the UAE crown prince confirmed to Putin that the UAE was ready to provide a venue for Ukraine negotiations, Ushakov said.
When the place and the date of such a meeting are agreed, Putin will determine who will head the Russian delegation at trilateral talks on a Ukraine settlement, he said.
Ushakov highlighted that a large number of issues still need to be agreed on before a trilateral meeting between the Russian, US and Ukrainian leaders.
However, progress on the territorial issue would make it easier to reach agreement on the remaining matters, he said.
Ushakov also said he believed US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had gained a better understanding of Russia’s position following their talks with Putin.
The two US envoys visited Moscow on Sept. 5 for talks with Putin before traveling to Kyiv on Sept. 6 for discussions with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Moscow and Kyiv have since signaled interest in resuming trilateral negotiations, with October discussed as a possible timeframe.

Russia strikes passenger train near Polish border as drone swarms reach deeper into western Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:10:51 UTC
22:10:51 KST

Russia struck a passenger train just two kilometers from Ukraine’s border with Poland on 13 September, as Moscow continued a second day of attacks on Ukraine’s railway network and expanded strikes against transport and logistics infrastructure far from the front line.
Russia is increasingly using its expanding drone fleet to reach transport, logistics, industrial and civilian infrastructure deep inside Ukraine. Western regions, long considered safer because of their distance from the front, are now seeing strikes on railways and border crossings, making even civilian travel and routes out of the country increasingly dangerous.
The latest attack took place in Ukraine’s north-western Volyn Oblast, near the Yahodyn border crossing with Poland. According to Ukraine’s state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia, a Russian drone struck the locomotive of a passenger train.
A monitoring team detected the threat in advance and warned the train crew, preventing casualties. The railway operator said trains to Warsaw and back were already running again after the strike, although with significant delays.
A gas station was also struck in a Russian drone strike near the Yahodyn crossing, causing a large fire, according to UNN, adding to the danger around a key transport route between Ukraine and Poland.
Poland also issued an air-raid alert for areas near the Ukrainian border, including Włodawa, Łęczyński and Świdnik counties and the cities of Chełm and Krasnystaw.
The attacks came alongside Russian strikes on railway infrastructure in several other parts of Ukraine.
Update: Diplomatic train may have been Russian drone’s target
Update 19:00: Ukrzaliznytsia later said a diplomatic train carrying security advisers from several EU member states and former European leaders, including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson, had been at Yahodyn shortly before the strike. Another train at the station during the attack carried former CIA Director David Petraeus.
Ukrzaliznytsia said the Russian drone may have been targeting the diplomatic train, which departed earlier than scheduled as railway staff adjusted train movements in real time because of the ongoing threat of Russian strikes. The operator said it continues to change routes and schedules as tracks are damaged or blocked by attacks.
Russia targets railways across Ukraine
Ukrzaliznytsia said this was the second consecutive day of Russian attacks on the railway network.
On 12 September, Russian drones struck railway facilities in Lutsk, Volyn Oblast, including a passenger train, as well as Fastiv, Kyiv Oblast. Passengers were evacuated after the threat was detected.
Ukrzaliznytsia said its monitoring center and railway personnel remain on heightened alert as Russia continues targeting the network. Evacuations and diversions have caused delays on several routes, including services toward Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih.
Russia also attacked a railway infrastructure site in Vinnytsia Oblast on 13 September, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
Russia’s drone campaign is expanding
Russian attacks are increasingly reaching critical infrastructure and civilian areas across Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia struck energy facilities, railway sites, businesses and residential buildings during the latest wave of attacks, including missile and drone strikes on Odesa.
Zelenskyy said Russia had launched around 2,100 drones against Ukraine in the past week, alongside nearly 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 78 missiles.
He said Russia is using jet-powered Geran drones to “destroy the economy and destroy people’s lives.”
Russia has sharply increased its use of upgraded Geran attack drones in recent months, which are faster than earlier versions and can cover the long distances needed to strike targets deep inside Ukraine. Their growing speed and scale are putting additional pressure on Ukraine’s air-defense system, which has to detect and intercept large numbers of drones across the country.
“Russia’s terrorism is a common threat for many,” Zelenskyy said, arguing that the threat must be defeated in Ukraine rather than allowed to spread further into Europe.
Border crossings increasingly targeted
The strike near Yahodyn comes after Russia began targeting Ukrainian border crossings farther from the front line.
Since late August, Russian forces have struck at least five Ukrainian crossings with Moldova and NATO member Romania. The crossings handle civilian traffic, trade and logistics that are increasingly important to Ukraine as the war continues.
On 9 September, Russian drones struck the Starokozache crossing with Moldova, killing two civilians and injuring three others. One Russian drone entered Moldovan airspace and flew toward Romania, prompting NATO aircraft conducting air-policing duties to scramble.
Russia also struck the Orlivka ferry crossing on the Romanian border twice in early September.
The attacks prompted growing concern in Poland. On 10 September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland expected Russia could target Ukrainian border crossings with Poland as Moscow expands its strikes against transport and logistics routes.
Tusk said Poland had received intelligence indicating that similar attacks could occur against crossings involving other countries. He also warned that Poland and Europe needed to prepare for different scenarios along Europe’s eastern flank.
The strike near Yahodyn came only three days after that warning.
Poland expects Russia to target border crossings as attacks on Ukraine escalate – Russia has already hit crossings with Moldova and Romania
“Russia is trying to expand the geography of its terror”
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russia was deliberately expanding the geography of its attacks.
“Moscow tries to expand the geography of its terror,” Sybiha said, arguing that Russia is trying to turn the entire territory of Ukraine into a battlefield as it fails to achieve its objectives on the front.
He said Moscow was targeting “civilians, trains, and the infrastructure that keeps the country moving.”
Sybiha called for stronger air defenses, interceptors and counter-drone capabilities, as well as measures targeting Russia’s drone production and supply chains.
In a separate statement after the Yahodyn attack, Sybiha said Russia’s strikes near the Polish border were “not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders.”
“This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” he said, urging European countries to respond with stronger sanctions.
Attacks moving closer to NATO
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said members of his ministry had been stuck at the same Ukrainian-Polish border crossing only hours before the latest images emerged because of the Russian drone threat.
“Russia’s attacks are becoming more intense and moving ever closer to NATO and the EU,” Tsahkna said.
