How Israel’s destruction of south Lebanon is making displacement permanent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:09:22 UTC
22:09:22 KST

How Israel’s destruction of south Lebanon is making displacement permanent
With lost livelihoods, destroyed homes and little security, many displaced Lebanese are faced with an entrenched reality.
Beirut, Lebanon – More than six months after Israel intensified its war on Lebanon, a displacement crisis is slowly solidifying.
At its highest point in April, more than 1.2 million people were displaced by Israeli attacks on Lebanon.
Today, the figure stands at about 330,000, according to estimates by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) – but humanitarian workers say the drop should not be interpreted as permanent or even durable.
Nadine Mazloum, of the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), said displacement patterns remain “highly fluid and often reversible” due to the possibility of renewed attacks.
While the “overall number of displaced people has fallen substantially from the peak of more than 1.2 million, that should not be mistaken for a resolution of the crisis”, she added.
‘This is our land’
Israel and the Lebanese group Hezbollah have been fighting since October 2023, with varying levels of intensity.
On March 2, 2026, Hezbollah responded to continued Israeli attacks on Lebanon for the first time in more than a year, saying it was in retaliation for more than 10,000 violations of a 2024 ceasefire and for the assassination two days earlier of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on the first day of the United States-Israel war on Iran.
Israel then intensified its air attacks on Lebanon, while also reinvading southern Lebanon for the second time in less than two years. It currently occupies more than 50 villages.
The offensive has killed more than 4,380 people and drove hundreds of thousands from their homes – predominantly in southern Lebanon but also in the eastern Bekaa Valley and parts of the capital, Beirut, and its southern suburbs.
Displaced people took shelter wherever they could. In Beirut, some set up tents along the waterfront or corniche, or rented apartments in neighbourhoods deemed safer. But many of the displaced were also attacked, including in double-tap strikes.
A series of ceasefire announcements and a June framework agreement, which came after direct, US-sponsored talks between Israel and Lebanon, has not stopped the Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon.
However, bombardment on the rest of the country has eased, with more than 810,000 people either returning home or to places nearby – often to damaged houses with destroyed infrastructure.
One of them is Soujoud Ramadan, a woman from Froun, a town on a so-called “Yellow Line” – a military zone claimed by Israel that stretches roughly 10km (6 miles) north of the Lebanon-Israel border.
Froun was included in June’s framework deal under which Israeli forces were supposed to withdraw from “pilot zones” and the Lebanese army was intended to enter and disarm Hezbollah.
While much of Froun lies in rubble from Israeli air attacks, the Israeli military has not set foot in the town since 2024.
Ramadan has returned to her village, but with her home in ruins, she is staying at the local school, which is operating as a shelter for the displaced.
“We came back after the ceasefire,” she said, sitting in front of a small makeshift corner store she manages at the school’s entrance. “We came back because this land is our land and it is impossible for us to give it up.”
‘Ongoing cycle’
Despite their resilience and determination, UNHCR’s Mazloum said many returnees are still not living in complete stability.
“The reality is that many households continue to move between locations as conditions change, making displacement and return part of an ongoing cycle rather than a one-time event,” Mazloum said.
Over time, the impacts of prolonged displacement also compound, extending beyond the immediate needs for food and shelter.
“Many are facing a different set of challenges centred on exhaustion, instability and the gradual erosion of coping mechanisms,” Mazloum said. “Savings have been depleted, debts have accumulated and support networks are increasingly stretched. Families that have been paying rent for months often face mounting financial pressure at the same time that livelihoods remain disrupted.”
According to the latest IOM data, some 80 percent of displaced people are concentrated in five districts: Beirut hosts about 31 percent of the displaced, while Sidon, Tyre, Chouf and Aley host 15 percent, 14 percent, 11 percent and 9 percent, respectively.
The data also said 17,566 registered displaced people live in 184 collective sites, though that number has likely spiked in recent weeks, particularly with the intensification of Israeli attacks on southern areas, including in the city of Nabatieh. Of the displaced, some 75 percent are living in rented accommodation.
“This area has suffered greatly from the war,” Kamel Jaber, a journalist from Nabatieh, told Al Jazeera about the recent attacks on his city. “Hundreds of shops, warehouses and other [infrastructure] have been destroyed.”
He said that after the 2024 ceasefire, business returned to Nabatieh, but the resumption of the war has devastated the area’s infrastructure and economy. He also said locals began to feel “great anxiety and despair seep into their hearts” as the war has carried on without an end in sight.
‘Not one single standing wall’
Multiple videos have gone viral in recent weeks showing Israeli demolitions in southern villages, with dust shooting into the sky as explosions go off.
Al Jazeera visited the “Yellow Line” in early September and heard loud explosions every few minutes – what locals said were detonations of houses and other infrastructure on the other side of the zone.
Witnesses who have been able to go south of the “Yellow Line” say the closer to the border with Israel, the more widespread the damage is.
Maureen Philippon, the Norwegian Refugee Council’s country director in Lebanon, said that on a journey south, she passed through villages where there is “not one single standing wall”.
She said that after the 2024 ceasefire, many locals from southern villages close to the border returned home, but a “significant number had to flee again” after the resumption of attacks.
“Today they are not envisioning any returns,” said Philippon, warning that “these cycles of violence and damage” add a heavy “psychological weight” for many of the displaced.
With lost livelihoods, destroyed homes and little security or stability to have the confidence to rebuild, many Lebanese straddle displacement while others see theirs become entrenched.
Reports have recently circulated that Israel may pull back to a so-called “Grey Line” that extends up to 4km (2.5 miles) into Lebanese territory. That would mean the border villages would likely stay uninhabited and extend the displacement of the people from those areas. For those from further north, they may return to areas that have been completely demolished, leaving them without a home, electricity, or water infrastructure.
Experts are warning that the permanence of displacement in Lebanon, caused by Israel’s continued war, has far-reaching consequences.
“Humanitarian assistance remains essential, but so too are debris removal, rehabilitation of homes, restoration of public services, and support for livelihoods,” UNHCR’s Mazloum said. “Without those elements, many returns may remain fragile or unsustainable.”

Poland is treating Russian drone strikes near its border with Ukraine and the attack on a passenger train with the "utmost seriousness," Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said Sept. 13.
Russia launched drones overnight at western Ukraine, striking a gas station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing and a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train just 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border.
Kierwinski confirmed that Russia first struck near the Dorohusk–Yahodyn border crossing and later hit the passenger train near the Polish border.
"We are treating these events with the utmost seriousness," Kierwinski wrote on X. "The situation is being constantly monitored. Russia is an enemy of the free world."
The overnight Russian drone assault brought the war unusually close to Poland's border, with multiple strikes reported in Volyn Oblast, Ukraine's northwest, near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk crossing.
Polish Armed Forces' Operational Command spokesperson Jacek Goryszewski said the threat to Poland was "real" as Russian forces attacked Ukrainian regions overnight.
"Drones were operating and even striking targets located very close to the Polish border — just a few to several dozen kilometers away," he said, according to Polish broadcaster RMF24.
The attacks also stranded Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna and members of an Estonian Foreign Ministry delegation at the border crossing. Tsahkna said they were unable to leave Ukraine because of the Russian drone threat.
"Russia's attacks are becoming more intense and moving ever closer to NATO and the EU. Our response must intensify, too," Tsahkna wrote on X. "Every Russian missile and drone Ukraine stops, every Russian capability we help Ukraine destroy, and every additional cost we impose on Moscow strengthens the security of Ukraine and all of Europe."
The overnight attack damaged a gas station near the Yahodyn–Dorohusk crossing in Volyn Oblast, Ukraine's northwesternmost region. Falling drone debris also sparked fires at the station and several trucks parked nearby, Volyn Customs spokesperson Valentyna Chernysh told Suspilne.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned the strike, warning that the attack brought Russia's war directly to the EU and NATO's doorstep.
"This is (Vladimir) Putin's terror, 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," Sybiha wrote on social media.
The Yahodyn border crossing itself was not hit and remains operational, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko told RBC-Ukraine.
Demchenko warned that Russian attacks in the area are intensifying and said the crossing could be temporarily closed if the security situation requires it.

Ukraine drone strikes kill four as Russia attacks close to Poland border
Russia says four people killed in Ukrainian strikes as both sides continue to attack each other with waves of drones.
Several civilians have been killed and more than 20 others wounded overnight as Russia and Ukraine continue to attack each other with waves of drones to try to shift momentum in the more than four-year-long war.
Russia launched 863 drones at Ukraine over the last 24 hours, the Ukrainian General Staff said on Sunday.
Russian forces shot down 389 Ukrainian drones during the night, the country’s Ministry of Defence said, including over Tatarstan, other Russian regions, and the occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Russia carried out two drone attacks near Ukraine’s border with NATO member Poland, Polish and Ukrainian officials said.
The Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing point had briefly stopped working after the attack on a truck about 0.8km (0.5 miles) from Poland, but the crossing has since resumed operations, Polish border guards told the Reuters news agency on Sunday.
Warsaw and Kyiv also said a Russian drone struck a Warsaw-bound train near the Polish border in Ukraine but caused no casualties.
The Russian Defence Ministry said its forces had struck Ukrainian logistics and energy facilities overnight. They also targeted infrastructure facilitating military cargoes from Europe in western Ukraine, it said. Ukraine is dependent on trade and arms shipments from across the Polish, Romanian and Moldovan borders.
In Odesa, at least nine people were injured in a Russian night-time attack, according to Serhiy Lysak, who heads the city’s military administration.
Odesa is home to Ukraine’s main port hub on the Black Sea and has for months faced sustained drone and missile strikes, with Kyiv accusing Moscow of trying to choke off its exports.
Meanwhile, the head of Russia’s Rosatom nuclear corporation, Alexey Likhachev, said two people were killed in a series of drone strikes which targeted fuel trucks near the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.
Separately, authorities in Russia’s Tatarstan region said two people were killed and 12 others were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk.
‘We don’t rule out talks’
Later on Sunday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said three-way negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the United States could take place in October, Russian media reported.
“We do not rule out such a possibility; we are talking about the foreseeable future,” RIA Novosti and TASS news agencies reported, quoting Peskov.
US negotiators have recently visited Kyiv and Moscow in a bid to ramp up negotiations to end the war, while US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, have held talks over the phone.
In an interview aired on Saturday, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami, US, in December for talks.
Several previous attempts at negotiations involving the US have failed.

Italian Ex-Foreign Minister Giulio Terzi: Italy Is Unequivocally on Ukraine’s Side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:04:00 UTC
22:04:00 KST

Giulio Terzi di Sant’Agata, Italy’s former foreign minister who currently chairs the Senate’s Committee on European Union Policies, discussed with the Kyiv Post Italy’s support for Ukraine, Kyiv’s path towards EU membership, European defense, post-war recovery and accountability for Russian aggression. During his diplomatic career, he served as Italy’s ambassador to Israel and the United States, as well as Italy’s permanent representative to the United Nations in New York. He was appointed foreign minister in Mario Monti’s government in November 2011.
                                                                                                                                                                         
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ugo Poletti: Senator Terzi, drawing on your parliamentary and diplomatic experience, what specific role can Italy play in relations between Ukraine and the European Union today, distinguishing itself without weakening the unity of the member states?
Giulio Terzi di Sant’Agata: Since the beginning of Russia’s military aggression, Italy has distinguished itself as a strong and unequivocal voice in support of the Ukrainian people.
At the most recent summits – the G7 meeting in Evian, the European Council, the NATO summit in Ankara and, finally, the meetings of the Coalition of the Willing and the integrated ballistic-missile defense coalition – as on many previous international occasions, Italy has consistently upheld the inviolable principles of freedom and national sovereignty for which Ukraine has been fighting for more than four years.
Ukraine Is Better Prepared for Winter Strikes, Koretskyi Says
Italy has also worked to foster dialogue and cohesion among EU and NATO members in reaffirming their support for Kyiv. It has endorsed and voted for all 21 packages of sanctions against Russia, as well as the decision to end Russian gas supplies to Europe.
There can be no doubt that Feb. 24, 2022 was a watershed. Since then, security, deterrence and defense against the tangible threat of extremely serious military aggression have once again become central concerns. Italy wants to help develop a stronger culture of security and defense throughout European society.
This is connected with the need to build an increasingly cohesive Euro-Atlantic community, within which a genuine and credible European pillar of defense can be defined and established as quickly as possible. I believe that Ukraine is already an integral part of that pillar, even though the necessary legal, political and treaty conditions have yet to be fully established.
Does support for Ukraine, therefore, also provide a foundation for strengthening a common European security and defense policy? How can this be achieved without creating duplication or tension with NATO?
At the latest NATO summit, Italy reiterated a principle that has become more important than ever. “It is time for Europe to guarantee its own security,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said.
In addition to the US commitment to authorize the production of Patriot missiles in Ukraine, the summit consolidated one essential point: the Alliance must be judged by the concrete capabilities each country contributes to collective defense.
As the Meloni government has consistently argued, the European Union must therefore become an increasingly credible security actor within NATO – in terms of its technological and military capabilities, operational readiness and political determination.
Europe’s contribution to the Alliance must become strong enough for the European pillar to serve as the principal foundation of our continent’s security. This would consequently be of vital importance to our non-European allies as well.
Europe’s collective security rests on the indispensable value of Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, but also on Article 42.7 of the Treaty on European Union. The latter stipulates that, if a member state is the victim of armed aggression on its territory, the other member states are obliged to provide it with aid and assistance by all the means in their power.
                                                                                                                                                                         
These are rights, duties and responsibilities that European and Atlantic Alliance countries have signed and ratified over the years, without qualification or reservation. In principle, these provisions take precedence over national legislation. This is reflected in Articles 11 and 117 of the Italian Constitution and in comparable provisions in the constitutions of other member states.
Ukraine regards membership of the European Union as a strategic choice and a matter of national identity. Which reforms should it undertake most urgently, and what must the EU do to ensure that accession does not remain an indefinite promise?
Kyiv is demonstrating a firm determination to join the European family. That ambition has roots extending well beyond Putin’s aggression. It dates back to the time when the Ukrainian people and their government were alone among the former Soviet republics in refusing to join the Moscow-led Commonwealth of Independent States.
The European Council meeting of June 18-19 welcomed the intergovernmental conference on Ukraine’s accession to the European Union and the opening of the cluster covering fundamental issues on June 15, 2026. It also looked forward to the opening of the remaining clusters, in accordance with the merit-based approach. That said, let us be clear: Kyiv is already European. Ukraine is already a member of this family.
The progress it continues to make – in the rule of law, the judicial system and public administration – shows that Ukraine is genuinely mobilizing all the resources at its disposal in its struggle for freedom and independence, and to affirm itself as a sovereign nation in the face of Putin’s bloody designs. The progress already recognized by the EU in Ukraine’s alignment with European standards represents a series of fundamental steps.
I recently met Oleksandr Vasiuk, a member of the Verkhovna Rada’s Committee on Legal Policy, who explained in detail how the government in Kyiv is implementing the reforms required by the EU. He described the important results achieved in reforming the judiciary and the institutions of both constitutional and ordinary justice.
I was also pleased to learn of Kyiv’s strong drive to digitalize administrative documents and procedures. We should also consider the reforms of the anti-corruption system, which has now been strengthened through an independent National Anti-Corruption Bureau with procedural autonomy and a specialized anti-corruption prosecutor.
In my view, all these reforms represent important progress along the path towards Ukraine’s gradual integration into the European Union. We must hope that this process can be completed quickly.
European support for Ukraine now encompasses military, economic, humanitarian and diplomatic assistance. How can a partnership born during an emergency be transformed into a lasting, structural relationship?
This is already happening. A structural relationship is taking shape within the defense industry. Ukraine’s operational capabilities have been amply demonstrated – not only in defending its territory, but also in significantly slowing what, until a year ago, appeared to be an unstoppable Russian advance. Ukrainian forces have shown that they can operate at long range, making Russia’s frontline supply routes increasingly vulnerable.
Consider Ukraine’s drones and cutting-edge technologies, which are effectively unique in the world today. Europe is seeking to build a robust security architecture. This will involve not only institutions, but businesses above all. In countries such as Italy and Germany, a large proportion of small and medium-sized enterprises contribute to defense supply chains.
What will happen next? These companies will require further investment and expansion because defense manufacturing is extensive and highly interconnected. The F-35 production program, for example, relies on more than 2,100 suppliers worldwide, almost half of which are small businesses. There is therefore enormous potential for cooperation with Ukraine, which has acquired technological and operational expertise of unmatched value during these years of war.
That is not all. Cooperation with Ukraine is also extremely important in countering Russia’s hybrid warfare against the EU, including interference, disinformation, cognitive manipulation and cyberespionage.
There is now far greater awareness of the hybrid threats Moscow directs against Europe and the West as a whole. Russian aggression against our democracies does not consist solely of incursions into European airspace. It also takes the form of propaganda, political interference, cognitive manipulation and attempts to subvert our electoral processes.
Ukraine has experienced direct Russian military aggression since the conflict unleashed against Donbas and Crimea, culminating in the full-scale invasion of 2022. Even before then, however, Kyiv had faced an extraordinary wave of manipulation, violence and subversion, particularly from the time of the Euromaidan protests onwards.
Both hybrid warfare and the evolution of conventional warfare require sophisticated, technologically advanced instruments of deterrence. The EU and its member states are now working to develop those capabilities.
What practical contribution can Italy make to Ukraine’s reconstruction – not only through funding and business involvement, but also in such fields as public institutions, culture, education, healthcare and the protection of cultural heritage?
Ukraine’s reconstruction was a priority during Italy’s G7 presidency and has long occupied a central place on the European agenda.
In recent months, numerous meetings have been held in Kyiv between Italian ministers, ambassadors and business representatives and members of the Ukrainian government, confirming our country’s strong interest. The Ukraine Recovery Conference was held in Rome a year ago, where important commitments were made. One prominent example is Italy’s leading role in the reconstruction of Odesa Cathedral.
Rebuilding a country means bringing it back to life. It means reconstructing schools, hospitals and energy infrastructure, restoring livelihoods and creating the best possible conditions for Ukraine’s revival. In other words, it means providing Ukraine with genuine security. That security cannot be limited to empty promises and declarations such as those contained in the three great deceptions shamefully inflicted upon the Ukrainian people in the past.
The first was the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, under which the United States, the United Kingdom and Russia provided security assurances concerning Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity in exchange for Kyiv relinquishing its vast nuclear arsenal, which was subsequently transferred to Russia.
The second was the 1997 Russian-Ukrainian Friendship Treaty, a bilateral agreement in which Russia recognized Ukraine’s territorial integrity and the inviolability of its borders, including Crimea.
The third was the vague promise of Ukraine’s eventual NATO membership made by the Alliance at the 2008 Bucharest Summit. We cannot allow Ukraine to be deceived again. This time, reconstruction cannot begin without a full understanding of what genuine security for Ukraine entails in practice.
Important humanitarian questions must also be addressed. I recently met Yana Zinkevych at the Italian Senate. She is a member of the Ukrainian Verkhovna Rada and commander of the Hospitallers volunteer medical battalion. She recalled some tragic figures: more than 4,000 schools are unusable, 330,000 homes have been destroyed, and more than 1,000 kilometers of railway lines and bridges need to be rebuilt.
The EU – and Italy is once again at the forefront – wants to participate in this reconstruction. In a majority resolution approved by the Senate in preparation for the June European Council, the government was called upon to work to ensure that “the European institutions provide full political, economic and operational support to associations and organizations working to address the humanitarian consequences of the war of aggression.”
What minimum conditions must be met for a ceasefire to begin and open the way to a peace process?
First and foremost, the aggression must stop. Russia must cease bombing Ukraine – its homes and the facilities essential to civilian life, including hospitals, nurseries, schools and power stations. Russian raids are killing civilians. That is unacceptable.
Russia’s systematic attacks on Ukraine’s agricultural industry, ports, grain terminals and merchant vessels also demonstrate Moscow’s intention to spread chaos and continue the madness of these crimes. All of this must end before there can be a ceasefire and the beginning of serious peace negotiations.
When negotiations between the two sides eventually begin, there will clearly be certain points – or preconditions – that cannot be negotiated away. Russia must compensate Ukraine for the immense damage caused by the war. Ukraine’s full sovereignty, complete independence and national identity must also be definitively recognized and effectively guaranteed.
How can responsibility for crimes committed during the war be established, and how can the victims’ right to justice be upheld?
There is broad agreement that a special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine is urgently needed, and its establishment is now taking shape. The Council of Europe and the European Union have signed an agreement concerning its financing.
I also want to emphasize the importance of initiatives such as the International Centre for the Prosecution of the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine at Eurojust.
Its work complements the arrest warrants issued by the International Criminal Court for Vladimir Putin and other Russian officials, including Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia’s Commissioner for Children’s Rights, in connection with the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia.
These issues cannot be relegated to the background. They concern human rights, the right to compensation for the damage caused by a war of aggression unleashed by President Putin, and the right of every family to be reunited with children deported to Russia.

Bangsamoro set for maiden elections in southern Philippines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:01:25 UTC
22:01:25 KST

Amir Latif 
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
The Philippines' Muslim-majority Bangsamoro autonomous region is set to hold its first parliamentary election on Monday, which is seen as a crucial step in the quest for self-governance and lasting peace after decades of resistance.
Nearly 2.4 million voters are set to make a choice, with 80 seats at stake in the elections that will determine members of parliament, the region’s legislative body, the state-run Philippine News Agency reported on Sunday.
These include 40 political party representatives, 32 district representatives, and eight sectoral representatives.
Voting will run from 7 am local time Monday (2300GMT Sunday) to 7 pm (1100GMT Monday).
The elections will use automated counting machines previously deployed during the May 2025 midterm elections.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is home to around 5 million people, the majority of whom are Muslims.
It covers five provinces, three cities, and 63 villages across eight special geographic area clusters.
In January 2019, a referendum approved the "Bangsamoro Organic Law," officially establishing the "Bangsamoro Transition Authority" in the region, following decades of resistance by the Murad Ebrahim-led Moro Islamic Liberation Front.
Ebrahim was appointed as the first interim chief minister of the autonomous region the same year. He was succeeded by Abdulraof Macacua in March last year.
 
1st elections after several delays
Monday's elections will be held after being delayed four times.
The Philippine Supreme Court postponed the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro region for the third time last year.
The election, originally scheduled for 2022, was postponed to May 11 of last year, then rescheduled for October, before being postponed again.
For young voters and women, the historic polls are more than an exercise in choosing leaders.
"Among those preparing to take part are women and young Bangsamoro, whose voices are being given space in the new parliamentary system not only through their votes, but also through sectoral representation, voter education and participation in the electoral process," said a statement from the Bangsamoro government.
Under the Bangsamoro Autonomy Act, regional parliamentary political parties are required to ensure that at least 30% of their party nominees are women. As far as practicable, at least one in every three party nominees must be a woman.
The provision establishes a gender quota aimed at increasing women’s representation in the first regular Bangsamoro Parliament.
The election commission also reserves one seat each for women, youth, traditional leaders, and the ulama, and two reserved seats for settler communities and Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples in the Parliament.
 
Long struggle until 2019
The chair of the Commission on Elections, George Garcia, said the polls represent a continuation of the Bangsamoro struggle for self-government through the peace process.
The Moro Islamic Liberation Front led the region’s struggle for autonomy since the mid-20th century, ultimately resulting in peace talks and the transitional government’s formation after a referendum on Jan. 21, 2019.
Before the Bangsamoro Transition Authority was founded in 2019 following the referendum, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, led by Murad Ebrahim, had asked for a six-year transition period during peace negotiations with the Manila national government.
But negotiations resulted in a three-year transitional government under Ebrahim as chief minister until 2022.
The two sides agreed to allow the transitional government to take control of regional governance and run affairs until 2022, when elections were agreed to be held.

Director who oversaw Grenfell cost-cutting given senior council housing role

Grenfell survivors and bereaved relatives have criticised the “outrageous decision” to hire a director who oversaw cost-cutting at Grenfell Tower in a £150,000-a-year senior council housing role.
Laura Johnson, the director of housing at the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea (RBKC) at the time of the 2017 Grenfell fire, has been appointed the permanent director of development and property at the Barnet Group, which manages the borough’s 13,000 council homes.
The Grenfell inquiry found that, in her previous role, Johnson pushed for a new contractor to carry out the tower’s renovation works on a lower budget, which ultimately meant metal cladding was swapped for combustible plastic-filled panels to save money.
It also found she slowed down the installation of self-closing mechanisms on fire doors in the tower for “financial and practical reasons”, despite warnings from the London fire brigade that their absence compromised fire escape routes.
Ed Daffarn, who escaped from the 16th floor of the tower after repeatedly warning about serious fire risks at Grenfell, said: “It is an absolutely outrageous decision.
“The fact that we, as bereaved survivors, haven’t received any justice nine years after the fire, and yet the people that were involved in senior decision-making are able to carry on working in the social housing sector, have responsibility for health and safety, and receive massive salaries – it feels so disrespectful.
“If I was a resident in a Barnet council home, I’d be absolutely petrified.”
Johnson had been working in her role at the Barnet Group on an interim basis before she was appointed permanently in August with a salary of £157,078.
A spokesperson for the Barnet Group said she was the “strongest candidate” in a competitive field.
“We were aware of the Grenfell inquiry findings and considered them carefully during the recruitment process,” they said. “We also took into account Ms Johnson’s professional experience, subsequent performance, references, qualifications and overall suitability for the role.
“Following a robust and publicly advertised recruitment process, we concluded that she was the strongest candidate and legally eligible to hold the position.”
Grenfell United, the group representing the bereaved and survivors, has urged Barnet Group – which is owned by Barnet council – to reconsider its decision to hire Johnson, saying it showed “a staggering disregard for the inquiry’s findings”.
“She should not be in a position of power,” Daffarn said. “No one named in the Grenfell inquiry should be while we are still awaiting the outcome of the police investigation.”
The Metropolitan police said it was seeking charges against 57 individuals and 20 companies in relation to the fire, with the Crown Prosecution Service saying it expected to make decisions on charges by June 2027, the 10th anniversary of the disaster.
“Although the police have not publicly identified those individuals, it is extraordinary that Barnet council would make this appointment permanent before the criminal justice process arising from Grenfell has concluded,” Grenfell United said.
A spokesperson for the Barnet Group said: “Barnet Homes and Barnet council will not discuss matters relating to members of staff which took place during previous employment.
“Our thoughts remain with the survivors and family and friends of all those affected by the tragic Grenfell Tower fire. The safety and wellbeing of our residents is our top priority.”

The bird that changed Ecuador: how a chance discovery of a rare species helped to save many more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:00:05 UTC
22:00:05 KST

I have to confess that I rarely enjoy birding in montane cloud forests. The birds that live in these mountainous, cool and humid habitats are masters of disguise, usually passing themselves off as a leaf or other form of foliage. But if I want to see antpittas – elusive, ground-dwelling birds that rarely show themselves – then I have no choice.
So, on a cool, cloudy morning my guide, Juan Carlos Crespo, Fredy Ramón Castillo, a local ranger, and I are standing on a steep, muddy path close to Tapichalaca Lodge, 2,500 metres above sea level in the eastern Andes, waiting for the jocotoco antpitta to emerge from the undergrowth.
Fortunately, antpittas have a soft spot for food, especially the large, juicy earthworms Castillo has placed on a low branch nearby. He calls the bird, with increasingly loud and urgent shouts of “venga, venga!” (“come on, come on!”). The minutes tick by, until I begin to wonder if this is a lost cause.
Then, out of nowhere, a plump, thrush-sized bird with a chestnut back, grey front, black crown and white face-patch materialises just a few feet away. It proceeds to gulp down the earthworms as if it has not eaten for days.
I have seen a lot of different birds, but never one that so changed the course of bird conservation. In November 1997, a group led by the influential US ornithologist Robert Ridgely was exploring this area of southern Ecuador to see what they could find.
As they ascended a forest trail at dawn, they heard the sound of a bird in the far distance. As Ridgely recalled many years later, “It had this crazy call, sounding like an owl; but we had no idea what it was, and to be honest I never thought we would find out.”
Ridgely walked ahead of the group, and heard the sound much closer than before. He recorded the call and played it back to the mystery creature, which came crashing through the dense bamboo, right out into the open.
“I knew right away that this was something really special, which no one apart from the local people had ever seen – an entirely new species to science.” It was, in fact, one of the greatest ornithological breakthroughs of the late 20th century: while new species are sometimes discovered, they are rarely so large, noisy and so obviously different from other members of their family.
Talking to local farmers, Ridgely discovered that they were familiar with the bird, which they had named “jocotoco” to represent its loud, barking call. Two years later, the species was officially described, and named the jocotoco antpitta; the scientific name, Grallaria ridgelyi, commemorating its proud discoverer.
Ridgely soon realised that if the bird was to be saved from extinction its forest home needed to be urgently protected. He and a group of like-minded friends created an organisation dedicated to saving the bird and its habitat, raising funds from donors in the US and Europe to buy and restore the land. In 1998 the Jocotoco Foundation was born.
Today, the foundation protects and manages 19 reserves throughout Ecuador, covering about 50,000 hectares (193 sq miles), and manages a further 82,000 hectares of privately and communally owned land. Together, these sites are home to more than 1,350 species of birds – that’s 80% of all those found in Ecuador, and an astonishing one in eight of all bird species on the planet, as well as many other plant and animal species. The foundation also works closely with nearby communities, employing local people as park rangers – many of whom grew up on the land they now protect – and through jobs in wildlife tourism.
The model for the foundation’s reserves is simple and very effective. First, it restores habitat by planting a variety of native trees and other plants, or in some places simply allows the vegetation to regenerate on its own. Park guards, all of whom come from local communities, protect the reserves against illegal incursions such as cattle grazing, logging and poaching, aided by new technology including camera traps and audio recorders.
They also use these to monitor the fortunes of key species, while providing nest boxes to encourage them to breed, making up for the loss of natural tree cavities while the old-growth forests are being restored.
A recent study at Canandé, in the Chocó region of north-west Ecuador, revealed that even after deforestation, nature can recover very rapidly. The study showed that in just three decades – a single human generation – of being managed for biodiversity, formerly cleared lands have recovered 90% of the biomass – the weight of all animals – and 90% of the number of species found in nearby mature forests. While the new mix of species is not fully the same as in a mature forest, 75% of the original species present in an old-growth forest have returned.
Mike Parr, the president of the American Bird Conservancy, has no doubt about the importance of this work. “Beyond safeguarding Ecuador’s rarest birds, migrating species and incredible overall biodiversity, Jocotoco’s strategic integration of ecotourism, public awareness, community engagement and scientific research are world class. They have done an amazing job covering the previously unprotected endangered species of Ecuador.”
During recent visits to Ecuador I have visited 10 of the foundation’s reserves, including those in the Chocó region north-west of Quito and Copalinga in the Amazon foothills, along with the Los Petreles reserve on San Cristóbal Island in the Galápagos, a refuge for a critically endangered seabird, the Galápagos petrel.
On a visit to Buenaventura reserve, a restored cattle ranch in the western foothills of the Andes, we went in search of an even rarer bird: the El Oro parakeet. This charismatic parrot was only discovered as recently as 1980, and has a tiny home range, with fewer than 1,000 individuals.
Another early start took us to an open area of grassland and scattered trees where the birds are known to gather. Moments later, we heard a raucous call, and there they were: several flocks totalling about 20 of these emerald-green birds, the males with a distinctive red forehead.
But even this memorable moment was eclipsed by my visit to the Chakana nature reserve, more than 4,000 metres above sea level in the páramo grasslands of the high Andes – yet just an hour south-east of Quito. On an unexpectedly fine and sunny day, against a stunning backdrop of the snow-capped Cotopaxi volcano, we enjoyed closeup views of the Ecuadorian hillstar, a specialist high-altitude hummingbird, along with nine Andean condors soaring right around us, before they rose high into the clear blue sky.
Numbers of the Andean condor, the world’s largest flying bird by a combination of weight and wingspan, have fallen rapidly in recent years, due mainly to deliberate poisoning. But here, these mighty raptors are now returning to their ancestral home.
Dr Martin Schaefer, chief executive of Jocotoco, believes that even in these dark times there is room for optimism. “The power to restore what we have lost is in our hands.”
Ian J Davidson, Americas regional director for BirdLife International, agrees. “By creating a network of protected habitat ‘arks’, Jocotoco has given these remarkable species a genuine chance not only to endure, but to recover and expand beyond their remaining strongholds.
“Their work stands as a global conservation success story, an inspiring example of what determination, science and long-term stewardship can achieve for nature.”
At a time when President Trump has withdrawn US government funding for conservation projects around the world, the Jocotoco Foundation is a classic model of how scientists and local people can work together to save endangered birds and the precious places where they live.

The end times fascists are plotting their escape from our world. Our mission is clear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
13:00:05 UTC
22:00:05 KST

When Jeff Bezos announced his plan for an opulent Venetian wedding in early 2025, many locals found the idea offensive, even obscene. A growing number of residents were struggling to find secure and affordable housing in a city overrun by tourists and Airbnb, and the billionaire was planning to, in effect, rent out the municipality for three days, forking over an estimated $50m for festivities that would clog central canals and block well-trafficked streets. Worse, Amazon’s carbon emissions were soaring, thanks to artificial intelligence and the datacentre build out – and that’s personal in Venice, where the streets already flood dozens of times a year.
Marta Sottoriva, a 35-year-old high school teacher, told us that she first heard about the wedding plans just when Bezos’s rocket company, Blue Origin, was grabbing headlines. Bezos had sent a “crew” of female influencers and celebrities, including his fiancee, Lauren Sánchez, and the pop singer Katy Perry, to the suborbital edge of space in a seemingly pointless publicity stunt. “The idea that you are so rich and powerful that you can use space as a 10-minute trip,” Sottoriva recalled, only intensified the “feeling that our city was being taken away from us in such an arrogant way”. Federica Toninello, another young activist, agreed, telling us that it felt as if both space and Venice were being “colonized”.
Colonizing space is exactly what Bezos hopes to do. Blue Origin, Bezos claims in his well-rehearsed sales pitch, will secure humanity’s survival by allowing a trillion people to one day spread across the solar system. The unbearable horror he imagines himself saving our species from? The threat of what he calls a “civilization of stasis”, otherwise known as having to contend with real ecological limits and devising a way to share the planet’s finite resources. To avoid this reckoning, Bezos imagines a future in which “Earth will be zoned residential and light industrial” and set aside as a sort of preserve out of reach for most of its native inhabitants. The vast majority of humans will pursue the nebulous benefit of “exponential growth” in the forbidding void of space, trapped on Blue Origin spacecrafts. It would seem that Bezos believes the prospect of humanity living sustainably and peaceably on our precious, singular home is a nightmarish possibility unworthy of his consideration.
Predictably, it turned out that most Venetians would rather continue living in magnificent Venice. Unlike Bezos, they don’t fret about hypothetical civilizational stagnation; they worry about economic stagnation as a result of government divestment, a lack of jobs and opportunity, and being forced out of the city and country they love. Young Italians often have little choice but to emigrate to find work; over the last decade, more than 1 million citizens have moved, a third of them between the ages of 25 and 34.
To date, the precarity and anger many Italians feel has mostly benefited the neofascist right. But those same forces also drew people to the anti-Bezos cause, helping to coalesce a budding, self-consciously antifascist movement.
The spirited, disruptive “No Space for Bezos” campaign tapped into wells of outrage against billionaires, climate breakdown and militarism – and it also gave the organizers a megaphone to broadcast ideas for different, less lethal ways we could choose to live together. Activists printed posters and stickers showing Bezos’s head on a rocket blasting into space. They made a dummy of Bezos clutching fistfuls of fake money while clinging to a giant buoyant Amazon package, then set it free to float down the canals. They unfurled banners from Venice’s iconic buildings and bridges and across its piazzas: “Tax the rich to give back to the planet.” And they chanted that the money for the wedding would be better spent rebuilding Gaza. For days, they caused gleeful chaos and relentlessly poked fun at the groom and his star-studded guest list, which included his billionaire bunker neighbors Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and a gaggle of Kardashians.
Not long before the wedding, officials announced that the event was being moved to a less central location due to the protests. Even Bezos’s two yachts, Koru and Abeona, were denied permission to dock locally. Organizers declared victory and celebrated. The international press devoured the visual-rich showdown. And the online right didn’t know who to root for: the Davos elites spraying one another with foam on a superyacht, or the leftist riffraff making agitprop?
Like Donald Trump’s enormous ballroom, Bezos’s extravagant wedding epitomized the obscenities of our networked gilded age. For the Amazon founder, it wasn’t enough to be part of one of Europe’s most beautiful cities – he needed to consume it and swallow it whole. A year later he would do the same with New York City’s Met Gala, sparking similar outrage and grassroots creativity.
The Venice protests, which dwelled on Bezos’s dreams of outer space at the expense of Earth, pointed to something fundamental about the age of end times fascism – a concept at the center of our new book, referring to an unholy alliance working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. Today’s battle lines are not simply between people who struggle to survive under increasingly degraded and costly conditions and an oligarch class thinking of ever more ludicrous ways to waste their wealth. They are more cosmological than that.
On one side are those of us who have no escape plan, no bunker in the sky or underground, and who therefore are committed to staying right here, in the complexity of our earthbound reality, with one another. We know we need to do what is necessary to make “here” – this planet and all of its ecologies and communities – and safer for the multitude of beings who rely upon them, fully aware this is our one and only home.
On the other are those with rapturous plans to shield themselves and their families from the political and ecological fires burning our planet, whether those plans take the form of heavenly ascension, earthly bunkers and fortressed nations, or fantasies of colonizing space and merging with machines. Instead of improving conditions for actual people on Earth (or even pulling back from pouring fuel on the fires), end times fascists are plotting their escape, indifferent and oblivious to all that’s worth saving.
An absence of awe
Bezos’s fixation on space gets at something else that is key to understanding end times fascism and its fixation on bunkering and abandoning our shared world: the apparent inability of the people driving this project to marvel at, or even notice, the wonders that surround them.
That was glaringly apparent in 2021, when Bezos sent another crew to space. This time William Shatner, best known as Star Trek’s Captain Kirk, was on board (to fulfill one of Bezos’s boyhood fantasies, of course). “Space. The final frontier,” Shatner had said at the start of each episode. But as the now 90-year-old actor watched our blue-and-green planet recede from the window, he was suddenly flooded with terror. “The contrast between the vicious coldness of space and the warm nurturing of Earth below filled me with overwhelming sadness,” he later recalled, explaining that he had gained a much deeper appreciation for our planet’s sublime and fragile gifts.
“Every day, we are confronted with the knowledge of further destruction of Earth at our hands: the extinction of animal species, of flora and fauna … things that took five billion years to evolve, and suddenly we will never see them again because of the interference of mankind,” Shatner wrote. He took the trip expecting to be awestruck by the universe and instead he longed for home the minute he left: “I discovered that the beauty isn’t out there, it’s down here, with all of us.”
Perhaps Shatner’s insight about our precious imperiled planet resonates with the Amazon founder, but the billionaire’s plans for space colonization and his company’s large expansion of carbon-spewing data centers both suggest otherwise. And among tech oligarchs, Bezos is all too typical. Peter Thiel, for one, once revealed that his three best ideas for achieving true freedom are “cyberspace”, “outerspace” and “seasteading” (the idea of building new countries on floating oil rigs). In other words, this man, whose enormous wealth affords him access to the most spectacular settings our planet has to offer, actually believes these three cold, dead places are superior to the Earth we have, verdant and alive.
Something similar seems amiss with Elon Musk, a man who seems to look up at the wonders of the night sky and see only opportunities to fill that inky unknown with his own space junk. The venerable novelist Joyce Carol Oates highlighted these apparent limits in the fall of 2025 when she roasted him ruthlessly on his own platform, X. “So curious,” she wrote, “that such a wealthy man never posts anything that indicates that he enjoys or is even aware of what virtually everyone appreciates – scenes from nature, pet dog or cat, praise for a movie, music, a book (but doubt that he reads); pride in a friend’s or relative’s accomplishment; condolences for someone who has died; pleasure in sports, acclaim for a favorite team; references to history. In fact he seems totally uneducated, uncultured. The poorest persons on Twitter [X] may have access to more beauty & meaning in life than the ‘most wealthy person in the world.’”
The observation clearly got under the tech baron’s notoriously thin skin: he called her “a lazy liar” and began posting approvingly about various movies to prove Oates wrong. Yet in Musk’s euphoria on the day his aerospace company, SpaceX, went public, he made no attempt to hide his boredom with our blue planet and its challenges: “We want to solve [problems] here on Earth and we should solve them. But there also have to be things that get you excited about the future, that make you glad to wake up in the morning because you can’t wait to see what happens next.” It would seem that only abandoning Earth provides that thrill.
Most people have the capacity for awe, to gasp at the jeweled beauty of a songbird or the otherworldliness of a whale’s exhalation or the intricate latticework of an ancient holy site. Children have the capacity for pure awe; so do 90-year-old actors in suborbital space. To experience awe is to dissolve into the swirl of the universe, to feel small in the best way. This sense of interconnection is also why we grieve when we witness strangers suffering, and feel the great sorrow of extinction. The fact that this capacity seems to be missing from the men who hold our collective fate in their hands is a personal loss for them – and an existential crisis for the rest of us.
One dangerous part of the tech oligarchs’ world-abandoning project is that the tools they are building are designed to remake us in their own broken image. Popular platforms and apps train us to share Silicon Valley’s dream of discarnate freedom, perpetually nudging us to forsake real places and in-person connection in favor of simulations – and to view Earth, our bodies and our relationships as prisons to hack and flee. Altman, for one, has made it clear that he sees “certain advantages to being a machine”, and he has repeatedly insisted that his own children will never be smarter than AI, as though intelligence can be reduced to no more than computation. Like similar services, ChatGPT is trained to hijack our empathic response systems so we, too, will elevate machines and imbue them with more significance than they deserve.
The inability to appreciate this planet and its marvelous cast of characters helps explain why they are so prepared to sacrifice it. Indeed, the tech right’s willingness to eliminate our life-sustaining labor and replace human relationships with synthetic ones cannot be separated from their indifference to what little remains of the planet’s fast-vanishing wildlife and plant diversity. They don’t seem to know how to love this place, to savor the pleasure of other people’s company, or to marvel at the mysteries presented by other species.
In short, we are up against an ideology that has given up not only on the premise and promise of liberal democracy but on the livability of our shared world – on its beauty, on its people, on our children, on other species. There is something treasonous in this. Treasonous not to an abstraction like a flag or a nation, for we are not nationalists. But treasonous to the unspoken pact made with the web of life that sustains us.
They are traitors to creation, to the wonders of here.
The antithesis of fascism
There is no cut-and-paste formula for fighting end times fascism. Whether it’s Venetians taking on Jeff Bezos or Albanians telling Jared and Ivanka Trump that their country is not for sale or a small town in Kentucky organizing against a sprawling datacentre, every front in this fight takes on the character and texture of its place. There are, however, some guiding principles that are beginning to emerge across locations, and Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for mayor of New York City – and his approach to governance since his election – embody many of them. Start from love of place, then conjure a radically inclusive future where everyone can afford dignified lives, embrace common goals across difference, get outside and gather offline and in person, take on the powerful joyously, draw on history and don’t be afraid to stir the soul.
Mamdani has pounded away at his core policies to make the city more affordable, and has made good on many of those promises in his pursuit, for example, to lower rent and expand universal childcare. But he has also done something more sublime, dwelling on the boisterous, charming corners of the city that are the reason so many people choose to endure the pressures pushing them to leave.
As Mamdani’s star was rising, fascists and neofascists across the country and around the world did what they do. They sorted and separated, ranked and expelled. They sowed confusion and division by claiming Mamdani wasn’t a real American, and blamed the left for every social problem and grievance. They held up multicultural New York as a supposedly terrifying example of what happens when the “great replacement” succeeds. JD Vance spoke out in defense of people’s right to not want to live next to people from “a totally different culture”, and Stephen Miller railed on X: “NYC is the clearest warning yet of what happens to a society when it fails to control migration.”
As the fascists drew their rigid lines – in versus out, protected versus disposable, “heritage” versus. invader – the campaign to elect Mamdani threw a year-long party that celebrated one of the most racially and ethnically diverse places ever known, five boroughs shaped by wave after wave of new immigrants who have made their homes on Lenape lands. With its every action, the campaign asserted that shared identity can be forged not just by ancestry but by a commitment to a shared home, and to a shared set of values about how to live together in that home.
New York is a city of people carrying countless hyphenations and keeping myriad cultural practices alive. But as Mamdani put it: “No matter what you eat, what language you speak, how you pray, or where you come from, the words that most define us are the two we all share: New Yorkers.”
So Mamdani explained the complexities of ranked-choice voting in the Democratic primary using a line of mango lassis as props. He canvassed for votes at queer clubs, shouted out Haitian revolutionary history at the massive Bayo concert, shared his favorite bagel order, and broke fast during Ramadan over biryani in the Bronx. Once in office, he also turned the now legendary Knicks playoff run and the 2026 World Cup into a summer-long party few will forget. In these ways and others, Mamdani re-enchanted a city that had faced relentless vilification from Washington as dangerous, dirty and dysfunctional.
It was a perfect encapsulation of “hereness” – an idea developed by the Jewish Labour Bund, a Yiddish socialist group that was founded in the 19th century and grounded in fierce commitment to place and community not based on bloodlines. Molly Crabapple, a proud New Yorker and artist who recently published a bestselling history of the Bund, made the connection in a piece published in the Guardian. “Like New York itself, Mamdani’s campaign was multicultural, multiracial, polyglottal,” she wrote. “When Andrew Cuomo tried to bait him as un-American, he released ads in Spanish and Bangla, Hindi and Arabic. He ran a campaign devoted to class-first politics that sought to speak to everyone in their own idiom, while never once apologizing for who he was.
Amid all this celebration of difference, Mamdani’s campaign also emphasized the kinds of daily experiences and anxieties that are common and unifying for nearly all New Yorkers, lingering in the ordinary places that are too often overlooked or reviled. Mamdani rubbed shoulders with commuters on packed subway cars, paid homage to the glories of the Staten Island Ferry, and visited countless bodegas, approaching the strangers he met with nonjudgmental curiosity and a smile so wide it became a punchline on Saturday Night Live.
But the campaign was not only antifascist – in the myriad ways that it celebrated the unruliness that makes New York lovable, it was also the antithesis of fascism. More than a rejection of hate, it was an invitation to kindness, to a world in which we avert our eyes from no one. That meant lifting up and honoring the very people fascists are most eager to eject and discard: the working-class, immigrant workforce that keeps the city functioning. The campaign shined a spotlight on delivery workers getting ripped off by platforms such as DoorDash, on Amazon warehouse workers fighting to have their unions recognized, and on taxi drivers in line at LaGuardia, one part of a nocturnal workforce that makes it possible for New York to boast of being the city that never sleeps.
Faced with the prospect of a fairer city funded by marginally higher taxes, some prophesied a billionaire exodus. Hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman threatened to leave along with other high earners and Fox forecast a “Mamdani Migration”. Luxury real estate agents reported being bombarded with calls from clients wanting to sell their penthouses and move to Palm Beach.
The threats of defection only underscored the mutually reinforcing nature of the two core themes of Mamdani’s campaign – the joyous love of here, even if here is kind of a wreck, and the concrete plans for repair and improvement. Because the more devoted you are to a place, the easier it is to put in the resources and energy required to improve it. It’s a politics based not on wanting to escape this earthly realm, whether our cities or our animate bodies, but on a deep desire to stay, and to protect all that is irreplaceable, human and alive.
This is the very same spirit that we’ve seen motivating people to protect their air and water from sprawling datacenters and to defend their immigrant neighbors from ICE. While reporting on the weeks-long uprising in Minneapolis, the journalist Adam Serwer memorably described the guiding ideology of the resistance as “neighborism”, or the “commitment to protecting the people around you, no matter who they are or where they came from”. It was an openhearted, welcoming ethic that united huge numbers of ordinary people to do something deceptively simple: protect the most vulnerable members of their community from what looked very much like an invading army. That meant everything from braving bullets, to cooking dinner to opening up spare rooms to families who were no longer safe at home.
In these and countless other ways, Minnesotans rose up to insist that their neighbors were already where they belonged, whether they were, as Serwer put it, born in Minneapolis or Mogadishu.
The human networks that neighbors are building, block by block, group chat by group chat, are about more than refusal. In our time of serial shocks and intersecting crises, they are also the basis for a different kind of survivalism. But while the various strains of fascists build bunkers for the few, ours are survival networks grounded in the principle that every one of us, without exception, deserves to live and thrive. They are also bound by a belief that keeping one another safe when the inevitable shocks arrive is a sacred duty. Part of that involves telling new stories, stories that are truthful and inspiring enough to help our depleted fellow humans fall back in love with our one and only home and defiantly recommit to defending it with all they’ve got.
Some worlds must end
Those stories cannot be about returning to something called “normal”, to what passed for calm before Brexit and Trump and Silicon Valley’s authoritarian turn. Those were the years during which too many problems were allowed to compound and fester: fascism is always a warped response to real crises. And end times fascism is a response to real planetary-scale crises, including ever-concentrating levels of carbon in the atmosphere and wealth in the hands of the super-rich. The responses it proposes – mass sacrifices of humans and non-humans alike – are monstrous and must be purged from our midst.
To achieve this, we will have to figure out how to address the underlying crises contemporary fascism feeds off of. Because boundaries are being crossed. Limits are being exceeded. Walls are being hit. Fascists want us to believe that what is hitting the wall is the human story: it’s over, so make sure you are among the chosen who transcend to the next world. Pray to your God for salvation. Implant the chip, merge with the machines. Militarize and purify your bunkered nation. Arm yourself to the hilt and hide behind your fortune. Don’t worry about the humans, the animals, the trees, the rivers and reefs that won’t make it.
But they are wrong. It’s not the human story that is hitting the wall. Rather, it is the story we have been trapped inside of. The one about how greed must be the engine of civilization. About how growth can go on for ever. About how there are always more efficiencies to be found, more workers to be rationalized, more resources to be sacrificed, more people, places and planets to colonize. These myths are hitting the wall of reality and much will have to change as a result.
The logics that must be abandoned should be clear by now. Unlimited violence. Unconstrained exploitation. Insatiable wealth. Unchecked dominance. Those are the drives that make coexistence impossible. Looking forward, two paths beckon. We can abandon and betray this world, or we can break with capitalism and build new economic and political systems that honor life and prioritize care and repair.
Thankfully we are not starting from scratch. Our movement ancestors have left us maps to earthly Zions where everyone is welcome, to inclusive futures where peace and safety are core principles. Not the post-human future desired by end times fascists, but a post-capitalist and pro- (all of) life one. Deeply democratic, socialist, feminist, multiracial, multispecies, internationalist, generous, courageous and animate. Embodied and sensory, proudly earthbound.
And that, fundamentally, is the prospect that terrifies end times fascists more than anything else. It’s why Thiel denounces anyone attempting to regulate fossil fuels and AI as the antichrist; and why Trump and Vance smear nonviolent Minnesotans defending their neighbors as “domestic terrorists”. What keeps these men up at night is … us. It’s the possibility that a popular and vigorous movement will rise up and defend this planet and the many life-forms who call it home.
We didn’t choose to be born into a fight quite so fateful, but we have reached a choice point. We can either follow end times fascists into oblivion, or we can commit to building the unruly, boundary-crossing movement they so deeply fear. One that wrests away their weapons, holds them accountable for their crimes, and defends the paradise of here.

Allameh Tabataba'i University Opens International Admissions for English-Taught Master’s Programs
Allameh Tabataba'i University (ATU), Iran’s leading specialized public university in the humanities and social sciences, has launched international admissions for its English-taught Master of Arts and Master of Science programs for the first semester of the 2026–2027 academic year.
Renowned for its rigorous academic traditions, influential faculty, and vibrant campus life in Tehran, ATU invites qualified international graduates and scholars from across the globe to apply for Master’s degree programs delivered entirely in the English language.
Available Master’s Degree Programs
Eligible international candidates may apply for admission in one of the following six disciplines (applicants must select a field corresponding to their Bachelor’s specialisation):
- Actuarial Science
- Cultural Studies
- English Language and Literature
- International Relations
- Regional Studies (Specialisations: Central Asia & the Caucasus / Middle East & North Africa / Southeast Asia)
- Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL)
Key Eligibility Criteria and Academic Regulations
To qualify for admission, candidates must meet the following official requirements:
- Non-Iranian Citizenship: Applicants must hold a valid foreign passport. In accordance with national regulations, dual nationals holding Iranian citizenship are not eligible to apply through the international student track.
- National Academic Clearance (ADAB Platform): Prior to registering in the university’s application portal, all applicants must register on the national ADAB system (https://adab.saorg.ir/PortalADAB/fa) and obtain an official tracking/clearance code designated specifically for Allameh Tabataba'i University. Note: Securing simultaneous clearance codes for multiple Iranian universities will result in automatic disqualification.
- Undergraduate Qualifications: Applicants must possess a recognised Bachelor’s degree in a discipline related to the intended Master’s program.
- Full-Time Commitment & Legal Status: All programs are strictly full-time. Distance, short-term, or part-time study tracks are not available.
- Language Training: Although academic instruction is conducted in English, enrolled international students are required under Ministry of Science, Research and Technology regulations to attend concurrent Persian language courses starting from their first semester, submitting a Persian language proficiency certificate prior to graduation.
Application Procedure and Timeline
The admissions procedure is fully digitised, centralised, and transparent:
Application Deadline: 15 September 2026
Application Platform: Submissions must be made exclusively through the official ATU International Student Admission Portal: https://apply.atu.ac.ir/. Applications submitted via email, postal mail, or in person will not be accepted. The portal is accessible in English, Persian, and Arabic.
Direct Registration / Agency Notice: Applications may be completed by the prospective student or an authorised, licensed international recruitment agency. Sponsoring agencies must register using the applicant’s verified personal email address. Submissions managed by unauthorized third parties or intermediaries will be rejected.
Required Application Documents
Applicants must upload clear, flatbed-scanned copies of the following documents to the admission portal (smartphone photos or blurred scans will be automatically disqualified):
Passport-Sized Photograph: Color photo with dimensions of 600 (H) × 400 (W) pixels (File size: 50 KB – 100 KB).
Passport Copy: Scanned copy of the primary photo and personal details page, with a minimum remaining validity of 9 months (Dimensions: 600 × 800 pixels; File size: 50 KB – 100 KB). Afghan applicants must also upload valid visa/extension pages.
Academic Credentials: Official Bachelor’s degree certificate and comprehensive academic transcripts.
Curriculum Vitae (CV) / Professional Resume.
Academic Letter of Recommendation from a qualified university professor.
Proof of English Language Proficiency: Official score report (e.g., IELTS, TOEFL, or equivalent recognized certificate) meeting the minimum threshold specified in the portal.
Tuition Fees and Financial Overview
Tuition fees for non-scholarship international students enrolling in the 2026–2027 academic year are priced competitively in Euros (€) and may be paid in their Iranian Rial equivalent based on the Central Bank's ETS exchange rate at the time of registration:
Fixed Tuition: €416 per semester
Variable Tuition (Theoretical Courses): €36 per credit
Variable Tuition (Practical Courses): €47 per credit
Variable Tuition (Remedial Courses): €11 per credit
Variable Tuition (Thesis): €376 per credit
Estimated First-Semester Total: ~€776
Estimated Total Program Tuition (4 Semesters): ~€4,220
Student Welfare and Accommodation
Subject to availability and regulations established by the University, international Master's students may access subsidized campus accommodation and meal plans for up to four academic semesters:
Dormitory Housing: Furnished 4-person rooms are available at a subsidized rate of 55,000,000 Rials per person per month (calculated on a 6-month semester basis).
Dining Facilities: Daily on-campus cafeteria meals range from 1,900,000 Rials (standard menu) to 2,300,000 Rials (premium menu) per serving.
Evaluation and Interview Process
Following initial document verification by the Center for International Student Affairs, eligible files are forwarded to academic departments for specialized review. Shortlisted candidates will be invited to participate in a departmental interview—covering specialized academic qualifications and general English language fluency—conducted online or in person. Attendance at the scheduled interview is mandatory.

Moscow reveals potential timeline for trilateral Ukraine talks
Trilateral talks between Russian, Ukrainian, and US representatives could begin in October, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, the official stated that Moscow “does not rule out such a possibility.”
“We’re specifically talking about the foreseeable future. That is, presumably of course, October,” Peskov clarified.
Earlier this week, the Kremlin spokesman stated that Moscow hopes “for a restart of negotiations between three parties – Russia, Ukraine, and America.”
The trilateral format was last used in Geneva in February, following two earlier rounds in Abu Dhabi. However, the talks later stalled without any significant breakthroughs, as the US shifted its focus to its war against Iran.
Peskov’s recent comments have followed a fresh round of shuttle diplomacy by US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who held a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow last week before visiting Kiev for talks with Vladimir Zelensky.
The Kremlin described the discussions with the US negotiators as constructive and “extremely candid,” while Witkoff said that progress had been made toward scheduling a three-way meeting. The potential resumption of talks in this format was also among the topics Putin and Trump discussed by phone on Tuesday, according to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov.
At around the same time, Zelensky suggested that the next round of trilateral negotiations could take place in the UAE, Türkiye, Switzerland, or another country as early as September or October.
Moscow has repeatedly said it remains open to diplomacy, as long as the root causes of the conflict are addressed and the new realities on the ground are respected. Ukraine has in turn ruled out making territorial concessions to Russia.

Saudi pipeline outage threatens loss of 4% of global oil supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:49:12 UTC

Breadcrumb
Saudi pipeline outage threatens loss of 4% of global oil supply
Saudi Arabia will run out of oil stocks for exports if it doesn't restart its major pipeline to the Red Sea within days, leading to a loss of up to 4% of global supply, Saudi oil buyers and traders said.
A further decline in Saudi flows will worsen the global supply crunch, which has already pushed global fuel prices to record highs, spurred inflation around the world and sent U.S. bond yields to the highest levels since the 2008 financial crisis.
Since drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to shut its huge east-west oil pipeline on Friday, Riyadh has not given full details about the extent of the damage or how long the route will stay off-line.
Sources that spoke to Reuters gave varying estimates, with one saying the damage could take as long as five to six weeks to repair, while another said it could be fixed sooner and could resume pumping partially while repairs are ongoing.
Saudi Arabia's government media office and energy ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
For the past six months, the pipeline running through the desert across the Arabian Peninsula has spared Saudi Arabia from the brunt of the impact of the wartime shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz that has crippled exports from its neighbours.
The world's biggest exporter has used the pipeline to reroute around 4 million barrels per day — around 4% of global supply — to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea.
But with the pipeline out of service, Yanbu now has stocks to maintain exports for just five to seven days, according to three industry sources familiar with Saudi exports.
Saudi Arabia also has stocks to supply customers for several days from Egypt's ports of Ain Sukhna on the Red Sea and Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean, a fourth source said.
Yanbu storage capacity stands at around 35 million barrels, according to industry estimates, with Ain Sukhna and Sidi Kerir able to store 18 million and 20 million barrels respectively.
Stocks are not full and will ultimately run out without the east-west pipeline resuming operations, the four sources said.
Saudi oil supply has already fallen to a more than three-decade low in August on reduced flows via Hormuz and the Red Sea, the International Energy Agency said on Friday.
World oil supply will decline this year by 5.7 million bpd, or about 6%, the IEA, which coordinates Western energy policies, said.
In addition to the attack on the pipeline, Houthi fighters in Yemen who have threatened Saudi oil shipments seized an island on Friday in the mouth of the Red Sea.
The Middle East supplied around 22 million barrels per day of oil before the war. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz have slowed to just 6 million to 9 million bpd, industry sources say.
Saudi Arabia told OPEC last week that its oil production had dropped to just 6.2 million bpd in August from 10.9 million bpd in February before the start of the war.
(Reuters)
