How personality and social context shape adolescent loneliness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:00:29 UTC
21:00:29 KST

Adolescents experience isolation differently depending on whether they are with close friends or mere acquaintances, and their underlying personality traits shape these daily emotions. A new study published in Development and Psychopathology reveals that while spending time alone is linked to momentary feelings of isolation, young people with maladaptive personality traits tend to experience chronic loneliness regardless of their social surroundings.
Adolescence is a period of intense social transition. Teenagers often shift their focus from family to peers, which can leave them feeling disconnected if they have not yet formed stable friend groups. The threshold for feeling lonely varies from person to person. Psychologists often look to the differential reactivity hypothesis to explain this variation.
This hypothesis suggests that individuals differ widely in how they respond to social situations. People who are prone to loneliness do not necessarily encounter more social stressors than their peers. Instead, they react more intensely to the social situations they do face. Personality traits can heavily shape this reactivity.
Maladaptive personality traits refer to enduring patterns of thinking and behaving that make it difficult to function in everyday life. These include extreme emotional sensitivity or a tendency to withdraw from others. Cara Luisa Wicher, a psychologist at the University of Wuppertal in Germany, led a team to investigate how these traits operate in daily life. Wicher and her colleagues Susanne Buecker, Paula Philippi, and Aleksandra Kaurin sought to map the daily fluctuations of adolescent loneliness.
The researchers used a method called ecological momentary assessment. Traditional questionnaires ask participants to remember how they felt over the past week or month, which can introduce memory bias. By prompting the youth multiple times a day on their smartphones as they went about their normal lives, the researchers captured the immediate context of their emotions.
The study included 294 adolescents and young adults between the ages of 12 and 21. For 14 days, the participants received up to seven alerts a day, along with a separate evening survey. They answered questions about how lonely they felt at that exact moment, who they were with, and where they were. The participants answered over 27,000 momentary prompts, yielding a highly detailed dataset.
Before the two week period began, the participants also completed baseline questionnaires. These surveys measured overall trait loneliness and maladaptive personality domains. The personality inventory assessed traits such as negative affect, detachment, antagonism, disinhibition, and rigid perfectionism.
The data showed a distinct pattern regarding solitude. When the adolescents were alone, they reported higher levels of momentary and daily loneliness compared to when they were in social company. Yet, individuals who generally spent more time alone over the entire two week period were not necessarily lonelier on average than their highly social peers.
The type of company played a major role in shaping emotional states. Being in the presence of close connections, such as friends, romantic partners, or family members, was associated with reduced loneliness. In contrast, spending time with weaker social ties, like classmates or colleagues, was not associated with any reduction in loneliness.
The environment also factored into these emotional states. The adolescents reported the highest levels of momentary loneliness when interacting with people on the internet. This was followed by time spent with roommates or strangers.
The researchers also noted shifts in social habits related to age. Older adolescents spent less time with their families and more time with romantic partners. At the same time, older participants experienced a stronger association between being alone and feeling lonely. This aligns with psychological theories of emerging adulthood, where spending time alone is a normal part of gaining independence, yet it can feel particularly isolating as young people navigate identity formation.
Maladaptive personality traits heavily factored into these daily experiences. Participants who scored higher on these traits at the start of the study reported greater and more variable levels of loneliness throughout the two weeks. They experienced steeper emotional fluctuations from day to day.
Two specific personality domains stood out in the data. Detachment involves withdrawing from social interactions and displaying limited emotional expression. Negative affect describes a tendency to experience intense negative emotions frequently.
Adolescents with high levels of detachment spent more time alone and experienced more frequent spikes in loneliness. Those with high negative affect felt especially lonely when they were by themselves. These traits seemed to affect the way the youth processed their social environments.
When looking at the broader picture, maladaptive personality traits seemed to disconnect loneliness from actual social contact. For youth with higher levels of these traits, being alone more often did not directly predict higher average loneliness. Instead, they appeared to experience loneliness as an ongoing state, rather than a reaction to a specific moment of solitude.
The researchers also found that daily satisfaction with social contact partially explained the link between being alone and feeling lonely. This suggests that the perceived quality of a relationship is a stronger predictor of loneliness than the sheer quantity of interactions. Adolescents with maladaptive personality traits reported lower social satisfaction overall, which was associated with their heightened feelings of isolation.
The study relies heavily on surveys based on self-reports, which can introduce personal bias. The sample was also relatively uniform, consisting primarily of young people born in Germany from stable socioeconomic backgrounds. This limits how well the findings might apply to more diverse populations or clinical groups.
To avoid exhausting the participants with long surveys seven times a day, the researchers used a single question to measure momentary loneliness. While this is a common practice in this type of research, a single item might not capture the full experience of feeling isolated. The act of answering the surveys could have also influenced behavior. If participants knew that reporting social company would trigger follow up questions, they might have underreported their social interactions to save time.
Because the study observed daily habits without introducing an experiment, the results show associations rather than direct causes. For example, it remains unknown if spending time online precedes feelings of loneliness or if lonely individuals simply seek out the internet as a coping mechanism. Future research could explore more diverse groups and investigate how specific coping strategies or emotion regulation skills might alter these daily patterns of loneliness.
The study, “Daily manifestations of maladaptive personality traits and loneliness across social contexts in youth,” was authored by Cara Luisa Wicher, Susanne Buecker, Paula Philippi, and Aleksandra Kaurin.

Iran says Monday’s meeting in Oman to focus on new maritime route in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:00:21 UTC
21:00:21 KST

Sahin Demir
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said a planned meeting in Oman on Monday will focus on a new maritime route through the Strait of Hormuz.
 
Araghchi told the London-based Arabic-language news outlet Al-Araby Al-Jadeed that the meeting will be held in the Omani city of Salalah with the participation of Iran, Iraq and five Gulf countries.
 
He said the gathering was initially envisaged as a meeting of eight countries bordering the Gulf, but Bahrain had decided not to participate, leaving seven countries at the talks.
 
“The main, and indeed the only, agenda of this meeting is the new maritime route in the Strait of Hormuz,” Araghchi said.
 
He said Tehran and Muscat had finalized an agreement on establishing the new maritime route and had prepared maps and a joint statement outlining the arrangements.
 
Participating countries will be briefed on the agreement, related maps and the joint statement, after which the documents will be submitted to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) for registration, he added.
 
He stressed that the agreement with Oman “by no means” signifies the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
 
Araghchi said the understanding instead sets out the framework and details of new entry and exit routes that would be used if conditions are created for reopening the strategic waterway.
 
Araghchi said Iran’s condition for reopening the strait is for the US to return to its commitments under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
 
“If the US returns to the commitments it accepted and signed in the Islamabad understanding and acts accordingly, the conditions will be created for the situation in the Strait of Hormuz to return to normal,” he said.
 
He accused Washington of undermining maritime security through what he described as a naval blockade and economic warfare, saying the Iran-Oman arrangements could provide the framework for navigation to return to normal if Washington fulfills its commitments.
 
He added that Tehran believes responsibility for ensuring security and stability in the region rests solely with regional countries.
 
Araghchi stressed, however, that Monday’s gathering is not aimed at establishing a new regional security mechanism, saying its agenda is limited to the new maritime arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz.
 
The foreign minister expressed hope that Monday’s talks would pave the way for further consultations on issues of common concern among countries in the region.
 
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Saturday that foreign ministers from regional countries would meet in Oman on Monday over the joint Iran-Oman shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, with the agreement to be communicated to the IMO. He reiterated that Iran would reopen the strait when the US ends its attacks and naval blockade.
 
The US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in February, prompting Tehran to retaliate against Israel and US military targets across the region. 
 
Washington and Tehran reached the Islamabad understanding in June with Pakistani and Qatari mediation, but its implementation later stalled amid disagreements over the Strait of Hormuz. The US resumed military attacks on Iran in August, with Tehran responding by striking US military assets in several Arab countries aligned with Washington.

Stitching our warped reality together: a cartoonist and art critic take different approaches to the Bayeux tapestry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

Our journalists often draw connections between seemingly disparate issues or events to give people a fuller grasp of how things interrelate. But not every story can convey the scope and complexity of today’s algorithmically warped reality.
One of the Guardian’s regular cartoonists has managed this feat by drawing inspiration from a medieval embroidery made almost 1,000 years ago. Edith Pritchett was asked by her editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine to draw a modern-day version of the Bayeux tapestry, the 11th-century artwork that has been capturing imaginations this month as it goes on public display in the UK for the first time since its creation. Her updated version was included as a pullout poster in the print edition of the Guardian last weekend and also published as a special scrollable digital feature.
Whereas the original Bayeux tapestry tells the story of the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England in 1066, Edith’s take on it depicts today’s battles with online trolls, social media addiction, the manosphere, AI agents and a natural world ravaged by fossil fuels. But her version is more than just a topical reimagining: it gives the viewer a genuine feel for how the different components of today’s dystopia amplify each other.
“I decided on the main topics such as techno-feudalism, the climate crisis, the super-rich, Elon Musk, the online swirling vortex of hatred,” says Edith, “then I tried to work out how to piece it together into a kind of flowing narrative.”
Unlike Edith, the Guardian art critic Jonathan Jones tried to avoid thinking about the Bayeux tapestry in contemporary terms when he encountered the actual artwork at the British Museum for his review of the landmark exhibition. “I’m always against grafting contemporary issues on to [historic] works of art,” he says. “Yet when I saw it, my genuine visceral response was to see some of those parallels. There is real horror in it – the horror of war – and it really did strike me very freshly.”
While the Bayeux tapestry might be made of frail linen, it’s hard to overstate its weight as a treasured artwork, historical document and, more latterly, an instrument of Franco-British diplomatic goodwill. Edith was understandably unnerved by the prospect of trying to update it: “I depressed myself by looking at the tapestry online and thinking about how beautiful and amazing it is. I thought, ‘Oh no, I’m going to do this cheap rip-off of it’.”
But she also felt inspired by the challenge. “I knew I was going to be wading into the big questions of today’s age,” she says. “I had an initial jumble of ideas and then picked out things that could be represented in an immediate visual language.” For instance, AI agents are depicted as retro-looking robots. However, she had to ditch some aspects of today’s tech-dominated world. “I would have loved to have included something about datacentres, but how do you draw a datacentre in a way that’s visually engaging? It would have looked rubbish.”
The prominent role of tech titans proved prescient: last week, the Guardian revealed that the tech billionaire Peter Thiel had been granted a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum ahead of the British and French heads of state.
Given the tapestry’s political significance and history, how did Jonathan avoid approaching it with preconceptions? “I have a fairly visual mind and when I go to an exhibition I avoid reading captions and text as much as possible. I don’t read catalogues until years afterwards,” he explains. “If you focus on the visual experience, what you see is fresh and raw – you’re not seeing it through other people’s words. One of the problems I have as a critic is that, for perfectly good reasons, curators want to talk to you in a show, and I have to politely ask them to leave me alone. It needs to be about what’s directly in front of my eyes. That physical, visceral experience in a direct, unmediated way so that you just open yourself to the images.”
The original artwork stretches to 68.3 metres long. Jonathan describes the experience of viewing it as almost cinematic. But as well as being swept along, his eyes were drawn to the intricate borders above and below the main narrative. These famously feature images of animals and symbolic portents that either mirror the story’s actions and emotions or provide a kind of ambiguous commentary. “So this felt like a whole multifaceted world that aspires to take in the whole of creation,” says Jonathan.
In today’s speak, you could say the borders reveal the vibes. Re-creating them gave Edith further scope to show how some of today’s dystopian tendencies work in tandem. “For instance, I drew an incel narrative along the bottom border,” she says, pointing to images of red and blue pills beneath a scene about the manosphere. Other details include a bitcoin symbol beneath a superyacht; wall-mounted mirrors that literally reflect the social media-induced misery of teenagers; dead animals above an oil rig, while other animals succumb to phone addiction and grapple with four-legged AI robots.
Edith refrained from illustrating some of the more horrifying consequences of today’s dynamics, such as droughts, wildfires and armed conflict, because she didn’t want to be reductive. “As an illustrator, you want to have a visual shorthand for things you’re trying to represent, but you also want to give them dignity. So there are certain things that, if you try to draw them, you would skip all nuance.”
Despite the horrors depicted in the original tapestry, Jonathan was surprised by the levity of some of the panels. “The surreal and comedy aspects were surprising. It felt more contemporary than I thought it would be. It was more raw and shocking as well as funnier.”
Did the tapestry also seem contemporary in terms of its format and the ways in which people consume narrative content today? “You could say its time has come because we’re more visual,” he agrees. “We don’t read as much, and here’s this raw masterpiece of visual storytelling.”
That said, building a digital version of Edith’s illustration presented unique challenges for our design team. “How do you show readers details in wide images when we’re all looking at these little vertical screens without chopping them up or pinching and zooming?” explains Tara Herman, the Guardian’s executive editor for design. The team’s solution was an interactive format that combines the act of scrolling vertically with the experience of viewing things unfold horizontally – almost as if you’re swiping instead of scrolling. “Our interactive format is an attempt to emulate the experience of being in a gallery where you’re taking your turn looking at a picture and pausing to take in different details.”

Pressure builds in Spain to deny US extradition request for leftwing donor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Attorneys for James “Fergie” Chambers, the US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects worldwide who is currently imprisoned in Madrid and sought in extradition, have submitted a brief ahead of a decisive government meeting on the case.
Meanwhile, Chambers’ partner, the actor and activist Stella Schnabel, met last week with multiple members of the Spanish parliament to assert his innocence.
The legal team’s arguments include that the US government has failed to identify specific acts of violence or damages personally attributable to Chambers and instead is seeking to criminalize acts linked to political protest.
They also assert that at least one figure of US law underpinning the request – “conspiracy to commit riot” – has no equivalent in Spanish law, which would also help render the extradition invalid.
It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas.
Chambers’ defense has submitted its brief to the government ahead of a meeting by Spain’s council of ministers expected to take place on 22 September. The council can decide whether or not to allow the US extradition request to proceed, based in part on an evaluation of supporting materials the Trump administration supplied to the government on 26 August.
Under Spanish law, at this “administrative” stage, the 22-member council has the power to deny the request, before it reaches a “judicial” stage.
The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m that he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support the Palestinian group Hamas. The exact details of the indictment against Chambers remain sealed.
Chambers’ team say he has been supporting humanitarian aid and other projects. The 41–year-old self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s additional charges of “international money laundering” don’t hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means. Chambers’ donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries for several years – including the Sameer Project, in Gaza.
“It would set an alarming precedent in all of Europe if Spain allowed the Trump administration to criminalize offering vital humanitarian aid to the Palestinian people and defending their rights,” said Baltasar Garzón, the acclaimed human rights lawyer and a member of Chambers’ legal team.
“That’s what Fergie has financed: humanitarian aid and support for people in a situation of great need,” said Garzón. “That’s not terrorism, according to Spanish and European legal standards.”
Meanwhile, Schnabel has met with members of Sumar and Podemos – progressive political movements vital to the coalition government of the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – and has written a one-page letter to Sánchez asking him to make “the only morally acceptable decision”, that of denying extradition. Sánchez forms part of the council of ministers.
Schnabel has not escaped scrutiny since her partner was detained on 10 July in Ibiza. On a recent trip to New York, the FBI pulled her aside at JFK airport and confiscated her phone, she said.
Support for Chambers in the lead-up to the 20 September meeting has come from Ione Bellara, leader of Podemos, who opened the party’s quarterly meeting last Saturday with a statement opposing the extradition request, saying that Chambers was “on the right side of history” with his financial support of Palestinians in Gaza.
Similarly, Sumar, the leftwing coalition that governs jointly with Sánchez’s Socialist party, filed a statement in Spain’s congress earlier this week urging the government to deny the petition, “given that the goal of the extradition request … is to criminalize, persecute or punish [Chambers] due to his political opinions, his public activity or his participation in political movements – in this case, in support of the Palestinian people”.
Irene Montero, member of Podemos and Spanish representative to the European parliament, told the Guardian that “Our laws don’t contemplate the actions he is accused of … [and] we can’t become a subject of the United States.”
Activists have held rallies in recent days in at least six cities across Spain in support of Chambers, with plans for more.
Other shows of support from farther afield have included a petition delivered to the Spanish government signed by actors, academics, activists and others, including Richard Gere, Greta Thunberg and Angela Davis. In Tunisia, supporters of the Club Africain football team displayed banners and T-shirts at a recent match that read, “Free Fergie”. In Portugal, at Festa do Avante, one of that country’s largest cultural festivals, fans held up a banner saying: “Free Fergie – supporting Palestine isn’t a crime.”
Schnabel told the Guardian last month that the $7.5m went to support Club Africain. Hamed Mbarek, one of the club’s supporters and an organizer of fans at last Saturday’s match, said Club Africain was “pro-Palestine” and that Chambers and the club had “synchronicity”.
Chambers’ money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time.
His views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media. He was interviewed on a TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group now proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”.
Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza have also brought controversy. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.”
He has also been a staunch critic of the US, telling a reporter in 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.”
Irene Zugasti helped organize rallies earlier this week and last weekend in support of Chambers in Madrid, Barcelona and several other Spanish cities. She sees the case as bigger than whether he is extradited or not. “If they go after Fergie, they’ll go after anyone … It’s a test – to see until what point European governments feel pressure from the United States.”

How to make chocolate mousse – recipe | Felicity Cloake's Masterclass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Years ago, a group of us cycled from Brittany to the Mediterranean, and along the way we ate a lot of chocolate mousse. Popular, easy to make and happy to sit in the fridge until required, it’s a mainstay of the modest French provincial restaurant and, as we discovered, it’s almost always good. Here’s my favourite version of the little black dress of the dessert trolley.
Prep 5 min
Cook 20 min
Chill 2 hr+
Makes 2
60g at least 70% cocoa chocolate
2 medium eggs
  1 pinch salt
  2 tsp sugar, or to taste
1 A note on the chocolate
You can use milk or flavoured chocolate here, if you like, but do bear in mind that if it’s quite sweet, you probably won’t need the extra sugar. Unless you’re using uniform chocolate drops designed for melting, roughly chop the chocolate – there’s no need to cut it into very tiny pieces, but they should be fairly even so they melt at the same rate.
2 Melt the chocolate over a bain-marie
Boil the kettle. Meanwhile, get ready a large heatproof bowl that can sit over a pan holding about 5cm of water without the base of the bowl touching the water. Pour the boiling water into the pan and turn on the heat to medium. Put the chocolate in the bowl, then put the bowl on top of the water pan and turn down the heat so the water is barely simmering. Stir occasionally, until the chocolate is completely melted.
3 … or use a microwave
Alternatively, use a microwave, which saves on washing up but carries a greater risk of burning the chocolate if you don’t keep your eye on it. Put the chocolate in a heatproof bowl, microwave for 20 seconds, then stir and carry on microwaving in five-second bursts until completely melted.
4 Carefully separate the eggs
While the chocolate is melting, separate the eggs – it’s important not to get any yolk in the whites or they’ll be tricky to whip up properly. To avoid this possibility, I break the eggs into a glass or metal bowl (plastic will make the job harder), then use a clean hand to scoop the yolks into a fresh bowl.
5 Beat the egg whites
Leave the chocolate to cool slightly. While it does so, use electric beaters or a large whisk to whip the egg whites and a pinch of salt to soft peaks – that is, to the point when the mix will hold a wave that flops over at the top rather than standing up straight. Add the sugar and carry on whisking until the mix is glossy and holds its shape.
6 Combine the egg yolks and chocolate
Mix the egg yolks one at a time into the melted chocolate. If at any point the mixture seizes and turns tight and grainy, don’t worry, it’s not a disaster. Simply add a small splash of boiling water and whisk again until the mix is glossy and pourable again (if that doesn’t work, repeat the process until it does).
7 Fold in the egg whites
Stir a spoonful of the whipped egg white into the melted chocolate and egg yolk mixture to loosen it up, then add the rest. Use a large metal spoon gently to fold it in, using a D-shaped action so you don’t knock too much air out of the meringue. Stop as soon as everything is uniformly mixed, with no streaks.
8 Chill to set
Spoon the mousse into a serving bowl or into two separate bowls or glasses (don’t worry if the serving looks ungenerous; this is a very rich dessert). Put in the fridge to chill (covered, if you like, especially if you have any strongly scented ingredients in there), preferably for a couple of hours, so the mousse has a chance to set properly. It will keep well for several days.
9 Variations on the theme
To ring the changes, when melting the chocolate, stir in the grated zest of a well-scrubbed orange, or two tablespoons of strong coffee, a pinch of cinnamon, nutmeg or chilli flakes, a little more salt, or a splash of vanilla extract or rosewater. Serve as is, or top it with whipped cream, cocoa nibs, orange zest, mint leaves or chopped nuts.

Iran to chair Tehran Convention, lead Caspian Sea environmental protection efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:59:13 UTC
20:59:13 KST

Iran to chair Tehran Convention, lead Caspian Sea environmental protection efforts
TEHRAN – Iran will host the seventh meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Tehran Convention on the protection of the Caspian Sea environment from September 20 to October 1, following a three-year hiatus, and will assume the convention’s rotating presidency at the conclusion of the meeting.
Arman Khorsand, head of the International Affairs and Conventions Center of the Department of Environment, said the Tehran Convention, which provides the main framework for cooperation among Caspian littoral states on environmental protection, marks its 20th anniversary of entry into force this year.
The seventh Conference of the Parties (COP7) will be held over four days, with the first three days dedicated to expert-level meetings and the final day to a high-level session, he added. Environment ministers and officials from the five Caspian littoral states, along with representatives of the United Nations, will attend the meeting.
Khorsand said reviewing and finalizing documents related to the convention’s various protocols, as well as a declaration by the environment ministers of the member states, are among the main issues on the agenda.
Holding COP7 after a three-year hiatus is particularly significant and could help strengthen regional cooperation to protect the Caspian Sea environment and address the environmental challenges facing the body of water, he noted.
The official further said that with the meeting being held in Tehran, the Islamic Republic of Iran will assume the rotating presidency of the Tehran Convention for the upcoming term.
In October 2025, DOE head Shina Ansari said Iran is willing to maintain and promote a collaborative relationship with the Tehran Convention, develop structures, as well as establish a permanent secretariat.
She made the remarks in a meeting in Tehran with Mahir Aliyev, the Secretariat of the Framework Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Caspian Sea (Tehran Convention), IRNA reported.
The two officials also discussed arrangements and preparations for holding COP 7, the perspectives of the Caspian Sea littoral states on cooperation for advancing the goals of the Tehran Convention, as well as reducing pollution and harmful substances in the Caspian Sea.
Tehran Convention
The need for joint protection and management of the Caspian environment and its resources has been a long-standing concern for the Caspian littoral states. In 1998, the Caspian Environment Programme (CEP) was established as a regional initiative aimed at stopping the deterioration of the Caspian Sea’s environmental conditions of and promoting sustainable development for the long-term benefit of the Caspian population.
Since its inception, the CEP has tackled various environmental issues by developing a coordinated management structure, creating Strategic and National Action Plans, and implementing transnational measures to address imminent threats to the Caspian environment. Funded by the littoral states, the European Union, and the international community through the Global Environment Facility (GEF), the CEP has worked to formalize its structure and activities by concluding the Tehran Convention.
In 2003, the Caspian littoral states: Republic of Azerbaijan, Islamic Republic of Iran, Republic of Kazakhstan, Russian Federation, and Turkmenistan, signed the Framework Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Caspian Sea (Tehran Convention). After the ratification by all the five Governments, the Tehran Convention entered into force on August 12, 2006.
The Tehran Convention serves as an overarching legal framework that establishes general requirements and an institutional mechanism for environmental protection in the Caspian Sea region. It is based on principles such as the precautionary principle, the polluter pays principle, and the principle of access to and exchange of information. The two major areas of focus are (i) prevention, reduction, and control of pollution, and (ii) protection, preservation, and restoration of the marine environment. The Convention includes provisions on environmental impact assessment as well as general obligations related to environmental monitoring, research and development.
COP 7 to focus on Caspian seal protection
Known for its unique biodiversity, the Caspian Sea is home to different kinds of valuable species and plays a vital role in the economy, food security, and ecological sustainability of the region.
Over recent decades, marine life, particularly sturgeon and Caspian seals’ populations in the sea, have sharply declined due to threatening factors such as illegal fishing, overfishing, oil, industrial, and agricultural pollution, climate change, reduced water flow, as well as habitat destruction.
The Caspian seal is the only marine mammal in the Caspian Sea. The species is now listed as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list, with its population declining due to various reasons, from one million in the past to 70,000, currently.
In recent years, the increase in the discovery of seals’ carcasses on the southern coast of the Caspian Sea has raised concerns among environmentalists that the Caspian seal is at greater risk of extinction than ever before. In just two months, 18 carcasses were discovered on Mazandaran coasts, IRNA reported.
Addressing the coordination meeting for the protection of the Caspian seal species, Ansari said that, given the recent losses of the seals and their critical status, conservation efforts need to be prioritized. Hence, COP 7, which will be held in Tehran, will focus on the preservation of the Caspian seal.
During the 11th Nevsky International Ecological Congress, held from May 22 to 23, 2025, in Saint Petersburg, Russia, the five Caspian Sea states (Iran, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Kazakhstan) discussed environmental challenges threatening, such as shrinking water level, pollution, habitat destruction, and decline in population of marine animals,” IRNA quoted Ansari as saying.
Underscoring the need for regional cooperation to protect the biodiversity of the Caspian ecosystem, Ansari said based on regional diplomacy, it is essential to focus specifically on the Caspian Sea environment to save endangered species, particularly the Caspian seals, through enhanced joint measures, the official noted.
The official went on to highlight the significance of promoting inter-sectoral cooperation among responsible bodies such as fisheries and veterinary organizations, saying that fostering joint efforts will reduce conflicts over the conservation of these species.

It comes amid reported friction between Le Pen and Jordan Bardella, the president of the National Rally party.
Back in her political stronghold in northern France, Marine Le Pen is delivering her first major campaign speech this Sunday. The far-right candidate for 2027 will be in Hénin-Beaumont as part of her presidential election, after MPs from her party met in Le Touquet (Pas-de-Calais) on Saturday.
Le Pen is currently leading in the polls, with 34% of voters declaring they intend to vote for her in the first round — across different tested scenarios — according to a survey carried out on 8 and 9 September by OpinionWay for Les Échos.
Despite this, recent weeks have been marked by a series of mishaps, amid alleged tensions between Le Pen and the president of the National Rally (RN) party, Jordan Bardella, as well as controversial remarks over aid to Ukraine and the release of a video in which a police officer — and former volunteered of the RN’s security team — makes racist, sexist and conspiracy-theory-based remarks.
Meanwhile, Le Pen has still not reacted to the signing of an immigration pact between Bardella and Nigel Farage, the leader of the UK's hard-right, anti-immigration Reform UK party, which provides for migrants intercepted in British waters to be sent back to France — should the two parties be elected.
What role will Bardella play?
In recent weeks, rumours around alleged tensions between Le Pen and Bardella — who is vying to be France's next prime minister — have been swirling.
According to French newspaper Libération, the president of the National Rally is said to have declared "it’s her or me" on 31 August, after Le Pen reportedly announced she intended to give her niece — Marion Maréchal — a greater role in the campaign.
During the 2022 presidential campaign, Maréchal backed Éric Zemmour, the leader of the rival far-right party Reconquête over her aunt.
Bardella subsequently denied any tensions, telling the French broadcaster BFM-TV: "Everything is going very, very well, I assure you. I support her 2,000%." He added that he had an "unbreakable political and personal affinity" with Le Pen while also denying that he wanted to "impose" his line on the party.
The two leading figures of the National Rally have presented different economic visions, especially concerning pensions. According to Bardella, the current French pension system "is not economically sustainable." He also seems hesitant to have his "boss" turn her proposed ban on the wearing of the veil in public spaces into a central campaign issue.
On 31 August, he insisted that the aim was not "to impose a dress code," stressing that a referendum on the issue would be held. The president of the Patriots for Europe group in the European Parliament also appears more pro-market than Le Pen, who has traditionally been more supportive of protectionist measures.
Support for Ukraine
Beyond this, the RN is also facing disagreements over international issues.
Speaking to BFM-TV on 4 September, Louis Aliot, the party’s vice-president and mayor of Perpignan, was asked about aid to Ukraine
"We turn off the tap. The health system, the education system, the whole economy, everything has been cut to the bone, and yet we still find money to fund more weapons (...) I’m willing to accept that, but who pays for all this? You also have to know how to stop a war," he said.
His comments quickly sparked a debate.
Taking to X, Édouard Philippe, the centre-right Horizons party’s candidate for 2027, seized the opportunity to accuse the RN of "its support for Putin’s regime," arguing that "turning off the tap for Ukraine means serving Russia."
"Weakening Ukraine, as Marine Le Pen wants, means threatening the security of Europe and France. I will do everything to stop her," he added.
Le Pen hit back within the hour, reminding the former prime minister that he was in office when the Russian president was "received with great pomp at the Palace of Versailles and then at the Fort of Brégançon," and that he himself had welcomed Dmitry Medvedev, then Russian prime minister, to his home city of Le Havre in June 2019.
National Rally grapples with police scandal
On 8 September, French regional daily Midi Libre released a video from November 2025 showing several municipal police officers in Carcassonne making racist, sexist and conspiracy-related comments during a nighttime patrol.
The patrol leader, responsible for nearly 90% of the remarks made that evening, is a former paratrooper, but he had also volunteered for the RN's internal security service.
He notably escorted Bardella on several trips, including during the promotional tour for his book, as well as at the launch of the RN's municipal election campaign.
The officer in question was expelled from the National Rally on Wednesday. Bardella, for his part, has described his comments as "despicable."
The Carcassonne public prosecutor’s office also announced on Wednesday the suspension of the four municipal police officers who appear in the video.

Are you smarter than a 15-year-old? Test your maths, science and reading with these PISA questions
Unknown

This week, the OECD's PISA report has revealed a global decline in 15-year-old's maths and reading skills — but how much better can the grown-up's fare?
Every three years, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD)'s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) evaluates 15-year-olds' reading, mathematics and science abilities through a standardised test.
The latest report, published on Tuesday, has revealed a concerning global decline in maths and reading skills in particular. Artificial intelligence (AI), smartphones and social media have been cited as contributing factors.
"The bottom line is quite simple: You don't get fit by watching sports. You get fit by doing sports," Andreas Schleicher, the founder of the OECD's renowned PISA tests, told Euronews.
"And the same is true with learning. Learning doesn't come through the consumption of content; learning comes by engaging with ideas to compare and contrast. And AI can hollow out that very process. That's what we observe."
But what about the adults? Are we any better? A 2024 study by Reading Agency found that half of the adults in the United Kingdom don't read for pleasure, while a Eurostat survey from the same year found that almost half of EU citizens have not read a single book in twelve months.
It begs the question: How much better than the 15-year-olds would we all fare?
Now's your chance to see — scroll to have a go at a sample of the OECD's questions. Answers can be found at the very bottom of the page (no cheating!)
Mathematics
Question 1: Alex drew the following pattern of red and blue triangles.
The first four rows of the pattern are shown below.
What percentage of the triangles in the first four rows of Alex’s pattern are blue?
A) 37.5%
B) 50.0%
C) 60.0%
D) 62.5%

- The number of DVDs sold declined by about 50% from 2008 through 2014
- The number of DVDs sold declined by the same amount each year from 2008 through 2014
- The slope of the line is the average yearly decline in DVDs sold from 2008 to 2014
Science
Question 1: Many people are concerned about the global environmental impacts of the manufacture and disposal of clothing.
Cotton fibres come from the outer layer of the cotton plant’s seeds. Compared to synthetic fibres, cotton fibres need less processing and biodegrade more easily.
The production of cotton textiles requires a lot of water, fertilisers, pesticides and other harmful chemicals. To try to solve these issues, sustainable cotton production methods are being developed.
Which of the following actions can be taken to reduce the negative environmental impacts of producing cotton textiles? Highlight all correct answers.
- Use water more efficiently
- Reduce the quality of the cotton textiles produced
- Increase the number of staff that cotton farms employ
- Use pesticides that are harmful only to the pest species being targeted
- Dispose of chemical waste in areas far away from the sites involved in cotton production
Question 2: When lightning strikes, an observer immediately sees a flash of light. Thunder occurs at the same time, but the observer hears it a little later.
The time taken before an observer hears thunder depends on factors including the distance between the observer and the location of the lightning strike.
Which one of the following statements best explains why lightning is seen before thunder is heard?
- The speed of light through air is faster than the speed of sound through air.
- Light does not need to travel through the air to be seen, but sound does need to travel through the air to be heard.
- Particles of light are not as heavy as particles of sound, so they are easier to detect
- Eyes detect light faster than ears detect sound
Reading
Question 1: In this test, you will read some sentences and decide if they make sense or not. Answer YES if the sentence makes sense and NO if the sentence does not make sense.
- The red car had a flat tire
- Airplanes are made of dogs
- The student read the book last night
Question 2: You are visiting your relatives, who recently moved to a farm to raise chickens. You ask your aunt, “How did you learn how to raise chickens?”
She says, “We talked to a lot of people who raise chickens. And, there are lots of resources on the Internet. For example, there is a Chicken Health forum that I like to visit. It was very helpful to me recently when one of my hens hurt her leg. I’ll show you the conversation I had.”

- Less than 600 zeds

Science 1. ’Use water more efficiently’ and ‘Use pesticides that are harmful only to the pest species being targeted'. 2. ‘The speed of light through air is faster than the speed of sound through air.’

Israeli troops call for 'conquest of Damascus' amid continued attacks on Syrian territory
Israeli reservists have called for the military to expand its illegal operations deeper into Syrian territory, with a senior officer saying many troops would favour advancing as far as Damascus, according to Israeli media.
Reserve officers serving with the Israeli army's 210th Division have criticised limits on the scope of its operations in southern Syria and called for increased activity inside Syrian villages and surrounding areas, Israeli news site Walla reported.
The officers reportedly argued that deeper incursions would help push what Israel considers potential threats further away from its border.
A senior Israeli officer defended the military's current approach but acknowledged the appetite among reservists for a more wide-scale invasion of Syria.
"Would the reservists like to conquer Damascus? Many of them would," Walla quoted the officer as saying.
The issue was also raised during a visit by Israeli military chief of staff Eyal Zamir around two weeks ago, according to the report.
The officer said reservists deployed to Syria often arrived after serving in Gaza and Lebanon, where the operational environment was significantly different.
"What is happening today in Syria is beyond anything we imagined and any activity we thought of - the activity is non-stop," he said.
Israel currently operates from 10 military positions inside Syrian territory, according to Walla, conducting operations around the clock based on intelligence and military assessments.
The report said Israeli forces have conducted raids well beyond the immediate border area, singling out Beit Jinn in the western Damascus countryside, around 11 kilometres from the occupied Golan Heights.
The senior officer said some reservists wanted to reach Beit Jinn "every day", saying that 14 militants had been killed in three separate Israeli raids in the area.
The comments come amid continuing Israeli military operations around Beit Jinn and elsewhere in southern Syria.
Israeli forces carried out a series of incursions in the Damascus and Quneitra countrysides on Saturday, sources told The New Arab.
An Israeli force comprising two tanks, a bulldozer and more than 10 other vehicles entered agricultural land surrounding the Beit Jinn farm area in the western Damascus countryside, according to the sources.
Another force of three military vehicles entered an area west of Saida al-Hanout in the Quneitra countryside, while four Israeli military vehicles entered the town of al-Rafid, where soldiers searched several homes.
Israeli forces also fired an artillery shell at agricultural land in the Ain al-Shaara area near Beit Jinn following similar shelling overnight.
Israeli military operations have become increasingly frequent in southern Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad's regime in December 2024.
Israel moved troops into the UN-patrolled buffer zone separating the two countries following Assad's fall and has since established military positions and carried out raids, arrests and strikes deeper inside Syrian territory.
Syria and the United Nations have said Israel's deployment violates Syrian sovereignty and the 1974 Disengagement Agreement governing the separation of Israeli and Syrian forces.
France on Friday called for Israeli troops to withdraw from Syrian territory, while reiterating its support for efforts to reach a security agreement between Damascus and Israel.
The French foreign ministry told Syria's official SANA news agency that any military deployment within the separation zone constitutes a violation of the 1974 agreement.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has condemned Israel's violations of Syrian sovereignty, saying Damascus had received support from more than 40 countries at the UN Security Council.
He reaffirmed Syria's territorial integrity and said it would continue defending its rights through "all legitimate political and diplomatic means".
A UN commission investigating Syria said earlier this week that Israeli military activity in the country's south had become "increasingly sustained and entrenched", warning that some Israeli actions could amount to war crimes.

Russia Weaponized Claude AI to Spy on Ukraine and Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:49:26 UTC
20:49:26 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Weaponized Claude AI to Spy on Ukraine and Europe
A Russian-linked hacking operation used Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence models to automate cyberespionage targeting Ukrainian government officials, military personnel, diplomats, defense companies, and drone technology suppliers, with more than 20 organizations identified as targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a threat intelligence report published by Anthropic on September 10, the company tracked the group as GTG-20006 and said its attribution was consistent with public reporting linking the activity to Midnight Blizzard, a Russian state-linked hacking group.
Anthropic said the hackers used customized AI-driven workflows to automate much of the attack process, including reconnaissance, acquiring infrastructure, phishing, maintaining access to compromised systems, and extracting stolen information.
The company identified more than 20 organizations targeted during planning, reconnaissance, or active operations. They included government ministries, intelligence and defense agencies, diplomatic missions, think tanks, and defense companies, primarily in Ukraine and Europe.
Ukrainian government, military, and diplomatic personnel were among the most frequent targets. The group scanned email and remote-access systems belonging to more than two dozen Ukrainian government organizations, according to Anthropic.
Drone technology was another major focus. The hackers exported mailboxes belonging to at least two drone component manufacturers, targeted a military drone producer, and stole a proprietary software development kit used for a drone vision system.
Anthropic said the attackers spent several days reverse-engineering the stolen software, reconstructing the system’s architecture, hardware components, supplier dependencies, and details of an unreleased product. Firmware related to military drone control and AI-based vision systems appeared to be of particular interest.
Claude was also incorporated into malware development and evasion. Anthropic found that AI agents monitored whether security software detected the group’s malicious programs. When a tool was flagged, the system could identify the affected component, modify it, rebuild the malware, and repeat the process until existing security products no longer detected it.
The hackers also used AI to research and register domains, configure phishing infrastructure, send malicious emails, monitor successful compromises, harvest credentials, and move through victims’ networks.
According to Anthropic, Claude assisted with processing and organizing hundreds of gigabytes of stolen information, including bulk exports from compromised email accounts. The AI was also used to help preserve access to infiltrated systems and automatically register attacker-controlled devices inside compromised organizations.
The operation sometimes targeted organizations connected to intended victims rather than attacking them directly. Anthropic said the hackers compromised at least three companies providing hotel guest Wi-Fi services and changed DNS records to redirect connected devices toward infrastructure controlled by the attackers.
The technique allowed the group to collect information about hotel guests and deliver malware to Windows, Android, and iOS devices. Individuals connected to Ukraine, including government officials and drone manufacturers, were among the targets.
The hackers also targeted WhatsApp accounts by linking attacker-controlled devices to victims’ profiles. Using automation tools, they suppressed read receipts while exporting conversations in Ukrainian and Russian. Anthropic said at least two former senior Ukrainian officials were targeted through the method.
In another part of the operation, the group exploited authorization weaknesses in video surveillance services to obtain tokens providing access to victims’ live camera feeds.
The same actor was linked by Anthropic to an intrusion into a North African government technology agency, where hackers stole a database containing more than 300,000 national identity records and commercial registry information covering more than half a million companies.
Russian-linked hackers have also been tied to major cyberattacks against Western companies. In June, The New York Times reported that Russian hackers were behind the 2025 attack on Jaguar Land Rover, which halted production for five weeks and caused an estimated $2.5 billion in damage to the UK economy.

AI giants call for slowdown over ‘serious’ risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:47:31 UTC
20:47:31 KST

AI giants call for slowdown over ‘serious’ risks
OpenAI chief Sam Altman and xAI owner Elon Musk have backed calls to immediately slow the development of increasingly powerful AI models. Their statements came after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI could outpace human control and cause catastrophic damage within months.
Four days ago, researcher Jacob Coxon publicly resigned from Anthropic, accusing both the company and his previous employer, OpenAI, of racing towards self-improving super-intelligence without “acting responsibly.” He also claimed that the technology could “kill us all” by the end of the decade.
In a 3,800-word essay published on his personal website on Saturday, Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela in 2021, outlined “serious” dangers, including loss of control over AI systems, their misuse for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and major economic disruption. He said commercial competition could fuel a “race to the bottom” and exacerbate the threats.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote.
Altman agreed that the industry needed to “pace the frontier,” describing Anthropic’s proposal to give independent evaluators employee-like access to its systems as “a great idea.”
Musk, whose xAI is among the companies competing to develop increasingly advanced models, endorsed the call on X. “Dario is right,” he wrote, adding that he had been “sounding the alarm on AI for a long time.”
Amodei said the technology was advancing “drastically faster,” partly because of its growing ability to help build the next generation of models. Citing an incident in which OpenAI agents reportedly escaped a confined testing environment, he said that within six to 12 months a more capable swarm could “take over the entire internet” and cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.
He proposed a three-step plan that he said could temper development without “sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States’ lead in AI.” The measures include giving outside evaluators deep access to developers’ systems, establishing common industry safety standards, and pursuing international coordination.
Anthropic was the first frontier AI company to deploy its technology on classified US government networks. Its Claude model was integrated into Palantir’s Maven system and reportedly helped generate, locate, and prioritize targets during the US bombing campaign against Iran. It was also reportedly used in the raid that captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
Anthropic later refused to lift safeguards against mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, arguing that current models remained too unreliable to make life-or-death decisions without human involvement.
The Pentagon insisted that providers must allow their technology to be used for “all lawful purposes” and subsequently designated Anthropic a national security supply chain risk. The company challenged the decision, with a California judge ruling in August that the department’s measures were “illegal and baseless,” although separate proceedings in Washington remain unresolved.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp has opposed calls to pause AI development, arguing that slowing progress would benefit US “adversaries.”

A dignified life is a ‘distant dream’ for many Iranian families amid US war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:45:24 UTC
20:45:24 KST

A dignified life is a ‘distant dream’ for many Iranian families amid US war
With constant degradation and no real prospects of improvement in the foreseeable future, people in Iran are losing hope.
Tehran, Iran – Iranians born in the 1980s have often considered themselves to be the “burned generation”, living in a period marked by the political and economic turbulence that followed Iran’s 1979 Islamic revolution.
The United States embassy hostage crisis, when Iranian activists in 1979 detained American diplomats and others for 444 days, set the tone for a decade ahead.
What followed in the 1980s was eight years of gruelling war with neighbouring Iraq, a cultural revolution undertaken by the nascent Islamic Republic, the executions of political prisoners, sanctions and economic uncertainty.
Bardia, a 23-year-old living with his parents in eastern Tehran, said many people his age feel they have it even worse than the 1980s generation, due to worsening sanctions creating an even more volatile job market and inflation.
“Becoming independent or forming a family, emigrating away, buying a home, a shop, a car or even a new phone is becoming more of a distant dream every day,” he told Al Jazeera, asking to remain anonymous due to security concerns.
Decades of woes
Decades of domestic mismanagement and corruption paired with external intervention have made life difficult for most of the about 90 million Iranians, even before the US and Israeli war on the country began on February 28.
Months of US bombing, intensified sanctions, and naval blockades have significantly worsened the situation this year, in addition to the January antigovernment protests and state-sanctioned restrictions on internet use by the population.
Last week, the government hiked petrol prices, which will likely have an inflationary effect, with a feeling that the situation will get worse before it gets better.
For people like Bardia, who works at a cafe in downtown Tehran while studying for a business administration degree, it is difficult just to get by.
Bardia’s pensioner father is working with online ride-hailing apps and using a 15-year-old low-quality Iranian car to make some money. His mother is a retired garment worker who makes intermittent earnings from sewing at home.
After accounting for government cash subsidies and food assistance, the family have about 800 million rials (about $350 at the current exchange rate) per month, while expenses are surging by the day.
“We buy meat maybe once every six to eight weeks,” Bardia said. They can no longer afford to eat out or get takeaway, buy new clothes or household appliances, and are hoping that their medical bill does not upend their household budget.
By late August, year-on-year inflation was at 89 percent, while food inflation stood at more than 127 percent compared with the same month last year, according to the latest figures released by the Statistical Center of Iran.
Iran’s national currency has also continued on a downward spiral, hitting a new all-time low of more than 1.37 million rials per US dollar in Tehran’s open market last week.
The rate slightly improved to about 1.31 million on Sunday, after Iranian media said an understanding with Oman over facilitating limited transit through the Strait of Hormuz might materialise before planned talks with regional states in Oman on Monday.
But Iran still insists that negotiations with the US will not happen until Tehran’s conditions for Hormuz, lifting the blockade, the sanctions and other demands are met. In the meantime, a maritime blockade has halted most Iranian oil exports, while US sanctions and regional tensions have blocked or hampered air, overland and rail routes, making life difficult for Iranians.
“I remember the day my dad bought a car with 10 million tomans [100 million rials – currently worth just $43]. I also remember the day my dad bought a piece of land with 10 million tomans. Today he came home with a little bit of meat and said it was 10 million tomans. I’m in shock; I’m just 24 and I’ve seen all of this!” one Iranian user wrote on X.
The number of Iranians posting videos online about the exorbitant amounts they paid for small quantities of food and other essentials has gone viral in recent weeks. But instead of complaining, they, likely ironically, claimed they were happy, because authorities might imprison or execute them if they protested.
Last week, a state television report said such videos were “a new project” of dissent by those wishing to overthrow the Islamic Republic by instigating “riots”.
‘Erosion of resilience’
After decades of pressure, the economy has shown immense resilience in the face of political upheaval, sanctions, currency fluctuations, and the deadliest COVID-19 pandemic of the Middle East. In less than a year, Iranians have lived through energy crises and two wars started by the US and Israel.
But Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and several other Iranian leaders have repeatedly expressed a desire to end the current “no war, no peace” status quo as it begets uncertainty for all Iranians and derails the economy.
Economist and market analyst Behnam Samadi said that status quo has come at a cost, with political and economic uncertainty making it difficult for decision-makers – whether the government or families – to act decisively to make the situation better.
“Households focus on preserving their purchasing power rather than planning for the long term; businesses set aside more resources to manage risk and maintain existing operations rather than undertake new investment; and the government is compelled to devote more resources to social support, securing foreign currency and crisis management,” he told Al Jazeera.
Many are not asking whether Iran’s economy is about to collapse, but how long the current state of degradation can last and at what cost.
Households are gradually changing lifestyles and consumption patterns, limiting expenditure on leisure, education and even healthcare, while credit purchases or instalment plans are rapidly on the rise. Iranians are essentially transferring some of the present financial pressures to the future.
“Perhaps the most accurate description is that Iranian households are adapting, but this adaptation does not mean their standard of living is staying the same. A substantial part of Iran’s economic resilience is sustained through reduced consumption, lower savings and a decline in household welfare,” Samadi said.
“And this is precisely the point that requires attention: If this situation persists, what we call ‘resilience’ today may gradually turn into an ‘erosion of resilience’.”

20:43:09 KST

Sources close to Otzma Yehudit chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir believe Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has already made a preliminary decision to try to form a broad national government after the election, even at the cost of leaving Ben-Gvir outside the coalition.
According to sources familiar with discussions in Ben-Gvir’s circle, Netanyahu’s change in messaging, from the “full, full right-wing government” slogan used in previous elections to the current emphasis on a “broad national government,” is seen as a sign that he is seeking to move in a more statesmanlike and centrist direction this time.
The sources claim that Ben-Gvir believes Netanyahu does not want to repeat a term in which he himself is positioned as the coalition’s leftmost member, with all his partners to his right. In their assessment, if election results allow it, Netanyahu would prefer to bring in a figure from the opposing camp, and in one possible scenario even former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, while leaving Ben-Gvir outside the government.
Ben-Gvir’s associates point to several signs that they say indicate this direction. One is Netanyahu’s use of the phrase “broad national government.” According to them, the choice of this wording, instead of the previous emphasis on a right-wing government, reflects a strategic shift.
They also point to Netanyahu’s political relationship with Ben-Gvir during the election campaign. Among other things, they cite the fact that Netanyahu did not appear with him at the Altalena event, as well as moves regarding surplus-vote agreements with right-wing parties, which they interpret as an attempt to create greater separation between the Likud and Otzma Yehudit.
From their perspective, these are not isolated incidents but part of a broader trend: an effort by Netanyahu to create greater room for maneuver ahead of the day after the election.
The assessment: Netanyahu will want to return to the center
The main argument among Ben-Gvir’s associates is also based on how they analyze Netanyahu’s political conduct over the years. They claim that the current coalition, in which all the partners are positioned to the right of Likud, was an exception and not necessarily Netanyahu’s natural preference.
They point to 2009, when Netanyahu brought Ehud Barak and the Labor Party into his government, while the National Union remained outside the coalition. According to them, National Union figures expected for an extended period to join the government but ultimately remained in the opposition.
They also note that in 2013, one of the first partners with whom Netanyahu reached agreements was Tzipi Livni. A government was later formed with Yesh Atid and the Jewish Home, while the haredi parties remained outside.
According to Ben-Gvir’s associates, beginning in 2015, Netanyahu’s room for maneuver gradually narrowed, partly because of political boycotts against him. That year, he was initially forced to establish a narrow government with 61 Knesset seats, and only later was Yisrael Beytenu added.
They claim that the peak of this pattern came after the 2019-2020 election cycles, when Netanyahu formed a parity government with Benny Gantz. Ben-Gvir’s associates note that in that government Netanyahu effectively abandoned advancing a broad judicial reform and agreed that the Justice Ministry would be placed under Avi Nissenkorn of Blue and White.
Judicial reform could also be abandoned
Ben-Gvir’s associates estimate that a move by Netanyahu toward a broader government would require him to give up some of the issues identified with the current right-wing government, foremost among them the continuation of the judicial overhaul.
According to their assessment, bringing a centrist party or a party from the opposing camp into the coalition would require significant compromises on issues related to the judicial system and would allow Netanyahu to present a more statesmanlike term in office.
The sources also link this to the assessment that this could be one of Netanyahu’s final terms as prime minister and that he may place greater weight on the legacy he leaves behind.
At the same time, Ben-Gvir’s associates acknowledge the argument working in the opposite direction. Netanyahu knows that Otzma Yehudit, if it joins a right-wing coalition, could provide him with a stable partner for a full term. By contrast, a government with Eisenkot could be more complicated and include significant ideological gaps.
Therefore, if the right-wing bloc wins 61 seats or more, leaving Ben-Gvir outside in favor of a government with Eisenkot could represent a gamble for Netanyahu: choosing a broader government that may nevertheless be less stable.
One scenario raised by Ben-Gvir’s associates is that Netanyahu may assume that even if a centrist partner later leaves the coalition, Otzma Yehudit could join at that stage and extend the government’s lifespan.
Their assessment is even more decisive in a scenario where the right-wing bloc fails to reach 61 seats even with Otzma Yehudit. In that case, Ben-Gvir’s associates are convinced that Netanyahu would prefer to bring in a party from the opposing camp rather than be dragged into another election campaign.
From their perspective, the central question ahead of the day after the election is therefore not only how many seats the right-wing bloc will win, but how much freedom of choice Netanyahu will have.
The more options available to him for forming a government, they believe, the greater the chance that he will return to the pattern that characterized him in the past: a broader coalition with a balancing force to the left of Likud, rather than a right-wing government in which he himself is the most moderate figure.

Putin’s Economic Growth Claims Diverge From IMF Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:43:00 UTC
20:43:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed during the BRICS summit in New Delhi that Russia’s economy had outpaced global growth rates over the previous three years, assertions that diverge from official International Monetary Fund (IMF) and European statistical data, The Moscow Times reported.
Addressing leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday, Sept. 11, Putin contended that Russia’s gross domestic product expanded by 10.3% between 2023 and 2025.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He attributed the performance to domestic structural realignment that he argued made Russia more resilient despite facing more than 30,000 international sanctions.
Putin further asserted that Western economies had suffered severe self-inflicted blowback, including mounting sovereign debt, widening budget shortfalls, and an 8% contraction in EU industrial production.
However, official data contradicts the Russian leader’s figures. According to Eurostat statistics, EU industrial output contracted in 2023 and 2024 before rebounding sharply in 2025, leaving a net three-year decline of approximately 0.6% rather than the 8% claimed by Putin.
Similarly, IMF figures show that the global economy grew by 10.7% from 2023 to 2025, marginally outpacing Russia’s 10.3% rate.
While the Russian economy expanded faster than the global benchmark in 2023 and 2024 on the back of historic wartime state spending, domestic growth decelerated to roughly 1% in 2025 as the global economy expanded by 3.5%.
Hard Times Ahead: Russian Attacks put Ukraine’s Finances Under Pressure
Stagnating momentum and widening fiscal deficits
Russia’s own official economic forecasts indicate that the growth divergence is set to widen further. The Russian Ministry of Economic Development projects GDP growth of just 0.4% in 2026, compared to the IMF’s global growth forecast of 3%.
Under those projections, Russia would substantially lag behind major economies such as the US at 2.3%, China at 5%, and India at 6.4%.
Moscow projects only modest acceleration in subsequent years, estimating growth of 1.4% in 2027, 1.9% in 2028, and 2.4% in 2029, representing cumulative growth of 5.8% over the three-year period.
The upbeat rhetoric at the summit also sits uncomfortably against recent domestic economic indicators. The Russian economy grew by 1.3% in the second quarter of 2026, while first-half growth reached just 0.6% – roughly half the pace recorded during the same period in 2025 and nearly seven times slower than the initial 2023–2024 wartime mobilization boom.
Fiscal pressures are simultaneously accumulating. On Sept. 3, Putin acknowledged that the federal budget deficit was expanding, with the January-July shortfall reaching 2.8% of GDP against a full-year government target of 1.6%.
Domestic supply constraints
Speaking at the BRICS Business Forum, Putin acknowledged that Russia has become the world’s most heavily sanctioned state, while claiming that the restrictions had ultimately strengthened national economic sovereignty and prompted a successful pivot toward non-Western trading partners.
Yet despite the official optimism, Western restrictions and persistent Ukrainian drone strikes against domestic energy infrastructure have exerted visible operational strains on the Russian economy.
Ukrainian strikes on refineries throughout 2026 have disrupted domestic processing capacity, prompting Moscow to enforce fuel export bans and compelling at least 26 major Russian airports – including St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo hub – to introduce severe refueling restrictions for commercial airlines.
Wartime labor shortages, persistent inflation, high central bank interest rates, and mounting fiscal deficits continue to weigh heavily on Russia’s economic outlook, even as the Kremlin continues to portray its economy as an insulated model for the Global South.

The first ministers of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland are set to meet in Cardiff on Monday to discuss the possibility of leaving the United Kingdom through constitutional change and cooperation between the three UK nations, according to The Telegraph.
Scotland's First Minister John Swinney, Wales' First Minister Rhun ap Iowerth, and Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill are expected to sign a memorandum of understanding calling for greater cooperation on economic, energy, European and constitutional issues.
Sinn Fein President Mary Lou McDonald is also due to attend the summit in Cardiff.
The agreement is expected to state that Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have the right to determine their own constitutional futures through democratic means.
The meeting comes amid renewed debate over Scottish independence and Irish reunification.

"I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Trump said.
"I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now."
Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum on Northern Ireland's constitutional status can be called if it appears likely that a majority would vote for the territory to leave the UK and become part of a united Ireland.
Swinney said Sunday that Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland being led by pro-independence parties represented a significant development in the debate over the future of the UK.
“For the first time ever, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are led by pro-independence first ministers,” Swinney said, arguing that the development demonstrated growing support for constitutional change.
The Scottish leader said he expected discussions in Cardiff to focus on cooperation between the nations and their respective approaches to independence.
Meanwhile, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that another Scottish independence referendum could take place if there were a "clear consensus" in Scotland in favor of holding one.
However, Burnham later wrote to Swinney to reiterate the government's position that another independence referendum would not be supported before the next general election.
He added that there was currently no consensus for another independence referendum in Scotland and no clear evidence that a majority in Northern Ireland wanted to leave the UK.

Americans have worse view of Muslims 25 years after 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
11:33:09 UTC
20:33:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Americans have worse view of Muslims 25 years after 9/11
A study released earlier this month found that Americans' view of Muslims is today twice as negative as it was in the wake of the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago.
Multiple US-led wars fought in the name of countering terrorism, namely in Afghanistan and Iraq; prominent politicians building their brands on demonising Muslims and other marginalised communities; and the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, have all contributed to a negative image of Muslims among Americans.
A Pew research survey found that 43 percent of US adults believed that Muslims were less patriotic than other Americans and 42 percent said Muslims were having a negative impact on the country.
“9/11 gave a pass to further demonise Muslims and invade Muslim countries,” Mirvette Judeh, president of the Arab American Caucus of California, told The New Arab.
“9/11 gave governments a pass to surveille everyone. It destroyed our countries and destroyed our communities here. Whole communities were demonised and terrorized. I feel like the hate and fear have gotten worse,” she said.
In March 2002, six months after 9/11, 25 percent of adults surveyed by Pew said Islam was more likely than other faiths to encourage violence. In another survey this year, 51 percent gave the same response to the question.
Despite these highly negative views of Muslims 25 years after 9/11, a growing number of Muslim Americans are becoming more civically engaged, with many running for elected office and taking on other public roles.
“There’s optimism in the fact that our community is getting more comfortable being visible,” Amr Shabaik, legal director of the Los Angeles chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, told TNA. “Other communities have gone though this and have seen increased participation.”
Arguably the most prominent example of a successful Muslim American politician is New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who gave one of the main speeches at the 9/11 memorial on Friday.
Though there was a petition to prevent him from speaking at the event, the mayor was warmly received and stood out as the only senior elected official to stay at the ceremony after all of the names were read.
Among family members of the victims at the ceremony was Michael Massaroli Jr., who lost his father in the September 11 attacks. As the last one of the victims’ relatives to speak, he urged people not to spread hate in response to 9/11.
"I think the one parting thing I want to leave everyone with is that you do to my dad’s legacy and the legacy of all these victims no honour by using this tragedy to spread hate," he said. "I've had to grow up and spend the past 25 years seeing people use it to hate on our Muslim brothers and sisters, do hate on people who don't look like them, and that's wrong and that does no honour to the victims here."
