Ukraine Reportedly Opens New Drone Front Against Russia in Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:06:01 UTC
19:06:01 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Reportedly Opens New Drone Front Against Russia in Africa
Ukraine is expanding its use of drone warfare beyond Europe, deploying specialists to Africa to support forces confronting Russian troops and Moscow-linked military structures.
Around 15 Ukrainian drone specialists are currently operating in Mali, helping local forces counter Russia’s Africa Corps through training, technical support, and operational planning, CNN reported on September 12.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian team works closely with the Azawad Liberation Front, a predominantly Tuareg rebel group active in northern Mali. Rather than taking part in frontline combat directly, the Ukrainian specialists assist local fighters with planning and conducting drone operations.
One Ukrainian drone operator told CNN that he coordinates local fighters remotely. “I coordinate their operations remotely. The signal from their drone comes to me via the internet, and I immediately tell them by radio what to do and where to fly,” he said.
According to CNN, the operator receives live drone footage over the internet and relays instructions to local pilots by radio. He said Ukrainian personnel have been ordered not to deploy directly to frontline positions.
Ukraine expands drone operations across Africa
CNN reported that Ukrainian specialists have also operated in Sudan, while personnel from Chad, Niger, and Burkina Faso have traveled to Mali to receive drone training from Ukrainian instructors.
The missions are part of a broader effort by Kyiv to apply expertise developed during Russia’s full-scale invasion in other regions where Moscow is expanding its military presence.
Ukrainian teams have also traveled to at least five countries in the Middle East, according to CNN, where they trained local forces to counter Iranian-made Shahed attack drones, which Russia has repeatedly used against Ukraine.
In exchange for Ukrainian technical expertise, Kyiv has received security cooperation agreements and commitments involving ammunition supplies, CNN reported. The deployments also allow Ukrainian specialists to test equipment and tactics in environments significantly different from the Ukrainian battlefield.
In Mali, daytime temperatures regularly exceed 43 degrees Celsius, while dust and sand accelerate wear on drones, electronics, cooling systems, filters, and batteries. A Ukrainian intelligence representative told CNN that the tactical environment is also markedly different.
“In Ukraine, it is high intensity, massed strikes, constant pressure. Here, it is more maneuver warfare across large areas, ambushes, control of routes, work by small groups and dependence on knowledge of the terrain,” the source said.
According to CNN, Ukrainian personnel teach local fighters how to use drones while learning desert survival and combat techniques from forces familiar with the Sahel.
Ukraine targets Russia’s position in Mali
Ukrainian personnel also described operations around Kidal, a strategically important city in northern Mali.
Earlier in 2026, Tuareg rebels and militants launched attacks against Russian forces in the area. Moscow later accused Kyiv of involvement and claimed Ukrainian and European instructors had helped prepare local forces for the operation.
CNN cited a Ukrainian intelligence source as saying that Kyiv views such missions as a way to increase pressure on Moscow and weaken Russia’s image as a reliable security partner in Africa. “We are turning our experience in drones into a foreign policy tool,” the source said.
Russia has significantly expanded its military presence across the Sahel following the withdrawal of French and other Western forces from several countries in the region.
After the Wagner Group was dismantled, Moscow transferred parts of its African operations into the Defense Ministry-controlled Africa Corps, which supports governments aligned with the Kremlin and helps protect Russian strategic and economic interests.
Ukrainian naval drone teams reportedly operate in Libya
Ukraine’s activities in Africa also extend to Libya, CNN reported. According to the outlet, Ukrainian naval drone operators are active in northwestern Libya and have used a base in Misrata to support operations against vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
The fleet consists of tankers used to transport Russian oil and reduce the impact of international sanctions, providing Moscow with continued export revenues.
CNN reported that one explosive-laden Ukrainian naval drone involved in such an operation later moved beyond the control of its operators and appeared near the Greek island of Lefkada. Greece issued a diplomatic protest, after which Kyiv formally apologized, according to the report.
The reported missions in Mali and Libya show how Ukraine is increasingly using drone expertise developed during the war against Russia to contest Moscow’s military and economic activity outside Europe.
“It puts pressure on them. This whole story has both psychological and real consequences,” a Ukrainian operator told CNN.
Russia, meanwhile, continues expanding its military footprint in Africa as it seeks political influence, access to natural resources, and strategic positions in countries where Western involvement has declined.
The reported missions come months after Ukraine unveiled its first comprehensive strategy to expand its presence and influence across Africa. In March, Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov said Kyiv aimed to strengthen its political, economic, and security role on the continent and more actively defend Ukrainian interests there.

Democrats are preparing large-scale investigations into Trump in the event of an election victory — WP
Kyiv • UNN
Democrats plan to investigate Trump's wealth, the family's business, and the administration's policies if they regain the majority in the House of Representatives. The White House is preparing to block the investigations.
Democrats in the United States are preparing a plan for investigations into Donald Trump and his administration in the event they regain the majority in the House of Representatives after the November midterm elections. Potential topics include the enrichment of the president and his family, the reorganization of the federal government, and the persecution of political opponents. The Washington Post reports, according to UNN.
Details
Democrats in the House of Representatives are eagerly preparing to take advantage of power they do not yet have. Democrats, who have a strong chance of regaining their majority in the November midterm elections—and given that little official business remains in the few days left before the end of the session—have focused their attention on developing an accountability agenda that would target President Donald Trump, his administration, and his family next year, the publication writes.
The publication spoke with 12 Democratic members and staffers who could chair committees if their party returns to power. They plan to examine Trump's business projects, his legal actions, the administration's policies, and the circumstances behind the growth of the president's wealth while in office.
There is so much corruption and fraud that Democrats will need the entire House of Representatives to conduct the investigations properly. We are all saying this, said Representative Robert Garcia.
However, according to the publication, some Democrats who worked on investigations into Trump during his first presidential term are urging their colleagues not to make premature statements about their results. At the same time, the White House rejected the Democrats' plans, and its representatives are preparing a strategy to block possible investigations if the majority in the House of Representatives changes.
Democrats have no plan whatsoever to improve the lives of the American people; they have only plans to obstruct and baselessly attack President Trump's common-sense agenda, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wiles said.
According to the publication, one of the main areas of future investigations could be the growth of Trump's and his family's wealth while he has been president.
Democrats are laying the groundwork for an investigation into how Trump and his family are becoming wealthier while he is in office. Garcia's committee has launched a system to track the Trump family's profits from cryptocurrency and foreign deals, calculating that Trump appropriated $2.25 billion from foreign payments during the first year of his second term, the publication writes.
In addition, according to available information, Representative Jamie Raskin (Democrat of Maryland), who could chair the House Judiciary Committee if Democrats win, has requested additional information about investments by the venture capital firms 1789 Capital and American Ventures, which are linked to Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump.
Raskin's investigation will cover companies in which Trump's sons invested and that received government contracts or favorable policies from the administration. Other Democratic targets include Trump's agreement with the U.S. Internal Revenue Service, which protects his family and businesses from future audits; his social media platform Truth Social, which sells fast access to his posts; and the business dealings of his son-in-law Jared Kushner, the publication writes.
We remind you
According to a financial report, the U.S. president received nearly $800 million from the World Liberty Financial cryptocurrency project and $635 million from the sale of memecoins. This became his largest source of income.

Russian forces launched approximately 2,100 strike drones, 78 missiles of various types, and nearly 1,700 guided aerial bombs against Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Sept. 13.
Zelensky emphasized that a substantial portion of the unmanned aerial vehicles deployed in recent days consisted of high-speed, jet-powered Shahed drones, which Moscow utilized to systematically batter Ukraine’s domestic economy, critical utilities, and civilian life.

Ukraine's refusal to give up territory to Russia stalls peace deal, Trump envoy says
A territorial dispute remains unresolved in efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine, but Kyiv is not prepared to make concessions, U.S. President Donald Trump's envoy Jared Kushner said on Sept. 11.
Speaking at the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference, Kushner said President Vladimir Putin outlined Russia's territorial demands during talks in Moscow on Sept. 5. Kushner appeared to be referring to Russia's demand that Ukraine cede territory in the Donbas.
"President Putin laid out his line of what he wants to achieve," Kushner said during a panel. "If Ukraine wanted to withdraw to that line, then obviously, you know, we have the rest of the deal set up and put together. Ukraine right now does not want to do that."
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv cede the partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Moscow is effectively demanding that Kyiv surrender territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front line and stressed the need for Western-backed security guarantees to deter future possible Russian aggression.
Kushner said the U.S., acting as a mediator, is seeking a "creative solution" that would protect Ukraine's interests while persuading Russia to end the war. He urged the sides to look beyond territorial questions and consider opportunities for economic development after the war.
The U.S. expects to announce the next steps in the talks in the coming weeks, Kushner said.
Kushner's remarks came after he and Trump's other envoy, Steve Witkoff, visited Moscow and Kyiv last week as part of efforts to break the deadlock in peace talks. The Kyiv visit was the envoys' first since the latest push to revive negotiations.
People familiar with the talks told the Kyiv Independent that the envoys brought revised peace proposals, but no breakthrough was achieved as Putin appeared intent on escalating Russia's war.
President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters after the meeting in Kyiv that he expected "the war will continue" into the winter months despite the renewed diplomatic push.
The most tangible outcome of the envoys' trip was an agreement between Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia to resume trilateral negotiations. Previous rounds produced little political progress but led to major humanitarian initiatives, including prisoner-of-war exchanges.

BRICS summit ends with call for greater Global South cooperation
Unknown

19:01:00 KST

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday called for stronger cooperation across the Global South as he warned that geopolitical tensions, disrupted supply chains and climate crises are increasingly affecting people worldwide.
Addressing the BRICS summit of leading developing nations on its second and last day in New Delhi, Modi also warned that the "weaponization of technology and critical minerals" could hinder global development and shared prosperity.
Founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, BRICS has expanded to 11 members, representing about half the world's population and a significant share of global economic output.
It has sought greater representation for developing countries in global institutions and promoted alternatives to Western-dominated financial systems.
"The number of conflicts and tensions in the world is increasing, increasingly impacting ordinary people," Modi said, alongside bloc leaders, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
"Pandemics, climate disasters and supply chain disruptions have shown that in today's interconnected world, no crisis remains confined to a single region," Modi said, announcing the bloc agreed to establish an integrated early warning system for infectious diseases aimed at boosting preparedness and response to future outbreaks.
The group in a joint declaration Saturday expressed concern over escalating tensions in the Middle East and Sudan and called for disputes to be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.
The bloc reiterated support for a multipolar world order and U.N. reforms, including its Security Council, as well as global financial institutions including the World Bank and International Monetary Fund.
The leaders opposed unilateral sanctions and coercive economic measures, and criticized sanctions not authorized by the U.N. They also criticized rising tariffs and nontariff barriers, saying they undermine global trade and supply chains.
The bloc backed greater use of local currencies in trade and stronger cross-border payment systems, and called for cooperation on food security, energy, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and climate action.
The declaration was a significant breakthrough, as forging consensus among Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – which hold competing positions on key regional and geopolitical issues – posed a complex diplomatic challenge amid ongoing conflicts and heightened tensions.

Federal science funding cuts push young U.S. researchers to consider moving abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:00:26 UTC
19:00:26 KST

Recent policy changes and budget reductions by the federal government have created immediate hurdles for young scientists building their careers in the United States. A new survey published in Frontiers in Sociology suggests that these abrupt funding disruptions have severely impacted the professional trajectories of early career researchers, pushing many to consider leaving academia or moving to other countries. The findings indicate how sudden halts in research funding can destabilize the long-term scientific workforce.
In early 2025, the Trump administration instituted rapid policy shifts across the academic landscape. Federal science budgets faced proposed double-digit percentage reductions, hundreds of existing research grants were abruptly frozen or terminated, and some diversity and climate programs were paused. Most basic scientific research in the United States happens at universities, relying heavily on federal grants. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation allocate taxpayer money to academic laboratories, paying for scientific equipment, experimental materials, and researcher salaries.
When this funding stops, the people most immediately affected are early career researchers. This group includes undergraduate students, doctoral candidates working on their dissertations, and postdoctoral fellows, who are scientists completing additional training before seeking permanent faculty positions. These trainees typically depend directly on grant money for their livelihoods. Even before recent disruptions, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 showed that many graduate students already face extreme financial stress because their stipends fail to cover basic living costs.
Sudden budget reductions tend to have long-lasting effects on the training pipeline. For instance, a 2026 computer modeling study indicated that abrupt cuts to federal health research funding create setbacks in scientist training that take decades to recover from. As an immediate reaction to the 2025 federal science funding cuts, a 2025 report indicated that universities across the country began shrinking graduate student admissions.
To better understand how the current generation of young scientists is experiencing these shifts, researchers led by Crystal Hammond at the University of California, Riverside, and Adriana Bankston at the STEM Advocacy Institute conducted a rapid-response survey.
The research team collected their data online during May and June of 2025, while the effects of the funding changes were still actively unfolding. They utilized two separate questionnaires. The first survey was a brief, qualitative tool that gathered personal stories and accounts of advocacy actions from six participants. The second survey was more comprehensive, collecting both quantitative data and open-ended responses from 30 early career researchers. The scientists recruited participants through academic mailing lists, social media, and direct outreach to university contacts.
In the comprehensive survey, 60 percent of respondents were doctoral students, 13.3 percent were undergraduate students, and 13.3 percent were postdoctoral researchers. The majority of the participants studied life sciences, such as biology or neuroscience, and most worked at large, public research universities. The respondents relied heavily on federal support for their work. About 63 percent reported that their research was funded by the National Institutes of Health, while 20 percent relied on the National Science Foundation.
The survey data provides evidence that the funding disruptions caused widespread professional distress. Half of the participants rated the professional impact of the cuts as severe, scoring the disruption an eight or higher on a ten-point scale. Another 40 percent rated the impact as moderate. When asked about specific negative consequences, participants reported a variety of issues, with 20 percent specifically noting that their stipends or benefits had been cut or delayed, and 10 percent reporting hiring freezes or rescinded job offers.
Looking to the future, the participants expressed widespread anxiety about their scientific careers. Ninety percent of respondents worried about their long-term job prospects in research. Over half of the sample, 56.7 percent, reported that they would not be able to complete their current research projects. Because of these barriers, 60 percent of the early career researchers said they were considering moving to another country to pursue their scientific goals.
The funding cuts also affected the broader well-being of the academic community. Nearly three-quarters of respondents reported that the budget changes negatively impacted their mental health and wellness. Additionally, 56.7 percent of participants said the disruptions harmed their sense of belonging in the sciences. Faced with these compounding pressures, 56.7 percent of the surveyed early career researchers indicated that they were considering leaving academic research entirely.
The qualitative responses offered more detail about the specific challenges these researchers faced. Graduate students described how canceled grants delayed their dissertation timelines, meaning they would run out of funding before they could finish their degrees. Postdoctoral researchers recounted how fellowships aimed at increasing diversity in the sciences were terminated abruptly. In response to these challenges, participants reported engaging in various forms of advocacy, such as organizing campus rallies, writing to their elected representatives, and trying to educate the public about the importance of scientific research.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2020. That earlier study examined perceptions of political interference and scientific integrity among federal agency scientists rather than funding cuts and career viability among university trainees, but it similarly found widespread disruption to researchers under the Trump administration.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The sample size of the survey was small, with only 30 participants completing the quantitative questionnaire. The authors utilized a rapid-response format with a short data collection window to capture immediate reactions, meaning the results are not a nationally representative sample of all scientists. Because the researchers used convenience sampling, it is possible that individuals who were most severely affected by the budget cuts were more motivated to participate.
Additionally, the demographic makeup of the respondents was fairly narrow. The majority of participants were White scholars working in the life sciences at research-intensive institutions. The effects of federal funding disruptions might look different for scholars in the humanities, social sciences, or at smaller colleges with different financial structures. Future studies with larger and more diverse groups of participants will be needed to fully capture how these policy shifts are reshaping the broader higher education landscape.
The study, “Early career researcher responses to 2025 United States federal science funding disruptions: a rapid-response pilot survey,” was authored by Crystal Hammond, John Patrick Flores, Siara Rouzer, Kassandra Fernandez, Amy Ralston, and Adriana Bankston.

‘It’s just straight bigotry’: Trump leads wave of Islamophobic rhetoric as midterms loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:00:06 UTC
19:00:06 KST

Within hours of Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic US Senate primary, Republican senator Tommy Tuberville of Alabama declared that the party had “just voted to send a TERRORIST” to Washington.
El-Sayed – or “Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed”, as Tuberville called him on X – was a “RADICAL ISLAMIST” who would “do everything he can to destroy America”, he claimed.
It was the opening shot in what researchers who track anti-Muslim sentiment describe as the most concentrated wave of Islamophobic rhetoric in US electoral politics since the 9/11 attacks, arriving at the exact moment Muslim candidates are winning office in unprecedented numbers.
“It’s probably the worst of what we’ve seen,” said Saher Selod, director of research at the non-partisan Institute for Social Policy and Understanding (ISPU), which has tracked anti-Muslim sentiment nationally for a decade. “We’re certainly seeing in 2025 and 2026, ahead of these midterms, really very Islamophobic ads – more so than what we saw after 9/11.”
ISPU’s 2025 Islamophobia Index, a 100-point scale built using common anti-Muslim stereotypes, rose from 25 in 2022 to 33 among the general public in 2025, with the sharpest increases among white and Hispanic Americans.
The Pew Research Center found in a survey this spring that 51% of US adults now say Islam is more likely than other religions to encourage violence, up from just 25% six months after the 2001 attacks.
The partisan gap on that question has widened sharply. Back in 2022 32% of likely Republican voters and 23% of Democrats in 2002 said Islam was more likely than other religions to encourage violence, according to the Pew survey. Today, 76% of Republicans say the same, and 29% of Democrats.
Anti-Muslim hate crimes reported to the FBI, which spiked to 481 in 2001 from 28 the year before, have never returned to pre-2001 levels, according to Pew’s research. The ISPU separately found that 63% of Muslims reported experiencing religious discrimination in the past year, the highest share of any faith group it measures.
Set against that backdrop is a wave of Muslim electoral success. There are four Muslim members of US Congress, with a fifth likely on the way, compared with zero in 2001. Ghazala Hashmi became Virginia’s first Muslim woman elected to statewide office this year, as lieutenant governor. Zohran Mamdani was inaugurated as New York’s first Muslim mayor in January 2025, and El-Sayed’s primary win put him on track to potentially become the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate.
The reaction to El-Sayed’s victory showed how quickly the rhetoric escalates. The Center for the Study of Organized Hate found Islamophobic posts naming El-Sayed rose by nearly 1,900% in the week after his win, from an average of 155 to more than 3,000 a day.
The attacks are also coming from the very top of the Republican party. Donald Trump infamously called in 2015 for a “total and complete shutdown” on Muslims entering the US when he was running for president, and attempted to enact one via executive order in early 2017. After years of legal wrangling, the supreme court did allow Trump to implement a limited version of his travel restrictions for majority Muslim countries.
This year, Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist” from the Oval Office, and separately claimed – without naming anyone – that “jihadists” were being elected to office “all over the place”. Vice-president JD Vance, meanwhile, called El-Sayed “very, very evil” at a Michigan rally and, separately, invoked his own late grandfather to attack comments El-Sayed made in 2022 defending a legal challenge to an Oklahoma anti-Sharia ballot measure.
The attacks go beyond one candidate, however. Senator Ted Cruz told Fox News that El-Sayed and Mamdani were “Islamists” who “want Sharia law” and “hate Jews, they hate Christians, they hate capitalism, they hate America”. Representative Nancy Mace posted that “every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic”, and followed up by writing that Islam “must be removed from civil society in the US”. In March, Representative Randy Fine of Florida wrote on X, “We need more Islamophobia, not less. Fear of Islam is rational,” while Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee posted that “Muslims don’t belong in American society”.
Republican leadership has been mostly silent.
For Mobashra Tazamal, associate director of Georgetown University’s Bridge Initiative, which studies Islamophobia globally, the shift is shockingly noticeable. “It is almost as if the veil has been lifted,” she said. “It is so bigoted, and it’s so crude, and there is no red line. It’s just straight bigotry.”
The rhetoric has also extended beyond individual candidates into policy fights.
In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott has spent much of the summer campaigning against what he calls the imposition of Islamic law, ordering a review of state grants to two major airports and referring both to federal regulators over privately funded wudu stations, ritual washing facilities Muslims use before prayer, which he called illegal religious favoritism. Abbott has separately fought a proposed mosque-anchored housing development outside Dallas.
Nationally, the Center for the Study of Organized Hate documented a coordinated campaign among 89 elected officials over 13 months, including 1,111 social media posts and eight bills, tied to a “Sharia Free America Caucus” that has grown to 65 members.
The anti-Sharia campaigns are not new: close to two dozen states passed largely symbolic anti-Sharia laws in the early 2010s. “This isn’t an issue. It’s not something that’s real,” said Tazamal. “It’s constructed, and then these politicians claim to be tackling this constructed problem that they create.”
The picture is complicated, though. Researchers caution against treating every attack on El-Sayed or Mamdani as bigotry.
El-Sayed drew criticism – including from Vance – after he responded to a March attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue by saying “hurt people hurt people”, noting that relatives of the attacker in Lebanon had recently been killed in an Israeli airstrike. El-Sayed eventually apologized, and said the remarks may have been misconstrued. He has also faced scrutiny over his public association with the hyper-popular leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, who mainstream Democrats and Republicans have attacked for past comments minimizing the 11 September attacks.
Mamdani has faced sustained criticism, including from rivals in his own mayoral race, over his refusal to unequivocally condemn the phrase “globalize the intifada”, a phrase Jewish groups say amounts to a call for violence against Jews, but one that he has never personally used. Mamdani subsequently said he would discourage the term after a rabbi told him it evokes memories of bus bombings and restaurant attacks for many Jewish New Yorkers.
The controversy among Jewish organizations, rival campaigns and national Democrats, was not, in the end, disqualifying in the eyes of voters who ultimately decided the race.
The devastation in Gaza, mass settler violence in the West Bank and the suppression of pro-Palestine speech in the US has brought an additional dimension to this discourse. US opinion on Israel has soured immensely in recent years, especially among Democrats, and criticism of Israeli policy by the likes of El-Sayed and Mamdani is cited by those describing Muslim politicians “jihadists”. Mahmoud Khalil, Rümeysa Öztürk and other Muslim residents in the US were among the first swept up for pro-Palestinian campus advocacy, even though most of the students protesting were not Muslim.
That pattern, criticism aimed at religious identity rather than positions or votes, is consistent with what researchers have documented since well before this election cycle. And the point, Selod and Tazamal say, is whether that criticism is being used as cover for a broader claim – that Muslim identity itself, not any specific position on issue or another, is disqualifying from US public life.
“With Abdul El-Sayed, we’re seeing these kinds of intense Islamophobic attacks against him, as opposed to attacking his platform or critiquing his policies,” Selod said. “It’s a playbook. They’re going to attack him for his religious identity to see if this will help pull voters away from him.”
That playbook resurfaced this week in New York, where Mamdani attended the ceremony marking Friday’s 25th anniversary of 9/11 at Ground Zero, as his predecessors have every year. A petition with more than 100,000 signatures, riddled with attacks, unashamedly asked him not to.
Rudy Giuliani, mayor of New York City at the time of the attacks, who is now closely aligned to Trump, claimed from thin air that Mamdani “doesn’t agree that September 11 was an Islamic terrorist attack”, and that his attendance “offends” him, adding even more venom against Muslims generally: “They have every desire to take us over … they want to dominate us. Mamdani is a clear supporter of that.”
Giuliani offered no evidence for either claim.
Cheri Sparacio, one of the petition’s organizers, whose husband died in the attacks, has said her objection is “not about the mayor’s background or faith, but his public actions”. Mamdani attended anyway, and on Friday morning, Mamdani and Giuliani shook hands at the ceremony.
Yet the current moment cannot be separated from the infrastructure built after 9/11, Selod said. “All of the surveillance programs that were put into place, your no-fly list, ICE – these are a product of 9/11,” she said. “We didn’t have Immigration and Customs Enforcement. We didn’t have the TSA, the Transportation Security Administration. These were all put into place to protect the nation against threats of terrorism.”
That architecture has since been extended well past its original target, Selod argued, pointing to the Boston Regional Intelligence Center, a post-9/11 “fusion center” built to detect terrorist plots. Local reporting and ACLU of Massachusetts records show the center has also been used to monitor Black Lives Matter demonstrators.
“It’s expanding beyond a Muslim population to target others,” she said. “Muslims are one to two percent of the US population. My hope is when people start to see how it’s expanding beyond that population, maybe they’ll start really critiquing these programs.”
ISPU polling suggests the sentiment tracks politics rather than faith. Americans who identify as somewhat or very conservative are 13 percentage points more likely than others to endorse anti-Muslim stereotypes, the ISPU found, while religiosity shows no correlation.
Tazamal ties the current spike partly to political calculation. “Polling for Trump is low, and the GOP is the sitting party, and they haven’t delivered on their promises,” she said. “So instead of focusing on institutional failures and policies they haven’t been able to put into place, they’re stirring up hate and bigotry towards a certain group, which is a routine tactic that they do.”
Caleb Elfenbein, a Grinnell College professor who has mapped Islamophobic rhetoric for years, sees a small, organized network reactivating on a predictable schedule. “It really looks, and feels, like a very cynical effort to take advantage of a general sense of fear that can be activated at any given time,” he said.
Whether it works for a GOP that polling indicates is likely to face heavy losses in November’s midterm elections is the open question hanging over this campaign.
Republicans are simultaneously contending with an unpopular war with Iran and rising costs that have squeezed their approval ratings.
Whatever happens, amid growing political mobilization among Muslim Americans and other groups, Tazamal does not expect the party to abandon this effort, or the Islamophobic rhetoric at the center of it.
“I don’t think the GOP is going to do away with it,” she said.

Sour times: pickled onions enjoy revival as Britons think outside the jar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

The humble pickled onion, long associated with classic pub culture, the ploughman’s lunch and cold festive buffets, is enjoying a revival as Britain’s appetite for pickles grows.
About 8.5m UK households bought pickled onions over the past year, according to the consumer data firm Worldpanel by Numerator, with particularly strong momentum in recent months.
In the 12 weeks to early August, the value of pickled onion sales rose 12% year on year, compared with 4% growth across total grocery. While higher prices have contributed to the increase, demand is strengthening, with about 300,000 more households buying them and more than 550,000 additional shopping trips made to buy them.
Pickles are more broadly moving beyond their traditional role as a side or accompaniment to become a flavour and ingredient in their own right.
Michelin-star chefs are even using them in their dishes, and this weekend marks the launch of London’s first major festival dedicated to pickling and fermentation: the Big Brine.
James Goodyear, the head chef at the Michelin-starred restaurant Gordon Ramsay High, said: “There’s a resurgence happening around pickling and preserving right now. Palates have evolved, so diners are naturally craving that sharp, mouthwatering punch of acidity and crunch to cut through richer dishes. Between social media demystifying the craft and a growing curiosity around gut health and natural fermentation, people are far more eager to explore beyond the basic supermarket jar.”
He said guests cared about “sustainability”, and having “jars quietly working away on the shelves” was a “smarter way of running a restaurant”. He added: “It lets us celebrate every single part of an ingredient and completely rethink surplus.”
Molly Scanlan, 39, from London is attending the Big Brine this weekend with her son and has noticed newer pickle brands in the supermarket. She “even noticed in a meal deal” recently the option of a “plastic sachet of snacking cornichons”.
Ocado data shows the pickles, gherkins and olives category is up 30% year on year, while fresh pickled and fermented products have grown 16%. Some individual products have had even more dramatic increases, including raw organic fresh ginger and lemon sauerkraut, up 393%, Opies cocktail gherkins, up 305%, Baxters sliced beetroot, up 246%, and Epicure spicy crinkle-cut pickles, up 242%.
Scanlan has been a fan of pickled foods from a young age. She says her son loves pickles, too, and he also likes kimchi.
Gherkins are Scanlan’s longstanding favourite, but she says there is a growing interest in a much wider range of fermented foods, with products such as kimchi and sauerkraut becoming more widely available. Part of the appeal, she says, is that “you can pickle anything”.
Matt Harris, the founder of Pickle Project, a London-based food brand that makes small-batch, handcrafted pickles using an ultrasonic brining process, said the brand had been created to bring “energy and fun” to what he described as an old-fashioned category. “Despite pickles having ‘a moment’, what’s available on supermarket shelves is very traditional,” he said.
Harris has introduced flavours such as deli dill pickle chips, while also experimenting with ultrasound technology to extract flavours from herbs and spices during the brining process. The brand has launched with Ocado and Whole Foods Market, and Harris said it had experienced “huge growth” over the past nine months.
Kat Goldin, a co-founder of the pickle brand Goat Rodeo Goods, said: “Over the last year, we’ve seen around 11-times growth in sales, which has been massive for us.” She added: “That also fits into this wider ‘lipstick effect’ culture we’re seeing. People might be cutting back on their grocery spending, but they still want to add a little bit of luxury or something special to everyday meals. A nice condiment or pickle can make a simple sandwich or salad feel more exciting without being a huge purchase.”
The pickle boom is also spawning entirely new formats, such as the UK’s first pickle sparkling water. Within its first week at Planet Organic, Yew sparkling water became the retailer’s bestselling soft drink, outselling even bottled water, while the brand says retailers have reported customers specifically asking for the pickle flavour.

AFP Photo
The leaders of France and Canada will visit France's North Atlantic territory of Saint-Pierre-and-Miquelon to underscore their support for national borders, the French presidency said on Sept. 13.
 The joint trip follows U.S. President Donald Trump's social media post displaying territorial ambitions across the region.
 Trump posted an image on Sept. 7 showing a North American map with Canada, Greenland, Mexico, parts of Central America, the Caribbean and Iceland covered by the U.S. flag.
 The altered map also encompassed French overseas territories, including Saint-Pierre-and-Miquelon, Guadeloupe and Martinique.
 French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney plan a symbolic visit to reaffirm shared values of freedom, democracy, rule of law and national sovereignty, the Elysee said.
 Macron will visit the territory on Sept. 19-21, with Carney joining the French leader on Sept. 20.
 Both nations share a common ambition to strengthen independent decision-making amid geopolitical tensions and power politics, the Elysee added.
 The archipelago of Saint-Pierre-and-Miquelon sits about 20 kilometers off Canada's Atlantic coast and houses around 6,000 residents.
 Macron will stop at the islands en route to New York for the U.N. General Assembly.
 The event marks the first official visit by a Canadian prime minister to the archipelago.
 The territory previously experienced tensions with Washington during World War II.
 General Charles de Gaulle's Free French forces seized the islands from the collaborationist Vichy regime in 1941 despite U.S. opposition.
 Francois Hollande made the last French presidential visit to the strategic archipelago in 2014.
 Macron will also address local climate change challenges, including the relocation of Miquelon village inland to escape rising sea levels.

Israeli regime besieged by self-made crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:56:23 UTC
18:56:23 KST

In recent years, the Zionist regime has faced a fundamental contradiction more than ever before; on the one hand, it possesses one of the most powerful armies in the region and extensive American support, and on the other hand, it has faced serious difficulty in converting this military power into a lasting political and strategic achievement. Tel Aviv has entered extensive operations on several fronts, but the end of none of these conflicts has been able to create the security and stability that Israeli leaders promised.
This situation became more evident especially after October 7. The Hamas attack was not only a major security and intelligence failure for Israel, but also called into question the image that Tel Aviv had built of its ability to control the security environment around it. Israel subsequently launched extensive operations in Gaza, and despite the high volume of military operations, it has still not been able to turn the Gaza issue into a sustainable political solution. The persistence of the resistance issue and the inability to create a political order desired by Tel Aviv show that military power alone is not sufficient to resolve a complex crisis.
On the northern front, the conditions are not much different. Israel has tried for years to limit the Hezbollah threat and reduce the group's military capability, but developments in Lebanon have shown that such a threat cannot be permanently eliminated simply through military operations. Even if heavy blows are dealt to a group's infrastructure and command, political, social, and regional factors can still provide the ground for rebuilding its capability. For this reason, Israel has once again faced the same issue it faces in Gaza: the ability to inflict a blow is different from the ability to end a crisis.
The confrontation with Iran has also highlighted this same gap. In recent years, Israel has repeatedly tried to limit Iran's strategic capacities through military and security operations, but these measures have not been able to remove the Iran issue from the region's security equations. Even in circumstances where Tel Aviv can achieve part of its military objectives, changing the regional balance and creating a stable situation is a far more complex matter. In fact, the more the scope of the conflict expands, the clearer it becomes that there is a considerable gap between "striking" and "winning."
Israel's problem, of course, is not limited to the military battlefield. Prolonged wars, economic pressure, political disputes, and social divisions have also placed the Zionist society under pressure. Since the beginning of the recent crises, the Netanyahu cabinet has faced extensive political disputes, and the controversy over the government's performance, the conduct of the war, and responsibility for the October 7 security failure continues. This situation has weakened the image that Israel presented for years of a cohesive, stable society enjoying intelligence and security superiority.
On the international stage, too, the costs of Tel Aviv's policies have increased. Although Israel still enjoys considerable American support, the continuation of the conflicts and the rise in international criticism have raised the political cost of the regime's actions. The important point is that Israel needs not only military power to maintain its superiority; it also needs political legitimacy, foreign support, and the ability to manage its relations with allies. The prolongation of the wars has ultimately placed all three of these areas under pressure.
Under such circumstances, the remarks of Yuval Noah Harari, a Zionist author and historian, take on greater importance. In an article in the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, Harari held Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet responsible for part of the recent failures and described the past four years as one of the most dangerous periods in the history of the Zionist regime. He stressed that the security institutions' warnings before October 7 about existing threats were ignored, and that the Netanyahu cabinet was preoccupied with its own domestic political priorities.
Harari went on to not only refer to the failure before October 7 but also criticized the way the war was managed afterward. From his perspective, Israel achieved successes in some military operations, but was unable to convert these successes into a lasting political and strategic achievement. He ultimately, using a very harsh expression, likened Israel's leadership situation to "lions led by donkeys."
The importance of these remarks lies in the fact that such criticism is no longer raised only by Israel's foreign opponents, but voices of criticism have also grown louder from within the regime's society and intellectual circles. In fact, the issue Harari refers to is not an individual weakness or merely a problem related to Netanyahu; rather, it is a larger question about the quality of strategic decision-making in Israel.
Israel today faces a serious contradiction: the regime's military capability remains high, but its ability to convert this power into a desired political order has declined. Tel Aviv can target facilities, infrastructure, and military objectives, but it cannot eliminate the roots of a political or security crisis simply through military operations. The experiences of Gaza, Lebanon, and the confrontation with Iran have each, in a different way, demonstrated this same reality.
From this perspective, Israel's failure should not be measured only by the number of operations or the amount of damage inflicted on the opposing side. The more important criterion is the extent to which Israel, after expending this volume of military and political resources, has moved closer to its strategic objectives. If the goal is to create lasting security, eliminate the main threats, prevent the expansion of regional rivals' influence, and preserve internal cohesion, the performance of recent years at least shows that Tel Aviv has still not achieved an important part of these objectives.
For this reason, Israel's current crisis is less a crisis of military power than a crisis of converting power into results. A regime that enjoys military superiority but cannot turn war into peace, operations into strategy, and temporary victories into lasting security will face a problem beyond a defeat on the battlefield. Perhaps the most important part of Harari's remarks is this; that Israel's problem is not only the enemies surrounding it, but part of the crisis goes back to the way decisions are made and managed by those who are supposed to contain these enemies.

Hard Times Ahead: Russian Attacks put Ukraine’s Finances Under Pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:55:00 UTC
18:55:00 KST

Ukraine’s finances face a “very difficult winter” as Russia hammers economic targets and the costs of war soar, the Ukrainian economy minister and other senior finance officials have warned.
Taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of interceptors, Moscow is now launching daily strikes on the country’s logistics and business infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The port of Odesa, which plays a vital role in exporting grain, has come under constant attack, reducing its ability to operate. At the same time warehouses, factories, logistics facilities and even filling stations have been targeted.
The strikes not only disrupt business activity and deprive the state of sorely needed tax revenue but also force the government to provide financial support for businesses, putting more pressure on the beleaguered budget.
There are also fears that come winter, an expected Russian blitz on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure will exacerbate the already tense financial situation.
“We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of the overall economic conditions in the country,” Oleksandr Kravchenko, Ukraine’s economy and environment minister, told the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv on Saturday.
“So what we estimate in the Ministry of Economy is that basically the total destruction of infrastructure and fixed assets is close to around $10 billion per year.”
Russian Strikes Hit Gas Station, Kyiv-Warsaw Train, Near Polish Border
He added that the financial instruments the government now has at its disposal will fail to cover the needs of businesses suffering from the attacks.
Cost of war
Roksana Pidlasa, a Ukrainian member of parliament and chair of the parliament’s budget committee, told the same conference that the war is now costing Ukraine around $190 million a day, compared to $140 million a day just two years ago, in a sober assessment of the state of Ukraine’s finances.
She added that preliminary reports on the “budget implementation” for the first eight months of the year show that national security and defense cost the government almost $42 billion in that period.
“We have raised only $39 billion from our own resources, which includes budget revenues and domestic borrowing. So unfortunately, this year the war has gotten so expensive that we can’t even cover our share of the costs... in the previous year our own resources were covering the basic military needs such as soldier salaries. We’re now using international money to pay soldiers’ salaries.”
As an example of how revenue has declined, Pidlasa cited VAT, which, she said, had “underperformed by $1.35 billion over eight months”. A quarter of this sum, she added, was lost in August alone—a month of intensive Russian attacks.
Hunting for cash
To mitigate the problem the government has said that it is preparing resilience strategies for the energy and logistics systems that will help them absorb Russian attacks.
Also speaking at the YES conference, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Saturday that the government can also draw upon the Special Program for Ukraine Recovery (Spur 2), a specialized financing initiative organized by the World Bank in which it matches funding for Kyiv provided by other international donors.
This money will be channeled into providing some support and relief for businesses affected by Russian strikes.
“We are in the process of negotiating with our European partners [on additional funding] and using the frozen assets of the Russian Federation, trying to identify sources outside the European Union and rationalizing all the spendings inside Ukraine,” he added.
Ukraine also intends to utilize military force, or the threat of it, to relieve the pressure on the budget.
“Russia knows that if they strike – and they are preparing to strike our energy system in the winter – Russia will receive the exact same,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday in a threat made, possibly, in the hope of deterring Moscow from attacking and thus saving Ukraine from associated financial costs.
“If they cause us blackouts, we will try to respond to them in kind,” he added.

Israel’s PISA collapse exposes a failing education system threatening its future - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:52:10 UTC
18:52:10 KST

On the eve of 5787, and as the election campaign gets underway, Israel has posted shocking results in this year’s PISA tests – the global benchmark for comparing education systems.
You might think this is because of the haredim (ultra-Orthodox) – after all, a growing share of Israel’s children belong to an education system that does not provide enough instruction in mathematics, science, and English.
But the problem revealed by results released this week is general – and disastrous.
Haredi schools are indeed included in the PISA sampling framework, but haredi boys are very poorly represented.
A Knesset Research and Information Center report on PISA 2022 found that haredi boys made up only 3% of the actual sample before weighting, whereas haredim are a sixth of the population and even more of the youth – mainly because most haredi boys’ schools refused to participate. Moreover, haredi girls performed rather well.
The figure that should truly alarm Israel is that the 2025 collapse is occurring not at the margins of the education system, but at its core.
Israel’s reading score fell by 38 points in just three years, from 474 in 2022 to 436 in 2025. Mathematics fell by 25 points, to 433, and science by 23 points, to 442.
In all three subjects, these are Israel’s lowest-ever PISA results, and they are significantly below the results recorded in 2012, 2015, and 2018. Israel is now below the average of the OECD – the club of developed economies – in all three subjects.
In mathematics, 46% of Israeli students fail to reach even the baseline level of proficiency, compared with an OECD average of 35%.
Similar gaps were recorded in all subjects, and the share of top performers is also below the average for developed countries.
The attitudes of students themselves toward learning and the education system should also set off alarm bells.
According to the organization’s report, “only 68% of students in Israel agreed or strongly agreed with the statement ‘I am curious about many different things,’ compared with 73% on average across OECD countries (and) 37% of students in Israel agreed or strongly agreed with the statement ‘School has been a waste of time,’ compared with just 24% on average across OECD countries.”
More children attend schools where principals say there are insufficient resources. More students report skipping school.
What about the Israeli Arab sector? There is actually a narrowing gap between students there and the Hebrew-speaking education system because the latter deteriorated faster. That is the sort of equality no country should aspire to.
Similarly, Israel’s educational gaps have narrowed somewhat – but again, not because weaker students improved, but because the share of top performers significantly declined.
Yet Israel remains among the countries with some of the largest gaps in the world between its strongest and weakest students – also bad.
The wars of recent years may be part of the explanation (COVID is not, because everyone went through it) – but the downward trend predates that.
What should be done?
First, obviously, a modern country cannot continue funding schools that fail to provide their students with meaningful core instruction in mathematics, English, and science.
As the haredi share of the population grows, the economic and social cost of this arrangement grows with it. Genuine core studies should be a condition for receiving public funding, and the matter is far too urgent to remain a bargaining chip in coalition negotiations.
But the 2025 PISA results make clear that this is not the main problem.
The emergency begins with the people the system manages to put in its classrooms.
Israel expects teachers to perform one of the most important and difficult jobs in society, yet for years it has failed to make teaching a profession in which enough talented people can build attractive professional and economic lives.
Add to this the workload, burnout, and a professional status that does not match the responsibility.
According to the OECD, Israel invests 22% less per student in education than the average, and far less than top performers.
Removing politics and placing education at the forefront
Above all of this lies the chronic politicization of Israeli education.
Education ministers come and go, each arriving with a worldview, flagship programs, and priorities of their own, while an education system requires planning measured in decades.
Education repeatedly becomes a battleground over identity, religion, nationalism, and politics, instead of having fundamental goals stable enough to survive the next minister and the next government.
The same applies to the place occupied by Jewish and traditional studies.
These are important and legitimate components of education in a Jewish state, and Israeli children should know the culture, history, and tradition from which the country emerged.
But classroom hours are a finite resource, which means this is also a question of proportion and effectiveness.
When the ability to read, write, calculate, and understand science is deteriorating rapidly, the curriculum cannot be managed as though these choices carry no cost.
Israel therefore needs a long-term education policy whose central elements are insulated as much as possible from changes of governments and ministers.
There must be broad national agreement on what an Israeli student must know, how much the country is willing to invest to bring excellent people into the classroom, and how to measure whether any of this is actually happening.
The education system cannot reinvent itself every time the person sitting in the education minister’s office changes.
Israel’s qualitative edge derives first and foremost from the quality of the people it produces and their ability to think, invent, research, and build.
That qualitative edge has been a major source of Israel’s economic and technological advantage, and from it has also grown a central part of its military advantage.
A small country with a small population cannot compete over the long term through mass; it competes through quality. If the education system stops producing that quality, there is no reason to assume the economic advantage will endure.
And if the economic and technological advantage erodes, the military advantage is not some permanent asset promised to Israel forever.
This connects to an even larger and more disturbing picture. Israel also depends on allies, foreign investment, scientific and technological cooperation, international legitimacy, and its standing as part of the developed democratic world.
As the country undergoes a process of nationalist radicalization, increasing religiosity, and damage to its liberal institutions, it places those assets at risk as well.
A society that allows sectoral politics to determine what children learn, that struggles to pay enough to attract excellent people into teaching, that changes its educational priorities with every minister, and that devotes ever more energy to culture wars and battles over identity is damaging the foundation from which the Israeli miracle arose in the first place.
The current right-wing religious coalition is not the source of every failure in Israel’s education system, some of which have been building for decades.
But it is deepening precisely the trends Israel now needs to reverse: politicization, sector preference, religious encroachment, and the prioritization of coalition demands over the construction of a modern education system with a uniform set of fundamental skills required of every child.
These are not separate crises.
Israel is accustomed to thinking of education as a demographic problem.
If only we take the haredim out of the equation, many secular and middle-class Israelis tell themselves, and if we also separate the Arab education system, what will emerge behind them is the “real Israel”: an educated, Western, technological country whose education system may be mediocre but is certainly not collapsing.
The 2025 PISA results should put an end to that illusion.
Add this to the long list of reasons why change is urgently needed in 5787.
The writer is a former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press. He served as chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and authored two books about Israel.

Russian airstrikes in several Ukrainian regions Saturday killed 10 people, injured dozens and damaged residential buildings and infrastructure, local officials said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, writing on Telegram, said Russia deployed nearly 500 drones against Ukrainian targets since morning.

Earlier, the ministry said its forces struck two cargo vessels overnight in the port of Chornomorsk.

The Togliattikauchuk plant specialized in the production of synthetic rubbers and fuel additives used in fuel for Russian missiles, it said.
Russian regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said industrial facilities in the Samara region were attacked by Ukrainian drones, without specifying which facilities or whether they were damaged, Interfax news agency reported.
Ilya Sukhikh, mayor of Togliatti in the Samara region, said several residential buildings were damaged and one person was injured.

A large-scale scheme involving the sale of counterfeit Biopatid has been exposed in Ukraine — 27 people have been notified of suspicion
Kyiv • UNN
The group illegally produced and sold across Ukraine a weight-loss drug containing tirzepatide without registration or certification. Twenty-seven people have been notified of suspicion.
Law enforcement agencies exposed and halted the activities of an organized group that had established the large-scale illegal production and nationwide distribution in Ukraine of a counterfeit weight-loss medicine called "Biopatid." This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, according to UNN.
Details
The drug contained the active substance tirzepatide and was sold without the relevant permits, state registration, or proper certification.
Law enforcement officers notified 27 participants in the criminal scheme that they were suspected of producing, transporting, sending, and storing knowingly counterfeit medicines for the purpose of sale. These crimes are provided for under Part 3 of Article 28 and Part 2 of Article 321-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
The drug was shipped to customers without observing the required temperature conditions. The cost of the main materials was approximately USD 17, while the finished product was sold for up to USD 1,200. Preliminary estimates indicate that, since the beginning of this year, products worth a total of more than USD 5 million had been manufactured
Investigative actions were carried out in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Poltava, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Rivne, Kharkiv, Khmelnytskyi, and Chernihiv. During the searches, counterfeit medicine and raw materials for its production, clandestine laboratory equipment, packaging materials and finished printed products, documents and draft records, mobile phones and computer equipment, as well as cash in various currencies totaling nearly UAH 15 million, expensive vehicles, and other property were seized.
Previously
Law enforcement officers are investigating the illegal production and sale of the counterfeit weight-loss drug Biopatid. More than 250 searches are underway in various regions.

EU sanctions rollover stalls over Russian oligarch Usmanov as Paris backs Bratislava's demand to delist him. Ambassadors broke up with no agreement on renewing the measures, and they have one sitting left before every restriction on the list runs out on its own.
The EU just released $7 billion for Ukraine to buy Patriot missiles and drones. The money comes from Europe's existing loan to Kyiv, and the decision finally lets Ukraine place orders for the American interceptors it cannot build itself.
Humanitarian and social impact
"There is real hunger there": Oleshky, occupied town in Ukraine's Kherson Oblast, turned 942 this week. Behind Russian blockade, its people eat roadside grass. The 942-year-old Kherson city has spent months cut off, its aid convoys shelled.
Ukraine's Third Army Corps won't just hold Donetsk fortress cities. It's building mission to pull civilians out of them. A dedicated fund is opening to pay for more trips, more often.
Political and legal developments
EU has never sanctioned Russia's nuclear sector. Activists say that gap just let Rosatom into German plant, and they're suing to close it. BUND says letting Russia's Rosatom help make fuel at the Lingen plant, amid the war and sabotage in Germany, hands Moscow critical infrastructure.

Ukraine's parliament changes how military budget is cleared, and freezes money behind one of war's cleverest supply schemes, defense-industry council says. The program lets Ukrainian units turn confirmed kills into new weapons, but a parliamentary rule change has frozen the payments.

'Putin's terror': Russian drone hits Kyiv-Warsaw train near Polish border as nationwide attacks kill 6, injure 43
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least six civilians and injured 43 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Sept. 13, as Moscow launched a mass drone assault that heavily targeted western regions far from the front line.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 453 Shahed and Gerbera drones, including some jet-powered Shaheds, as well as Parodiya decoy drones and S8000 Banderol missiles.
Ukrainian forces intercepted 405 drones and six S8000 Banderol missiles. Hits were recorded at 13 locations, while falling debris was reported at seven other sites.
The assault was particularly heavy in western Ukraine, which typically sees fewer Russian attacks than Kyiv, Odesa, and front-line regions.
The strikes prompted air raid warnings in neighboring Poland, where the country's Government Security Center issued an air threat alert for several counties in Lublin Voivodeship near the Ukrainian border.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, said Russia used rainy weather to launch gasoline-powered Shahed drones against areas farther from the front line, apparently expecting the conditions to make the drones harder to intercept.
In Volyn Oblast, in Ukraine's northwest, over the past day, Russian forces attacked with drones, injuring at least five people, according to regional Governor Roman Romaniuk.
Separately, a Russian drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw train near Ukraine's border with Poland, Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) reported. The train was about 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border. No passengers were injured.
"This is (Vladimir) Putin's terror, 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and NATO. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Katerina Sergatskova, an award-winning journalist and entrepreneur who witnessed the attack, told the Kyiv Independent that Russian drones struck a gas station and a train locomotive near the Yahodyn border checkpoint on the Ukrainian-Polish border.
Following the attack, she and other passengers were left standing outside for several hours.
"We were told to evacuate immediately, but there was no shelter," Sergatskova said. "We were simply told to move away from the train cars toward the lake."
Ukrzaliznytsia later confirmed a diplomatic train was present at the site shortly before the Russian drone arrived.
"Shortly before the locomotive was hit on the border between Ukraine and Poland at the Yagodin station, a diplomatic train was present, carrying, among others, security advisors from several EU member states, as well as former European leaders, including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson," Ukrzaliznytsia Wrote.
"Another train, which was at the Yagodin station at the time of the attack, carried former CIA Director David Petraeus."
In neighboring Rivne Oblast, Russian attacks caused power outages in parts of the city of Dubno and in the Rivne district, according to regional Governor Oleksandr Koval. An unspecified enterprise in the Sarny district was also destroyed in the attack.
No casualties were reported, and energy crews were working to restore electricity, Koval said.
In Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast, a Russian attack at dawn damaged an industrial facility. One person was injured. An apartment building in Ivano-Frankivsk was also damaged, with windows shattered, Governor Svitlana Onyshchuk said.
Russian drones also struck Ternopil, damaging a transport infrastructure facility and an industrial building, acting head of the Ternopil Regional Military Administration Taras Pastukh said. One person has been reported injured.
In Khmelnytskyi Oblast, falling drone debris sparked a fire at an enterprise. In Lviv Oblast, several residential and utility buildings, as well as a school building, were damaged. No injuries were reported in either region.
In Odesa Oblast, Russian forces attacked civilian infrastructure, damaging the upper floors of a residential building and several private homes. A fire also broke out in the Botanical Garden, while warehouses and a children's sanatorium were damaged, regional governor Oleh Kiper said. Information on casualties is still being clarified.
In Mykolaiv Oblast, a 71-year-old woman was killed in a Russian drone attack overnight. Russian forces also targeted energy infrastructure in the city of Mykolaiv, leaving part of the city without electricity, acting head of the regional military administration Heorhii Reshetilov said.
Four people were injured in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia Oblast, while Russian forces carried out 964 strikes across 58 settlements in the oblast over the past day, co-head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Defense Council Ivan Fedorov said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed, and 11 were injured as a result of Russian attacks, the Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Residential houses and administrative buildings were damaged.
In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian forces killed one person and injured three others, according to the Governor Viacheslav Chaus. The region has been under an air raid alert for more than 24 hours.
Three people were also injured in Kharkiv Oblast, where civilian infrastructure was damaged and destroyed, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kherson Oblast, one person was killed and nine were injured in Russian attacks, the Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Apartment buildings and private homes were damaged, along with a cultural center, gas pipeline, garages, and cars.
Six people, including a 6-month-old child, were injured across multiple settlements in Sumy Oblast, according to the military administration. The region has also been under an air raid alert for more than 24 hours.
Western Ukrainian regions have repeatedly come under Russian long-range drone and missile attacks targeting energy, transport, and other infrastructure.
Although they are targeted less frequently than Kyiv and Odesa, and far less frequently than front-line areas of Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, Russian drones have increasingly reached western Ukraine during large-scale nationwide assaults.
The latest strikes on western Ukraine were part of a wider Russian drone assault on Sept. 12. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched nearly 500 strike drones at Ukraine during the day.

UN Warns Ukraine Faces Toughest Wartime Winter Yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
09:28:00 UTC
18:28:00 KST

Ukraine could face its most grueling winter since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 due to systematic and expanding aerial bombardments targeting civilian and energy infrastructure, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Administrator Alexander De Croo warned in an interview with the BBC.
Speaking to the broadcaster, De Croo said Ukraine is entering the cold season from a “very weak position” as Russian strikes continue to pound the power grid, fuel distribution networks, and commercial centers across the country.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This includes gas stations, shopping malls, and business centers, but above all, energy infrastructure, transmission lines, and similar assets. There is absolutely no justification for this,” De Croo stated, emphasizing that the UN remains deeply concerned about the potential humanitarian consequences as temperatures drop.
De Croo cautioned that extensive destruction of heating plants, electricity networks, and municipal utilities could disrupt water supply, heating systems, and sewage networks in sub-zero weather.
He noted that if temperatures drop toward -20 degrees Celsius, the compounding damage to municipal life-support systems would create conditions bordering on a humanitarian catastrophe.
The UN official described current recovery efforts as an urgent “race against time” to repair battered power plants and distribution substations before freezing weather sets in.
‘A Way for Russian Occupiers Go Home’: Ukraine Intel Reveals Why Kerch Bridge Still Stands
Through the UNDP, international agencies are assisting Ukrainian authorities in restoring damaged assets while accelerating the deployment of decentralized, smaller-scale energy generation units designed to be more resilient and less vulnerable to concentrated missile and drone strikes.
However, De Croo characterized maintaining and rebuilding the energy system under persistent Russian bombardment as an almost impossible task.
Repair crews must routinely operate during active air raid alerts, fully aware that the facilities they are fixing are prime military targets, frequently forcing emergency pauses in critical restoration work.
Domestic resilience plans and decentralization
The UN’s assessment follows statements by Ukrainian officials outlining domestic preparations to counter expected winter strikes.
Speaking at the Yalta European Strategy (YES 2026) forum in Kyiv, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi stated that while fully shielding every facility remains unfeasible, Ukraine is better prepared to withstand grid attacks than it was ahead of last winter.
Koretskyi noted that the government has formulated comprehensive resilience plans, with primary efforts directed toward decentralizing heating, water, and power infrastructure across municipalities to prevent regional grid collapses.
The prime minister acknowledged that Russian strikes have multiplied over the past two months, creating additional economic and logistical burdens, but affirmed that the state possesses the resources and technical reserves required to manage the heating season.
Ukraine met its baseline winter natural gas storage target a month early, accumulating 14.6 billion cubic meters in underground facilities by late August, according to First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal.
Concurrently, municipal utility crews had prepared approximately 100,000 residential buildings alongside 12,400 local boiler facilities and 11,700 kilometers of district heating pipelines by late August.
The Ukrainian government has allocated approximately Hr. 6.8 billion ($152 million) toward grid repairs, decentralized backup generators, and physical blast protections to ensure critical municipal services continue functioning during localized blackouts.
