Europe dominates ranking of the world’s most beautiful cycling routes – these are rides to try
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

From the vineyards of Tuscany and lavender fields of Provence to the rugged Scottish coast and the peaks of the French Alps, Europe is home to some of the world’s most spectacular cycling routes, according to new research.
Tourism on two wheels is on the rise with a surge of 292% in Google searches for “cycling holiday”. There’s so much more to a cycling trip than just the bike, though, and new research has revealed the most beautiful routes worldwide.
It’s good news for European cycling fans, as a majority of the top 15 in the ranking are based on the continent.
A study by adventure booking platform Explore used eye-tracking software to assess the reactions of 200 participants to 52 renowned and attractive cycling routes from around the world.
The technology measured how quickly each route caught their attention and how long it held it for, and the metrics were combined into a weighted "eye-catching" score out of 100 to provide a definitive ranking.
“There's something about seeing a country from the saddle that no other kind of travel can match; you're moving fast enough to cover real ground, but slow enough to take it all in,” said Luke Judd, travel expert at Explore.
“What's interesting about this research is that it puts science behind what cyclists have always debated: which views genuinely stop us in our tracks.”
Canada’s Bow Valley Parkway, a scenic winding route between Banff and Lake Louise, was far and away the most popular option, with a score of 97 out of 100.
It was followed closely by Australia's Great Ocean Road, on the southwest coast of Victoria, which was awarded a score of 94.
Despite the top two being some distance from Europe, and the list spanning four continents, eight out of the 15 are actually in Europe itself.
Here’s where to head for a beautiful cycling experience closer to home.
European destinations dominate the rankings
In third place, with a score of 91, are the stunning Tuscany Gravel Routes in Italy. Most famous for the professional one-day race held there in the spring, the stunning route features cypress tree-lined climbs, working vineyards and centuries-old hilltop towns.
With a score of 90, the Elbe Cycle Route in Germany is in fourth place.
It follows the Elbe River for around 1,220 kilometres from Czechia towards the North Sea, and the route passes through Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt, skirts several German states and travels right through Hamburg, offering a journey through historic cities, countryside and some of eastern and northern Germany’s most interesting landscapes.
In sixth place, Amsterdam Cycle Route 10 has a score of 86. The Netherlands goes hand in hand with cycling, and there’s arguably no better way to explore Amsterdam than by bike.
This circular route offers a brilliant introduction to the city and its surroundings, taking you past canals, parks and historic neighbourhoods before heading into quieter countryside.
In seventh and eighth places, with scores of 82 and 81 respectively, are Italy’s Stelvio Pass and the Provence Lavender Route in France.
While the Stelvio Pass is notorious as one of the most difficult cycling routes in the world – and the second-highest in the Alps – the Provence Lavender Route is, mercifully, significantly easier.
The scenic trip is best taken in the summertime when lavender plants are in full bloom. It winds through rolling countryside, hilltop villages and the Luberon and Valensole Plateau’s vast fields of purple blooms.
It’s back to challenging routes with Scotland’s North Coast 500, which is in 11th place with a score of 78.
Starting and finishing in Inverness, this route is more than 800km long and can take even the most competent cyclists up to five days to complete. Despite its trickiness, it’s well worth it for those who want to experience the rugged beauty of the Scottish coast.
The Route des Grandes Alpes is one of Europe’s great mountain road trips, stretching from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean through some of the French Alps’ most spectacular scenery.
It’s in 13th place, with a score of 78 – the same as the North Coast 500 in Scotland – and isn’t easy either. Expect towering peaks, deep valleys, mountain passes and picturesque villages along the way. It’s fairly challenging, with long, winding and sometimes steep sections, so it’s best suited to experienced cyclists.
The last European entry in the top 15 is the Lake Ohrid Circuit in 14th place, with a score of 76. The trip covers roughly 90 to 96 kilometres and crosses an international border between North Macedonia and Albania.
Those tackling it will take in the historic towns of Ohrid and Struga and the Monastery of Saint Naum near the southern border, as well as Pogradec on the Albanian lakeside. Just remember to bring your passport in order to experience the whole route.
The world’s top 15 most beautiful cycling routes
How each route is ranked according to an “eye-catching” score out of 100:
- 1. Bow Valley Parkway (Banff–Lake Louise), Canada - 97/100
- 2. Great Ocean Road, Australia - 94/100
- 3. Tuscany Gravel Routes, Italy - 91/100
- 4. Elbe Cycle Route, Germany - 90/100
- 5. Carretera Austral, Chile - 86/100
- 6. Amsterdam Cycle Route 10, Netherlands - 86/100
- 7. Pacific Coast Highway, USA - 82/100
- 8. Stelvio Pass, Italy - 82/100
- 9. Provence Lavender Route, France - 81/100
- 10. Road to Hana, USA - 78/100
- 11. NC500 (North Coast 500), Scotland (UK) - 78/100
- 12. Route des Grandes Alpes, France - 78/100
- 13. Slickrock Trail, USA - 76/100
- 14. Lake Ohrid Circuit, North Macedonia/Albania - 76/100
- 15. Vancouver Seawall, Canada - 75/100

Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

Ukraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life. Wave after wave of terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroying supermarket distribution hubs, pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia will again try to blow up Ukraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.
Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, was going to plan. Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t. Failing militarily and taking huge casualties, his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.
This prospect of daily mass killings, rampant war crimes, malnutrition, homelessness and renewed, large-scale displacements of Ukrainian civilians – this intensifying Russian campaign of terror – is intolerable. So why don’t the western allies and Nato intervene to stop it?
The principal reason is chronic US ambivalence and unreliability, which has turned Ukraine into a seemingly irresolvable forever war. Former president Joe Biden tossed lifebelts to the Ukrainians in 2022, then left them to sink or swim. Trump has since tried to drown them. Despite halting the ground invasion and taking the fight to Russia’s heartlands, Ukraine is more vulnerable than ever to air attack. That’s largely because Trump has backtracked on allowing Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors and paused weapons deliveries. Europe has so far failed to fill the gap. Trump’s fawning and feting of Putin, seen at last year’s nauseating Alaska summit, and his bullying of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, undermine Ukraine’s resistance, European security and hopes of an expedited settlement. Vulnerable civilians pay the price.
Many Ukrainians are weary of war. About 60% oppose ceding Donbas land to Russia but a similar number would support a ceasefire, backed by western security guarantees, that freezes current positions, a recent poll suggests. Most Russians also want it to stop. And like Moscow, Kyiv is feeling the financial pinch, notwithstanding a $100bn EU loan. There’s plainly a deal to be done. But Putin (like Trump over Iran) ignores public opinion. The indifference of authoritarian leaders to the popular will, let alone global opinion, is another reason forever wars proliferate. Whether the conflict is Ukraine, Gaza or Iran, ordinary people, watching from the margins, feel powerless to influence events. Familiarity deadens the senses over time. The horror of it all is scary and upsetting. It’s easier to look away.
Efforts to halt the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February and has now extended to the Red Sea (Trump, remember, said it would only last a few weeks), and relentless post-2023 violence in occupied Palestine, are hampered, as in Ukraine, by the absence of credible, independent peace processes. This is another major factor fuelling the modern forever war phenomenon. Trump clumsily inserted himself into the Kyiv-Moscow argument, blatantly favouring one side. At no point did he trouble himself about the rights and wrongs of Putin’s war of choice. He aimed not to save lives but to win a Nobel peace prize (plus lucrative Russian energy deals).
Self-serving motives have similarly upset hopes of rescuing Gaza’s civilians from the Israeli military and Hamas. Trump’s “board of peace” and 20-point plan are primarily vehicles for his ego and greed, not a plausible route out of a political, military and humanitarian dead-end. As for ending the Iran debacle, the US president has lost interest. His refusal, like Putin, to accept the obvious, admit he failed to achieve his war aims, and seek a compromise with Tehran undercuts regional mediators and Gulf state allies, who rightly fear fighting will drag on indefinitely. Desperately needed: impartial, UN-empowered peace envoys to knock heads together.
Forever wars develop and grow entrenched in the absence of authoritative, universal legal frameworks respected and observed by all. The contempt shown by Trump, Putin and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, for basic principles of the post-1945 world order – rule of law, national sovereignty, oversight and enforcement by the international court of justice and international criminal court – directly contributes to the prolongation of conflict. Once the rules are cast aside, anything goes. That has ineluctably led to war crime atrocities such as those experienced in Gaza since the 7 October massacres; in Bucha, Mariupol and other towns and cities across Ukraine; and in Minab, southern Iran, where a US Tomahawk cruise missile allegedly killed more than 100 schoolgirls in February. Almost invariably, the culprits escape punishment. It’s impunity made law. It’s forever anarchy.
Another increasingly common feature of endless wars is the obstruction of full public scrutiny and accountability through independent media and UN investigations. Since the war with Hamas began, Israel’s army has tightly restricted international journalists’ access to Gaza. Despite the efforts of brave reporters, this policy has inevitably disguised and distorted the true picture of what happens there, not least for Israelis. Likewise, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, releases only limited, selective information about Iran-related operations. This has led, for example, to under-reporting of the extent and cost of successful Iranian strikes on US bases in the Gulf. Russian state media routinely censor news from Ukraine. Most Russians have little idea how badly the war is going. Generally speaking, public ignorance facilitates abuses and prolongs conflict.
Forever wars are ultimately caused by failing, foolish leaders. For sure, generals foul up. In battle, things rarely go as expected. Clever strategies backfire. But the core problem is politicians who promise too much, underestimate their opponents, ignore less macho, peaceful alternatives, think they are above the law, will not admit mistakes – and, without shame or compunction, lie to your face. This is an age-old problem with no quick solution. But Ukraine’s people, facing a season from hell, urgently need additional assistance now.
Western democracies cannot sit on their hands as the civilian toll from Moscow’s barbarous onslaughts mounts daily. Nato must finally switch to the offensive, make clear more war crimes will not be tolerated, threaten to strike Russian drone and missile launch sites from the air (as previously, repeatedly, urged here) – and force Putin to back off before his forever war becomes everybody’s war.
- 
  Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

Burnham must understand Wales is ‘not a region in England’, says first minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

Andy Burnham has to be serious about devolution and understand that Wales is a nation and “not a region in England”, according to the country’s first minister.
Rhun ap Iorwerth, who is the first non-Labour leader of the Senedd since devolution, told the Guardian that while he was encouraged by initial discussions with the new UK prime minister, he was wary about Burnham being captured by a consensus Westminster view against relinquishing further powers.
Separately in the interview, ap Iorwerth said his party, Plaid Cymru, would be willing to cooperate with Labour in the future to keep Reform UK out of power, as he would always want to block the “destructive politics” of Nigel Farage’s party.
Ap Iorwerth became Wales’s first minister in May, days after he led Plaid Cymru to victory in Senedd elections, breaking a 100-year period of Labour dominance, which included Labour being the biggest party in every vote to the Welsh parliament since it was created in 1999.
He has pushed for more powers to be given to his government, particularly over policing and the justice system, where Wales is the only UK nation not to have control.
Burnham’s background as Greater Manchester mayor was a positive, ap Iorwerth said: “He clearly understands the benefits of getting devolution right for Manchester. I’ve had really positive, constructive discussions with him.
“He now needs to know what devolution means for Wales, and it’s very, very different. We’re a nation. We’re not a region of England. There are different needs. We will work closely with the UK government on what empowering communities means. But it’s a totally different model, and it’s really important that Andy Burnham doesn’t confuse the two.”
Speaking in London after meetings with UK government officials, ap Iorwerth said, although Burnham had assured him he would “not bypass devolution”, he was concerned about institutional resistance to handing over police and justice powers.
In July, Burnham’s Welsh secretary, Stephen Kinnock, said he was not “entirely convinced” about the idea of devolving powers such as policing. Ap Iorwerth said: “The arguments for the devolution of policing and justice are very, very strong. Commission after commission and study after study have concluded this really needs to happen.
“Andy Burnham had more control over policing as the mayor of Manchester than I do as first minister of Wales, and it’s just not right. Burnham gives me the impression, and I believe him, that he’s ready to take a different approach.
“What I’m also acutely aware of is that those forces around him are probably equally as averse to devolving policing and justice as they have been under previous Labour leaders.”
With 43 Senedd seats, Plaid is the biggest party in the expanded 96-member chamber, with Reform forming the opposition. Reform enjoyed “a very significant result” in May in going from two members – both defectors from the Conservatives – to 34, ap Iorwerth said.
However, he pledged to stand against what he termed Reform’s “kind of politics that runs contrary to my core beliefs of cooperation and tolerance and supporting each other and looking after the weak”.
Asked if Plaid would potentially cooperate with Labour to block a potential Reform government, whether in Cardiff or Westminster, he said it would: “It’s not about keeping a political party out, it’s about keeping a kind of politics out, the negative influence that it has, and of course we do and will cooperate with Labour.”
At a press conference earlier this month to mark the start of the new Senedd session, ap Iorwerth took a somewhat downbeat approach, warning about a “very challenging” financial picture, with a real-terms decline in both day-to-day and capital spending this year.
Asked if he risked mimicking Keir Starmer’s sometimes gloomy approach in assessing the task of government, ap Iorwerth said that was not his intention: “I would certainly hope not, because I think a mistake Keir Starmer made was that the government almost gave up on its values, gave up on its beliefs under that administration, because things were difficult.
“We’ve taken a completely different approach, and if there was a sense of gloom, it was certainly not meant to be like that.”
On Monday, ap Iorwerth is due to hold a meeting in Cardiff with his equivalents in Scotland and Northern Ireland, John Swinney of the Scottish National party and Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin, an event labelled by one Telegraph columnist as a “sinister cabal … plotting nothing less than the end of the United Kingdom”.
Asked about this description, ap Iorwerth smiles. “It’s just not the way that I see it,” he says. “I don’t come from the base of working, either ourselves or with any other partners, to break up the UK. I want to build up my nation. That’s all it’s about.”
Wales is, he says, on a “constitutional journey”, one in which he sees the ultimate destination as being independence – but without any set timetable or rush: “That’s in the hands of the people of Wales.”

Rosina, London SW17: ‘Bella Italia in Bolton this is not’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Rosina is a serene, heavenly-white neighbourhood Italian restaurant just off Wandsworth Common, on the same stretch as the much-celebrated Chez Bruce. It is Adam Byatt’s fifth place – he’s probably best known for Trinity, his Michelin-starred restaurant up the road in Clapham – and, lately, his very good, recipe-driven YouTube channel ran a Road to Rosina series in which he visits suppliers, eats pasta with nonnas and learns peak tiramisu skills from a woman called Pina (more of her tiramisu later). If any neighbourhood can stomach an achingly civilised, Emilia Romagna-influenced, candlelit trattoria where the cloakroom tags are actual Amalfi Coast pebbles engraved with numbers, it is Wandsworth Common, land of the hedge fund/interior design power couple who wouldn’t think twice about sipping a basil gimlet with a plate of melon with culatello di Zibello or gnocco fritto with mortadella. Bella Italia in Bolton this is not.
Rosina’s cocktail bar leans on art deco shapes, with a pale, marble-topped counter and walls covered in David Steen portraits. There’s a small second bar area for those bridging the gap between light dinner and semi-serious drinking, and a larger, linen-tableclothed area for the restaurant proper, with a back room for private dining. Rosina’s intimacy is an optical illusion: the place is as big as a tennis court, and the weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weep.
The day-to-day cooking is in the hands of Will Bee, previously of Michelin-starred Lita in Marylebone and Paul Ainsworth at No 6 in Padstow, and the menu is hearty, as well as littered with little in-jokes; like all the most promising neighbourhood joints, however, it would take at least five visits before they began to grate. Small plates of fried taleggio, melanzane fritte and smoked sardines on toast give way to a list of pleasingly substantial pastas ranging from caviar linguine at £30 to a staggeringly pocket-friendly cavatelli cacio e pepe at just £8. There is also what’s dubbed as “post-service pasta” (spaghetti with anchovy, chilli and garlic) at £16, which is the first time I’ve seen a restaurant give a glimpse into what its owner eats after hours. More of this, I say. I want cocktail lists that offer “post-service fernet branca plus howling into the abyss about business rates”. Let the light in on the magic.
Hugh, my companion, ordered bruschetta of rabbit livers braised in chianti, and ate them with Lecter-ish lust. Two plump sardines, coated in breadcrumbs and with their little tails sticking out of one end, resembled something out of a cartoon. Carpaccio of wild sea bass came flecked with chilli and amalfi lemon, and doused in the kind of olive oil you hide from house guests: clean, sharp, precise. It was at this point that something shifted for me, from “this is perfectly pleasant” to “holy god, this is really quite special”. The arrival of the ’nduja strozzapreti only confirmed that: hugely simple, but wonderfully layered, with a rich tomato sauce enveloping a nourishing bowl of priest-stranglers.
Risotto bianco, made with Riso Buono carnaroli rice and topped with a bold, sunshine-yellow egg yolk, was rich, but it’s meant to be: risotto bianco is for people who laugh in the face of blood sugar spikes. There is nowhere to hide in a white risotto – it is a sensory bombardment of unctuous gloop – and Rosina’s is wonderful. Although, if I want to squander calories willy-nilly on genuine death row delicacies, it is to their fried potatoes that I might turn instead: tiny baby spuds no bigger than fingernails, roasted, crushed and tossed in herbs and oil. Absolutely remarkable. A hugely generous plate of roast summer vegetables came charred from the grill and drizzled with syrupy grape must saba from Modena. We ate those with perfectly cooked roast turbot.
Around us, Wandsworth Common conducted its typical Saturday business. The tyranny of school fees. The agony of basement excavations. The management of several homes at once, with only one housekeeper directing all the other housekeepers internationally. The true trials of life. These people deserve a good dessert menu, and Rosina offers an embarrassment of teeth-chattering riches. Dreamy, yesteryear-sounding things: orange riccarelli, marzipan fruits, iced cherries and a sharp, classic amalfi lemon tart with blackcurrant leaf ice-cream, which I demolished. And a bowl of Pina’s tiramisu, too, of course, of which we entertained a rather large amount. My congratulations to Pina: hers is a very good recipe: wet, light and stodgy in all the right places.
If this rather sumptuous spot needs anything quite as crass as my feedback, Rosina is a surefire hit. If you’re south of the river and on the lookout for an oasis of calm and fanciness at a range of prices, somewhere you can talk and be heard, Rosina is the perfect woman.
- 
  Rosina 35 Bellevue Road, London SW17, 020-8672 5888. Open all week, lunch noon-2.30pm, dinner 5.30-10pm. From about £50 a head à la carte, plus drinks and service

Addressing the BRICS Outreach/BRICS+ session on Sunday, Putin said international interest in the group “continues to grow,” arguing that its commitment to an “independent and autonomous course” and international law appeals to countries around the world. He also said BRICS accounts for 49% of global GDP growth and that its potential for further development is “far from exhausted.”
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, speaking at the same session, said the trust of Global South nations in BRICS has grown because “their voices are heard, their experiences are respected and solutions are crafted not just for them, but with them.”
Modi also announced that members had reached a consensus on a BRICS Integrated Early Warning System for preventing and responding to infectious diseases, as well as guidelines for integrating early-warning data in disaster management.
The expanded session brings together the leaders of BRICS member and partner countries, as well as outreach invitees and representatives of international organizations, with discussions focused on resilience, innovation, cooperation and inclusive global growth. Further bilateral meetings are also possible on the sidelines.
On Saturday, BRICS leaders unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration, which calls for the reform of global institutions to give emerging markets and developing countries greater representation and condemns unilateral economic measures that violate international law. The document also calls for “maximum restraint” in the Middle East and stresses that dialogue and diplomacy are the only appropriate means of resolving international disputes.

Saudi oil delivery times to Asia could rise 2.5-fold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:49:37 UTC
13:49:37 KST

TOKYO, September 13. /TASS/. Voyage times for deliveries of Saudi oil to Asia would increase 2.5-fold to around 100 days round trip if the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is closed, according to data from the Japanese Shipowners' Association cited by the Asahi newspaper.
A voyage through the Strait of Hormuz, the traditional route for oil supplies from the Middle East to Asia, previously took 40 days round trip. A route through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which could serve as an alternative, takes roughly the same amount of time, between 40 and 50 days.
However, a route via the Suez Canal and the Cape of Good Hope, which would become necessary if the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is closed following the current blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, would take around 100 days round trip. This would inevitably lead to higher transportation costs, Asahi noted.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been blocked due to the US conflict with Iran, which has been ongoing since February 28.

OpenAI pushes IPO to 2027 amid fears of rogue AI, calls to slow down development, Altman confirms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:42:02 UTC
13:42:02 KST

OpenAI will not go public in 2026, Chief Executive Sam Altman said in remarks published on Saturday, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence that render "unacceptable" even a 10% risk that AI could cause human extinction by decade's end.
The comments come as more US lawmakers urge new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing AI could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.
"I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don't feel pressure on that," Altman told business magazine Fortune.
Asked if there was a 10% chance of AI-driven extinction, Altman said he didn't know how to make such an estimate, but warned the risk was serious enough that AI companies and governments should act as though it could not be tolerated.
"Whether it's 10 or eight or six, the point is, we all have a tremendous amount of responsibility, and cannot let egos or incentives for profit or anything else get in the way," Altman added.
"We need to act such that we are not taking any of those numbers of risk, and I believe we can."
Instances of AI agents going rogue
Politicians, both Democrat and Republican, have responded with alarm and calls for more action after cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies out of concern at the technology risks.
In June, the New York Times said San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off until next year on a potentially trillion-dollar IPO.
At the time, shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company's valuation to $1.8 trillion.
Asked by Fortune if an IPO date of 2026 was off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said, "I would say not 2026.
"We got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together."
Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI firms may be close to unveiling a pact to slow AI development and work together to tackle safety risks, Fortune said.
Call for deliberate approach
On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged AI companies to take a more deliberate approach to development.
"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote in an essay on X.
Altman later posted that he agreed with the sentiment.
"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," Altman wrote. "This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks."
Safety concerns have not slowed Anthropic's own IPO plans. It is expected to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at the earliest and complete the listing days before the US midterm elections in November, people familiar with the matter told Reuters this month.

Trump on Tucker Carlson: 'I dumped him a few months ago. He said some very bad things'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:41:59 UTC
13:41:59 KST

US President Donald Trump criticized conservative commentator Tucker Carlson in a Friday interview with Jewish radio host Sid Rosenberg, saying he ended their relationship several months ago because he felt Carlson’s comments had crossed a line.
The discussion came after Vice President JD Vance said that despite political disagreements with Carlson, he still considers him a friend and would not “throw him under the bus” over political differences.
Rosenberg asked the US president about the contrast between Vance’s approach and Trump’s own decision to distance himself from Carlson.
“You were friends with Tucker Carlson for many years, and a few months ago, maybe even a year ago, you decided you were done with him,” Rosenberg told Trump. “JD comes out and says: I’m not going to do that, the guy is a good friend of mine, we’re best friends, and I’m not going to let politics dictate who my friends are.”
Rosenberg warned that the issue could become a challenge for Vance if he seeks to succeed Trump and run for president in 2028.
Rosenberg warns Vance over Carlson ties ahead of 2028
“If he really wants to win in 2028, beyond the issue of Jews with Tucker Carlson, Tucker Carlson also called you ‘the Antichrist.’ So if I’m a Trump supporter and I’m Jewish, JD Vance needs to be careful. That’s my advice to him, Mr. President,” Rosenberg said.
Trump did not criticize Vance or say that his vice president was wrong to maintain his friendship with Carlson. Instead, he reflected on his own complicated relationship with the former Fox News host.
“You know, I’ve known Tucker Carlson for a long time, and my relationship with him was on and off for years, very on and off,” Trump said. “He’s very inconsistent. And maybe I am too, but I’m telling you, he’s very inconsistent.”
Trump also described Carlson as “a fair weather guy,” referring to someone who is supportive mainly when circumstances are favorable.
He then confirmed that he had decided to cut ties with Carlson.
“Of course, I dumped him a few months ago, because I just felt it wasn’t appropriate,” Trump said. “He said bad things, very bad things.”
Trump said his decision was not primarily related to comments Carlson made about him personally.
“Not so much about me, but about a lot of other things that are going on. And you understand that,” Trump said.
Trump says Carlson’s attacks on Levin crossed a line
Trump pointed to Carlson’s criticism of conservative Jewish radio host and commentator Mark Levin as one example of remarks he objected to.
“He would attack somebody like Mark Levin, who in my opinion is fantastic, by the way,” Trump said.
Rosenberg responded that he was very close with Levin. Trump continued: “And others. And I just, personally, didn’t like it.”
Trump later described his relationship with Carlson as one that had gone through repeated periods of tension.
“I would say Tucker Carlson never really liked me,” Trump said. “I did a lot for him, in a sense, but I would say he never really… in other words, you know, with people you have chemistry, right?”
Trump then turned to Rosenberg and added: “Like I have chemistry with you. With people you have chemistry. Sometimes you don’t. And if you don’t have it, there’s nothing the hell you can do about it. And Tucker and I had a very bumpy relationship.”
Trump avoids criticizing Vance over Carlson friendship
Trump’s remarks were notable because he did not say that Vance was wrong for continuing to describe Carlson as a friend, nor did he directly address Rosenberg’s concerns about how the relationship could affect Vance’s potential 2028 presidential campaign.
Instead, Trump focused his criticism on Carlson, describing him as inconsistent, a “fair weather guy,” and someone he decided to distance himself from after Carlson “said some very bad things.”
The exchange highlighted a difference between Trump and Vance’s views on political relationships. While Vance has argued that friendships should not be abandoned because of political disagreements, Trump said that, in his own relationship with Carlson, he decided months ago that it was over.

More than 2,000 Yemenis flee to Djibouti as fighting intensifies
Yemeni refugees arrive in Obock, Djibouti, within 24 hours as Houthis tighten their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
More than 2,000 people have fled from Yemen to Djibouti as fighting between the Houthis and government forces intensifies.
Renewed conflict in Yemen has displaced 85,818 people to date and 82,000 since the start of September, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Sunday.
Recommended Stories

Djibouti’s Economy and Finance Minister Ilyas M Dawaleh said on Saturday that 1,400 Yemenis had arrived in Djibouti in the last 24 hours. That number has now exceeded 2,000 people, according to Sunday’s IOM figures.
In a separate post on Friday, Dawaleh said that 500 refugees had arrived in the coastal city of Obock, including women and children, after they were rescued at sea when their boats ran out of fuel while crossing the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Obock, a city only about 20 kilometres (12 miles) across the water from the Yemeni coast, has for several years been a preferred arrival point for those seeking refuge from war-torn Yemen. The Bab al-Mandeb strait is also used in the opposite direction by migrants from the Horn of Africa, who transit through Yemen on their way to Gulf countries.
Safiya Ibrahim, humanitarian response coordinator for the IOM, told AFP that “vulnerable groups such as women and children have reached the shores of Obock, with more expected in the coming days”.
Djibouti hosts tens of thousands of refugees and asylum seekers. United Nations Refugee Agency figures from March 2026 show a registered population of more than 36,000, with the majority from Somalia, Ethiopia and Yemen.
The Houthis seized the Red Sea port city of Mocha on Thursday and have since overrun the coastline and islands surrounding the Bab al-Mandeb strait. The rapid offensive has forced thousands of families to flee, with entire villages reportedly emptied in districts such as Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi and al-Maafer.

'Second life': Nepal hydropower tunnel survivor recalls ordeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:17:14 UTC
13:17:14 KST

'Second life': Nepal hydropower tunnel survivor recalls ordeal
Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah survived in total darkness inside a tunnel flooded by the deadly flash flood that struck the China-Nepal border on August 26, drinking muddy water and praying that rescuers would find him. The survivor, who was rescued on September 4, recalls the 10 days he spent stranded.
For 10 days, Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah survived in darkness inside a flooded tunnel, drinking muddy water and losing all sense of time as he desperately prayed for rescue.
When a disaster response team finally pulled him to safety on September 4, Sah's first question showed how deeply the ordeal had disoriented him.
"When I was rescued I first asked, how many days has it been?" Sah, 30, told AFP in an interview, while on his way back home in Saptari district Sunday.
"He said that it has been 10 days. I thought it had been just a few days."
Sah was among hundreds of workers at a series of hydropower projects hit by the catastrophic August 26 flood, triggered by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border.
Sah's extraordinary survival was a rare ray of hope after a disaster that killed at least 1,429 people and left more than 5,640 missing, the majority in Nepal.
Family, friends and neighbours celebrated Sah's return with garlands and a cake, and his home was adorned with balloons and colours.
His mother, Kapur Devi Sah, embraced him tightly as she cried, and later washed his feet for an auspicious welcome.
"My son has returned, I am very happy," she said.
Struggling to hold back tears, Sah recalled how the disaster had struck with stunning speed.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
"I was on duty, and then suddenly an unthinkable flood hit us, with tsunami-like waves that were several metres tall," he said.
Workers had received warnings that floodwaters were approaching, but did not get enough time to escape, he said.
"We did get information to stay alert, that a big flood is coming. As much as possible, we tried to be alert and evacuate our friends," Sah said.
"But the water did not give us much time ... we shut down everything, and tried to rescue and evacuate our friends."
Within minutes, however, the tunnel was engulfed by raging waters.
The sheer scale of the flood was unlike anything witnesses had seen before, with the government pointing the finger at the dire impact of rising global temperatures on Nepal's Himalayan mountains.
'Divine energy'
Separated from his colleagues, Sah found himself stranded with little idea whether anyone would ever reach him.
His Hindu faith helped carry him through the days of darkness and isolation.
"I survived because of my deep belief and confidence," he said.
"I was chanting Maha Mantra (Hindu prayers), and the divine energy I received because of that allowed me to not be scared or despair," he said.
"I was able to stay there."
With no clean water to drink, he survived on whatever he could find.
"There was water, but it was muddy," he said. "I only had that."
The darkness and isolation might have been overwhelming, but Sah was not entirely alone.
Another trapped worker, Kabir Maharjan, 45, had survived nearby.
"We were separated but speaking to each other."
The ability to hear another human voice offered a lifeline to Sah.
Eventually, after days of excavation and painstaking rescue efforts, search teams broke through to the trapped men and brought them out alive.
Sah's wife, Lakshmi Kumari Sah, said she never gave up hope of seeing her husband again.
"God has helped us, we had our hopes," she said, holding her daughter in her arms.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Sah, who spent several days recuperating in a Kathmandu hospital, says he has mixed emotions.
"I am happy, but I feel sad too," he said. "I was able to get a second life, to survive there. But many of our friends were there."
As rescuers continue searching through the tunnels, Sah urged authorities not to abandon the effort.
One Chinese worker was rescued on September 5, the day after Sah – but no signs of life have been heard since.
"I hope the government continues its search and rescue. It is possible there might still be someone alive," he said.
"Or they will be able to find bodies of friends who have passed away and hand them over to their families."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Drones attack oil refineries in Russia's Tatarstan – photo, videos
Drones attacked the industrial zone of Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Republic of Tatarstan on the night of 12-13 September, where major Russian oil refineries are located.
Source: monitoring Telegram channels; Russian media outlet ASTRA
Details: Local residents reported hearing drones flying over the city overnight, followed by a series of explosions.
Witnesses also reported that Russian air defence systems were active near an industrial area.
Local authorities have not yet reported the extent of possible damage to processing facilities or any casualties.
Nizhnekamsk is home to one of the Russian Federation's largest oil-refining hubs. The attack targeted facilities that play a key role in financing the war and supplying the Russian military with fuel.
In particular, the TANECO oil-refining and petrochemical complex is among the five largest oil refineries in Russia, with a designed crude oil processing capacity of more than 16 million tonnes per year. The refinery is one of Russia's main producers of diesel fuel, aviation gas for fighter jets and petrol for cars.
Another major oil refinery, TAIF-NK, is located nearby. The plant can process more than seven million tonnes of oil and gas condensate annually. TAIF-NK specialises in the production of petrol, diesel and other petroleum products. Its products are actively supplied both to the domestic Russian market and for the needs of the Russian forces.
Another facility in the Nizhnekamsk industrial zone is Nizhnekamskneftekhim, part of the Sibur petrochemical holding company and one of Europe's largest petrochemical plants. The plant is effectively a monopoly in Russia for the production of many types of synthetic rubber and plastics.
Background:
- Nizhnekamsk is located more than 1,200 km from Ukraine's state border.
- This is not the first attack on strategic oil-refining facilities in the region. In August 2026, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported a successful strike on the TANECO oil refinery.
- In addition, in early July, a Ukrainian strike drone captured on surveillance cameras fell on the neighbouring TAIF-NK plant in the Nizhnekamsk industrial zone.
- On 10 August, drones attacked Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Tatarstan, where an oil refinery is located.

BRICS leaders reject forced displacement in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:09:45 UTC
13:09:45 KST

AA Photo
BRICS leaders on Sept. 12 called for greater efforts to prevent and peacefully resolve conflicts amid the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
 The leaders opposed any forced displacement of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip.
 These calls were part of the New Delhi Declaration, unanimously adopted on the first day of the bloc's two-day summit in the Indian capital.
 Expressing deep concern over continued violence in Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, the leaders demanded an end to any policies aimed at forced displacement.
 The declaration also expressed concern regarding arrangements prejudicing the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people and legitimizing or prolonging occupation.
 A just and lasting solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict can only be achieved by peaceful means and depends on fulfilling the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, including self-determination and return, the declaration read.
 The bloc rejected unilateral measures seeking to alter the legal and historical status of occupied Jerusalem.
 The declaration urged full respect for the sanctity of all religious sites in the city and for the rights of all to access and observe their religious rites without hindrance.
 The bloc also condemned attacks on the U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) installations and personnel.
 Such attacks are a violation of international law, the declaration emphasized.
 Noting a current global context of polarization and distrust, BRICS members urged the international community to respond to security threats through politico-diplomatic measures to lower conflict potential.
 The bloc stressed the need to engage in conflict prevention efforts by addressing their root causes.
 The declaration encouraged the active role of regional organizations in conflict prevention and resolution.
 It supported all efforts conducive to the peaceful settlement of crises.
 BRICS leaders expressed concern over the growing risks of nuclear conflict and called for disarmament, arms control and nonproliferation.
 The declaration voiced serious concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities.
 Nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm, the bloc said.
 The leaders noted the multilateral trading system has long been at a crossroads.
 The statement highlighted the proliferation of trade-restrictive actions inconsistent with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules.
 The bloc voiced serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures distorting trade.
 BRICS condemned the imposition of unilateral coercive measures contrary to international law.
 Such measures, including unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, have far-reaching negative implications for human rights, the bloc reiterated.

BRICS summit: Members, partner countries discuss ‘resilience, innovation, cooperation’ on day 2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:02:36 UTC
13:02:36 KST

Saadet Gokce
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Leaders of the BRICS grouping and its partner nations met Sunday on the final day of the two-day 18th BRICS Leaders’ Summit in India’s capital, New Delhi.
 
The leaders attended an open session titled “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.”
 
The expanded grouping of 11 countries includes longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa – the origin of the BRICS name – plus more recent additions Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
 
The group has also welcomed partner countries into the framework, including Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam.
 
Among those attending the weekend summit are Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, besides host Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and other leaders representing the expanded group.
 
Other attendees include leaders and top officials from Kazakhstan, Vietnam, Malaysia, Uzbekistan, Thailand, Cuba, Belarus, Nigeria, and Uganda, among others.
 
On Saturday, the bloc unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration, which recognized the “valuable contribution” of partner countries to BRICS cooperation, according to a joint statement.
 
It emphasized its “strong belief” that advancing the BRICS partnership with Emerging Markets and Developing Countries (EMDCs) would “further contribute to strengthening the spirit of solidarity and international cooperation for the benefit of all.”
 
The declaration also reaffirmed the bloc’s commitment to “fostering inclusive, mutually beneficial and development-oriented partnership with Partner countries.”
 
“We encourage their increasing participation in BRICS engagements and practical cooperation in areas of shared interest,” it added.
 
The group now represents about 49.5% of the world’s population, 40% of global GDP, and 26% of global trade, according to figures cited by BRICS.
 
The last summit was held in Rio de Janeiro in 2025, and the next is scheduled to be held in China.

Making Iraq ‘normal’ again: do mass arrests and cash seizures signal end to corruption?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
04:00:52 UTC
13:00:52 KST

The gates of the Green Zone in Baghdad are made of five-metre-high armoured steel, reinforced with horizontal girders, and strung between concrete pillars and anti-blast walls. Police water cannon trucks are stationed nearby, along with armoured personnel carriers and squads of heavily armed soldiers.
At the first sign of street protests – over failing electricity, unemployment or, more recently, the US-Israeli attacks on Iran – the gates are shut. X-shaped vehicle barriers, made from welded iron beams and mounted on wheels, sit ready at the roadside alongside coils of razor wire; both are slid across the street, sealing off the sprawling neighbourhood, home to the presidential palace, parliament, the prime minister’s office, the massive fortress-like US embassy, and other institutions, including the homes of scores of politicians and members of parliament.
When the gates are closed, traffic is diverted, creating monumental jams lasting for hours for most Baghdadis who lack the coveted Green Zone badges.
In the early hours of 28 June, the gates were shut, US-made Abrams tanks prowled through the streets, and black-clad counter-terrorism units fanned out across the area. Only this time, the measures were meant to prevent those inside from leaving, rather than to keep those outside from getting in.
By dawn, Iraqis woke to the news that nearly 50 people, including a dozen MPs and senior officials, had been detained, along with the seizure of hundreds of millions of dollars in cash and gold. Pictures and videos, purporting to show masked officers hauling out safes full of money, piles of jewellery and suitcases filled with dollars, circulated widely.
The arrests were met with the greatest Iraqi schadenfreude since the beginning of time. For if Iraqis – of all persuasions, sects, ethnicities and social backgrounds – agree on one thing, it is the rottenness and corruption of the political parties that have held power since 2003, and the greed of a clique of party bosses, businessmen and militia leaders.
‘Not just something every PM does’
On the day of his inauguration as Iraq’s new prime minister in early May, Ali al-Zaidi, a 41-year-old with a round face, thin beard and sharp eyes, delivered, in stilted language riddled with grammatical mistakes, the standard repertoire of promises made by every prime minister before him, Iraq’s own version of making the country great again: supporting local industry, agriculture and youth; fixing the electricity supply and solving the housing crisis. But the two issues the wealthy businessman with little political experience emphasised as most urgent were disarming the pro-Iranian factions and fighting corruption “with no red lines”.
With Iraq’s coffers nearly empty after the near-total halt of its oil exports since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, these two issues – militias and corruption – are interlinked and, in the shadow of war, are threatening the state itself.
But the prime minister before him, and the one before that, had both begun their tenures with similar gestures – declaring the exposure of vast corruption networks – and both had ended their time in office mired in corruption charges of their own, while the country’s public services remained in ruins. So why should this time be different?
“No, this isn’t just something every prime minister does,” a government insider told the Guardian. “No, this is unprecedented – a real earthquake inside political circles, because it’s a signal to all the politicians about what could happen to them. To everyone, without exception.”
What we are seeing, he said, is a prime minister trying to dismantle the financial empires of the political parties – empires built on corruption that is naked and clear for all to see, and that implicates every single politician without exception. “So when you pick four or five of them and strike,” he said, “you are sending a message to everyone: what happened to those people can happen to all of you, if you don’t do such and such.”
Division of the spoils
Al-Zaidi came to power as a compromise candidate after months of negotiations among the Coordination Framework, the bloc of major Shia parties and figures in parliament, and after the Trump administration vetoed the leading candidates.
The negotiations – really a haggling over the division of spoils – are a well-rehearsed exercise, repeated after every election for the past two decades, under a system known as muhasasa, which has become the cornerstone of Iraqi politics, devised by Iraqi opposition parties in exile in the 1990s as a power-sharing arrangement that would prevent Iraq from again sliding into a dictatorship. The arrangement was imported wholesale after the 2003 US invasion by those same parties and the Americans; under muhasasa, the prime minister is a Shia, the president a Kurd. But muhasasa also came to mean the division of government posts among all the political factions: Sunni, Shia, Kurdish and others.
Party bosses and militia commanders feud, threaten and cajole, some claiming to represent the historical rights of their community, others decrying the historical injustices imposed on theirs, all in an attempt to increase their share of the lucrative ministries and state institutions, turning them into party fiefdoms, running every possible scheme to defraud the treasury.
“The parties have built states within the state,” an international banker, who was hired by a previous government to help clean up the system, said. “We probably have seven or eight of these mini-states, siphoning between 5% and 10% of every government contract.”
The stooge?
In the muhasasa power-sharing system, if the minister of oil is Shia, at least one of his deputies – and it is always “his” – will be Sunni.
Here a second round of haggling and horse-trading begins within the Sunni blocs and parties over the lucrative post. It usually comes down to a kind of exchange rate – how many directors of education, health and culture is one deputy oil minister worth?
Once a party has won the post, the contest shifts to finding the right candidate. Sometimes the parties bring in someone from within their own ranks, ideologically committed to them, or a relative of the party boss. But in most cases, they choose someone from the bureaucracy instead – someone familiar with the running of the state, versed in the rules and regulations of an archaic and dysfunctional system: mandarins who have succeeded in weaponising these often-conflicting regulations accumulated over more than a century, from the Ottomans, to the British who imported a system for the Indian Raj, to the military dictators who added a socialist flavour, and finally the young American zealots who arrived in Baghdad after the 2003 war that toppled Saddam Hussein and wanted to create a neoliberal free market state, without any knowledge of Iraq or its history.
The regulations are deployed at every level to obstruct every state function – from the issuing of an ID card to the signing of a multibillion-dollar contract – until a bribe is paid to ensure the task’s smooth completion.
In January 2025, Adnan al-Jumaili – a young engineer with a pleasant, smiling, square face, lean, with a trim moustache and thick, prematurely greying hair – was appointed deputy oil minister responsible for refineries.
His fast rise through the ranks, first as director of a single refinery, then as director of the state institution overseeing the northern refineries, responsible for several plants, was celebrated in some pro-government local press as the placement of a young, honourable and efficient talent at the helm, one who would end years of mismanagement and setbacks.
He appears in several videos alongside the then prime minister, Mohammed Shia al-Sudani, who had been chosen by the same Shia parties to lead a government focused on delivering essential services.In video after video, al-Sudani is shown with his chest puffed out, wearing black sunglasses, cutting ribbons to inaugurate projects and showcase his government’s achievements, while beside him, a smiling al-Jumaili, in a hi-vis vest and helmet, briefs him on the details. In one clip, he even receives an “honourable employee” award from al-Sudani.
But soon after al-Sudani lost his bid for a second term and al-Zaidi became prime minister, it all came crashing down.
Al-Jumaili was the first to be arrested, on 30 May, and arraigned on television in a yellow jumpsuit, surrounded by dozens of machine guns and boxes of ammunition found at his home. Investigators said they had also recovered $10m (£7.4m) in cash, 3bn dinars (about $2m) and 1.5kg of gold, along with around 40 properties across Baghdad and other provinces. In the weeks that followed, more wealth surfaced: cash stuffed into plastic water bottles, hidden down a rainwater drain, concealed in walls – and, allegedly, 7bn Iraqi dinars that his wife was caught trying to burn in an outdoor oven. By mid-July, the total seized in the case had reached 127bn dinars ($96m) and $24m in cash, plus properties, vehicles and 375kg of gold, and 70 properties as well as a number of cars.
What shocked many Iraqis was the sheer vulgarity of it all – the way the money, the product of elaborate schemes devised to siphon millions, only for it to end up buried underground or stashed in boxes and large, family-size plastic pickle jars.
According to the judicial investigation, al-Jumaili ran a scheme that had yielded hundreds of millions of dollars.
In a meeting with Iraqi journalists the next day, al-Zaidi said that al-Jumaili had tried to bribe him before his arrest with $200m to keep his post – in some reports, the total offer was said to reach $600m.
Whether al-Jumaili was the mastermind of all the corruption, or whether it had been laid out for him in advance, is unknown. But from the moment he arrived at the ministry of oil, he began amassing huge commissions from contracts and awards handed to companies and contractors and from diverted shipments of fuel.
As last year’s elections neared, he became a conduit for delivering millions of dollars to candidates, many on the prime minister’s list, though not all.
One politician told the Guardian: “Many parties came in and benefited from working with al-Jumaili, and he regarded all of this as protection for himself.” As his connections to political parties expanded – not only to the Sunni bloc that had nominated him, but allegedly to his bosses at the ministry of oil and in the prime minister’s office – he came to believe he was untouchable. And as his political cover grew, he began to commit catastrophic mistakes, the politician said. “Because, you see, he was telling himself he was now beyond reach – that it was impossible for anyone to touch him.
“So he began making mistakes, overreaching – faking warehouse deliveries, for example, and diverting fuel to create phantom storage stock that didn’t exist. We started hearing about thousands of phantom day-labourers, whose wages were being paid out even though they didn’t exist in the first place. We heard about transport contracts inside the refineries worth millions of dollars – contracts at astronomical figures.”
“The Adnan al-Jumaili affair is, I think, a model of the way things are run, the way the process of placing people in particular positions works,” the government insider said. “These positions are responsible for generating large revenues, illegally, for a party or for several parties. It’s like bitcoin mining, you see, they generate money.”
Investigations into al-Jumaili’s financial dealings had begun the previous October, when the judiciary began looking into spending irregularities in the elections and discovered that he had funnelled money to numerous candidates. This eventually led to his arrest and, after his confessions, to the mass arrests on 28 June.
‘That chapter must close’
The investigations and arrests coincided with two things: severe pressure on Iraqi finances brought on by the war, and a more active role by the US in shaping Iraqi politics.
According to government insiders, members of parliament and a source close to the judiciary, the Americans – weary of dealing with Iraqi politicians continuously failing to achieve any reforms – had built a rapport instead with the Iraqi judiciary. The new American envoy, Tom Barrack, played an active role, encouraged by the judiciary’s increasingly assertive statements on the state’s monopoly of weapons.
For many months, investigators searched for a corruption case that could be exposed publicly. The challenge was finding one that, when exposed, would make headlines domestically and internationally, while guaranteeing that the fallout would not bring down the entire post-2003 political system. Al-Jumaili’s case was perfect: it implicated a number of prominent politicians, but stopped short of naming the big party bosses.
As one official put it: “You don’t know, in the end, if you keep pressing on these parties – what might the armed factions do? What might Iran do?” The case also touched a nerve sensitive to the Americans specifically: the smuggling of Iraqi oil.
“The government and judiciary are aiming to achieve two goals,” the government insider said. “The first is to recover as much as possible of the money that the parties and political leaders have siphoned over the years.” (In several statements, the prime minister has hinted that if the money is returned, there will be no further legal repercussions.) “The second is to sever, in all its forms and details, the relationship between the parties and the state – meaning the relationship between the economic offices of these parties and every corner of the state apparatus. In other words: the parties will no longer be able to extract anything from the state.
“The idea that the parties live off quotas they receive from the state – through projects, commissions and so forth – must come to an end. That chapter must close. And I believe this is the most important thing that could happen in Iraq’s modern history.”
It seems that bringing in al-Zaidi, or at least the support he is getting from the US and the judiciary, was calculated precisely for this moment, he and other officials said. Someone with sufficient experience and knowledge of the mechanisms involved in routing money out of the state, who knows how money is smuggled, channelled and extracted through contracts, projects, commissions and so forth.
Will this latest drive to fight corruption deliver any serious results? Or will it turn out to be, at best, another cosmetic operation – if not a case of political score-settling? And how can Iraq become a normal state, capable of reform, while it sits on a regional faultline, caught amid a multi-pronged war fought across its land and skies – and can that reform ever be achieved without accountability for the party bosses and the mini-states they’ve built?
“There are no guarantees that corruption will end, and that parties will stop looting the state,” the government insiders said. “But what we’re hearing is that there really is a governmental and judicial desire to end a certain phase and begin a new one – a situation where things are normal, where basic services are available, where this constant crisis over fuel, electricity, water and every other detail comes to an end. Where the situation becomes normal, meaning: our state becomes like any other state in the world, with its successes and its failures.”

Russian region offers record $18,000 reward for recruiting foreigners to fight in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
03:58:00 UTC
12:58:00 KST

Russian region offers record $18,000 reward for recruiting foreigners to fight in Ukraine
Siberia’s Irkutsk Oblast has raised payments to people who recruit foreign nationals into the Russian military to 1.5 million rubles ($17,800) per recruit, the highest such reward offered by a Russian region, independent outlet Vyorstka reported on Sept. 11.
Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev signed the decree earlier this week, establishing the 1.5 million-ruble payment for anyone who helps a foreign citizen or stateless person sign a contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The region has offered payments for recruiting contract soldiers since at least April. Recruiters could previously receive up to 400,000 rubles ($4,700), meaning the maximum payment for bringing in a foreign national has risen almost fourfold in seven months, according to Vyorstka.
The new decree also creates a separate category for foreign nationals and stateless people for the first time. Payments for recruiting Russian citizens registered outside Irkutsk Oblast were doubled from 400,000 to 800,000 rubles ($9,500).
Other Russian regions have also increased incentives as Moscow seeks additional manpower for its war against Ukraine. Smolensk Oblast raised its recruiter payment from 115,000 rubles ($1,300) to 1 million rubles ($11,900), while Ryazan Oblast increased some recruitment payments to 805,000 rubles ($9,500).
The increase comes amid mounting evidence that Russia has relied on foreigners, particularly people from lower-income countries, to replenish its forces.
Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said in April that at least 28,391 foreign nationals from 136 countries had been identified as fighting in the Russian military, not including regular North Korean troops. Amnesty International cited the figures in a report published on Sept. 10 but said it could not independently verify them.
Amnesty said Russia’s recruitment of foreign nationals has frequently involved “deceptive, coercive and exploitative practices,” including false promises of civilian jobs, high salaries, residency rights, or Russian citizenship.
The rights group documented cases in which recruits said they signed contracts they did not understand, had their passports confiscated, received little military training, had their movements restricted, and were threatened when they attempted to leave.
Amnesty concluded that in many cases, Russia’s recruitment practices amount to human trafficking.

Fewer people in Türkiye believe in ‘extraordinary power’ of Russian army – writer
Ukrainian writer Olena Lytvynenko, author of The Viburnum Flavor of Turkish Tea, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Many people have already realized that the perception of the ‘extraordinary power of the Russian army’ does not correspond to reality. At the same time, some Turks still believe that Russia has not yet begun to use its military potential to its full extent,” Lytvynenko said.

However, she noted that decades of Soviet and later Russian propaganda, including the notions of Russia’s “strength and greatness” that it helped shape, continue to influence the views of part of Turkish society.
Olena Lytvynenko came to Türkiye to study in 2013 and later worked as a diplomat at the Embassy of Ukraine in Ankara. Her first book, The Viburnum Flavor of Turkish Tea, was recently published.

Canada turning to Europe as trade tensions with US escalate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
03:33:03 UTC
12:33:03 KST

Esra Tekin
13 September 2026•Update: 13 September 2026
Canada is accelerating efforts to deepen economic and strategic ties with Europe as its relationship with the US faces its worst trade tensions in decades, according to a Sunday report by the Wall Street Journal.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has held talks with European leaders, including those in France, Germany, and Italy, exploring ways to bring Canada closer to the EU without pursuing full EU membership, it said.
Canadian officials are examining the possibility of an “associate membership” arrangement that could provide closer access to the EU’s $21 trillion single market, particularly in strategic sectors such as energy, AI, critical minerals, and defense.
Two developments – US President Donald Trump’s efforts to gain control of Greenland and his war with Iran – have strengthened the case for some European leaders for closer ties with Canada. Carney has expanded his outreach to leaders who are traditionally closer to Trump, including Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni, while maintaining frequent contacts with French President Emmanuel Macron and Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
By the summer, Canadian and European officials had stepped up discussions through multiple diplomatic channels. During preliminary G7 meetings in France, they identified 11 areas for deeper cooperation aimed at reducing dependence on US technology, defense equipment, and trade.
- Surprised by speed and scales of proposals
Carney’s meeting with Macron in Paris ahead of the G7 summit in Evian this June reportedly surprised French officials with the speed and scale of Canada’s proposals. At the same time, Carney was in frequent contact with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as the two countries finalized negotiations on Canada’s planned $25 billion purchase of German submarines.
The discussions could also include easier movement of workers, expanded research and university exchanges, as well as cooperation on data centers, undersea cables, cloud infrastructure, and satellite networks.
Carney is also seeking to strengthen Canada’s energy links with Europe, including infrastructure that could allow Canadian natural gas to reach European markets and reduce reliance on Russian energy.
The initiative reflects Ottawa’s attempt to reduce its heavy economic dependence on the US. Canada sends two-thirds of its exports across the border, making diversification a major challenge.
Carney, who previously served as governor of the Bank of England, is betting that closer European ties can help Ottawa withstand pressure from Washington while reshaping its long-standing economic orientation toward the US.
European governments, however, have approached the proposal cautiously, with some concerned that a dramatic shift in Canada-EU relations could further strain ties with Washington.
