How to watch Sweden’s election like a pro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Magdalena Andersson and Ulf Kristersson are seen ahead of Swedish state television's final debate in Gävle, Sweden on Sept. 11, 2026. | Anders Wiklund/AFP via Getty Images
STOCKHOLM — Millions of Swedes will vote in a tense general election on Sunday that is set to deliver a new left-wing government or bring far-right ministers into power for the first time.
The Social Democrat-led left bloc enjoyed a comfortable lead for months but polls tightened significantly in the final two weeks of the campaign, with one 11th-hour survey suggesting a dead heat.
“Two or three weeks ago, we were saying this is a done deal,” said Gustav Karreskog Rehbinder, who is running results forecasts for Sweden’s public broadcaster SVT on election night. “Now it seems that it will be a more exciting night than expected.”
Advertisement
The vote will have potentially significant consequences for security in Europe and the wider debate over integrating the far right into mainstream politics. Here is POLITICO’s guide to the contest, the candidates and the countdown to declaring a winner.
How does the election work?
There are 349 seats in the Riksdag, Sweden’s parliament, which is located in an imposing waterside building on an island in central Stockholm.
The country chooses its lawmakers every four years using a proportional representation voting system, meaning that if a party gets about 20% of the votes across Sweden, it will have about 20% of the seats in the Riksdag. Coalitions are the norm.
But there’s a catch: Very small parties are eliminated and get no seats at all if they do not meet the minimum threshold for support of 4% of the national vote. This could be a vital element in a closely fought contest, when the smaller parties may hold the balance of power.
Nearly 8 million people are registered to vote and turnout tends to be high — more than 80%. This year, a record number of people are expected to have cast their ballots early, which they’ve been able to do since Aug. 26. If they change their minds, these early voters can vote again on Sunday, canceling their original choices. Regional and local elections take place at the same time.
Who gets to govern?
After the last contest in 2022, eight parties were elected to parliament and they have been fighting this summer’s campaign in two blocs — one on the left and one on the right.
Advertisement
That means there are only two realistic candidates to be prime minister: the incumbent, conservative Moderate party leader Ulf Kristersson; and Magdalena Andersson, the former PM who leads Sweden’s biggest party, the center-left Social Democrats.
Kristersson speaks to the media in Stockholm on Sept. 10, 2026 ahead of the country’s general election. | Jonathan Nackstrand/ AFP via Getty Images
Kristersson has run the right-wing coalition for the past four years thanks to influential support from the second biggest party, the far-right Sweden Democrats. They backed him in votes in parliament and drove policy in a hardline direction, including crackdowns on crime and especially immigration. But the Sweden Democrats did not join the coalition cabinet. That could now change.
Can the far right enter the government?
Kristersson divided opinion in 2022 when he broke a decades-long taboo against working with the far right and did his deal with the Sweden Democrats, who had won 20% of the vote. The SD was founded in the 1980s and some members in those days had roots in neo-Nazi movements. The party has taken steps to clean up its act in recent years, though not to everyone’s satisfaction.
Now Kristersson says he will give the SD ministerial seats in government if his side wins on Sunday, as part of an agreement with the far-right leader, Jimmie Åkesson. That would be another huge step for Sweden and one that the opposition has seized on.
“Of course this would be a different country with a government with half of the ministers from the Sweden Democrats,” opposition leader Andersson told AP recently. “It would not be good for Sweden if they would get the keys to the ministry of defense or the ministry of foreign affairs.”
Kristersson insists he would still be in charge overall. He points to his work with Åkesson over the past four years which he says has revived the economy and cut rates of violent crime and immigration, both of which had been major public concerns. “I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government,” he told POLITICO.
Advertisement
For his part, Åkesson says it’s time for the SD to take the next step and assume the responsibility of governing. He is eyeing up the chance of becoming prime minister himself at the next vote, due in 2030. The SD sums up its vision for the country with the phrase: “Sweden should be safe, free and Swedish.”
What is at stake for Sweden and Europe?
Apart from the question of far-right power — which is a political preoccupation across the continent, especially after recent state elections in Germany — both the left and right leaders have traded blows on the question of security, and who will be strongest in standing up to Russia.
In a POLITICO interview Andersson demanded that Kristersson come clean after it was claimed that an SD official allegedly promoted pro-Russia narratives and linked up with a Russian state group inside Sweden. For his part, Kristersson in his own POLITICO interview questioned the left bloc’s commitment to NATO, which Sweden has only been a member of for two years.
Tim Ross/POLITICO
One thing unites both candidates for prime minister: continuing Sweden’s support for Ukraine. In its long history, Sweden has been at war with Russia multiple times and the threat Moscow poses is seared into the national consciousness.
Otherwise, the campaign focused on consumer politics — helping ease the cost of living and improve Sweden’s famous welfare state. The two sides made competing promises of a better deal on taxes, housing, health and dental care costs, as well as warnings over the impact of their rivals’ migration policies.
When will we know who has won?
Swedish broadcasters will release exit poll findings when the voting ends at 8 p.m. local time on Sunday.
Advertisement
Karreskog Rehbinder said he hoped to be able to give an early indication on SVT of how the election will unfold once 10% of the votes have been counted, which he expects to be around 9.15 p.m.
If the final tally is extremely close and it’s not clear which side is ahead in the first hours after the voting ends, he said it would likely not be clear until all the counting has finished — which isn’t expected until Wednesday 16 Sept. or later.
The Swedish Election Authority usually publishes “an initial provisional allocation of seats” in the Riksdag at around 10.30 p.m. on election night, if enough voting districts have reported their results by then.
But even once the final results are known, it will take weeks or perhaps even longer before a new coalition is formed. And if the parliament cannot ultimately agree on a new prime minister, a fresh election could be called.
Parties on the right are largely settled in their so-called Tidö alliance — named after the castle where their agreement was signed in 2022. But there have been deeper splits between some of the smaller parties in Andersson’s left bloc, which could prove a challenge to her attempt to stitch together a majority government.
“If you look at the prediction markets and polling aggregations, they say exactly the same thing — there’s about a 70% probability of a left-wing win, which is of course much narrower than it was three weeks ago,” said Karreskog Rehbinder, who is the founder and CEO of political tech startup Vera Policy. “That would still be my best guess but it is far from sure.”

Why Spain’s new Sahrawi citizenship law matters to Morocco
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
01:41:10 UTC
10:41:10 KST

Why Spain’s new Sahrawi citizenship law matters to Morocco
The new citizenship bill for Sahrawis touches a sensitive fault line in Madrid’s ties with Rabat.
Spain’s Congress has approved a bill that would open a special route to Spanish citizenship for Sahrawis born in Western Sahara while the disputed territory was under Spanish occupation.
The bill passed by 168 votes to 31, with 145 abstentions. It must still go through the Senate before it can become law.
So what exactly would the measure do, and why is Morocco watching it closely?
What does the bill do?
The proposed law would allow people born in Western Sahara before September 29, 1977, to apply for Spanish nationality through a special procedure without having to meet the normal residency requirements. First-degree descendants would also be covered.
It would also shorten the duration of the residence requirement for eligible Sahrawis legally living in Spain. Instead of the usual 10 years, they would be able to apply after two years.
Supporters describe the measure as a way of addressing what they see as a historical injustice.
Spain was the colonial power in Western Sahara until it ended its administration of the territory in 1976. The territory has remained disputed ever since, with Morocco considering it part of its sovereignty, while the separatist Polisario Front seeks independence.
Why does Morocco care?
The law would not change the territorial status of Western Sahara. It would not recognise an independent Sahrawi state, nor would Spanish citizenship give its holders sovereignty over the territory.
The concern in Rabat is instead about the relationship the law could create between Spain and people with direct links to Western Sahara.
Reuters has reported that between 70,000 and 110,000 people could eventually qualify, although estimates vary. Anyone who obtains Spanish nationality would also become a European Union citizen and acquire the rights that come with that status.
Potential beneficiaries could include eligible Sahrawis living in Western Sahara as well as members of the Sahrawi refugee population around Tindouf in Algeria, where the Polisario Front is based.
For Morocco, that could mean a larger community of Spanish and EU citizens with personal or family ties to an issue at the centre of its relationship with Madrid.
Why is the timing important?
The bill comes after a significant change in Spain’s policy towards Western Sahara.
In 2022, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government backed Morocco’s autonomy proposal for the territory, describing it as the most serious, realistic and credible basis for resolving the dispute.
That decision helped repair relations between Madrid and Rabat after a major diplomatic crisis. Since then, the two countries have strengthened cooperation on migration, security, trade and other areas.
The new citizenship measure does not formally change Spain’s support for the autonomy proposal. Madrid can argue that supporting autonomy as a political solution is one matter, while dealing with the consequences of its former colonial rule is another.
But the two issues are difficult to separate completely from Morocco’s perspective because both concern Western Sahara.
What is the debate inside Spain?
The bill has also divided Spain’s political parties.
The governing Socialist Party and its allies in Sumar supported it. The conservative People’s Party abstained, while Vox voted against it.
The disagreement has centred partly on how Spain should address the legacy of its former rule in Western Sahara and on the legal route proposed for granting nationality.
The debate is important to the Moroccan side because it shows that the measure is not simply a technical change to Spanish nationality law. It has also become part of a discussion inside Spain about its colonial past and its relationship with Western Sahara.
Moroccan and international media have also focused on the measure. While Moroccan media have highlighted its potential implications for Spain’s policy towards Western Sahara and its relations with Rabat, Reuters has reported that the move could further strain relations between Spain and Morocco.
Does the bill recognise the Polisario?
No. The proposed nationality route does not recognise the Polisario Front or an independent Sahrawi state.
Nor does acquiring Spanish citizenship indicate support for the Polisario. Nationality is a legal status, and Sahrawis hold different political positions.
The connection to the Polisario is nevertheless relevant because many Sahrawi refugees live around Tindouf, where the Polisario has its headquarters and administers the refugee camps.
If eligible people from those communities acquire Spanish nationality, they would become Spanish and EU citizens while retaining their existing personal and political identities.
Why is Spain referring to its colonial past?
Spain was the colonial power in Western Sahara until it ended its administration of the territory in 1976.
Supporters of the bill argue that people born in the territory during Spanish rule were left in a difficult legal position after Spain withdrew. They therefore present the measure as a way of addressing what they consider a historical wrong.
Spain has used historical ties in nationality policy before.
In 2015, it introduced a procedure allowing Sephardic Jews who could establish their Sephardic origin and a special connection with Spain to apply for Spanish nationality. The measure was linked to the expulsion of Jews from Spain beginning in 1492.
That precedent is relevant to the Moroccan debate because Spain has previously used historical ties to establish a special route to nationality.
And what about Ceuta and Melilla?
This is where the issue becomes particularly sensitive for Morocco.
Morocco considers Ceuta and Melilla an integral part of its territory and sovereignty. The two cities are located on Morocco’s northern coast in North Africa and are under Spanish administration.
Spain rejects Morocco’s claim and considers the cities Spanish territory. Successive Spanish governments have maintained that their sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla is not negotiable.
The Moroccan argument here could be about how historical ties are treated.
If Spain can draw on its historical and colonial relationship with Western Sahara to create a special nationality route for Sahrawis, and has previously used historical ties with Sephardic Jews, whose connection to Spain dates back more than five centuries, Morocco could ask why its own historical and geographical relationship with Ceuta and Melilla should be considered irrelevant when it makes its claim to sovereignty over the two cities.
For eight centuries, Muslim dynasties, including the Almoravids and Almohads, ruled parts of the Iberian Peninsula.
Morocco’s potential argument is therefore narrower: if historical ties can help establish present-day legal rights, then history and geography can also form part of the case it makes about two cities located on the North African coast.
What would the law change for Morocco?
In territorial terms, very little.
The citizenship measure would not change who controls Western Sahara, determine the territory’s final status or alter the United Nations-led political process. Nor does it, in itself, change Spain’s official position in support of Morocco’s autonomy proposal.
Its significance lies mainly in the relationship between Spain and Morocco. The measure brings Spain’s colonial history in Western Sahara into a broader domestic political debate, raising questions about how that history should be addressed and what its growing political significance could mean for the delicate relationship between Madrid and Rabat.

Risk of humanitarian catastrophe: UN "very worried" about upcoming winter in Ukraine
Alexander De Croo, Administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), has said Ukraine faces its "toughest winter" since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion, which could turn into a humanitarian catastrophe if Russia continues its attacks on the country's energy infrastructure.
Source: De Croo in a comment to BBC
Details: De Croo, the third-highest-ranking official in the UN, accused Russia of carrying out "very systematic" attacks on Ukraine's civilian and energy infrastructure. He said the targets include petrol stations, shopping centres and business centres, but primarily energy facilities.
"There is absolutely no justification for that," the senior official stressed.
De Croo said there is now a "race against the clock" to repair the power grid before winter begins and temperatures drop sharply.
He noted that Ukraine is entering this winter "from a very weak base". The senior official added that the UN is "very, very worried... about what this winter could become".
He said there is a serious risk of a humanitarian catastrophe if the population experiences a critical shortage of electricity needed to run heating systems and if the water supply and sewage systems stop functioning.
"With the temperatures that you would get here, that would lead to circumstances which would be really close to humanitarian catastrophe," De Croo noted.
"This winter is going to be the toughest one since the [beginning of the full-scale] war," he stressed.
The UNDP is currently helping repair damaged parts of the energy system and establish decentralised generation facilities that are less vulnerable to missile and drone attacks.
Meanwhile, De Croo acknowledged that carrying out this difficult work under the current security conditions is "almost an impossible task".
Quote: "They [Ukrainian power engineers – ed.] are reconstructing these sites under constant, constant air alarms. And they know that they are working at a site which is a target. So you try to reconstruct, but part of your day you can't work because it's just too dangerous."
Background: On 12 September, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that Ukraine is significantly better prepared this year for Russian attacks on its energy sector than it was last winter.

Houthis claim attack on Saudi base as fighting flares with Yemeni forces

Houthi fighters have said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southern Saudi Arabia, as Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government described the rebels’ swift advance along the Red Sea coast as a “painful” development in a new front in the Iran war.
The UN said on Sunday that nearly 86,000 people had fled Yemen, most of them since early September when the Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched a large-scale offensive that last week resulted in the capture of a key port city and an island on the Bab al-Mandab strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the strait of Hormuz.
The overnight attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted “weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people”, the Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on X. The date of the operation was not specified.
The Saudi civil defence force said a projectile had fallen in al-Tawwal governorate near the border with Yemen along the Red Sea, injuring two people and damaging a mosque and several other buildings. The statement blamed the Houthis. It also said sirens had sounded in Sharurah governorate but no damage was reported.
Yemeni government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha and later attacked other Houthi positions in the south-west of the country.
“Air force of the armed forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three airstrikes” in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said on Sunday.
A senior government official in Yemen said its forces would return to the Red Sea coast and fight back, after people fleeing the Houthi advance told the Associated Press they had seen forces withdrawing and urging people to run.
Sultan al-Arada, a member of the ruling presidential council, described the collapse of government forces in Mocha and elsewhere on Yemen’s west coast as “painful and regrettable”.
Al-Arada, who is also the governor of Yemen’s central Marib province, said in a televised interview broadcast late on Saturday night that forces “are currently regrouping and will return to the battle in one form or another”. The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
The US news site Axios reported that the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, twice called Donald Trump to request strikes on the Houthis last week, but that the request was rejected. Trump acknowledged the conversation on Saturday but did not say whether Washington would take any action. “Everything’s gonna work out fine and dandy,” he told reporters.
The clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing the remainder of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and several strategic islands, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab strait at the sea’s southern entrance.
The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on the strait of Hormuz in response to the US-Israeli assault on the country.
Reuters reported last week that the Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast came with direct guidance from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Iran describes the Houthis as an ally but publicly denies giving them military direction.
Iranian ship struck near Hormuz, state media says
State-run Iranian media said on Sunday that an Iranian commercial vessel had been struck early in the morning off Qeshm Island, with one person killed and four injured.
The state-run IRNA news agency quoted the Qeshm governor as blaming a “terrorist enemy”. There was no immediate comment from the US military, which has struck Iranian-flagged vessels during its blockade of Iranian ports.
Several explosions were reported overnight around Qeshm, the largest island in the Hormuz strait. The island, about 14 miles (22km) from the port city of Bandar Abbas, is key to Iran asserting control over the strait.
Maritime trackers also received new reports of a separate attack on a ship in the strait on Sunday, adding to concerns about threats to energy supplies after Saudi Arabia shut down a vital oil pipeline.
The British navy-affiliated agency UKMTO said it had a report of a projectile hitting a vessel as it moved through the strait, later adding that a fire had broken out and local authorities were evacuating those onboard.
The Houthis, mountain fighters who seized the capital, Sana’a, 12 years ago and withstood years of deadly Saudi airstrikes during Yemen’s civil war, said on Saturday evening that over the past 48 hours, “Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes” on areas under their control.
Yemen’s civil war, which began in 2014, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but reignited in July. Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration.
The civil war has uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes, with the fall of Mocha on Thursday driving many residents to Aden.
The UN’s migration agency said on Sunday that more than 2,000 people fleeing Yemen had landed in Djibouti last week.

Ukraine war briefing: Nine killed and dozens wounded in Russian strikes as Kyiv braces for harsh winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
01:22:31 UTC
10:22:31 KST

- 
  Russian airstrikes killed nine people, injured dozens and damaged buildings and infrastructure across Ukraine on Saturday, as Kyiv braces for a “very difficult” winter amid intensified attacks on the country. The civilian death toll has risen sharply in Ukraine over the past two months as Russia steps up attacks on power plants and other infrastructure. Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses in distant parts of Russia, and both sides have targeted each other’s shipping.
- 
  Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, writing on Telegram, said Russia had deployed nearly 500 drones against Ukrainian targets since early morning. “Basically, the Russians have expanded the war away from the front, where they have no success, into the economy, and their tactics are as basic as it gets: destroying every site that could help people cope with the conditions of war,” he wrote. “Russia wants to kill the Ukrainian economy and break our resistance.”
- 
  The city council in Kramatorsk, one of Ukraine’s frontline “fortress cities” that Russia wants to capture, said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over a 90-minute period. Four people were injured. “These are not military targets,” the council said. “They are ordinary civilian cars. People were going about their business.”
- 
  The governor of Ukraine’s Zhytomyr region, Vitaliy Bunechko, said a Russian strike on a grocery store killed two people in the town of Zviahel, west of Kyiv. Bunechko said two petrol stations also came under attack.
- 
  Earlier, Zelenskyy reported attacks on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih, his home town. The governor of Zaporizhzhia region, Ivan Fedorov, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other localities.
- 
  In Odesa region, governor Oleh Kiper said 37 people, including an infant, were injured in a series of overnight attacks, while two people were missing. Russia’s defence ministry said Russian forces have maintained their strikes on Ukrainian ports, hitting a cargo ship in Odesa that it said was carrying goods for military use.
- 
  Ukrainian officials said the country was bracing for a brutal winter as intensified Russian attacks on infrastructure and key export industries compound a deepening budget crisis. The economy minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko, said damage to infrastructure and fixed assets from Russian airstrikes was estimated at close to $10bn this year, while the broader economic costs of the attacks and the de facto blockage of its ports had cut 1.5 percentage points of GDP. “We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country,” he said.
- 
  With fighting on the frontline largely stalled, Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted logistics networks and other economic assets in an effort to undermine each other’s war effort. For more than two weeks, Russia has carried out near constant attacks on Kyiv using faster jet-powered drones, disrupting life, business and government operations. Moscow has also effectively blocked Ukraine’s Black Sea ports by intensifying its air attacks on the country’s southern regions. Ukraine’s main exports – agricultural products and iron and steel – are shipped via these ports.
- 
  In Moldova on Ukraine’s western border, authorities closed national airspace for nearly an hour after a drone was detected near the border. Seven border crossings were temporarily closed.
- 
  Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami for talks on ending the war, in a media interview released Saturday, but the Kremlin immediately ruled it out. “It is impossible,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told AFP in New Delhi on Saturday, repeating Moscow’s demand that a meeting can only take place in the Russian capital. The gathering of world leaders takes place on 14-15 December and there has been no confirmation yet as to whether Putin would attend. Putin has repeatedly rejected offers for a face-to-face meeting with Zelenskyy.

Houthis claim missile, drone attack on Saudi military base

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
00:59:43 UTC
09:59:43 KST

Yemen's Houthi group has carried out an attack using ballistic missiles and drones against a military base in southern Saudi Arabia, the group announced.
In a statement posted on X platform, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the attack targeted weapons depots and command-and-control facilities at the Sharurah military installation.
Saree stated that a large barrage of ballistic missiles and unmanned aircraft was deployed, claiming the strikes successfully hit their designated targets.
He framed the attack as direct retaliation for ongoing Saudi military strikes on Yemen, warning of expanded attacks deeper inside Saudi territory should air strikes persist.
Saudi authorities have not formally commented on the claims regarding the Sharurah base.
However, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence reported earlier on Saturday that a projectile landed in Al-Tuwal governorate in the southwestern Jazan region, injuring two people and causing material damage to a mosque, several residential buildings, and civilian vehicles.
Shifting front lines
The strikes coincide with significant shifts across Yemen's territorial map amid escalating clashes between government forces and the Houthis since July, which ended years of relative calm.
According to the group, the Houthis now control the entirety of western Al-Hudaydah province following advances in western Taiz province, where they captured the strategic coastal city of Mokha and its Red Sea port.
The advance has placed Houthis in close proximity to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, one of the world's most critical maritime choke points.
Meanwhile, Yemeni government forces have made territorial gains in the northern Al-Jawf province along the Saudi border, advancing toward its provincial capital, Al-Hazm.
Active combat also continues across contested fronts in Marib, Al-Bayda, and Al-Dhale provinces.
Yemen has remained gripped by conflict since the Houthis captured the capital Sanaa and large swathes of the country in 2014, prompting the military intervention of a Saudi-led coalition in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.

Palestine hails BRICS' declaration supporting Palestinian rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
00:49:09 UTC
09:49:09 KST

Palestine has welcomed the declaration issued at the weekend summit of the BRICS grouping of 11 countries, praising its positions in support of the rights of the Palestinian people and the Palestinian cause.
In a statement on Saturday, the Palestinian Foreign Ministry welcomed the declaration from the New Delhi summit and its "positions and affirmations supporting the Palestinian cause," particularly its rejection of attempts to forcibly displace the Palestinian people from their land, including occupied East Jerusalem; its call for an end to Israeli occupation; its commitment to the two-state solution; and its support for the state of Palestine's full UN membership.
It also welcomed the declaration's support for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) and its mandate, as well as its call to protect holy sites and ensure access to them in occupied East Jerusalem, protect the Palestinian people, and ensure the unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid to besieged Gaza.
The ministry said the positions are consistent with international law and relevant UN resolutions, and stressed the need to translate them into practical and concrete steps.
The ministry underlined that "implementing the positions and affirmations contained in the BRICS declaration requires ending the Israeli occupation and enabling the Palestinian people to exercise their inalienable rights," including the establishment of an independent and sovereign Palestinian state on its land, with occupied East Jerusalem as its capital.
Calls to preserve Gaza ceasefire
Earlier on Saturday, a final declaration issued at the conclusion of the BRICS leaders' summit expressed opposition to the forced displacement of Palestinians from Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The joint summit declaration called for respect for UN Security Council resolutions concerning Gaza.
"We call on all parties to ensure the preservation of the ceasefire in the Gaza Strip and the full and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid," it said.
It also expressed concern about Israel's continued violence in the region in violation of the ceasefire reached last October.
"We call for an end to any policies aimed at the forced displacement of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, and express concern over any arrangements that could undermine the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights or could lead to legitimising the occupation or prolonging it," the statement added.
The declaration called for an urgent and lasting solution to the Palestinian issue and reaffirmed its support for the State of Palestine obtaining full membership in the United Nations.
BRICS is made up of longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa – the origin of the BRICS name – plus more recent members Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.
With its expansion to 11 members since 2024, BRICS has become a bloc representing roughly half of the world’s population and around 40 percent of global economic output.

Ex-CIA officer caught with $40 mn in gold bars seeks plea deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
00:47:11 UTC
09:47:11 KST

Ex-CIA officer caught with $40 mn in gold bars seeks plea deal
The US Justice Department has reached a tentative plea agreement with an ex-intelligence officer suspected of faking a classified CIA assignment to steal more than $40 million in government-provided gold bars as “work-related expenses.”
David Rush, who once worked as a senior CIA official with top-secret clearance, was arrested in May after an internal probe discovered he had lied about his education and Navy service. A search of his Virginia home uncovered a trove of 303 one-kilogram gold bars, some $2 million in cash and 35 luxury watches.
Rush has so far been formally charged only with theft of public funds for falsifying pay records to obtain around $77,000 in military-leave compensation. The case has not yet been presented to a federal grand jury.
In a joint motion filed on Friday, Rush and federal prosecutors said they had reached a “plea agreement in principle” and asked the court to extend the indictment deadline from September 17 to October 8, giving them another 21 days to resolve the matter.
“The parties need additional time to prepare the paperwork,” Assistant US Attorney Raizza Ty and Rush’s attorney, Jessica Carmichael, wrote in the filing. “A pre-indictment resolution promotes the public interest by conserving government and judicial resources.”
The document did not disclose what charge Rush would plead guilty to or any possible sentencing recommendation. The parties said proceeding with an indictment and trial would require extensive litigation involving classified material. A deal could avert a public trial and keep key details of the case under wraps.
The court filings said that, beginning last November, Rush requested and received “a significant quantity of foreign currency and tens of millions of dollars in gold bars for work-related expenses,” but official details remain scarce. According to media reports, Rush invented a special-access “continuity of government” operation, ostensibly intended to preserve federal functions during a nuclear war or other catastrophe.
The case has also prompted officials to scrutinize US Deputy Secretary of Defense Stephen Feinberg, a private equity billionaire who reportedly oversees the Pentagon’s $33 billion military intelligence budget. Earlier this week, NBC News reported that Feinberg had recommended Rush for sensitive assignments and praised his performance to senior CIA officials. The outlet also said footage showed both men at a government-affiliated residence used by Rush.
Feinberg has not been accused of wrongdoing, and the Pentagon has denied he endorsed Rush for any position, describing reports of a close professional relationship as “false and embellished.”

Ukraine helps shape global policy on developing clean sports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:35:00 UTC
09:35:00 KST

Ukraine helps shape global policy on developing clean sports
According to the press service of the Ministry of Youth and Sports, Ukraine is actively involved in shaping international anti-doping policy, as reported by Ukrinform.
Matvii Bidnyi has been elected as Europe’s representative on the WADA Executive Committee for the 2025–2027 term. In 2026, Ukraine will chair OneVoice—an international platform that coordinates government representatives in the field of anti-doping efforts.
During the WADA Executive Committee meeting, a series of decisions were adopted aimed at strengthening the independence and effectiveness of the international anti-doping system.
One of the key decisions was to strengthen the independence of anti-doping testing at major international sporting events—the Olympic and Paralympic Games and world championships. From now on, the host country’s anti-doping organization will not be directly involved in planning testing or collecting doping samples from athletes. This should help eliminate potential conflicts of interest and strengthen guarantees of fair testing.
Special attention was given to the work of WADA’s independent intelligence and investigations unit. Plans call for expanding its tools to detect potential violations while adhering to national legal procedures and practices.
During the meeting, the list of prohibited substances and methods for 2027 was approved, and the areas of funding for anti-doping research and WADA’s draft budget for 2027 were agreed upon. Work continues on the issue of regulating unintentional doping.
“Ukraine’s presence and representation within WADA give the country the opportunity to influence decisions that shape the future of global sports, as well as to defend and represent the interests of the European continent within the international anti-doping system. We must influence the shaping of the international agenda, rather than passively implement decisions made without our participation,” noted Matvii Bidnyi.
On the eve of the Executive Committee meeting, the Ukrainian delegation participated in the work of OneVoice and a meeting between the platform’s representatives and the Olympic Movement. As the chairing country for 2026, Ukraine coordinates the work of government representatives within the platform and participates in the formulation of common positions. Within OneVoice, government representatives from five continents coordinate their positions with WADA regarding the development of the international anti-doping system.
Ukraine continues its work within WADA and OneVoice, upholding the principles of clean sport and the independence of the anti-doping system. Ukraine’s representation in international anti-doping organizations enables it to participate in shaping decisions that determine the development of the global anti-doping system.

08:53:57 KST

By virtue of our big brains, we humans not only have free will but are aware of it, which doesn't mean we're not constrained. The universe may be infinite but our resources aren't, so we have to make choices along the continuum enabled by circumstances – such as the weather, geography, our banker, et cetera, and theoretically also by law. Different societies have different rules, but all have some. In most, you're not supposed to choose to murder the neighbor because he ate your dog. It will end in tears, or at least in court, where you will have to explain your choices.
The question is when language emerged, evolving beyond animal modes of communication such as physical gestures and fixed vocalizations. When did our considerations become loftier, rising above fight it, flee it or eat it? From what point could we not just signal the kids how to make choices, but explain? The evidence is entirely circumstantial and opinions differ vastly.
At one end is the camp favoring "sudden emergence" of language ability, which suggests that language did not arise early in our evolution, or even gradually, for the sake of social communication. Animals have nothing like it, this camp points out, and suggests that one day, one guy was born with a beneficial mutation enabling him to generate complex thoughts inside his head, as an internal process, and the trait spread.
At the other end is the camp advocating for early language development. The escalating complexity of our productivity and evidence of thoughtful choices suggest the necessity for speech to evolve, starting more than a million years before the Homo sapiens species even emerged.
Underlying this view is evidence of skills that plausibly had to have been learned. For instance, some early humans chose specific types of rock to knap into tools, as evident from a bias towards one rock out of the local varieties; and deeply prehistoric import of stone from afar to make tools. How deeply? Lomekwian tools from 3.3 million years ago were made using local stone, but archaeologists have reported that archaic hominins in Kenya made the energetically expensive choice to haul quality stone over a whopping distance of 13 kilometers (8 miles) 2.6 million years ago. That suggests they had standards 2.3 million years before our species first opened its baby blues.
In other achievements of early humans, some archaeologists think that hominins were braving the briny in deep prehistory, which is how they reached remote islands. Others suspect that hominins floated there by accident, as other animals did.
What have we so far? Accidents aside, to achieve all that, some posit that early humans, possibly even before the rise of the Homo genus about 3 million years ago, had to have had communication skills that surpassed pointing and calling. Recent research showing that the building blocks to create and teach complex vocalizations existed before the dawn of our species supports this hypothesis.
Do animals speak? Yes. Do they have language? Research shows that cats emit dozens of vocalizations beyond "meow" but that's short of language. A key difference between human and cat communication is our use of phonemes, which are meaningless sounds on their own that can be combined to create "words" (think of combining the meaningless sounds "com" and "bine" to create "combine"). Cats and dogs don't build "words" from smaller meaningless units like our phonemes. They teach the offspring by example.
But some other animals do pass that bar. Humpback whales and Bengalese finches exhibit cultural learning, teaching their group's unique vocalizations based on their version of phonemes. Vocal learning has also been identified in bats. Science has not identified grammar or syntax in our aviating friends, but these animals' capacity for vocal learning might suggest that from early on, hominins had the innate ability to mix 'n' match phonemes, resulting in "words" and ultimately, rudimentary language.
There's a caveat: Similarities in learning communication in humans, bats and whales may be down to convergent evolution – and our closest relative, the chimpanzee, evinces no ability to create words. Chimp communication seems confined to a range of about 13 call types, though possibly variations on their grunts may convey more than we realized. Research shows that the structure of grunts in certain chimps differs systematically with fruit-tree size and species. One suspects complex communication, enabling a higher level of choice, emerged in the Homo genus only after the split from the chimp some 7 million years ago.
But how early? Could the emergence of language have predated the emergence of the Homo genus? Did archaic forms such as australopithecines, who could walk upright and make tools, develop proto-language before the brain assumed "modern human" structure? The argument rages on.
Drop that rock, Oggie
Other animals make tools too, but none are known to do so at the complexity level of humans knapping stones. Stone tool manufacture began over 3.3 million years ago, based on finds at Lomekwi, Kenya, and who made those hammerstones is quite the question. Whoever it was, researchers posit that the knappers over the eons gained a "developing understanding" of the fracture properties of different rocks. That understanding, we infer, was conveyed to the next generation. Still, who made the tools at Lomekwi and do they suggest communication beyond hoot and point?
Archaeologists guess that the Lomekwi manufacturers were australopithecines and/or Kenyanthropus platyops, a flat-faced species whose skull was found in proximity to the tools. Some think Kenyanthropus was an alternative australopithecine. Maybe it was all of them, explaining how to choose and work a rock.
In any case, the candidates for making tools 3.3 million years ago were small-bodied, small-brained hominins, and there is argument over whether australopithecines should be encompassed in the Homo genus (presently they're in the "australopithecus" genus).
Homo genus or not, the majority thinking is that at best, australopithecines had nonverbal proto-language. If so, their mentors managed to convey tool-making lessons with grunts and gestures, with the kids learning through observation and imitation: australopithecine see, australopithecine do, australopithecine slap the wrong rock out of baby's hand and point at another.
A more verbal protolanguage only emerged in advanced species with big brains in the Homo genus, such as tall, big-brained, long-legged, wanderlust-stricken Homo erectus, according to mainstream thought. Researchers – from the linguist Daniel Everett of Bentley University, the archaeologist Steven Mithen of the University of Reading and the cognitive researchers Dan Dediu and Stephen Levinson of the Max Planck Institute – think that's where rudimentary symbolic language began, basically, because just look at what erectus achieved!
Increasingly complex stone tools, for one. Also, as erectus spread out of Africa to all ends of Eurasia insofar as glaciation permitted, he may or may not have known how to light a fire, but he could control it from early on. Fire use is reported inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa 1.8 million years ago. Lightning did not strike inside a cave; a hominin harvested a wildfire and transported a burning bush or branch back home.
In Israel, where erectus (and others) crossed between Africa and Asia, fire use signs go back a million years. In Zhoukoudian, China, fire use by the peripatetic erectus is identified about half a million years ago. He did get about, erectus did; and all that just with grunting, hooting and pointing?
Have brain, will travel
Based on erectus' brain size and achievements, Mithen suggests that proto- language arose in erectus as part of an emerging suite of "human" characteristics. Unrelated work supports the genesis of language about 1.5 million years ago, based on the little we can infer about the evolution of Broca's area – a region in the frontal lobe associated with processing grammar, producing language and coordinating the muscles needed to speak.
Earlier hominin skulls suggest their Broca's area was chimp-like, researchers say, adding that maybe hominins who developed a bigger Broca's area had improved communication, facilitating their evolutionary survival compared with hominins with smaller Broca's areas, who were disadvantaged.
A different sign of erectus' putative progression appears in the Sakhnin Valley in northern Israel, where the self-taught archaeologist and anthropologist Muataz Shalata deduced that hominins living there hundreds of thousands of years ago had developed the capacity to be moved by beauty. A subset of the stone tools littering the Sakhnin Valley floor shows clear choices of striking flints, worked to showcase their beauty: a crystal or fossil inclusion, for instance.
The energy a hominin expended in shaping a hand axe around an exotic feature would have been greater than the cost of making an ordinary tool and smacks of active choices – of a stone and a process. The investment of effort is a meaningful choice, because a deer doesn't look at an aesthetically pleasing weapon and faint. In any case, the focus on beauty suggests higher, abstract levels of thinking in erectus.
Apropos Shalata, he did weaken one argument proffered by some early-linguistics theorists, that making stone tools without language is impossible because making stone tools is so complicated and difficult. Shalata picked up a flint and a crystal geode to use as a hammer, and knapped it into a decent hand axe in about 15 minutes, making it look easy, while talking to Haaretz about something else. He had a lot of practice, he added.
So what have we? At least from the time of erectus, we have decisions and clear evidence of aesthetic choices – investing the energy in finding pretty rocks and taking the extra trouble to shape them in a way that highlighted the attraction. Maybe that is where early linguistic ability reached its finest level, enabling one erectus to lord it over the others with his pretty hand axe.
Never mind erectuses – some resist the notion that even the most advanced of alternative humans, the Neanderthals and Denisovans with whom we had intimate relations, could talk like we do. There is research into the Neanderthal hyoid bone (which is like ours), larynx structure and so on.
Moreover, like humans, both had FOXP2, a gene associated with the neural control of speech. We know little about Denisovan lifestyles but are confident that Neanderthals lived in groups and had a complex social life. They were capable of making very complex tools, including hafted spears. Also, while we never found anything smacking of Neanderthal or Denisovan figurative art, we are pretty clear that they had symbolism. And did they achieve these lofty heights by gestures and grunting?
Plausibly not, but just this month, a new paper suggested that actually, early humans didn't need more than ape communication to achieve any of the things we wrote above – fire, co-travel, or making stone tools and living in small groups. Fire was key, they posit. Until then, the assumption was that language predated storytelling. This paper suggests that groups sitting around the flickering fire were inspired, which catalyzed the transition from hooting, throwing feces and flipping each other the bird to defending our investment choices.

From the Pacific to Jerusalem: The special alliance between Nauru and Israel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:58:15 UTC
08:58:15 KST

A senior delegation from the Republic of Nauru (Naoero) arrived in Israel this week, led by Vice President and Foreign Affairs, Trade and Justice Minister Lionel Rouwen Aingimea. The delegation included ministers and members of parliament.
At the heart of the visit was a historic event in relations between the two countries: the official opening of Nauru’s embassy in Jerusalem, Israel’s capital.
The ceremony was attended by Aingimea; Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar; Foreign Ministry Chief of Protocol Gil Haskel; Foreign Ministry Deputy Director-General for Asia and the Pacific Aviv Ezra; Israel’s honorary consul in Nauru, Sean Oppenheimer; Nauru’s honorary consul in Israel, David Ben-Basat; members of the senior Nauruan delegation; and other guests.
The occasion marked a significant milestone in diplomatic relations between the two countries.
At first glance, Nauru may appear to be a small and distant country, an island in the heart of the Pacific Ocean. But in relations between nations, the importance of friendship is not measured by population or territory.
For years, Nauru has demonstrated that when Israel needs genuine friends in the international arena, it stands firmly and consistently by its side, sometimes in the face of considerable pressure.
Nauru is one of the smallest countries in the world. It lies in the Pacific Ocean, just south of the equator. Its nearest neighbor is Banaba, an island belonging to Kiribati, about 300 kilometers to the east. The Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau are also located in the region.
Nauru became an independent nation in 1968, and for many years its economy was based primarily on phosphate mining.
Nauru has repeatedly supported Israel
Despite its tiny size, Nauru is a sovereign nation with an equal vote in the United Nations General Assembly, a vote it has repeatedly chosen to cast in support of its friend Israel.
For Israel, the story of Nauru is first and foremost one of diplomatic loyalty and a friendship that does not depend on prevailing international opinion.
In UN institutions, where Israel often finds itself facing an automatic and hostile majority, Nauru has traditionally been among the countries that stand by it.
It is regarded as one of Israel’s most consistent supporters at the UN and has also expressed support for Israel in proceedings brought against it before the International Court of Justice in The Hague.
This special relationship has been particularly evident on the issue of Jerusalem. In 2019, Nauru recognized Jerusalem as the capital of Israel, joining a small group of countries willing to take a clear position on the matter.
The United States moved its embassy to Jerusalem in 2018, followed by Guatemala. Paraguay also moved its embassy to Jerusalem that year, but returned it to Tel Aviv several months later.
The Nauruan initiative also has an important Israeli chapter.
During Israel Katz’s tenure as foreign minister, he met with Nauruan Ambassador Marlene Moses during her visit to Israel. At that meeting, a request was made to further strengthen relations and give practical expression to Nauru’s recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital.
At the time, Katz was working to expand the circle of countries recognizing Jerusalem and encourage the opening of diplomatic missions in the capital. The years passed, but the idea was never abandoned.
The decisive step came during Sa’ar’s visit to Fiji. There, he met with Aingimea.
The two reached an understanding on opening a Nauruan embassy in Jerusalem. The government of Nauru approved the move, and what had remained a diplomatic aspiration for years has now become a reality.
This policy is driven by the leadership of Nauruan President David Ranibok Adeang, who has demonstrated warm friendship toward the State of Israel.
His support extends beyond words and diplomatic gestures. It is reflected in the positions Nauru takes in international institutions and in its willingness to stand with Israel even when doing so cannot be taken for granted.
In this context, I particularly recall a story that illustrates the nature of this friendship.
At an international conference, a representative of a wealthy Gulf state approached the president of Nauru and asked him to change his country’s policy and end its support for Israel.
The request was accompanied by a suggestion that such a change could bring substantial financial assistance to Nauru.
According to the account brought to my attention, the president’s response was unequivocal in spirit: Nauru’s integrity is not for sale, and Israel will continue to receive its support.
It is difficult to imagine a statement that better captures the meaning of genuine friendship.
In the diplomatic world, where economic interests, political pressure, and shifting alliances often influence votes and positions, there is special significance in a small country declaring that some principles are not for sale.
The opening of Nauru’s embassy in Jerusalem is therefore far more than a ceremonial event. It transforms many years of friendship, trust and diplomatic support into an official and permanent presence in Israel’s capital.
At a time when Israel is facing diplomatic pressure, fierce criticism, and struggles in international forums, it is especially important to recognize countries that do more than issue statements of friendship.
These countries are prepared to vote, act, and stand alongside Israel.
President Isaac Herzog, who hosted and honored the members of the delegation at his official residence, described it well.
Nauru may be small in territory and population, but in its relationship with Israel it repeatedly demonstrates a simple truth: friendship between nations is not measured by their size, but by their courage to stand together precisely when friendship comes at a price.
The Nauruan flag now flying above its embassy in Jerusalem is a tangible expression of that friendship. It is also a promise of a new and even deeper chapter in relations between the State of Israel and the Republic of Nauru.
The writer is the CEO of Radios 100fm, Nauru’s honorary consul in Israel, deputy dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, and president of the Israeli Radio Communications Association. He previously served as a monitor for Israel’s Army Radio and as a correspondent for NBC News.

Fifth season of 'Fauda' sparks viral international reactions to October 7-focused episodes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-13
23:57:31 UTC
08:57:31 KST

The fifth season of the Israeli television series Fauda sparked controversy and a new understanding of the October 7 massacre around the world after it devoted several episodes to October 7, with episodes 7 and 8 focusing specifically on the Hamas-led attack.
Both episodes received a 9.3 rating on IMDb, sparking widespread reactions on social media. Within a day of its release on Netflix, the series had already ranked seventh among the platform’s 10 most watched shows in 43 countries.
Israeli social media influencer Lee Malach wrote: “My entire feed is filled with tweets from Dutch and German people; I have no idea why, about the October 7 episodes of ‘Fauda.’ They are in total shock over what happened here, and the posts are difficult to read and very supportive of Israel. It is crazy to me how little these people know about what happened here and how much they talk about the subject.”
Show brings new understanding of massacre
Brazilian cartoonist Luciano Pires wrote: “I watched the fifth season of ‘Fauda.’ It has always been an unsettling series. But the fifth season is particularly shocking and painful. Episodes 7 and 8 recreate the October 7 massacre, making them far more difficult to watch than a fictional drama. After all, we have all seen dozens of real videos from the attack, many of them filmed by the terrorists themselves, and they were horrifying enough. But this time, the fictional work takes us directly into the horror.”
Pires also reflected on what filming the scenes may have meant for the show’s Israeli cast and crew.
He continued: “I was genuinely horrified, not only by watching the massacre through the eyes of the victims, but also by thinking about the Israeli actors, many of whom are Jewish. The image accompanying this post shows actor Yaakov Zada Daniel, who plays the operative Eli, as he enters his home in a kibbutz attacked by Hamas terrorists. It is a breathtaking moment. He was not acting out a scene about a distant tragedy; he was recreating on camera an event that struck his country, his family, his friends, and the series’ own production team. Idan Amedi, an actor in the series, was seriously wounded during the fighting in Gaza. Matan Meir, a member of the production team, was killed in the war.”
Pires concluded: “Perhaps that is why these episodes have a different quality. They do not feel like an attempt to imagine the horror. They take us directly into it.”
The episodes also prompted strong reactions from viewers in Italy. One man wrote: “I could barely keep my eyes open.” Another woman wrote: “Yesterday, a friend called me and told me the same thing. She added, ‘Who knows, perhaps this series will help people understand the atrocities committed by Hamas on October 7.’ And I replied, ‘I’m afraid it won’t.’ P.S. My friend is neither Jewish nor Israeli, but she is free and knows how to use her own mind.” Some users also shared real footage of the massacre in southern Israel in their replies.
An influencer from India wrote: “Sleepless nights. Can someone please erase my memory of this episode?? I can’t stop thinking and worrying. Episode eight of ‘Fauda’ really disturbed me. I don’t understand how there are still Hamas supporters among us. God, please help me get over this series.” Another user responded: “I am a huge fan of ‘Fauda’ and of Israel, but I don’t have the courage to watch the fifth season.”
Viewers argue series only showed small portion of attack
A different user from India argued that the series had shown only a small portion of the violence committed during the attack.
The user wrote: “Contrary to claims that the fifth season of ‘Fauda’ went too far, I think it is remarkably restrained. The series offers only a small glimpse into the atrocities of October 7. The reality was far more disturbing: murder, abductions, sexual violence, brutal abuse, torture, and the deliberate targeting of innocent civilians.
“It spared viewers descriptions of women who were gang raped and burned alive, families who were tied together and whose bodies were dismembered, the killing of pregnant women and children, the sexual desecration of bodies, the mutilation of genitalia, and horrific injuries suffered by children. Many children were also abducted, including infants as young as nine months old. Kfir Bibas was only nine months old when he was kidnapped; he was later murdered in captivity alongside his four-year-old brother, Ariel. The series did not show fathers who had kerosene poured over them and begged for their lives moments before being set on fire as their attackers laughed.”
The user continued: “No film or television series can truly recreate the horror of such a pogrom. ‘Fauda’ is a fictional work, but it draws inspiration from real events. October 7 was not a fictional story; it was a real tragedy, and the victims deserve to be remembered as events truly occurred.”
A woman from the UK responded: “I just finished watching episodes 7 and 8. This will stay with me forever. What Israelis went through... and the world simply does not care.”
A social media user from Texas asked his followers whether they had watched the season and what they thought of it. Responses included: “Well made, but heartbreaking. Not for the faint of heart,” and “Episodes 7 and 8 are simply unforgettable.”
He concluded: “It seems that episodes 7 and 8 of ‘Fauda’ moved everyone; it looks like a phenomenal season, as usual.”
